case_name: Coral North FLNG, Mozambique
headline: The project at the coastline of Mozambique, managed by ENI, involves the development of six subsea wells to extract natural gas from the offshore Coral reservoir. The project has faced strong resistance from civil society organisations due to concerns over environmental damage, human rights violations and inadequate community consultation specifically targeting financial institutions.
description: The Coral North project approximately 50km from the coastline of Mozambique (at Cabo Delgado), managed by the Italian company ENI, involves the development of six subsea wells to extract natural gas from the offshore Coral reservoir [5] . Similar to the Coral South floating LNG (FLNG) project, the gas will be liquefied, stored, and exported, with a planned production capacity of 3.55 million tonnes per year  [1]   [2]   [5] . The project's three main shareholders are ENI (50%), ExxonMobil (25%) and China National Petroleum Corporation (20%) [3] . Additionally, ENH, KOGAS and XRG are also involved with the project  [10] . In the beginning of 2025, the final investment decision (FID) for the FLNG looked conclusive, yet, in reality, the project was constantly postponed due to several reasons  [1] . Firstly, the FID was not confirmed as scheduled causing a delay of about 10 months  [1] . Therefore, banks and export credit agencies were unable to assess the financial risk of such a major infrastructure project  [1] . Furthermore, socio-political instability during the election period—marked by protests in which dozens of people were killed—intensified the situation. For nearly eight years, the region has experienced ongoing armed conflict between Mozambican government forces and insurgent groups  [2] . Even after the election of Daniel Chapo, tensions persisted, with reports of continued repression by the armed forces  [1] . Lastly, Centro de Integridade Publica (CIP) revealed that ENI was pressuring Felipe Nyusi’s government with “the possibility of paying the production tax in kind such as gas, rather than cash; and the requirement for local content, meaning that a significant part of the goods, services and labour employed in the projects comes from Mozambique”  [1] . Environmental and Societal Impacts The Coral South FLNG has been involved in several flaring incidents (inaccurately reported by ENI) since the start of its operation in 2022  [1] . ReCommon’s publication the ‘Hidden Flames’ reveals the devastating environmental impact of this plant, particularly focusing on flaring  [2] . Furthermore Data Desk shows that “LNG terminals tend to flare for significantly longer than the industry claims once they start producing, and that flaring remains persistent for decades at many facilities”  [2] . A group of civil society organisations argue that the participation process of EIA was also inadequate with several essential documents kept unavailable for commentators.  [5] . Additionally, the assessment did not properly account for climate change impacts, which heavily affect the vulnerable coastline areas, undermining the local communities’ ability to adapt  [5] . The project would also not benefit the population substantially as it increases national debt and sovereign liability, and conditions have only worsened since gas exploitation began  [5] . The impact on women and other vulnerable groups is also not accounted for, despite legal requirements to do so  [3]   [5] . Lastly, as the region is heavily conflict-affected, the project could lead to even more human-rights violations such as deaths, displacement and other security concerns  [5] . This lack of involvement also shows what many human rights experts say: “Previous LNG projects in Cabo Delgado have suffered from inadequate consultation, which has undermined local participation in key project decisions and resulted in loss of livelihoods and long-term socioeconomic disruption for communities who depend heavily on fishing, agriculture and natural resources. Despite promises of employment creation, high illiteracy rates and limited access to education mean that local communities have reportedly benefited little from job opportunities generated to date”  [2] . The erosion of Mozambique’s sovereignty has reportedly intensified since gas exploitation began around 2010, as legal agreements increasingly limited the government’s regulatory capacity and created fiscal risks without guaranteed economic returns [6] . The fossil fuel sector has also been linked to corruption-driven debt, and Kete Fumo of Justiça Ambiental argues that “the projects make use of tax avoidance mechanisms, unfair contracts and investor protection clauses”  [6]   [7] . In addition, the growing military presence in the region has affected traditional coastal communities by restricting access to fishing areas and livelihoods (7). Resistance Regarding the delays in closing deals, ENI argued that the Mozambican authorities’ approval of the development plan only in April 2025 was responsible, although ongoing negotiations with private financial institutions suggest continued challenges in securing financing [8] . Several civil society organisations (Friends of the Earth Mozambique / Justiça Ambiental!; ReCommon; BankTrack; Reclaim Finance; urgewald; Les Amis de la Terre France; Friends of the Earth Japan) gathered under the coalition of “Say No! To Gas Mozambique”, aiming to influence financial institutions not to support the Coral North FLNG or any future projects in the country  [7] . Italy’s UniCredit, the Dutch bank ABN AMRO, and three French banks BNP Paribas, Crédit Agricole and Société Générale, are all institutions which were involved in the Coral South FLNG and decided not to support the second FLNG due to new policies  [7] .  ActionAid Italia and ReCommon specifically campaigned against the participation of Italian financial institutions in new ENI-led fossil fuel projects [4] . Their advocacy included pressure campaigns directed at UniCredit and Intesa Sanpaolo, with over 600 letters sent in April requesting commitments not to finance Coral North FLNG  [4] . In October 2024, the organisations reported that UniCredit was not involved in the project, referencing both sustained public pressure and the bank’s existing restrictions on ultra-deepwater oil and gas financing  [4] . Furthermore, more recently First Rand Group, which includes Rand Merchant Bank, has also confirmed it is not financing the floating LNG platform  [7] . Additionally, a South Korean civil society organisation, Solutions for Our Climate (SFOC) engaged in similar activism against state investments in the project by the Korea Gas Corporation  [6]   [8] . They pointed out how the FLNG and involvement would be economically risky for South Korea and violate the rights of future generations to a healthy environment  [6]   [8] . As of April 2026, StopMozGas? Campaign members expressed concerns over the African Development Bank’s involvement with a 150$ million loan to support the project  [2] . The Coral North project have currently reached the final investment decision (FID) and is expect to be finalised in 2028  [9] .

case_name: Andes LNG, Chile
headline: The Andes LNG project proposed building a liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminal, a 90 km pipeline and a 540 MW power plant in Bahía Chascos (Atacama Region, Chile), an area of high biodiversity with marine meadows, endangered sea turtles, seabirds and cetaceans.
location: Bahia Chasco, near Caleta Punta de Choros
description: The Andes LNG project proposed a liquefied natural gas terminal, a 90 km pipeline, and a 540 MW power plant in Bahía Chascos, a high-biodiversity area home to marine meadows and endangered green turtles  [1]   [2] . The companies behind the proposed developments are Mitsui OSK Lines, Shell Gas & Power International and Wartsila  [1] . The project was submitted to Environmental Impact Assessment System (SEIA) in 2016 and received a favourable assessment from the Atacama Environmental Assessment Commission on June 13, 2019  [2]   [3] . The LNG constructions were expected to start in 2022 and enter into operation by 2024  [1] . The LNG would have received liquefied natural gas from the United States and after converting it to a gaseous state it would have been sent further through the pipeline to a gas-fired thermoelectric power plant in Canto del Agua, in the municipality of Vallenar [4] .   Environmental impacts Chasco Bay is a unique area with a high ecosystem value with seagrass meadows, sea turtles, Humboldt penguins and kelp forests (Huiros)  [4] . The main damage of the construction would have been the creation of the floating docks, which meant the installation of pilings that require blasting the seabed with more than 180 explosions  [3] . This operation would have led to the complete destruction of seagrass beds, which is the primary food source of the endangered green sea turtle  [3] .   Public representatives, such as the mayor of Atacama, Patricio Urquieta argued that this project would be a move towards sustainable development, balancing different interests [5] . Similarly, the Regional Secretary of Energy, Kim Fa Bondi stated that all necessary processes had been carried out that led to a favourable environmental assessment vote (5). The operation aims to mitigate its effect by involving cooling engines, The discharge water is expected to be between 39.2 and 3.9 °C, which is 24.5 degrees Celsius higher than the suction temperature, exceeding maximum permitted limits [6] . Additionally, the expected suction speed is 0.385 m/s, while the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) only recommends 0.15 m/s  [6] . Furthermore, the extraction would suck away microorganisms which are the main food source for cetaceans  [6] . On the surface, it affects four archaeological sites, and the pipeline would be built in a region where flowering desert is particularly prevalent  [6] . Lastly, a potential spill could heavily impact the area which would be mitigated by the construction of a Marine Species Rescue Centre, where in case of accidents, turtles and other marine species would be taken  [5]   [6] .   Resistance Local communities, the municipalities of Caldera and Copiapó, and organizations such as CODEMAA and ONG FIMA led a preventive resistance based on multi-track strategic litigation and "community baseline" activism. This mobilization stood out for creating alternative knowledge: fishermen and neighbours documented species and seagrasses that the company had omitted from its technical reports. Supported by scientific and professional networks, the community overwhelmed the system with irrefutable evidence of the project’s deficiencies. Additionally, territorial advocacy and the use of alternative media, like Radio JGM, prevented the bay from becoming a "sacrifice zone."   More specifically, as the project threatened tourism, the municipalities of Copiapó and Caldera submitted several concerns and objections during the study phase, but they were all disregarded  [3] . This led to an appeal against the environmental study, in the First Environmental Court  [2]   [3] . Lawyers of the municipalities of Caldera and Copiapó, Rodrigo Flores and Guillermo Ortega argued that as the municipalities are the representatives of citizens, the Environmental Assessment Service (SEA) must consider observations made by municipal bodies  [2] . In contrast SEA the lawyer aimed at pointing out that municipalities lack standing under the law 20.600 with limited and residual powers  [2] . This appeal was accepted in May 2020 and ratified by the Supreme Court in February 2021  [3] .   Eventually, on June 6, 2022, the Committee of Ministers (the highest body of the Environmental Impact Assessment System) definitively rejected the project  [3] . This decision was made due to the deficiencies in the marine baseline, which made it impossible to “rule out significant and severe impacts on endangered marine species and ecosystems in an area proposed for conservation”  [3] .   Success Ultimately, constant pressure on the Committee of Ministers and successive judicial victories led to the project's definitive rejection in 2022. The case is considered a landmark for environmental justice, as it prioritized the protection of a fragile ecosystem and citizen participation over a 650-million-dollar industrial investment.

case_name: Groningen Gas, Netherlands
headline: The biggest gas field in Europe has caused more than 1000 earthquakes. The houses of up to 100,000 people have been damaged, some of them beyond repair. Shell, Exxon and the Dutch state owned company EBN refuse to fully compensate. As of 19th of April 2024 the Wet beëindiging gaswinning Groningenveld (Groningen Field Gas Extraction Termination) Act entered into force, marking the end of gas extra
description: The Groningen field is Europe's biggest gasfield. Supplying low caloric gas to households, buildings and greenhouses for heating in the Netherlands, and parts of Germany, Belgium and France. It is operated by Shell, in a joint venture with Exxon Mobile and Dutch State company EBN. On 22 July 1959, the Slochteren 1 well, drilling to a depth of 3,000 metres (9,800 ft), discovered the huge 2.8 trillion cubic meters (100 trillion cubic feet) gas field in the porous Rotliegend sandstone formation, which is 130 metres (430 ft) to 140 metres (460 ft) thick and 45 kilometres (28 mi) long from north to south by 25 kilometres (16 mi) long from east to west. The field started production in 1963 and produced around 100 billion cubic meters (3.57 trillion cubic feet) per year in the first decade of production but gradually the annual production fell to around 35 billion cubic meters (1.25 trillion cubic feet) per year.   Since 1986 earthquakes are felt in Groningen. At first Shell denied any link with the gasfield, but after a few years they acknowledged that the depletion of the gasfield might cause 'minor tremors' In 2012 a 3.6M earthquake occurred. The Dutch Mining Authority ordered that gas production should be shut in 'as much as possible and as quickly as possible' . The year after production was ramped up to 54 BCM. In succeeding years political pressure, court cases and actions managed to cap in production at 24BCM (2017).   Experts suggest 12BCM would be a safe upper limit, but several groups are campaigning to shut down the gas field completely.  The earthquakes are caused by the depletion of the field. The field pressure has dropped so much that the formation is shrinking. Causing a lowering on surface level of about 1 meter over the long run, and over a 1000 small earthquakes. Although at a low level on the Richter scale they cause a huge amount of damage. They come from a low depth (3km) , are frequent and are amplified by the clay surface.   The Netherlands is still the EU's biggest gas producer. Next to the Groningen gas field there are 250 smaller gas fields, mainly supplying high caloric natural gas. UPDATE March 2018 by EJAtlas editorial team: According to Reuters, the Dutch government said it will phase out gas production at the Groningen field by 2030 as part of efforts to reduce the danger caused by small but damaging earthquakes. However, Reuters add, "the Netherlands is building a conversion plant to make high-calorific foreign gas suitable for use in Dutch systems." Will this mean that exploration is banned in the country but tolerated elsewhere, despite the ecological and social impacts in causes? [1] UPDATE April 2026: As of 19th of April 2024 the Wet beëindiging gaswinning Groningenveld (Groningen Field Gas Extraction Termination) Act entered into force, marking the end of gas extraction in the Netherlands [2] .  Between 2019 and 2020 the gas extraction was approved despite growing phase out initiatives in order to ensure security of supply [3] . Around 2020-2021 the Minister put out that gas from the field will be no longer needed after 2022 and phase-out can proceed without jeopardising security of supply  [3] . The Nederlandse Aardolie Maatschappij (NAM) (owned by Shell and ExxonMobil) is required to pay around “€270 million for physical damage claims from 2020 and more than €500 million towards compensation for the fall in house prices in the gas extraction area” [5] . Next to physical damage to homes, compensation can also be requested due to the stress and anxiety caused by the earthquakes  [5] . The reasoning behind this initiative is that “non-homeowners can experience the same degree of suffering and grief as homeowners” [6] . Recently, there have been several ongoing legal disputes regarding the closure of the gas field. First, based on the 2018 agreement that originally set a phase-out path, Shell and ExxonMobil initiated arbitration seeking compensation for lost profits due to the accelerated closure of Groningen gas production [10] . Second, there is a disagreement between the government and the NAM on who should pay the repairing earthquake damages  [5] . On one hand, the ministry of economic affairs argues that NAM should contribute as the damage caused by the earthquakes happened due to the extraction activity  [5] . In a 2018 agreement the government and NAM discussed compensation for lost income and the costs of repairs and reinforcement work, stating that the government makes the initial payments up front and sends over the bill to NAM  [5] . On the other hand, NAM argues that the approach of the government led to payments for damages that are not directly connected to the extraction activities  [5] . The scheme of compensation allows residents to claim up to €60,000 for repairs without having to prove the exact cause and reasoning  [5] . Third, Shell sues the Netherlands over the gas field closure under the Energy Charter Treaty which aims to protect investments in the energy sector [7] . It empowers corporations to sue countries in private over government laws and policies that ‘damage’ business interests  [7] . Despite the Netherlands withdrawing from this treaty in 2025, investment remains protected for 20 years from the effective date of withdrawal [7] . The Groningen case clearly illustrates that certain dispute resolution mechanisms in contracts and treaties can erode democratic oversight, strengthen the influence of corporations, and restrict states to act in the public interest  [10] . Furthermore, there have been some initiatives on keeping the reserve open for strategic interest due to the war in Iran and its impact on growing oil prices  [4] . The far-right wing party, JA21, made suggestions to preserve the possibility to re-tap certain wells, in contrast with the commitment of the Dutch government to permanently seal all wells with concrete, never reopening them [8] . This proposal was supported by the Freedom Party, including Geert Wilders who stated "In ​the current geopolitical situation, keeping our own gas ​wells as an emergency reserve makes sense,"  [8] .  The Dutch research institute TNO, has also warned about permanently sealing the Groningen gas field as it “could leave the Netherlands at risk of a sudden gas shortage”  based on the principle to keep it available, but not use it [9] . This was made in light of a potential Russia sabotage over pipelines, Iran closing the Strait of Hormuz or the United States blocking LNG tankers over political disputes with Europe  [9] .

case_name: Protests in Huelva against the use of liquefied gas, Spain
headline: Activists in Huelva oppose the expansion of Enagás’ LNG infrastructure, arguing that investments in liquefied natural gas projects reinforce fossil-fuel dependence while worsening local environmental and social impacts.
description: Enagás (acronym for Empresa Nacional del Gas), the Spanish gas transmission network operator  [6] [7]   [11] . In May 2022, the company announced a potential increase in the liquified natural gas (LNG) shipments due to the growing energy tension unravelled by the war in Ukraine [2] . Huelva is home to the Polo Químico, one of the main industrial complexes in Southern Europe, where the chemical, energy and petrochemical industries are concentrated, including Enagás’ LNG regasification plant  [1]   [2] . Enagás aims to expand the Huelva plant to become “one of the most important regasification plants in Spain” according to the Port of Huelva’s director  [2] . Currently the plant has five storage tanks with a total capacity of 619,500 m³ of LNG  [12]   [13] . This capacity allows it to have a regasification capacity of up to 1,350,000 m³/hour, which is the maximum volume of gas it can convert from liquid to gas per hour  [12]    [13] . Environmental and Societal Impacts The province of Huelva is “one of the worst affected in Europe by the dynamics of its chemical and gas industries, which have been a source of danger and unhealthiness for its inhabitants for decades”  [2] . Phosphogypsum ponds, radioactive waste, and the release of industrial pollutants into the atmosphere have been harming the health of local populations and ecosystems for years  [3]   [4] . This is due to the fact that the area has become a hub of highly toxic industrial and mining sectors which have contaminated the entire surrounding area and public institutions instead of addressing the issue continue to promote such industries  [2] . The Enagás facilities with the regasification plant, storage tanks and gigantic LNG carriers in the Port of Huelva accelerates the dangers that the energy and chemical industry poses to the area, its population and the natural environment  [1] . Numerous civil society groups have been demanding an end to the production and consumption model based on fossil fuels, which has systematically violated human rights and accelerated climate change  [3]   [4] . The growing international gas prices put large segments of society at risk, and unravelled a much more severe energy crisis in the Global South  [3]   [4] . Rebelión por el Clima (Climate Rebellion) also points out that 78% of the gas consumed in Spain is used by industries and electricity generation  [3]   [4] . In Andalucia this figure is even bigger, 84.6% with Huelva and Cádiz being the provinces with the highest rates  [3]   [4] . In contrast, families experience energy poverty due to the soaring prices and inflation  [3]   [4] . Therefore Rebelión por el Clima (Climate Rebellion) demands the dismantling of these infrastructures and the establishment of renewable energy and energy conservation practices including conversion to renewable heating, self-consumption systems and improving insulation by 2035  [3]   [4] . Resistance Around September 2022, a protest by Ecologistas en Acción (Ecologists in Action) gathered at the Juan Carlos I pier, which is opposite to the gas facilities at the port of Huelva  [1] . The organisation demanded a stop to fossil fuel companies and greenwashing  [1] . Following, in October the same year around a hundred activists from the Rebelión por el Clima (Climate Rebellion) movement (of which Ecologistas en Acción (Ecologists in Action) is part of) blocked the headquarters of Enagás at the Huelva Chemical Complex  [2]   [5] . The group used the slogan “Families are freezing while their future burns here” criticising the company and shedding light that the most vulnerable people are suffering due to the price surge and the climate crisis  [2] . They have also highlighted the inadequacy of the Plan Más Seguridad Energética (More Energy Security Plan), approved on October 11 by the Government, which has been heavily influenced by industrial corporations and binds citizens on fossil fuel dependence  [2] . Expansion of the project Despite the protests in 2022, the LNG terminal in Huelva has continued to expand. In 2023, Alberto Santana, President of the Port of Huelva, and Arturo Gonzalo, CEO of Enagás, signed a protocol to explore innovation opportunities related to renewable gases such as hydrogen and Bio-LNG [8] . During the same period, LNG bunkering activity increased significantly, with the company quadrupling fuel supply to ships between 2021 and 2023 [9] . Operational activity also continued to grow. In 2024, the Huelva terminal received 38 LNG carriers and unloaded more than 5 million m³ of LNG. That same year, the facility obtained authorization to upgrade its mooring system to accommodate vessels of up to 180,000 m³, allowing it to receive larger methane carriers and reinforcing its role as one of Spain’s major LNG terminals [10] .

case_name: Resistance against the Permian Highway Pipeline, Texas, USA
headline: The development of the Permian Highway Pipeline triggered widespread resistance in Central Texas, including grassroots protests, municipal opposition and multiple legal challenges over environmental risks, landowner rights and regulatory oversight.
location: Not specified clearly in live EJAtlas metadata.
description: Kinder Morgan’s Permian Highway Pipeline project is transporting 2.1 billion cubic feet of fracked gas every day, crossing hundreds of properties, rivers, creeks, karst aquifer recharge zones, springs, and endangered species’ habitats in Central Texas [1] . The $2 billion pipeline project is part of the industry’s Trump-backed project to build new oil and gas pipelines from West Texas Permian Basin to refineries near Houston and Corpus Christi, and also to LNG terminals in the Gulf area for export [7] . Despite the intent for exporting, the company argues that the pipeline is in the public interest as it will generate $1 billion for state and county revenues annually  [7] . Leaseholders in the Permian Basin are expected to earn significantly more, with annual royalty revenues exceeding $2 billion once production bottlenecks in West Texas are resolved  [7] . Environmental and Societal Impacts Yet, the Texas Real Estate Advocacy and Defense Coalition argues otherwise, as the pipeline’s path impacts residential areas due to being in the area (incineration zone) that is at risk in the event of an explosion  [7] . Furthermore, under Texas state law, such companies as Kinder Morgan can chart their own pipeline routes under the ‘right of eminent domain’ (a process by which public and private entities can take private property, even if the owner does not want to sell) [3] . Several landowners had stated that Kinder Morgan is bullying them to give away their properties for prices below their market worth  [7] .  Since the pipeline project does not go beyond state lines, it is only regulated by the Texas Railroad Commission, which does not require an environmental assessment study  [7] . According to David Baker, executive director of The Watershed Association of the Permian Basin Highway is the “worst thing to ever happen to the Texas Hill Country and that even the construction would cause harm to our fragile karst aquifers”  [1] . The potential impacts of the project could affect the land’s sensitive karst topography with many underground cavities, fractures and drainage systems which supply the springs around Hill Country, flow into Trinity and Edwards aquifers (which provides drinking water to 80% of San Antonio)  [7] . The construction would also cross Blanco and Llano Rivers and also affects the popular Jacob’s Well  [7] . The landscape of this area makes potential spills or leaks impossible to clean up, which can be accelerated by the Hill County’s prone to flash floods and heavy rains  [7] . The pipeline would also affect the endangered Austin blind salamander and the Barton Springs salamander  [2]   [15] . The city of Austin argues that Kinder Morgan has not followed the necessary steps under the U.S. Endangered Species Act to obtain the necessary permits for the project  [2]   [7] . Specifically, the company failed to apply for a permit from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service for construction plans over the Edwards Aquifer Recharge Zone  [2]   [7] . It also impacts the endangered golden-cheeked warbler, which migrates annually from Mexico to Central Texas and only nests in the Hill Country’s cedar breaks  [7] . Resistance Early Public Opposition (2019) In the beginning of January, 2019 there was a public meeting held regarding the Permian Highway Pipeline in Central Texas, where Hays Country residents loudly shared their concerns regarding the projects, and many speakers vowed to fight it [8] . Similarly, many concerned individuals filled the Wimberley Community Center to hear from elected officials, lawyers and experts, many bringing petitions and posters against the project  [8] .  Local governments soon began to respond to these concerns. In the following month, the Kyle City Council unanimously signed on a resolution, opposing the pipeline due to its route through Hays County [9] . Similarly, the San Marcos City Council passed a resolution on 5th of March to oppose the development, requesting immediate action from the Texas Legislature to protect landowners [10] . Legal and Political Escalation (Mid-2019) Opposition increasingly moved into the legal and institutional framework during the summer of 2019. In June 2019, the Austin City Council directed the Watershed Protection Department to assess the pipeline’s potential water-quality impacts  [13]   [15] . The report concluded that current laws may not fully prevent environmental harm and noted limited public information from Kinder Morgan about the route and potential impacts, making risk assessment difficult (13). In the same month, Hays County, the Travis Audubon Society and private property owners also filed a“notice of intent to sue due to the endangered golden-cheeked warbler  [5]   [14] . The plaintiffs argue that Kinder Morgan did not obtain the necessary federal permit from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; instead, the company used a “work-around agreement with the Army Corps of Engineers” in violation of the Endangered Species Act  [5]    [14] . At the same time, landowners also challenged the regulatory oversight of the project. In June 2019, a Travis County judge ruled that construction of a natural gas pipeline through the Texas Hill Country could proceed, despite arguments that the Texas Railroad Commission would not provide sufficient oversight of the project’s construction and maintenance  [3] . The landowners argued that the Commission failed to properly regulate the pipeline routing and eminent domain powers  [3] . While expressing concern about private entities exercising powers that would normally require public scrutiny if held by a government body, Judge Livingston noted that the court’s role is to apply existing law rather than determine state policy  [3] .  As a counter reaction in July, 2019, Kinder Morgan filed a legal complaint against the City of Kyle, arguing that the newly adopted pipeline safety ordinance is illegal [4] . The new law (following the above-mentioned water-quality impact report) requires more permitting and fee requirements, increasing setbacks around pipelines and mandates requiring them to be buried 13 feet underground in some places  [4] . Later that year, in October, the City of Austin filed a Notice of Intent to sue Kinder Morgan, joining opposition by cities such as San Marcos, Kyle, the Barton Springs Aquifer Conservation District and the property-owner group TREAD Coalition  [2]   [13] . They argued that Kinder Morgan and the Army Corps of Engineers violated NEPA during the permitting process as “NEPA requires full consideration of the impacts of the action you’re undertaking, as well as looking at alternatives” [6] . Protests and Construction Incidents (2020) In the following year, in January, just before construction started, a group of Hays County residents gathered at the downtown Kyle square to protest the pipeline [11] . Soon after, in March, during construction due to an accident about 36,000 gallons of drilling fluid leaked into the Trinity Aquifer while drilling under the Blanco River, contaminating nearby drinking-water wells  [6] . In response, Trinity Edwards Spring Protection Association (TESPA) argued that the spill was in violation of the Safe Drinking Water Act, with the Army Corps of Engineers also being at fault as they allowed Kinder Morgan to skip over the NEPA analysis through the “Nationwide Permit 12 process”  [6] . The Sierra Club attorney requested a temporary injunction to halt construction based on this violation of NEPA  [6] .  Attorneys also issued a notice of intent to sue Permian Highway Pipeline LLC (PHP) and its managing partner Kinder Morgan for contamination of an underground source of drinking water caused by construction operations in Blanco County on March 28, 2020  [1] . The notice identified four federal environmental laws that may have been violated: the Safe Drinking Water Act for injecting fluids into an underground source of drinking water; the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act for creating an imminent and substantial endangerment to the public; violations of the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers’ Nationwide Permit 12 due to the discharge of pollutants; and discharging pollutants into waters of the United States without a permit  [1] . Continued Mobilisation and Legal Action (Mid-2020) From June 29, 2020 to August 1, 2020, a small local coalition united around stopping the action, organising a ‘Week of Action’ which resulted in a car caravan on 1st of August  [13] . Organizers supplied a social media toolkit and coordinated activities through a Facebook page  [13] . In the same month, the Wimberley Valley Watershed Association (WVWA) and Trinity Edwards Springs Protection Association (TEPSA) filed lawsuits due to violations of the federal Safe Drinking Water Act  [13] . The plaintiffs stated that the company must clean up the March 28 spill and asked developers to agree on stopping using a drilling chemical that contains known human carcinogens  [13] .  In the following month (July 2020), approximately 100 gallons of drilling fluid appeared close to the Pedernales river. The Houston Chronicle reported that this incident followed an earlier accident in March 2020 along another section of the project in nearby Blanco County, where a mixture of non-toxic bentonite clay and water reportedly seeped into drinking-water wells used by local landowners  [13] . Soon after, in August 2020, a federal judge in Texas denied the Sierra Club’s request to stop construction arguing that “Unfortunately, granting an injunction at this stage of the pipeline’s completion would not unring the bell,” [12] . According to the judge, the environmental group failed to showcase a definitive threat of future harm (12). By this time works were 72% complete and trenching 87% finished  [12] . In contrast, the Sierra Club attorney said that the “construction has already done significant damage to waterways and will do more if completed”  [12] .  Despite continued protests, legal challenges and construction-related incidents, the pipeline was ultimately completed and began transporting natural gas in early 2021.

case_name: Bratislava LNG terminal cancellation, Slovakia
headline: Sustained protests, guerrilla campaigns, policy advocacy, and financial pressure halted an LNG terminal in Bratislava.
description: In Bratislava, Slovakia, the state-owned investor Public Ports company Verejné Prístavy proposed the construction of a liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminal on the Danube, with an expected lifespan of 20 to 40 years  [1]   [18] . Following a planned environmental impact assessment study, construction of the new terminal was supposed to begin in 2022 and end in 2026, with an estimated cost of approximately 40 million euros  [17]   [18] . The port would cover 5,500 square meters on the Pálenisko port peninsula and would be located in close proximity to the city centre, just a short distance from a cycle path, a gardening area, and the Žitný ostrov Nature Reserve, which is the largest source of drinking water in Central Europe  [1]   [17]   [18] .. The terminal would be used to refuel road tankers, provide LNG storage, and serve as a bunkering facility for ships  [17]   [20] . It would involve storage tanks, technological equipment to maintain the fuel at low temperatures, and a dispensing point for pumping fuel into ship tanks, classifying it as a small-scale LNG bunkering facility  [20] . The company claims that the project would introduce alternative fuels and reduce greenhouse gas emissions as part of the EU plan to develop the Rhine–Danube transport corridor  [17]  . Environmental Impacts However, Greenpeace Slovakia claims that the plan to build an LNG terminal in Bratislava is outdated and does not take into account the latest developments of climate change mitigation plans, as currently wind and solar are the cheapest forms of energy supply in most major markets  [1] . The claim that the LNG terminal reduces greenhouse gas emissions is a fallacy, as considering the entire life cycle, it does not reduce emissions compared to conventional fuels  [1] . Natural gas is 80% methane, a greenhouse gas that has up to 82.5 times the global warming potential of CO2 over a 20-year period  [1] . Furthermore, Transport & Environment has calculated that uncontrolled methane leakage may even increase emissions from shipping  [1] . Establishing a new LNG plant would accelerate climate change, which has already resulted in some places in Slovakia up to 50% reduction in water resources, devastating droughts lasting several years or increasingly intense torrential rains  [1] . Additionally, an LNG terminal would pose a severe safety risk for the city centre and residential areas, as LNG is a highly flammable substance, and over the past 30 years, more than 19 LNG accidents have been documented  [1] . It can potentially worsen the city’s air quality as it increases freight traffic density  [1] . Moreover, while LNG tanks have a double-walled structure with thermal insulation layers making leakage unlikely, pollution can occur from other chemicals used, such as in the storage and transportation of LNG (corrosion inhibitors, coolants, cleaning agents, emulsion agents, various additives), which can impact the Natural Reserve waters  [1] .  Greenpeace Slovakia claims that a report analysing 104 LNG-related accidents between 1944 and 2024 highlights that areas within a two-kilometre radius of LNG facilities face the highest risk [15] . In the case of Bratislava, this zone includes densely populated areas such as Eurovea, Mlynské Nivy, and Ovsište in Petržalka, as well as the Slovnaft refinery located only 1.5 km from the proposed terminal, which could amplify accident-related impacts  [15] . The report warns that risks such as vapour cloud explosions, pool fires, and jet fires may be underestimated by the industry by a factor of 15 to 20, posing serious threats to nearby populations and infrastructure  [15] . These risks are further intensified by climate-related extreme events, as the planned terminal site was flooded during recent floods, raising concerns about the facility’s resilience and environmental safety  [15] . Resistance tactics The civil society in Bratislava has employed a wide variety of tactics against the proposed LNG facilities. In 2021 June, on the day of the hearings of the LNG plans, Greenpeace protested in front of the Ministry of Transport; furthermore, together with other partners, the organisation submitted allegations against the Environmental Impact Assessment  [2] . In the same year, they have also put out guerrilla campaigns all around the city, advertisements about “greenwashing” by gas companies and posters in local restaurants with a link to sign and oppose fossil fuels  [3]   [4] . Greenpeace also established an infostand around the city weekly, and organisers on bikes and kayaks went around the city with short infomercials about the terminal  [5]   [6]   [8] . There were also collaborations with influencers and content creators, spreading information about the proposed LNG plans and their impacts  [10]   [11] . Greenpeace, in collaboration with expert James Turitt from the Clean Air Task Force, monitored methane emissions from gas infrastructures in Slovakia through an infrared camera [7] . In total, 31 cases of methane emissions were documented at seven locations, four compressor stations in Veľké Kapušany, Veľké Zlievece, Ivanka pri Nitre and Lakšárská Nová Ves, an underground gas storage facility in Plavecký Štvrtek, a national transfer station in Špačince and an SPP Distribution control station near Lozorno  [7] . Greenpeace held advocacy meetings with the City Hall and the Mayor of the city district, which was in close proximity to the planned terminal. Furthermore, they had a lobbying meeting with the Ministry of Transportation. Activists from Friends of the Earth-CEPA, From Benches to Streets, Turning Point, Concerned Mothers, Extinction Rebellion and Greenpeace Slovakia, before the discussion of the Bratislava Public Port Development Strategy, symbolically expressed their opposition to the construction of an LNG terminal in Bratislava  [12] . Greenpeace Slovakia have also disrupted the Central European Energy Conference during the initial discussion on increasing energy security with a banner stating “gas = energy crisis”  [1]   [9] . Just a short distance from the conference, a second 20-meter banner was hung outside of the MR Štefánik Square in Bratislava by activists from Slovakia, Poland, Croatia, Austria and Hungary, which drew attention to energy security with renewable resources, not oil, natural gas or coal  [1]   [9] . A Greenpeace activist, Katarína Juríková, stated that the energy crisis will not be solved by “replacing one gas supplier with another”, rather “investment should go into renewable energy sources (...) with a sufficient financial support for people so that everyone can afford these changes”  [9] . Moreover, Greenpeace Slovakia, Friends of Earth - CEPA, Concerned Mothers and From the Benches to the Streets launched a public appeal for residents to express their opposition to the planned construction of the LNG terminal [13]   [21] . Yet, the Ministry of Environment rejected the appeal, arguing that the terminal would not be in conflict with the Paris Agreement and that the transition to low-emission alternatives in river transport is not realistic in the near future [14] . The Ministry also stated that methane leaks, which can have an impact during construction and operation, need to be addressed at a global level  [14] . In contrast, Greenpeace stated regarding low-emission alternative technologies that “His argument is in direct contradiction with the conclusions of the European Parliament and the Council, which state in the proposal for a regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council on the deployment of alternative fuels infrastructure and repealing Directive 2014/94/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council that “unlike maritime transport, in inland waterway transport, where smaller vessels are commonly used and cover shorter distances, zero-emission propulsion technologies such as hydrogen and electricity should enter the market more quickly. LNG is not expected to play a significant role in this sector anymore.”   [14] . The contract governing the provision of a non-refundable financial contribution stipulates that the state-owned joint-stock company, Verejné prístavy, must take out insurance [16] . Therefore, insurance companies such as Allianz, Kooperative, Komunálna poisťovňa, Uniqua, Generali, Union, Collonade, ČSOB, and Wüstenrot received letters from Greenpeace Slovakia asking them not to insure the planned LNG terminal, as the company then would not fulfil the obligation and would have to return the funds obtained  [16] . Success As of 2026, the LNG terminal in Bratislava was cancelled, and the Public Ports stated, “The project plan is in the phase of completed pre-project preparation, specifically at the level of processing the feasibility study and related analytical and evaluation documents […]. The LNG terminal project in the Port of Bratislava has not yet been approved or has a valid implementation schedule. After the completion of the pre-project preparation, a decision was not made to transition the project to the implementation phase. The project is currently not being implemented,” [19] . Greenpeace stated that the cancellation was mainly due to financial and strategic reasons, as the terminal did not receive support under the AFIF (Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Facility, which is an EU financial instrument for alternative fuels in transport) call, as it was primarily focused on infrastructure for low-emission and zero-emission technologies  [19]   [20] . The organisation also stated that this decision has been impacted by the fact that the current demand for LNG as a fuel for inland waterway support on the Danube is limited and that out of the three projects planned (two in Bratislava, one in Komárno), none was implemented (19). Without enough customers, the terminal would not have been stable economically  [20] . Yet, even with successful cancellations, Greenpeace also noted that  “hundreds of thousands of euros of public funds were wasted just on the preparation of the project documentation required for the EIA. As much as we welcome the fact that the project will not be implemented, the fact that any investment was made in its preparation at all has drained money from real decarbonization measures."  [19]   [20] .

case_name: Washington Park and South Providence Residents Oppose Allens Avenue Waste Transfer Station, RI, USA
headline: Residents of Washington Park and South Providence successfully organized to defeat a proposal to build a waste transfer station in their neighborhood.
description: Residents of Washington Park and South Providence successfully organized to defeat a proposal to build a waste transfer station in their neighborhood. The facility would have processed 2500 tons of waste daily and created particulate pollution and environmental odors which would have negatively impacted the quality of life and health of those who live, work, and play in the area.  The 1.8 miles of Allens Avenue that runs along the Port of Providence is “arguably the most unpleasant stretch of road in Rhode Island,” according to journalist Frank Carini. [1] Marked by noxious odors from industry, diesel fumes from cars and trucks, and giant piles of materials such as scrap metal, asphalt, and road salt, many of the businesses on Allens Avenue have created negative health impacts for people in the nearby neighborhoods of South Providence and Washington Park, which have some of the highest asthma rates in the state and country. The lot at 481 Allens Avenue has hosted many polluting industries since the 1950s, including metal casting, scrap-metal processing, and waste storage. As a result, the site is classified as a brownfield because the soil has been contaminated with petroleum hydrocarbons, lead, and arsenic. [2] Operations on the site were written up several times over the years by the RI Department of Environmental Management (DEM) for safety violations, improperly stored material, and taking unauthorized items. The site sits next to Motiva, a petrochemical distributor; National Grid, a natural gas liquefaction facility; and Univar, a chemical processing plant, and is across the street from Meeting Street School, a school inclusive of students with disabilities that serves early childhood through grade eight students.  On Feb. 18, 2018, William Thibeault of Allens Providence Recycling LLC, a company based out of Everett, Massachusetts, bought 481 Allens Avenue for $950,000. [2] Between 2018 and 2020, the lot was used as a scrap-metal recycling facility and a tow yard. In December 2019, Allens Providence Recycling announced plans to build a construction and demolition (C&D) waste transfer station at the site. Residents were outraged at the proposal, as the project would further burden neighborhoods already bearing the brunt of a myriad of environmental harms. [3] The proposed facility would handle 2500 tons of residential waste, commercial waste, and construction debris daily, all of which would be brought in and removed by truck. This would result in an estimated 188 truck deliveries daily. These trucks would have to idle in a queue outside of the facility or circle the area if the queue was full, increasing the diesel pollution on Allens Avenue and nearby areas. [2] Residents also voiced concerns about the lack of adequate dust and odor control plans. C&D facilities produce fine particulates, which are especially dangerous because they can be inhaled into our lungs and/or be absorbed into our bloodstreams. Fine particulates are linked to cardiovascular diseases and short-term breathing problems, including asthma. Odors reported by residents, likely associated with volatile organic compounds (VOCs), lessen quality of life and cause health symptoms, including headaches, nausea, and respiratory irritation. The facility had no odor control plan, and its only dust control plan was to spray the facility with leachate, the liquid that accumulates from trash dumped onto the waste processing floor ( sometimes called “garbage juice”). Leachate has been found t o contain toxic heavy metals and PFAS (also known as “forever chemicals”). [4] PFAS can increase cancer risk, cause problems with fertility and pregnancy, compromise immune systems, and interfere with natural hormones and with liver, thyroid, and pancreatic function. [5]   A group of activists led by Linda Perri of the Washington Park Association and Monica Huertas of No LNG in PVD (now the People’s Port Authority), along with support from their city councilor, Pedro Espinal, quickly got their community involved in opposing the project. A meeting was held on January 8, 2020, to strategize and prepare for an upcoming City Planning Commission (CPC) hearing that would address the project proposal on January 21. [3] Seventy-five ( 75) community members attended the CPC hearing to oppose the project, which took place at 4:45 in the afternoon. [6] As journalist Steve Ahlquist noted, “Going to a public hearing that begins at 4:45 pm in downtown Providence is a very difficult thing for many people. It requires leaving work early and finding parking downtown during rush hour. It requires missing classes or losing paying wage hours at your job. It means securing childcare, transportation, [and] paying for parking.” Despite the efforts many residents went through to attend the meeting, they were told once they arrived that the company and requested a last-minute continuance, such that the agenda item had been postpone d. Residents who had shown up and wanted to speak were not allowed to do so, even though the CPC could have voted to allow them to do so under RI’s Open Meetings Act. Undeterred, they moved outdoors, into the cold winter evening, and held an impromptu rally with speeches against the transfer station, where activists vowed to come back with an even stronger turnout for the next meeting. [7] In the interim, the Racial and Environmental Justice Committee held a visioning session for residents to describe what they wanted the Port to look like going forward, and the Washington Park Association organized another community meeting with several elected officials and organizers to gather more opposition to the transfer station. [13] In late February, Providence City Council members, including Pedro Espinal, introduced a resolution calling on the CPC to deny the proposal. [8] This resolution amplified the concerns of community members and those raised in a staff report about zoning. 481 Allens Avenue is zoned as General Industrial (M-2), which allows for “a facility for the incineration and/or processing of waste, including sewage disposal facilities or solid waste transfer station, operated by or for a state or municipal agency.” [9] However, because the proposed transfer station would not be operated by the state or the municipality, it would not be allowed under current zoning laws. In the lead-up to the rescheduled CPC meeting on March 17, No LNG in PVD ran a door-knocking campaign to encourage neighbors to turn out for the meeting. Contextualizing th e transfer station within the longer fight for environmental justice in the Port of Providence, Monica Huertas of No LNG in PVD told volunteers, “It didn’t start with the transfer station and it’s not going to end with the transfer station. It’s not going to end on March 17, and even if the City Council says no, or whatever, this is not where it ends with the Port and all the issues we’re having with the Port.” [10] Ahead of the March 17 meeting, Allens Providence Recycling asked for another extension on their application, and then withdrew the application shortly afterwards. [11] While community members argued that the transfer station never should have been proposed at all, they celebrated the victory that the transfer station would not be built. Linda Perri of the Washington Park neighborhood association declared, “This was a win for the community. It is so great that everybody got behind this. It became a movement. It showed that real people really do care about injustice and the climate. It put a laser-like focus on South Providence. I would like to see that land developed into a green, clean solar field, something to benefit the community.” [12]

case_name: Koa-Gas movement against gas drilling, Bavaria, Germany
headline: As of December 2025, exploratory drilling for natural gas is underway in Reichling, southwest of Munich. If successful and economic viable, investors might develop additional gas wells in the region. There is significant media coverage across Bavaria, accompanied by protests from activist groups.
description: Currently, exploratory drilling for natural gas is underway in Reichling, a village located in southwest Bavaria near the picturesque Ammersee. Should the prospecting of the gas field prove successful and be economically viable, investors might develop additional gas wells in the region. The site in question is designated as Kinsau 1A and is managed by Energieprojekt Lech Kinsau 1 GmbH, based in  Düsseldorf. [1]   The primary investor of this GmbH is MRH GmbH, which holds a 80% stake, while the remaining shares are held by Genexco GmbH, a direct subsidiary of MCF Energy from Canada. This highly topical issue has received extensive coverage in  Bavarian  media, with  protests mounted by activist groups against the drilling activities. Notably, concerns have been raised by non-governmental organisations such as Greenpeace and BUND Naturschutz, but also the District Administrator of Landsberg am Lech, who issued an open letter to the Bavarian government. [2]   According to Greenpeace, the site may contain 300 to 500 million cubic meters of natural gas, potentially contributing to a total of up to 3 billion cubic meters in the Alpine foreland. [3] Natural gas, by definition, is a naturally occurring hydrocarbon gas mixture found beneath the earth's surface used as fuel. “Natural gas originates from any one or more of three major processes: thermogenic, biogenic, and abiogenic processes.“ (Faramawy et al. 2026: 35) When broken down linguistically, "natural" indicates that the substance is not made by or substantially altered by humans, while "gas" refers to a state of matter distinct from liquids or solids. [4]   [5]   [6]   Natural gas originates from the slow transformation of ancient organic matter—largely plants, algae, and microorganisms—that was deposited and buried in sedimentary basins over millions of years. Subjected to escalating heat and pressure within deep geological formations, these materials chemically altered to form hydrocarbons, which migrate into porous reservoir rocks. Compared to oil, natural gas typically forms under conditions of greater burial depth and thermal maturity, often emerging from shales, coal seams, or carbonate reservoirs.  [7]   [8] The area surrounding the drill site is an ecological important nature reserve and various habitat zones. It also harbours various activists who express their concerns through protests. The planned natural gas drilling project near Reichling, located in Bavaria’s Landsberg am Lech district, illustrates the interplay between technical considerations and socio-ecological factors. Official communications of the Drill Company it is emphasized that the project is a controlled intervention, supported by legal permits, protective buffer zones, and environmental safeguards such as media-resistant containment areas, leak detection systems, and closed-circuit drilling fluid recycling. (Daborer 2023) Nevertheless, the project exists within a complex context where ecological concerns, regulatory frameworks and the economic needs intersect.  Local opposition arises primarily from concerns about the proximity of the drilling site to protected natural habitats and residential areas.  Specific worries include the potential for groundwater contamination, seismic activity, and accidental releases. These concerns are situated within a broader critique related to climate policy and the future role of fossil fuels. (Reinbeck 2025: 7) The estimated gas reserves are sufficient to cover only a short period of regional consumption, raising questions about the strategic relevance of the project within energy transition efforts.  The regulatory process of the Südbayrisches Bergamt had to include a detailed consideration of adjacent protected areas such as drinking water protection zones, biotopes, Fauna-Flora-Habitat (FFH) sites, and bird conservation areas. [10]   Special species protection assessments conclude that, contingent on mitigation measures, legal prohibitions are not expected to be breached. And if this were the case, compensatory measures are defined in the landscape ecology reports that are proportionate to the impact and meet the legal requirements for compensating habitat impairments. Assessments indicate that protected areas will not be directly affected, that hazardous materials are concentrated within designated zones, and that emissions during exploration are relatively low. (Daborer 2023: 15) But the design of infrastructure and the framework for environmental impact assessments influence which ecological effects are documented, and which are less apparent. Activists are concerned that the drilling process can cause significant noise and light pollution, which can threaten vulnerable wildlife in conservation areas. Furthermore drinking water incidents could lead to the entry of pollutants into groundwater and surrounding waters, with these pollutants originating from the depths of the earth and oil and substances used in drilling operations. (Reinbeck 2025: 9) However, this approach may overlook wider, system-level impacts associated with fossil fuel extraction. According to Greenpeace there is an inherent risk of incidents, such as blowouts. Such events could lead to the release of gas, causing ecological damage that would be difficult to mitigate. (Reinbeck 2025: 10)  Methane emissions represent a significant area of concern. While frequently underestimated, methane is a potent greenhouse gas with a substantially higher climate impact than carbon dioxide over short time horizons. Methane release tends to occur not only during combustion but throughout production, transport, and storage stages. Existing monitoring measures may not fully capture these emissions. (Anderson/ Broderick 2017: 25) The extraction and distribution of natural gas is also accompanied by the unintentional release of methane. If total anthropogenic methane emissions remained at current levels, it would cause a significant temperature increase of around 0.6°C. (Anderson/ Broderick 2017: 5)    In general, the media coverage on the topic in Reichling is very present. Not only local news broadcast like Landsberger Tagesblatt   [11] , Gong 96.3   [12 ] , Augsburger Allgemeine,   [13]   or Merkur  [14]   wrote various articles, also Süddeutsche Zeitung and Bayrischer Rundfunk   – also the Bavarian Government published a press release on their website   [15]   The drill would be the first new extraction point of fossil energy in Bavaria in a long time, and it created a big public discussion. The first public information evening was in 2022, also the media reported then  about the reopening of the site. [16]   Over the last few years has been a lot of different protests. Seven stakeholders from environmental organisations are involved, often organising protests together, spreading awareness through information meetings, and collecting data on the project, forming a large network. They organised protest marches, planted trees on site, delayed the project by insisting  on nature conservation assessments, held information forums to raise awareness and spread hope.   There are also various protests in form of petitions. Greenpeace   [17] , Umweltinstitut München e.V.   [18] ,  BUND Naturschutz,  [19]   and FridaysForFuture   [20]   did all call for signatures against the gas drill. They are addressing the petition as an open letter to Finance Minister Aiwanger: „Mr. Aiwanger, don't put the business interests of international gas companies above the protection of our homeland and the well-being of the rural population!“.  We will now dwell on design and aesthetics—both corporate and oppositional—tracing how the visual and material choices of all parties work to persuade, obfuscate, or destabilize dominant narratives.   In the open interview format “ Jetz red I ” the Head from MRH GmbH Daniel Jürgensen talked about the probable future aesthetic of the well, if they find enough gas and it gets a permission to use the gas: there will be no tower flaring fracked gas, but the gas will flow upwards by itself into two containers, where it will be analysed, purified and then fed into the grid, by a pipeline system which will be laid in the streets. They will build a green fence around it so that it cannot be seen, smelled or heard.    [minute 28:30–33:20 /21]   So here is a very clean aesthetic promoted.   Greenpeace in contrast highlights, that the clean aesthetic comes from the region itself and that the gas well is still an ultra-deep entanglement with the fossil strata underneath the nature conservation area. The energy itself is a non-renewable fuel and should be recognized as it. Therefore, the imagery of the protest is filled with Posters against emitting climate-damaging gases like Methane or CO2. The protest in the moment is focussing on the messages: “No new gas!” and “Stop gas drillings in Bavaria!”  Their main protest colour is bright yellow, possibly taking inspiration from the large yellow X that was originally used for the Lützerath protests. They have placed this X in front of the drill site to make a more permanent statement against the project.  The activists are trying to undermine the clean look of the company as a provider of a bridging technology by emphasising the role of gas exploration in causing temperature rise. This enables them to present a different perspective on the topic to that of the drilling company, or Minister Hubert Aiwanger.   Jane Hutton’s notion of reciprocal landscapes elucidates how the contrasting visual and material strategies employed by corporate and activist actors not only shape local perceptions but also reveal the deep entanglement of cultural narratives with the physical environment, underscoring the dynamic interplay between identity, place, and resource extraction.  The Application for a mining licence for Kinsau 1A project was in May 2022, one month after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine had begun. Because of the war Germany and the EU have significantly reduced their dependence on Russian gas,  [22]  aiming for a full phase-out by 2027 under the REPowerEU plan. Russian gas imports dropped from 45% in 2021 to around 19% in 2024, though a partial rebound caused concern. [23]   [24]   To replace Russian supplies, the EU has increased “Liquified Natural Gas” imports (later only referred to as LNG), especially from the United States, which provided nearly 50% of EU LNG in 2023. Recently, the EU pledged to import $250 billion worth of U.S. energy by 2030, deepening reliance on American LNG. [25]   A key issue for debate is whether domestic gas reserves are large enough to make them a more sustainable option than imports from overseas. The Federal Institute for Geosciences and Natural Resources (BGR) has compared the extent to which natural gas imports from various countries pollute the atmosphere, even before the gas is burned in Germany. The study shows that emissions from locally extracted gas are presumably lower because the extraction distance is shorter, resulting in a reduction of overall emissions and uncertainty.   [26]   However, new infrastructure for gas extraction in Reichling and the surrounding area would tie the region to gas use for a long period, since such investments in pipelines and facilities cannot easily be abandoned. Therefore, the capacities of LNG terminals remain in place for a long period, limiting the displacement of LNG imports despite local supply claims.  So in what ways does the village of Reichling become a microcosm, or indeed a proxy battlefield, for competing visions of Germany’s energy future? Genexco GmbH insists that it is seeking co-operation with the municipality of Reichling and the regional utilities and that the benefits should be felt locally. These could include the payment of taxes and 2-3 permanent jobs during the funding phase.   It should be noted that neither the Lech Kinsau 1A energy project (based in Düsseldorf), in which MRH GmbH from Mülheim a.d. Ruhr holds an 80% stake, nor the Canadian company Genexco GmbH, which holds a 20% stake, are based in the Landsberg district. As trade taxes are primarily paid in the jurisdiction where the company is registered, in this case no financial contribution is made to the regional municipalities. In contrast to other federal states, the state of Bavaria does not impose a tax on the extraction of natural gas, as the current extraction tax is zero percent. This means that the State of Bavaria is effectively ‘giving away’ the fossil natural gas to the extracting companies. (Reinbeck 2025: 7)  The debate over domestic gas extraction versus imports aligns with Hutton’s call to understand energy systems as material circulations that connect local sites to national and global scales, revealing the intricate interdependencies across ecological, economic, and technological domains. The German government has to master various issues: remaining a leading industry, diversifying the energy sources while reducing fossil dependencies and steering continuously to climate neutrality. This also applies to Bavaria. The State has the climate protection law – which came into effect at the start of 2021,   [27]  and decided to be climate-neutral by 2024. [28]   But the question is, which of these do we prioritise? In case of Reichling, the minister for economic affairs Mr. Aiwanger often refers to the Bundesbergrecht  [29]     where it says that the local german resources should be utilized and thus extracted for ongoing infrastructure requirements. And that he cannot do anything about the legality of gas extraction.   For many years, the German Federal Environment Agency has proven to be surprisingly resistant to the incorporation of ecological and environmental preservation requirements. [30]   There are also critical voices apart from environmental NGO’s from the District Administrator from Landsberg Thomas Eichinger who wrote an open Letter to the minister for economic affairs Mr. Aiwanger. Generally the Communal Politicians are struggling with the public communication considering what measures are suitable for the planned energy transition until 2040 in Bavaria. [31]     In the Interview format: Jetz red’ I in ARD television from the 02.10.2024 the mayor Sandra Perzul from the neighbor village Dießen is pleading to the governmental organization to give coherent instructions for the necessary infrastructural investments for the energy transition on a local level. [32] In conclusion, the reactivation of the Kinsau 1A gas well in rural Bavaria embodies a complex entanglement of deep geological history, contemporary climate activism, and contested visions for Germany’s energy future. Situated in the ecologically sensitive Molasse Basin near the Ammersee, the project represents a significant technical and financial undertaking to access fossil fuels formed over millions of years, while simultaneously raising substantial socio-ecological concerns. Despite comprehensive regulatory assessments and corporate efforts to frame the project as transparent and minimally disruptive, local and environmental opposition emphasize the risks of groundwater contamination, methane emissions, and the contradiction of expanding fossil fuel infrastructure amid urgent climate goals. The project also highlights tensions between energy security and climate policy, as domestic gas extraction seeks to reduce dependency on imports, yet potentially locks the region into continued fossil fuel reliance. Visually and rhetorically, stakeholders deploy contrasting aesthetics—corporate actors promote a clean, cooperative image tied to local natural heritage, while activists use bold symbolism to challenge the narrative and call for a rapid transition to renewables. Politically, the village of Reichling acts as a microcosm where global energy politics, regional economic interests, and grassroots advocacy intersect, revealing the complexities of managing resource extraction under climate imperatives. Financially and legally, the project benefits from lenient regional policies, with the Bavarian state not taxing natural gas extraction and tax revenues leaving the local municipalities, further fueling local dissent. Media coverage and public discourse around Kinsau 1A underscore the high stakes and polarized perspectives on the future of energy in Bavaria and Germany more broadly. Ultimately, the Kinsau 1A case exemplifies the persistent challenges in reconciling fossil fuel dependency with the urgent global mandate for climate neutrality and equitable energy transitions.  Bibliography:  Anderson, K. and Broderick, J.
