case_name: No LNG in PVD Opposes National Grid Liquefaction Project, RI, US
headline: National Grid built a natural gas liquefaction at Fields Point in Port of Providence despite vast opposition from residents in the nearby South Providence and Washington Park neighborhoods.
description: National Grid built a natural gas liquefaction at Fields Point in Port of Providence despite vast opposition from residents in the nearby South Providence and Washington Park neighborhoods who were concerned that the facility would create additional dependency on fossil fuels in the state and increase air pollution in their communities which were already burned by asthma rates. Natural gas is responsible for nearly 90% of energy generation in Rhode Island. [1]   The vast majority of this natural gas is produced in Appalachia, the Gulf Coast, or Canada and is transported to Rhode Island by pipelines developed and operated by Algonquin Gas Transmission Company and the Tennessee Gas Pipeline (TGP) Company. [2] On its coldest days  (around nine days per year), when an additional supply of natural gas is needed, Rhode Island relies on Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG), which is transported into the state via tanker truck. [3] LNG is produced as a liquid in facilities by cooling room temperature natural gas by around 162 degrees Celsius. The LNG is then transported and reheated to a gas form once it reaches its final destination, in a process known as regasification. Regasification is costly and extremely energy-intensive. National Grid, a British multinational electricity and gas utility, began operating an LNG storage facility at Fields Point in the Port of Providence in 1974, and in 2015, the company proposed building a liquefaction facility to produce LNG at the site. [4] When justifying the need for this facility, National Grid cited demand for more LNG from their customers, Narragansett Electric Company and Boston Gas Company, both of which are their own subsidiaries. [3] The Fields Point site is located near the residential areas of South Providence and Washington Park, which resident Gina Rodriguez described as “a beautiful, diverse, vibrant, strong Black and brown community.” [5] In the neighborhoods surrounding the proposed facility, 75% of residents are people of color, 56% are low­ income , and 17% are linguistically isolated. [6] South Providence and Washington Park are directly adjacent to the Port of Providence, where air, water, and soil pollution are produced by toxic industries, including fossil fuel infrastructure, petrochemical facilities, asphalt plants, and scrap yards. The air pollution from the port contributes to the neighborhoods having some of the highest childhood and adult asthma rates in the state. As soon as the liquefaction facility was proposed, community groups quickly mobilized to oppose it. The “No LNG in PVD” coalition was formed to spearhead the charge. Monica Huertas, an environmental justice advocate and mother of four from Washington Park, served as the coalition's coordinator. The Coalition which was made up of environmental justice groups, including the Environmental Justice League of RI (EJLRI) and FANG (Fighting Against Natural Gas), and youth-led activist groups, such as the Providence Youth Student Movement (PrYSM) and the Providence Student Union (PSU), began attending public meetings and hearings, holding street protests, and producing research to demonstrate the harms this facility would cause. [7] Residents communicated how the liquefaction facility’s existence posed a direct and immediate threat to their health and safety, and was fundamentally misaligned with their vision of a cleaner, safer, climate-resilient port for the following reasons: The facility would pose significant risks of natural gas leaks and explosions, which have notably occurred at other LNG facilities, including a liquefaction plant in Skikda, Algeria. [8] The facility sits close to the Rhode Island Hospital Complex, which contains the only Level 1 trauma center in the state, Women and Infants’ Hospital, and Hasbro Children’s Hospital, all of which could be impacted by an accident at the facility. [9]  The increase in truck traffic from tankers transporting LNG from Fields Point to other storage facilities will worsen air pollution and asthma in the neighborhoods surrounding the facility.   In the event of hurricanes or storm surges, LNG spills could be caused by flooding or storm surges. The facility would sit unprotected on the coastline and would have no emergency access once the water rises. The project would lead to an increased dependence on natural gas in Rhode Island, which is fundamentally misaligned with the residents’ interests and the city and state’s stated goals of transitioning to renewable energy. [10] Some of these fears were brought to bear when there was a major gas leak at the Fields Point LNG storage facility on March 29, 2017. 19 million cubic feet of natural gas and about 2 gallons of polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) were released. [11] The leak led to the shutdown of the I-95 highway as response crews took measures to prevent a deadly explosion. Residents could hear and see the leak from their homes. Residents argued that if the current facility was already being mismanaged in ways that posed serious safety threats to their community, they could not trust National Grid to ensure safety at the new liquefaction facility. [6] From the outset, the processes for accessing information about the project and participating in the public approval process were made difficult for community members. Dates and times of public meetings were not available on National Grid’s website; rather, residents had to individually email the company to gain access to that information. All materials about the project published by National Grid were written solely in English, making the information unavailable to the large Spanish and Khmer-speaking populations in the neighborhoods impacted by the project. [12] And when residents did make it to public meetings, they were heavily policed, reinforcing a lack of recognition of challenges between local police and residents. Indeed, one meeting was even held in the Providence Public Safety Complex, which made many residents of color, who represented the majority of people impacted by the project, feel unsafe. [5]   Additionally, the required Public Participation Plan that National Grid submitted to the Federal Environmental and Regulatory Commission (FERC) included numerous nearby fossil fuel and chemical facilities like Univar, Sprague, Energy, and Motiva. The only community organizations included, the South Providence Neighborhood Association and the Washington Park Neighborhood Association, were either not in existence or inactive at the time the plan was released. [13] At a public meeting that the community had fought for months to have, Gina Rodriguez directly called out National Grid representatives for the lack of transparency in the process, declaring, “The fact that you keep calling this a public engagement process or a public involvement plan when we’ve had no involvement and no input is a farce. It is a lie. And it just shows how racist you are.” [5]  After the fraught initial public meetings held by National Grid, the next phase of the process began: the Coastal Resources Management Council’s (CRMC) approval process. CRMC is a planning and regulatory agency that oversees activity in Rhode Island’s coastal zone. The council includes staff scientists who serve in advisory roles and politically appointed voting members. In summer of 2017, a few months before the CRMC was set to hear the National Grid case, Rhode Island Governor Gina Raimondo replaced three environmentalist members of the CRMC whose terms had expired (there is no limit to the number of terms members can serve; most had only served 1-2 terms despite the norm being at least two full terms). [14] They were replaced by Lisette Gomes, Michelle Collie, and Jennifer Cervenka, the latter of whom was appointed as the new chair of the council. [15] The makeup of this council was much more favorable to National Grid, whose employees contributed $20,165 to Governor Raimondo’s campaign between 2014 and 2017. [17]   A public CRMC hearing on the project was scheduled for November 14, 2017. So many community members showed up to testify that an additional hearing was scheduled for November 28th. [18] At the second hearing, more than 50 people testified for over four hours. Residents implored the CRMC to consider how these facilities would impact their children, who were already growing up in a neighborhood surrounded by environmental hazards. Members of the council showed disinterest in residents’ testimony, including by looking at their phones, demonstrating particular disrespect towards testifying residents of color, such as when Chair Jennifer Cervenka interrupted activist Justice Gaines’s testimony about environmental racism. [18] Cervenka and CRMC member Grover Fugate walked out during resident Gina Rodriguez’s testimony and called on police to surround her. [19]   In response, No LNG in PVD issued a letter condemning Cervenka’s actions and calling attention to potential conflicts of interest that she had failed to disclose before presiding over the National Grid Case. Cervenka was previously employed at a law firm where Robin Main, who represented National Grid in the CRMC hearings, was a law partner and had oversight over her. [20] Cervenka also served as the chair of the RI Chamber of Commerce Coalition, an organization whose members have various professional ties to National Grid. Cervenka held this position concurrently with her position on the CRMC. [21] After No LNG in PVD’s letter was published, 427 community members, 32 organizations, and 9 elected officials called for Cervenka’s resignation from CRMC. [22] Cervenka ignored these calls, and days later, the CRMC unanimously issued its approval of the facility after nineteen minutes of deliberation. [23] In the following months, the project also obtained the necessary permits from the RI Department of Environmental Management and was approved by the Federal Energy and Regulatory Commission (FERC). [16] After multiple construction delays, the project was completed and became operational in May 2023. [24] [25]   In 2020, No LNG in PVD became the People’s Port Authority, shifting its focus to combat systemic problems in the regulatory oversight and decision-making processes in the Port, in addition to continuing to fight against harmful projects like this one. [26]

case_name: Balama graphite mine in Cabo Delgado, Mozambique
headline: A large mine belonging to Syrah Resouces of Australia encountered local resistance in 2024 because of lack of compensation to farmers, and labour issues. Mozambique exports graphite, a component in lithium-ion batteries.
description: Cabo Delgado, which is the scene of the violent conflict between the TotalEnergy company (and other LNG companies) and the local inhabitants, is a province in Mozambique which also sees other conflicts related to the extraction and exports of minerals for the so-called energy transition (which so far, by 2025) is still an "energy addition"). Foreign companies are involved. According to Business and Human Rights,   graphite mining in Cabo Delgado, Mozambique, as also graphite mining in Madagascar, stand to play a pivotal role in the global battery market. It is well known that graphite is a polluting materiasl, not less because of reports from China, the largest producer of graphite. [7]   The Australian mining company Syrah Resources owns a 95 per cent share in a large graphite mine complex in the Balama district in Cabo Delgado. This mining project involves two open-pit mines and is operated by Twigg Exploration and Resources, a subsidiary of Syrah. Syrah Resources is a public company from Melbourne listed on the Australian Stock Exchange. It grew rapidly from being a low-profile exploration miner with a handful of mineral prospects in the Arab Peninsula and African countries to controlling what the company describes as the world’s  largest graphite extractive project outside of China.   Here we describe the Balama project until 2024, the stoppage for nine months after December 2024 because of local protests and blockade, and the restart of the project (with strong police force intervention) after June 2025. The value of the shares went down, and then up again.  [4]  Over 700 families were protesting for lack of payment of indemnity for the land, and there were also labour issues that caused the blockade.  External support was given by so-called Namparamas.  [5]  The local revolt and blockade had international echo.  [6] Syrah is not the only multinational corporation extracting graphite from the impoverished and conflict-prone region of Cabo Delgado. Next to Syrah’s operations is the  Balama Central Graphite Project  , a mining concession that Battery Minerals recently sold to the UK-Indian multinational Tirupati Graphite together with another graphite site in Montepuez district, a few dozen kilometres east of Balama. [1]  Additionally, just about 10 kilometres north of Syrah’s mining site, another Australian company called Triton Minerals has a large-scale concession with  an estimated 5.7 million tons of graphite  for at least 25 years. Triton also controls the graphite extraction Grafex project in the Ancuabe district, where insurgent attacks  reportedly killed two security guards  in June 2022. Next to this is the GK Ancuabe Graphite Mine, a mining company ultimately controlled by the Dutch multinational AMG Advanced Metallurgical Group through a German subsidiary. GK Ancuabe was the first multinational to  start producing graphite in north Mozambique  , and did so with the financial support of a German development bank. All of these companies and mine operations show the heavy interests at play in controlling the graphite that lies under Mozambique’s soil. It is worth noting that  Chinese companies are also investing in the region . There is no replacement for lost livelihood options for most communities living around the extraction sites, as the mining industry rarely offers broad employment opportunities for local people. Likewise, there is no replacement for their cultures, as their lives are tightly intertwined with their lands and forests. The ‘local benefits’ the industry points to are often a reality for only a small number of business people and the few who gain employment. The Mozambique organization Justiça Ambiental JA!  has complained. Other international observers have noted the closing down of the mine in December 2024 because of the protests.  The company explained, “the disturbances at the Balama mine began in late September 2024 when a group of farmers with historical land resettlement grievances initiated protest actions.” Protests continued throughout the post-election period, and Syrah demobilized most of its operational staff, maintaining “only a full contract security presence at the site.”   The new Mozambican government was scheduled to be installed in January 2025. However, the protests could force a different outcome.  Since suspending operations in mid-2024, the Balama mine did not produce a single ton of graphite. In the first quarter of 2025, Syrah sold just 1,300 tons of the product, a much lower volume than in previous periods.  The company declared force majeure     [2] [3]  By 2025 it is recuperating levels of production. The company asserts that globally Balama will enable Syrah's participation for many years in the electric vehicle markets. Graphite is a component in lithium-ion batteries  serving as the primary material for the  anode  (negative electrode) , where it stores and releases lithium ions during charging and discharging.

outcome_text: This is an explanation of what happened in May 2025, to start production again. "Maputo (MOZTIMES) – TWIGG Exploration & Mining Limitada, a subsidiary of the Australian multinational Syrah Resources Limited, resumed operations at its graphite mine in Balama, Cabo Delgado province, on 5 May, after an eight-month blockade by local communities demanding fair compensation for the loss of land use rights. In a statement released this week, Syrah announced that the protests at the mine had ended and that access to the facilities had been restored. “Following a formal agreement being reached between farmers, Mozambique government authorities and the company”, the statement read. However, it added that “a small group of individuals continued to block access to the site for no legitimate reason nor claim against Syrah, over the weekend, Mozambique Government authonties cleared the remaining illegal protestors and restored site access for Balama operations”. Local sources told MOZTIMES that access was re-established through police force. “On 2 May, around 50 agents of the Rapid Intervention Unit (UIR) were deployed to disperse the protesters who, since September 2024, had been camping in the Nkwide area, near the mine,” a local source said, adding that “the police used gunfire and tear gas to disperse the demonstrators”. As a result of the operation, several farmers and members of the community defence militia Naparama were arrested, including the traditional leader of Balama, Mualia Issa, and Tobias António, a farmers' representative and former TWIGG employee. Since 2014, the local population has been demanding fair compensation for land expropriated in favour of mining activities. ...The use of force to reopen access to the mine may further damage relations between TWIGG and the local population, in a context already marked by allegations of labour abuses, unfair dismissals, and environmental impacts". (Noemia Mendes, MOZ Times, 9 May 2025).

case_name: Jordan Cove LNG and connector pipeline cancelled in Oregon, USA
headline: Canada’s Fossil Fuel company Pembina faces decade-long battle over Oregon’s largest proposed energy development.
location: Not specified clearly in live EJAtlas metadata.
description: Pembina, a Canadian fossil fuel company, is the parent company behind the proposed Jordan Cove Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) project [7] . The corporation’s plan involves constructing the Jordan Cove LNG terminal and the Pacific Connector Pipeline, which together would have formed the largest construction project in Oregon’s history [1] [2] [4] . The project aims to connect Coos Bay and Malin, exporting 7.8 million metric tons of LNG per year and liquefying roughly 1.04 billion cubic feet of natural gas per day [1] [2] [4] [15] . According to the Permitting Dashboard, an official U.S. government website, the terminal would include gas inlet facilities, a metering station, a gas conditioning plant, five liquefaction trains with supporting equipment, two full-containment LNG storage tanks, an LNG transfer line, ship-loading facilities, a marine slip and offloading area, a new access channel connecting the Coos Bay Navigation Channel to the marine slip, and upgrades to four bends of the existing Coos Bay Navigation Channel [2] [4] . Additionally, the terminal would have emergency and hazard systems, security control and support systems, administrative buildings, and temporary workforce housing [2] . Furthermore, the pipeline would be 230 miles (370 km) long and would have a 36-inch (91 cm) diameter between Malin and Coos County [4] . The aboveground components would include a new 61,500-horsepower Klamath Compressor Station near Malin, along with three meter stations, five pig launchers and receivers, seventeen mainline block valves, and a gas-control communication system [2] [4] . The proposed pipeline and terminal would affect more than 600 landowners, heighten wildfire risks, cut through 80 miles (129 km) of national forests and public lands, and cross 485 rivers, streams, and wetlands [5] [6] [9] . It would also significantly damage old-growth forests and further fragment already vulnerable wildlife habitats, especially those of steelhead and salmon [5] [7] . Moreover, the company would receive the authority to seize land from any American property owner, jeopardising Indigenous territories (approximately 10 sites), and Native Tribes also warn that the influx of construction “man camps” could threaten the safety of Indigenous women [6] [9] . It must also be highlighted that there was no free, prior, and informed consent from the Klamath, Yurok, Krauk, or Siletz Tribes, which violates the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples [5] . Although the project intended to export gas to Asia, many also questioned its economic feasibility, considering that industries were unlikely to abandon cheap local fuel for more costly, imported North American gas [9] . Firstly, as the federal government is responsible for LNG siting, in 2016 the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) denied the application for the proposed project, citing costs that outweighed public benefits [1] [10] [11] . However, during the second application submitted by lobbyist David Urban, the pro-fossil fuel administration in Washington D.C., granted approval in March 2020, stating that the project served the “public interest,” despite the gas being intended entirely for export [1] [9] [10] . In May 2020, FERC also issued a denial of rehearing for its approved decision [5] . The justification for the choice rested on two claims frequently stated also by President Donald Trump: 1) creating jobs within the country, and 2) countering the influence of China as an energy exporter [9] . Critics argue that this benchmark for permits diverges significantly from the intent of the Natural Gas Act of 1938 [9] . Section 7 of the Act further states that the use of eminent domain “only applies to pipelines that are carrying gas considered to be interstate commerce,” which does not apply in this case, as the project involved gas from Canada as well [10] . Furthermore, the political environment, including initiatives such as the US BUILD (Better Utilization of Investments Leading to Development) Act and the Asia EDGE (Enhancing Development and Growth through Energy) initiative, demonstrated a clear plan by the Trump administration to expand the energy infrastructure [9] .  Despite this reversal on the federal level, the project continued to face resistance from state-level regulatory barriers [3] . For instance, the Oregon Department of Environmental Quality, Department of State Lands and Department of Land Conservation and Development have the authority to deny further approvals, permits and certifications [6] . Furthermore, even with Pembina’s request in February 2021, FERC did not override the permit denials [5] .  At the local level, opposition to the project came from tribal members, fishermen, residents, artists, and environmental advocates between 2016 and 2021 [7] . Tools of environmental advocacy ranged from environmental art installations, which illustrated the scale and impact of the project, to submitting letters to regulatory agencies such as FERC to challenge approvals [1] [7] . Advocates also formed support networks and nonprofits, such as Greater Good Oregon, to pool resources and fund legal representation for those unable to afford attorneys, ensuring broader participation in the fight [7] . The Klamath Tribal Council has issued letters, while the Krauk Tribe of California has formed protests at the Klamath Falls [15] . These efforts were long-term continued, gathering approximately 200-400 peoples at subsequent protests [15] . A group of landowners, represented by the Niskanen Center, also took FERC to the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals over the company seizing citizens’ land for profit [8] [10] . They argued that FERC failed to consider information showing that the proposal was not in the public interest (eventually the case did not go to Court due to the cancellation in 2021) [11] . Moreover, Oregon Senators Ron Wyden and Jeff Merkley introduced two bills to protect landowners from exploitation for pipelines by barring the use of gas exports as justification for eminent domain (as of 2025 there is no progress, the bills remain as “introduced”) [10] [13]   [14] . However, Pembina mounted heavy opposition. Locals reported that FERC “tolling orders” were used to block landowners from accessing the courts, allowing construction to begin before appeals were resolved [9] . This tactic was used 74 times in 12 years, enabling construction in 64% of cases [9] . Furthermore, the company employed aggressive political strategies, including donating to state legislators and PACs, paying Coos County $25,000 per month, funding local grants, sending promotional mailers, and even financing sheriff’s deputies who surveilled activists [9] . Finally, in December 2021 the owner of Pembina Pipeline withdrew the FERC application and halted the project development due to the inability to secure required permits [1] [2] [5] . Because these crucial permits were denied at the state level, the project could not meet federal requirements, leading the company in May 2021 to file a letter seeking to pause the project [5] . Key cancelled or denied permits included: Department of the Interior: Right-of-Way Authorization (DOI-BLM); Endangered Species Act Consultation (DOI-FWS)) Department of the Army: Section 408 Permit; Section 10 Rivers and Harbors Act of 1899 and Section 404 Clean Water Act, and Department of Commerce: Endangered Species Act Consultation (NOAA-NMFS); Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act, Section 305 Essential Fish Habitat (EFH) Consultation) [4] . Manly these instances were due to violations of state and local land use protections, with Pembina failing to justify changes to these protections [16] [17] . In addition, the company did not properly request water quality certification, and the project posed unacceptable environmental, public health and climate risks [18] .   Furthermore, between 2019 and 2020, the project faced delays and extensions from: the Department of Energy (Natural Gas Export Authorization),  the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity for Interstate Natural Gas Pipelines; Authorization for Liquefied Natural Gas Terminal Facilities, Onshore or in State Waters; Environmental Impact Statement (EIS)), and the Department of Commerce (Marine Mammal Protection Act (MMPA) Incidental Take Authorization (DOC – NOAA/NMFS)) [4] . Yet, as of 2025 OA Partners filed a petition with the D.C. Court of Appeals to revive the terminal project and waive permit requirements due to Donald Trump’s executive order to “unleash American energy” and “speed up permitting for LNG export projects” [2] . The applicant claims that permit denials have violated federal supremacy, unreasonably delayed a federally approved project, and opposed LNG exports which would have supported national economic and security interests [12] .

case_name: San Carlos Power Station, The Philippines
headline: The San Carlos Power Station, first proposed by San Miguel Corporation as a coal plant in 2018, and later as an LNG power station in 2022 was cancelled after opposition from local youth and religious leaders
description: San Miguel Corporation (SMC) initially proposed a 300MW coal fired power plant in San Carlos City, Negros Occidental, Philippines in 2018 . SMC’s application for a Grid Impact Study was approved by the DOE in August of that year [1] . Th is proposal for a coal-burning facility met with immediate local resistance, with Negros Occidental governor Alfredo Marañon Jr issuing an executive order and calling for an ordinance declaring Negros Occidental a ‘coal-free’ and environmentally friendly province. Although Negros is the largest solar electricity producer in the country, producing more solar than the island's total electricity demand, most Negrosanons are being sold expensive coal or diesel power produced on neighboring islands. The island lacks grid infrastructure to efficiently distribute solar oversupply. [9] In March of 2019, at least 7,000 people formed a ‘human chain’ that stretched 229 kilometers from the communities of Manapla to La Libertad in opposition to SMC’s coal plant. Most of the participants were youth or members of the Diocese of San Carlos. [3] Amidst global student strikes demanding climate action from governments worldwide, student organizations in Negros such as Youth for Climate Hope (Y4CH) led student mobilizations against coal development in Negros. [8] Proposal for LNG plant (2022) In 2020, the Department of Energy (DOE) announced a moratorium on new coal fired plants, [4] and by 2022, SMC had altered plans for the San Carlos Station to a proposal for an LNG plant along with a shipping terminal and regasification facility to receive fuel for the generating station [5] . SMC subsidiary Reliance Energy Development Inc (REDI) carried out an Environmental Impact Statement for the proposed San Carlos LNG power station in 2022 and the project was expected to be complete in early 2024 . REDI said the plant would address the country's need for reliable and affordable power while using a cleaner source of energy than coal [5] . The new proposal for an LNG plant also met immediate local resistance from youth and religious leaders, and by November 2022, the company had canceled the project. Resistance to the project was spearheaded by Bishop Gerardo Alminaza of the Diocese of San Carlos and climate organizations including Youth for Climate Hope and REpower Negros [6] . Other groups voicing objection to the project included fisherfolk, mangrove conservationists, barangay kagawad and health workers, and teachers [7] . REDI did not provide official statements to state or local governments explaining their cancellation of the project. The Environmental Management Bureau informed the Center for Energy Ecology and Development (CEED) that REDI had not pursued an environmental compliance certificate for the project. The governor speculated that the cancelation was a business decision. [10] [11] Opponents of the plant argued to maintain Negros as a renewable energy hub, especially given the island's vulnerability to climate change. They also expressed concern that LNG sourced from unidentified 'far-off suppliers' might be expensive and wouldn't benefit Negrosanons. The proposed power station was near the Tanon Strait, which is rich in biodiversity, and opponents also expressed concern about exposing the Strait to shipping traffic and pollution. Participants in the struggle against the San Carlos Station saw themselves as inheritors of a legacy of successful struggle against fossil power on the island. case_name: Coal power plant to be built by Jiuquan Iron & Steel for alumina production at Nain, St Elizabeth , Jamaica
headline: In February 2017 it seemed that the Chinese company Jiuquan Iron & Steel would build a 1000 MW coal power plant at the Alpart bauxite-alumina factory. Opposition arose. Bauxite mining might also become contentious.
province: Not specified clearly in live EJAtlas metadata.
description: This is a conflict on a coal fired power plant, and at the same time could become a conflicts on bauxite mining. In July 2016 it was reported (4) that "Russian mining company signed a deal for the US$300-million sale of its 1.6-million-tonne Alpart alumina refinery in Jamaica to China’s Jinquan Iron and Steel Company (JISCO). In a separate pact with the Jamaican Government, JISCO agreed to the rehabilitation and expansion of the plant and its conversion to 500,000-tonne-a-year aluminium smelter. The inking of the agreements happened in Beijing, where Jamaica’s mining minister, Mike Henry, and his energy colleague Andrew Wheatley have been having talks with Rusal, JISCO, as well as the Development Bank of China. The bank, according to Gleaner Business sources, has signalled a willingness to commit, over the next several years, up to US$2 billion to the project. An abundance of cheap energy is a critical ingredient in aluminium smelting, and its absence in Jamaica has been a barrier to the country’s ambition to convert its bauxite through all the stages to the production of the metal. After 2008, Alpart refinery was mothballed for seven years in face of a soft market for alumina " (4). Opposition arose to the proposed coal fired power plant. The 1,000-MW coal-fired plant to be built by the Chinese company Jiuquan Iron & Steel at Nain, St Elizabeth would be linked to the upgrading of bauxite-aluminium manufacturing. Environmentalists said "No to Coal-Fired Power Plant in Jamaica". (1). More than 21,000 people signed a petition opposing coal-fired power in Jamaica. The #SayNOtoCoalJA initiative, being led by theJamaica Environment Trust (JET), is calling on the Government of Jamaica not to turn to coal as a fuel source for industrial development here. In July 2016, the Jamaican Government announced the sale of the old Alpart bauxite plant at Nain in St. Elizabeth to Jiuquan Iron & Steel Company Limited (JISCO) of China, as well as a 2 billion dollar investment in an industrial zone, powered by a 1000 megawatt (MW) coal-fired plant, creating 3,000 jobs. JET wants the government instead to continue the transition to a new energy future for Jamaica, as outlined in many government documents which emphasise energy conservation, renewables and liquefied natural gas (LNG) as a transitional fuel for the Jamaica, a nation of 2.7 million people. “Coal-fired plants have several negative impacts on public health and the environment,” said JET’s Chief Executive Officer (CEO) Diana McCaulay. “Coal plant emissions cause respiratory illness in humans, and affect the environment by creating acid rain and contributing to global climate change.” “Coal, in fact, is the dirtiest of the fossil fuels,” said McCaulay. “It emits greater quantities of carbon dioxide than other fossil fuels.” Carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions represent the largest share of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, which are blamed for climate change. A modern coal-fired plant emits 762 kilograms of CO2 per megawatt-hour of electricity generated, if there is no CO2 capture. The 1000 MW plant alone would emit roughly 6.7 million tonnes of CO2 per year, just over half of Jamaica’s 2025 target under the 2015 Paris Agreement on Climate Change. Jamaica was among 150 nations to sign the Paris Agreement, which signalled the commitment of the international community to combat climate change. “The building of the proposed coal-fired plant would be in direct contradiction to that agreement,” said McCaulay. Coal-fired power plants also typically emit a host of other pollutants besides carbon dioxide. The possible mercury, lead, arsenic, sulphur dioxide, dust and soot emissions associated with a coal-fired power plant also have significant impacts on public and environmental health. According to the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), 59 percent of all sulphur dioxide and 18 percent of all oxides from nitrogen emissions come from coal-fired power plants. Another environmentalist, Wayne Chen, described the proposed plant as “short-sighted”, adding that it poses danger to residents in the vicinity of the plant. “While there will be immediate gains for the owners, in particular, and for the country, the extent to which is still not clear, the losses in the long run will cancel these gains,” he explained. “Contrary to popular belief, Jamaica’s greenhouse gas emissions are not insignificant. In 2011, our emissions, based on World Bank data, compared with those of Uruguay in South America and Georgia in Europe. With an additional 1,000 MW coal plant, our GHG emissions will more than double...". , e For his part, Jamaican Energy Minister Andrew Wheatley dismissed the disquiet over reports of the coal plant as much ado about nothing. "Where we are right now, we have not received any application, any proposal, as it relates to a coal-fired plant at Alpart,” Wheatley told IDN. (1). Meanwhile, it was asserted (2) that "Coal is the only feasible option for a 1000-megawatt power plant being contemplated for the new owners of bauxite alumina company, Alpart. So said former Chairman of the Jamaica Bauxite Institute and Co-Chair of the Energy Monitoring Committee, Dr. Carlton Davis. The Chinese-owned Jiquan Iron and Steel, JISCO, was finalizing arrangements to take over Alpart, as part of a planned USD$2-billion investment in Jamaica. There’s been opposition to JISCO’s intention to build a 1000-megawatt coal-fired plant to run its operations. But Dr. Davis says coal is the only feasible option." (2) . At the end, by November 2017, it was said that "It'a LNG and not coal for Alpart plant". (5)

case_name: Floating Storage and Regasification Unit in the port of Piombino, Italy
headline: Amid soaring gas prices and Russia-related tensions, Italy placed a Floating Storage and Regasification Unit (FSRU) in Piombino to boost LNG imports. The project sparked protests over environmental risks, limited local benefits, and fossil-fuel dependence, mobilising unions, citizens, and environmental groups, reflecting decades of industrial decline and social frustration.
description: Normal 0 false false false EN-GB X-NONE AR-SA /* Style Definitions */ table.MsoNormalTable {mso-style-name:"Table Normal"; mso-tstyle-rowband-size:0; mso-tstyle-colband-size:0; mso-style-noshow:yes; mso-style-priority:99; mso-style-parent:""; mso-padding-alt:0cm 5.4pt 0cm 5.4pt; mso-para-margin-top:0cm; mso-para-margin-right:0cm; mso-para-margin-bottom:8.0pt; mso-para-margin-left:0cm; line-height:115%; mso-pagination:widow-orphan; font-size:12.0pt; font-family:"Aptos",sans-serif; mso-ascii-font-family:Aptos; mso-ascii-theme-font:minor-latin; mso-hansi-font-family:Aptos; mso-hansi-theme-font:minor-latin; mso-font-kerning:1.0pt; mso-ligatures:standardcontextual; mso-fareast-language:EN-US;} In the context of heightened natural gas prices and geopolitical tensions with the Russian Federation that characterised 2022 and 2023, the Italian government chose the port of Piombino as the docking place for a new FSRU (Floating Storage and Regasification Unit). An FSRU is a maritime vessel designed to receive, store, and convert liquefied natural gas (LNG) back into its gaseous state for distribution into the onshore gas grid. According to its proponents, importing LNG and injecting it into the national gas grid via FSRUs moored in Italian ports would increase supply and reduce reliance on pipeline-delivered gas from Russia. However, critics argued that the project threatened local ecosystems, offered limited economic benefits, and reinforced dependence on fossil fuels. This led to widespread protests, including street demonstrations, public assemblies, appeals to administrative courts, and campaigns organised by trade unions, local associations, and environmental groups, highlighting the population’s frustration with both the FSRU and decades of industrial decline. The first confirmation that Piombino had been chosen to host an FSRU came on 6 April 2022, when Roberto Cingolani, then the Minister for Ecological Transition, announced to the Chamber of Deputies' Foreign Affairs Committee that the port would accommodate a regasification plant for a period of one or two years. [1]  According to SNAM, the part state-owned company to which the government had already entrusted the management of new FSRUs, Piombino was chosen because of its central location on the Italian peninsula, its proximity to the National Gas Transportation Network, and the suitability of its existing port quay for docking an FSRU. [2] Piombino is a medium-sized coastal city in southern Tuscany whose economy has long depended on large state-owned steelworks that shaped both employment and urban life. From the 1980s onwards, privatisation and successive industrial crises triggered a gradual deindustrialisation. Following privatisation in the 1990s, decades of industrial decline, failed investments, and recurring promises of regeneration left the area marked by unemployment, pollution, and social fatigue. Repeated unfulfilled plans for redevelopment fostered a deep mistrust toward institutions and a shared sense of economic stagnation. [3] [4] The government's plan was met with immediate suspicion by local authorities and businesses, due to the lack of consultation and the evident fact that the FSRU would occupy a large part of the port. [3]  In this sense, the government’s attempt to deal with this matter as quickly as possible was the initial cause of friction between the Ministry and local communities. In an effort to reduce opposition, the Minister organised several meetings with local and regional authorities, [5]  promising that as a compensation Piombino would soon benefit from plans to revitalise its industrial sector, [6]  and later appointing Eugenio Giani, the President of Tuscany, as Special Commissioner for the FSRU project. [7] Despite government assurances, opposition to the project intensified as details emerged. Local administrations and associations raised environmental and economic objections: the daily discharge of around 50 kilograms of chlorine into the sea threatened marine ecosystems;  the construction of an 8-km pipeline risked disrupting the landscape and port activities;  and local fishermen feared damage to fish and mussel farms. [8]  Additionally, Greenpeace and WWF warned that the terminal’s location in a marine sanctuary endangered protected cetacean habitats. [9]  The government’s decision to bypass standard environmental assessments, citing urgency, further eroded public trust. [10] At the same time, the Federation of Basic Unions (USB) condemned the project for diverting space and investment from sustainable redevelopment of the historical steel and tourism sectors, industries capable of creating far more employment than an FSRU requiring only about twenty specialised workers and creating no prospect of long-term local development. [11]  Similar concerns were cited by local businesspeople and industrialists, as well as by all local sections of national parties across the political divide. [1]  This unusually broad mobilisation reflected not merely environmental and economic concerns related to the FSRU, but a wider frustration rooted in chronic unemployment, industrial decline, pollution, and decades of political disillusionment. [3] Beyond the local level, national and international environmental groups challenged the project on systemic grounds. Legambiente, Greenpeace, and WWF criticised it as part of a broader expansion of fossil-fuel infrastructure that prolongs dependence on methane, a major greenhouse gas subject to significant leakage throughout its supply chain. They argued that this policy perpetuates extractivist and neo-imperialist dynamics, linking Italy’s energy security to environmentally and politically destabilising practices in the Global South. [9] [12] Despite the early concerns and widespread opposition, in June 2022 SNAM acquired Italis LNG , a 293-metre vessel capable of storing 170,000 cubic metres of liquefied natural gas and regasifying up to five billion cubic metres annually. [2]  Preparatory works in the port continued throughout 2022, and on 19 March 2023 the vessel was moored at the eastern quay of the northern dock. [13] During this preparatory phase, opposition in Piombino unfolded on multiple fronts. At the grassroots level, public assemblies and street demonstrations were organised by citizens’ committees, local branches of all major parties, trade unions (with USB even calling for a general strike [14] ), and national environmental organisations.  [3] [13] [15] [16] [17] [18] [19] [20] [21] [22]   The mobilisation extended beyond the local context: activists from Ravenna joined in, connecting the two movements opposing FSRU projects launched under the same national LNG expansion plan. [22] [23] [24]  At the institutional level, municipal authorities submitted dozens of critical observations to the authorising committee [25]  and filed appeals before administrative courts. [26]  In response to the mobilisation, the government’s only concession was to formalise the FSRU’s three-year operation. [8]  Meanwhile, no progress was made on the promised compensations outlined by the President of Tuscany, which included long-delayed projects such as road access, environmental remediation, and plans for the FSRU’s eventual relocation. [27] In all other respects, the government and regional authorities remained firm: the observations were disregarded, [28] and the administrative court dismissed all appeals. [29]  After technical adjustments and testing, operations officially began in July 2023. [13] Opposition to the FSRU in Piombino eased after its launch, becoming one of many grievances linked to local deindustrialisation. Tensions resurfaced in 2025 as the three-year operational period neared its end. SNAM’s CEO and the President of Liguria announced plans to move the Italis FSRU offshore near Savona, Liguria for 17 years. [30] [31]  Local organisations in Liguria opposed the move, echoing Piombino’s earlier concerns, prompting the regional council to vote against the transfer. [32] In March 2025, ARERA, the national energy regulator, argued that relocating the regasification plant installed two years earlier would be too costly and recommended it remain in Piombino, contrary to government agreements from 2023. [33] [34]  The local section of Confindustria, the main organisation representing business interests, also shifted position, endorsing the FSRU’s stay as potentially beneficial for port development. [35] So  far, opposition to the departure has been limited, mainly a signature-collection campaign, far less mobilised than the initial protests.

case_name: Wind power electrification of the Muolkkut (Melkøya) LNG plant, Sapmi (Norway)
headline: The Norwegian government plans to transform the power supply of the Melkøya LNG plant. It faces opposition from the Sámi Parliament, which considers a lawsuit because the wind power plants and infrastructures on land will have socio-cultural and environmental consequences for ancestral reindeer herding practices.
description: The island of Muolkkut (Melkøya) is the Sámi homeland and was previously used for fishing and reindeer herding on the mainland surroundings. However, in 2007 a liquified natural gas (LNG) refinery has been developed on the island and consequently completely changed the island of Muolkkut. The refinery processes natural gas produced from the Snøhvit offshore field in the Barents Sea which is transported through an almost 200 km long pipeline and operated by Equinor company  [2] [1]   [6] . On top of this, now in 2023, the Norwegian government put a new "green" project plan forward to decarbonize power supply to the LNG plant, including several hundred kilometres of power lines from land along with wind power industrial complex (see also Kokelv Wind Farm in project description)  [3]  . “We want development and growth in all of the country,” "it will be the single biggest climate measure ever taken by a Norwegian government" , the Prime Minister of Norway, Jonas Gahr Støre, stated.  Although the project has been approved, this decision raises significant concerns due to the extensive wind power development it involves   [4]   [7] .  The Sámi people and the Sámi Parliament have emphasized the project's extensive size and the inadequate consultations concerning its significant impact, especially on ancestral lands and reindeer herding. Due to these concerns, they feel that pursuing a lawsuit must be considered  [1] [4] . In September 2023, the Sami Parliament addressed the government's decision regarding Melkøya. The Parliament agreed that the decision on the electrification of Melkøya needed to be withdrawn. A member of the Sámi Council stated, "No one is taking responsibility for the numerous interventions and the serious consequences of the government's decision. The cultural practices, businesses, and use of nature by the Sámi people are not being considered in the current situation." Therefore, the president of the Sami Parliament announced that they would pursue legal action, further contributing to the discussion about the problematic project  [4]   [5] . In May 2024, 75 Members of the Norwegian Parliament urged the government to find an alternative to electrification, as it is strongly opposed by many residents of Northern Norway and the Sami people. In contrast, 94 members did not support this alternative. A proposal to halt the ongoing construction of the electrification infrastructure received a much closer vote, with 85 members voting against it and 84 in favor. As a result, work on electrifying Equinor’s Melkøya facility off Hammerfest will continue [9] under the excuse of cutting emissions from the industry at local peoples' socio-environmental and cultural costs [6]   [8]  .

case_name: Port Qasim, LNG Terminal Expansion, Pakistan
headline: The activities at Port Qasim have caused pollution along the surrounding coastal area, impacting the local community of Rehri Goth and leading to environmental and social imbalance. Fisherfolk can no longer fish due to the polluted waters and restricted access to the ocean. Despite this, the Qasim Port Authority has proposed further expansion with additional LNG terminals.
province: Not specified clearly in live EJAtlas metadata.
location: Not specified clearly in live EJAtlas metadata.
description: Located in Karachi’s Phitti Creek in the Indus Delta, the port began operations in 1980, initially handling the import of raw materials for Pakistan Steel Mills. It is considered one of the largest contributors to Pakistan’s national economy, accounting for 51% of sea trade. The port handles a wide range of commodities such as mineral and edible oils, coal, wheat, and rice as general cargo. It also hosts the only LNG terminal in the country. Additionally, the port contains the largest industrial zone in Pakistan, with more than 400 industrial and commercial units in operation [1] . According to the Port Qasim Authority [1] , the port has potential for expansion with two new LNG terminals and multifunction berths. One proposed project is the Energas LNG Terminal, also known as Energas FSRU [2] . The project is owned by Qasim Terminal Holding Co. (49%), along with Lucky Group, Sapphire Group, and Halmore Power [2] . Another proposed LNG terminal project is the Tabeer LNG Terminal, whose parent company is Bison Energy, formerly Mitsubishi Corporation [3] .   Lucky Electric Power, one of the shareholders of Port Qasim and operator of a coal-fired power plant at the port, claims a commitment to planting 200,000 mangrove trees annually over the next ten years. This initiative is part of their stated CSR efforts aimed at improving the living conditions of local communities by revitalising mangrove forests within the Indus Delta. The initiative is said to support biodiversity, enhance coastal resilience against flooding and rising sea levels, and protect fishing villages. The company claims the project "safeguards lives and strengthens bonds" with neighbouring communities [4] .  However, local residents and the ecosystem of the area have already been affected by port activities. Locals, have been complaining that the government is expanding the problems instead of solving the existing ones by constructing additional LNG terminals just a few kilometres from the village of Rehri Goth. Current port operations are already polluting the coastline due to the presence of massive industrial and commercial facilities within a 5 km radius of the village.  The existing LNG terminal and the coal-fired power plant operated by Lucky Power are among the sources of pollution, which the company claims to offset by planting mangrove trees. Furthermore, the constant movement of ships in the area has restricted fishermen’s access to the sea and worsened pollution. A local fisherman, whose family has practised fishing for generations, noted that his catch has dropped significantly, from 30 to 40 kg per trip to just 5 to 10 kg. The reduced catch is not the only issue; fishermen now have to travel further into the ocean to find fish. The construction of another terminal is expected to make the situation even worse for locals who rely on fishing as their primary source of income [5] .   In 2022, the Alliance for Climate Justice and Clean Energy (ACJCE), a coalition of five non-governmental organisations and research institutes, wrote a detailed letter to Mitsubishi questioning the environmental and social impacts of the proposed LNG terminal. The letter urged the corporation to address the negative consequences of the terminal’s construction.  The letter was endorsed by 30 civil society organisations, research institutions, and individuals from various fields. It also highlighted that the terminal would be built at the confluence of the Chhan Wado and Chara creeks, which are home to extensive mangrove forests. These forests not only provide a safe breeding ground for fish but also play a vital role in the growth and protection of seaweed and coral reefs [5] .  ACJCE further pointed out that Tabber Energy, a subsidiary of Mitsubishi, misled the government in its report by stating that the nearest human population was 10 km from the terminal site, whereas in reality, it is only 5 km away  [5] . The report, conducted by Indus Consortium, also failed to include any input from the local communities, people who have lived in the fishing villages for over 400 years [3] .   Moreover, a public forum was organised by the Pakistan Fisherfolk Forum and attended by a large number of women fisherfolk, civil society representatives, and community leaders to urge the Asian Development Bank to halt funding for fossil fuel projects in Pakistan.  Participants also rejected the further expansion of LNG and fossil fuel dependency, instead advocating for energy independence through investments in solar and wind power, particularly for marginalised communities that lack access to the national grid [6] [7] .   In 2024, the Tabeer LNG terminal project was cancelled [3] , while the Energas FSRU project appears to still be ongoing [2] .

case_name: Aqaba Port and Arab Gas Pipeline, Jordan
headline: Jordan signed a 15-year gas deal with Israel worth over 10 billion US dollars. Jordanians demanded the deal be stopped even before it was signed, but the government dismissed their demands and instead arrested activists for raising their voices, claiming that this is a deal between companies rather than politics.
province: Not specified clearly in live EJAtlas metadata.
description: Jordan has its only port and coastline in Aqaba town, sharing a border with occupied Palestine (Israel), Egypt, and Saudi Arabia. This geographical position has allowed the country to participate in international trade [1] . The Arab Gas Pipeline, which is a natural gas pipeline operating through different Arab countries (Egypt, Jordan, Syria, and Lebanon), began operating in 2003 [2] . In Jordan, this pipeline runs in three sections, two of which pass through the Aqaba region. The first section extends from Arish in Egypt to Aqaba, with a total length of 265 km, including 15 km offshore running under the Gulf of Aqaba. The second section runs from Aqaba to El Rehab, covering a distance of 390 km and located around 30 km from the Jordan–Syria border [3] .   In 2016, Jordan signed a deal with Israel to import gas that would cover over 40% of Jordan’s energy consumption for 15 years. The deal was signed under US pressure, with an estimated cost of around 10 billion US dollars, and the majority of the profit goes to Israel [4] [5] . The gas deal was signed between Jordan’s state-owned National Electric Power Company (NEPCO) and the Leviathan field partners, which include Texas-based Noble Energy, Israel’s Delek Group, and Ratio Petroleum [8] . The gas is exported from the Tamar and Leviathan fields in Israel, not only to Jordan through the Arab Gas Pipeline but also via a connecting pipeline from northern Israel [6] . In 2022, Israel’s energy ministry approved the start of gas flow to Egypt through Jordan using the Aqaba route, which will then transmit it to Egypt [7] .    Furthermore, the Aqaba Development Corporation signed an agreement to expand the Aqaba LNG terminal, known as the Shaikh Sabah Al Ahmed Al Sabah LNG Terminal. This development will enable the conversion of compressed natural gas from the  Arab Gas Pipeline  into  liquefied natural gas , which can then be shipped overseas  [17] . While it has not been explicitly stated,  considering the long-standing and close Jordanian-Israeli gas relations,  the expansion of the LNG terminal in Aqaba is likely to benefit  Israel with  additional LNG export capacity with direct access to the Persian Gulf.   The opposition to the agreement stems from widespread public resistance to normalising ties with Israel, particularly after the 1994 treaty between Jordan and Israel. Many Jordanians view Israel as a settler-colonial entity and an enabler of state violence, which is why the National Campaign deliberately avoids mentioning “Israel” by name. Beyond political objections, critics are also alarmed by the strategic importance of natural gas, which grants the supplying country significant influence. Additionally, they are frustrated that the deal denies economically struggling Jordan billions of dollars that could instead be invested in developing its own energy resources, such as domestic natural gas, shale oil, and solar power, or in strengthening the national economy and creating employment opportunities for thousands of jobless citizens  [4] [8] . Jordan’s parliament approved a draft law to prohibit the import of Israeli gas just days after the gas agreement, which has faced widespread public opposition. All 130 members of parliament voted in favour of the motion. However, the government has claimed that the deal was a commercial agreement between companies rather than a political issue  [10] . Additionally, t housands of Jordanians raised their voices to stop the gas deal with Israel, with protests, petition signings, and meetings with various associations also forming part of the mobilisation [9] . In 2019, the Arba Group for the Protection of Nature, for example, prepared a petition that was submitted to the Prime Minister during a parliamentary session. It was signed by thousands of Jordanians, amplifying their opposition to the import of gas from Israel [9] .  Activists were also arrested for their participation in protests calling for the cancellation of the gas deal shortly after it was signed. However, protests had already been taking place since 2014, two years before the agreement was finalised. Hisham Bustani, the director of the Jordanian National Campaign against the gas agreement with Israel and the 'Enemy’s Gas Is Occupation' campaign, stated:  'It seems that the government is fed up with the peaceful protests held by the campaign and the civilised way of expressing our rejection.'  [12] The resistance to the gas deal was not limited to Jordanians; international mobilisation groups also demanded the deal be stopped, arguing that it would undermine collective efforts to isolate Israel and sustain its occupation and apartheid in Palestinian territory. Protests against the deal were held in the US, with demonstrators in Colorado gathering in front of the headquarters of Noble Energy in Denver; in the UK, in front of the Jordanian Embassy in London; and in South Africa, where protesters called on the Jordanian government to cancel the deal  [13] .   Regardless of all the opposition, the deal was eventually signed, and the Israeli Ministry of Energy and Mining reported that Israel’s natural gas exports to Egypt and Jordan increased by 13.4% in 2024  [11] . This confirms that, despite citizens’ efforts, there appears to be no long-term shift away from the normalisation of relations with Israel, despite it being a colonial state committing genocide. The relationship with Israel and the import of gas to Jordan through Aqaba was not the only concern, local communities and even marine life have been directly affected by the operations of the Aqaba port. Pollution caused by these operations has impacted local fishermen, with fewer than half of them receiving compensation. Since the fishermen in the area rely on fishing as their main source of income, pollution, oil spills, and waste discharged from the port have harmed both fishing activity and the overall ecosystem of the Aqaba marine environment, which is known to host unique fish species.  When fishermen raised their concerns about these issues, they were told to fish in international waters, such as off the coast of Yemen, an unreasonable suggestion considering the long travel time and the limited resources available to them for such a journey, which could take weeks  [14] [15] [16] .

case_name: The Kakhovka Dam Destruction, Ukraine
headline: On 6 June 2023, occupying Russian forces destroyed Ukraine’s Kakhovka Dam, unleashing mass flooding, widespread contamination, and long-term damage to water, energy, and agricultural systems. The attack marked a deliberate act of environmental warfare, exposing the imperial roots and military weaponization of Soviet-built infrastructure.
description: On 6 June 2023, occupying Russian forces detonated the engine room of the Kakhovka Hydropower Plant in Ukraine’s Kherson Oblast. Satellite data, seismic recordings, and open-source intelligence confirm that the dam—under uninterrupted Russian military control since February 2022—was destroyed using internal explosives placed by retreating units. This intentional act drained the 240 km-long reservoir, flooded over 600 km², displaced thousands, and collapsed critical infrastructure across water, energy, and agricultural systems. It marked a deliberate case of environmental warfare: an ecocidal strategy executed in occupied territory with precision and intent [1] . Built in 1955 as a keystone of Soviet hydro-industrial ambition, the Kakhovka Dam was a geopolitical instrument as much as a technological one. Intended to assert Soviet supremacy in engineering, impress Cold War allies, and discipline unruly nature, it was a signature piece of Stalinist-Khrushchevite infrastructure. The reservoir submerged the Velykyi Luh floodplain—an ecologically rich and culturally significant landscape—while displacing over 90 villages. Its design formalized the violent redirection of the Dnipro River to serve metallurgical expansion, industrial monoculture, and centralized control. Ukraine’s position was that of a subordinated territory: extracted from, flooded over, re-engineered without consent. That the dam’s destruction was foreseen by its own Soviet designers—as a potential tactical move in wartime—only reinforces how destruction was built into its imperial logic [2] [1] . The 2023 detonation was not merely sabotage, but a reiteration of extractive territorial violence. The immediate effects were severe and multidimensional. Floodwaters inundated both Ukrainian- and Russian-occupied banks of the Dnipro, mobilizing industrial pollutants, pesticides, petrochemicals, and decomposing organic matter from storage sites, flooded infrastructure, and submerged ecosystems [3] . Toxicological analyses in mid-2023 detected hazardous concentrations of cadmium, arsenic, lead, and petroleum hydrocarbons in water and sediment samples, exceeding EU safety thresholds [4] . Over 10,000 hectares of agricultural land were rendered temporarily non-arable due to contamination, waterlogging, and erosion-induced topsoil loss [1] . The collapse of the reservoir system left an estimated 700,000 people without reliable drinking water, as centralized pumping stations failed and groundwater resources were disrupted or contaminated [5] . Ecological collapse was spatially differentiated. Downstream, the sudden flood devastated over 40 protected areas, caused massive fish mortality, disrupted amphibian breeding, and obliterated wetland ecotones along the Dnipro-Bug estuary  [6] .  Upstream, over 80% of the former reservoir bed was initially predicted to undergo desertification. Yet by early 2024, multi-agency field studies documented widespread spontaneous revegetation—riparian willows, sedges, reeds, and floodplain shrubs—emerging even in previously barren sections. These dynamics suggest a provisional trajectory of biotic recovery, though one acutely vulnerable to anthropogenic disturbance, especially hydropower redevelopment and militarized land use  [7] . In occupied areas like Oleshky, Russian forces blocked evacuations. Ukrainian residents lacking Russian passports were denied exit; volunteers attempting rescues were shot at or shelled; boats were confiscated [8] [9] . Informal rescue networks formed via Telegram, mapping stranded civilians and navigating crossfire to save lives [10] . Days later, bodies surfaced in once-flooded streets. Many more likely drowned in locked-down settlements, their deaths uncounted and unacknowledged. Beyond the local catastrophe, systemic shocks reverberated. Kakhovka had supplied irrigation to five oblasts and cooling water to the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant. Its destruction slashed 334.8 MW of hydropower capacity [1] , undermining both national energy security and regional agricultural viability. But these losses were not isolated—they exposed the lasting vulnerability of Ukraine’s infrastructural dependence on centralized hydro-industrial systems inherited from the Soviet model, designed for control rather than resilience. Civil society responses emerged rapidly and unevenly in the face of institutional vacuum.  On 6 June, Razom We Stand, led by climate advocate Svitlana Romanko, condemned the dam’s destruction as an ecological war crime and linked it to Russia’s fossil-fuel militarism. They demanded a total embargo on Russian oil, gas, and LNG as a matter of environmental justice [11] .  Simultaneously, Let’s Do It Ukraine, a youth-led environmental movement with prior experience in civic cleanup and disaster response, deployed volunteer researchers—often without state coordination or protection—to collect sediment and water samples, revealing toxin levels far above safety norms   [12] . UAnimals, an animal rescue group, conducted decentralized evacuations of pets and wild animals under shelling, filling the gap left by absent official relief structures [13] . Legal mobilization followed. Ukraine’s Prosecutor General opened a criminal case under Article 441 (“ecocide”)—a precedent-setting wartime application aiming to anchor environmental devastation in international criminal law [14] . The Submerged report by Truth Hounds and Project Expedite Justice provided a forensic and legal analysis of the dam’s destruction, framing it as a potential violation of Article 8(2)(b)(iv) of the Rome Statute based on disproportionate environmental harm [1] . Climate Counsel, in coordination with the Prosecutor General’s office, developed a prosecutorial guide to identify and frame environmental war crimes, marking the first operational toolkit of its kind [15] . The case also became the basis of a mock trial organized by the Environmental Justice Project, advancing it as a legal test case and calling for ICC engagement and reform of war crimes thresholds [16] . Meanwhile, in February 2024, the European Parliament adopted a revised Environmental Crime Directive that criminalizes large-scale environmental destruction “comparable to ecocide”—a move shaped by mounting international pressure, though without explicit reference to Kakhovka [17] . By July 2023, contestation over reconstruction emerged. On 18 July, Ukraine’s Cabinet of Ministers announced plans to rapidly rebuild the dam—without environmental impact assessment or public consultation—echoing technocratic, extractivist logics [18] . The Kakhovka Platform, a coalition of over 40 civil society and environmental groups, issued a sharp rebuttal, rejecting the revival of Soviet-style hydrological authoritarianism and proposing democratic, ecologically attuned alternatives. These included restoring the Velykyi Luh floodplain, relocating water intakes, and replacing centralised energy infrastructure with distributed solar and wind systems. Recovery, they argued, must dismantle Soviet spatial inheritances—not reproduce them—and be rooted in participatory planning, not imposed developmentalism [19] . Across the Lower Dnipro, the future of restoration remains uncertain and politically charged. While spontaneous rewilding of the exposed reservoir bed reveals significant ecological potential, military hostilities, unexploded ordnance, and contamination by toxic sediments severely constrain access [7] . Recovery is both viable and precarious—shaped not only by ecological processes, but by contested decisions over infrastructure, territorial control, and postwar development trajectories  [20] . The Kakhovka Dam’s destruction exposed more than just structural weakness. It revealed the layered violence of an imperial project—first in construction, then in demolition. Russia’s targeting of the dam enacted a strategy of territorial de-sovereignization: the use of ecological collapse to fracture Ukraine’s ability to reproduce life, autonomy, and infrastructure. Legal cases may eventually assign responsibility, but political accountability lies in reconstruction. What is rebuilt, who rebuilds, and for whom—these will determine whether imperial logics are broken, or reinstalled under new management.

case_name: Masela Block and Abadi LNG, Indonesia
headline: The Abadi LNG project, led by INPEX, faces criticism for environmental and social harm, despite claims of sustainability. Indigenous communities have been displaced, compensation disputes remain unresolved, and the project contradicts Indonesia’s climate goals.
description: The Abadi gas field, discovered in 2000, is located in deep offshore waters near the maritime boundary between Indonesia and Australia. INPEX holds a 65% operating stake in the project. Although situated within Indonesian territorial waters, the field is approximately 400 kilometres from Australia's Northern Territory and may partially extend into Australian waters. Due to its remote location, it is far from major demand and supply hubs in Indonesia  [1] , which adds the need to develop a liquefaction terminal to export the extracted gas. The Abadi LNG project is scheduled to begin production by January 1, 2030. As per its development plan, INPEX has committed to supplying at least 2 million metric tonnes of LNG annually for domestic consumption, according to Indonesia’s Minister of Energy and Mineral Resources, Arifin Tasrif  [2] .   Indonesia ranks as the world’s eighth-largest exporter of liquefied natural gas (LNG), following major exporters such as Australia (108.1 billion cubic metres), Qatar (106.8 billion cubic metres), and the United States (95 billion cubic metres) in 2021. In comparison, Indonesia exported over 14 billion cubic metres in the same year  [3] .  Despite this, domestic gas reserves are declining at an estimated rate of 3% annually, while demand continues to grow by approximately 7% each year. At the same time, the Indonesian government has pledged to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 29-41% by 2030. Notably, this emissions reduction target coincides with the planned start of production at the Abadi LNG project in 2030  [4] .   While INPEX, the main operator of the Abadi LNG project, claims on its website that it aims to neutralise CO₂ emissions from gas production through carbon capture and storage (CCS), concerns have been raised about the selective application of sustainability measures [5] . A petition by Friends of the Earth Indonesia (WALHI), titled  "Stop Prolonging the Life of Fossil Fuels and Destroying the Environment and Livelihoods in Indonesia,"  cites previous cases such as the Tangguh LNG project, where INPEX was also involved, as evidence of the harm that CCS projects can cause when local communities are excluded from environmental decision-making. In Tangguh, the environmental impact assessment failed to involve residents, leading to the destruction of ecologically sensitive areas such as mangroves and coastal zones, restricted fishing activities, and the displacement of three Indigenous tribes, who lost access to their ancestral lands, farming, and hunting grounds [6] .  As an instance, in 2020, an official from the Indonesian government stated that the land on which the Masela Block assets are located is state-owned. The same official referred to the Maluku Indigenous community as "those" who claim it to be customary land within the forest area, yet again asserted, based on government data, that the land is state-owned  [7] .  Despite this claim, two years later, the Tanimbar Islands Nustual community submitted a complaint to the presidential office objecting to the compensation price offered for the land, which was Rp. 14,000/m². Eventually, the Saumlaki District Court determined that the appropriate compensation should be Rp. 172,000/m². INPEX filed an appeal to the Supreme Court, which ultimately overturned the Saumlaki District Court's decision, reinstating the original compensation price of Rp. 14,000/m².  [8] [9]  This incident is deeply troubling and clearly illustrates how those in power can consolidate more control, while local and Indigenous communities, who have a profound understanding of the land, receive nothing, all under the guise of sustainability and carbon neutrality. And this is not all: it was not only the local people who were affected, but also the forest itself, which had sustained and regenerated for hundreds, even thousands, of years, that is also mentioned in the petition which further stresses that the exploration of new oil and gas fields is incompatible with the goals of the Paris Agreement, a point supported by findings from the International Energy Agency (IEA)  [6] [13] . Additionally, the involvement of CCS as part of the fossil fuels project will not address the main problem, which is fossil fuels [12] , but will overlook its harm to the environment and the local community affected by it, under the cover of carbon neutral project, as carbon is the only main concern here. According to the same petition  [12] , Jokowi, the president, issued Presidental Regulation on CCS activities in 2024, that additional incentives will be provided for fossil fuel industry to adopt the CCS, which will also allow other countries to import carbon and to eventually inject it in Indonesia, and based on the petition, this is just another form of "Waste Colonialisim." and this will bring nothing but the suffering of people in accidents like inhaling harmful gases due to gas leak following by other symptoms, explotions and other accidents, and there is a history of such events occuring  [12] . Not to mention that the expansion of LNG in Indonesia is not directed to fulfill the domestic energy demand, but to export it to developed countries  [13] .   Despite these conflicts, the Abadi LNG project has recently advanced into a new phase, receiving formal approval from the Indonesian government less than a month ago, April 2025  [10] [11] .

case_name: Occupation in 2023 of Fluxys' LNG terminal in Zeebrugge, Belgium
headline: Greenpeace activists occupied a gas terminal, calling attention to the environmental impacts of LNG and the need to phase out gas.
description: On April 29, 2023, Greenpeace activists blocked Fluxys ’ LNG terminal in Zeebrugge [1] . On rubber boats and kayaks, they entered the terminal and attached a “Gas kills, Fluxys guilty” banner to the terminal’s loading and unloading quays [2] . The occupation lasted 6 hours, after which the activists were removed by police, and 14 of them were detained for 48 hours.  Fluxys, a Belgian gas operator, operates a 12,000-kilometre pipeline network across Europe [3] . The company’s LNG terminal in Zeebrugge is an important re-exporting hub for Russian LNG. Since the beginning of the war in Ukraine, European imports of LNG from the United States increased by 140%  [2] . Greenpeace wants to raise attention to the role of gas operators like Fluxys in the stark increase of US-based LNG to Europe. Gas projects have severe environmental and climate impacts  [1] . The organization demands a halt to new gas infrastructure projects and a European-wide plan to phase out gas by 2035. Two years later,  eight activists from Greenpeace Belgium confronted an LNG tanker coming from the US, and heading for the port of Zeebrugge. "They approached the US Marvel Swallow   and unfurled banners featuring Trump and Putin, and reading “Their gas, your cash” to denounce how Europe’s reliance on fossil gas fuels geopolitical instability, while leaving households burdened with skyrocketing energy costs".  On board the Arctic Sunrise,  Joeri Thijs, spokesperson for Greenpeace Belgium , said: “Autocrats like Putin fund their wars with gas revenues, while political bullies like Trump use their dominance as gas suppliers to pressure European countries economically and politically." [5]
