case_name: Shimizu LNG power plant project in Shizuoka, Japan
headline: In 2015, the proposed construction of a LNG power plant in Shimizu Port was started in Shimizu Ward, Shizuoka City, Japan. However it faced strong opposition from local residents due to concerns over environmental impact and safety risks. After three years of sustained efforts by residents, the construction plan was cancelled in 2018.
description: The planned LNG power plant at Shimizu Port faced strong opposition from local communities, ultimately leading to its cancellation in 2018. This case illustrates how grassroots mobilization can stop corporate-led infrastructure projects. The Shimizu Natural Gas Power Plant Project was a plan to construct a thermal power plant burning Liquid Natural Gas (LNG) at Shimizu Port in Shizuoka Prefecture, approximately 150 km southwest of Tokyo. [1] This project was initially launched in 2015 by TonenGeneral Sekiyu K.K., a Japanese petroleum products manufacturer and distributor. During the construction phase, TonenGeneral merged with JX Energy Corporation, forming JXTG Energy Corporation, Japan’s largest energy company in 2017. The company was later renamed ENEOS Corporation in 2020. [1] The proposed construction site was a former oil terminal at the Port of Shimizu, owned by TonenGeneral. This port is a key logistics hub, accommodating international container ships and large cruise ships due to its strategic access to Tokyo and other metropolitan areas, ranking the 12th largest among Japanese ports in 2023. [2] [3] [4] At the time of planning, Japan was experiencing an increasing dependence on fossil fuels. From 2011 to 2016, the share of nuclear power generation had declined from 26% to 1.7%, after the 2011 Fukushima nuclear accident. Meanwhile, fossil fuel-based power generation had surged from 65.4% to 83.6%. [5] The planned LNG-fired power plant was expected to have an output of 2 million kW, enough to supply electricity to approximately 700,000 households. [6] The operating company emphasized the project's benefits, highlighting two main objectives: “Provide a stable supply of inexpensive, environmentally friendly electricity” and “Contribute to the economic development of the Shimizu region through job creation and tax revenues.” [7] The proposed construction site is located next to an LNG terminal, allowing for the efficient use of existing infrastructure. [3]   In addition to the fact that LNG-fired power generation emits less CO2 than coal-fired power generation, the company also planned to further reduce its environmental impact by introducing the latest high-efficiency combined-cycle power generation equipment. [7] Based on these factors, the company determined that the project would have a minimal impact on the local environment and proceeded with the construction plan. [7] [8] On the other hand, the public, local government, and fishermen's associations raised concerns about the project's impacts. The four main issues were environmental assessment and health risks, disaster risks, impacts on tourism, and ecological impacts. First, the new power plant was only 400 meters from a train station in the city centre. As an industrial city, Shimizu residents had suffered from the influence of factory fumes for years, especially children. [1] Residents feared that the power plant would worsen air pollution and affect public health. [ 1] [9]   Furthermore, the City Council highlighted the plant's negative contribution to global warming, noting that its CO2 emissions would be approximately 1.6 times that of Shizuoka City. [10] Second, the location is at risk of being affected by a tsunami in the event of a large-scale earthquake, and the resulting secondary disasters due to damage to the plant were considered unavoidable. [1] Third, the local government aimed to attract cruise ships but feared that the power plant would damage the landscape, ultimately harming the tourism industry. [9] Fourth, the Shimizu Fisheries Cooperative and the Yui Port Fisheries Cooperative opposed the project, fearing that the discharge of wastewater would disrupt the marine ecosystem, harm fishery resources such as cherry shrimp and whitebait in the Shimizu area, and ultimately impact the livelihoods of local fishermen. [10] [11] In short, the potential winners and losers of the project were as follows; Winners: ENEOS Corporation, energy sector, government authorities pushing fossil fuel expansion. Losers: Local residents (air pollution risks), fishermen (marine impacts), tourism industry (landscape concerns). The environmental assessment consists of four stages: “Statement of Consideration,” “Methodology,” “Preparation,” and “Evaluation.” [11] The Statement of Consideration was submitted to the Shizuoka city government and the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry on January 30th, 2015. [12] However, due to these concerns, the first citizens' group, “the Council for the Construction of LNG-Fired Power Plants”, was established on March 10th, 2015. Around the same time, Yoshihiro Matsuda, professor emeritus at Tokai University, also submitted an opinion letter raising concerns about the document. [11] Citizen groups began holding weekly study sessions to engage in discussions with the government on equal terms and express their opposition. [1] By July 14th, 2016, six major citizen groups had been formed, including “Mothers’ Group to Protect Citizens from the Shimizu Thermal Power Plant.” This movement also included an association of high-rise apartment residents who were expected to be directly affected by emissions from the power plant. Each group carried out activities from their respective perspectives. [11] [13] .  Meanwhile, ENEOS revised the power generation scale twice, on August 24th, 2015, and August 25th, 2016, ultimately reducing it from 2 million kW to 1.1 million kW. [11] In 2017, a coalition group, “The LNG-Fired Power Plant Issue Liaison Group,” was formed to unite the various citizen groups. On May 11th, they submitted a formal opposition request to the Shizuoka Prefectural Assembly and the governor. [11] In response, the governor of Shizuoka Prefecture and the mayor of Shizuoka City publicly opposed the project in July and August. Their statement was “The program itself is not in line with Shimizu's urban development direction.” [9] On September 15th, ENEOS postponed the submission of the preparation document, the next environmental assessment stage. [14] By March 2017, the citizen groups had organized 17 demonstrations, 21 study sessions, and over 30 leaflet distribution campaigns. [11] In addition to distributing and posting flyers in front of nearby train stations, residents also took buses to the ENEOS headquarters, where they distributed flyers and made appeals on the road in front of the company's headquarters. To raise awareness among citizens, they also released a song Guarding Our Beloved Shimizu, which opposes the thermal power plant, and uploaded it to YouTube [17] . They even strategically purchased shares in ENEOS, using shareholder meetings to voice their concerns directly to corporate leadership. [1] Their activities further expanded, and a petition with 25,829 signatures opposing the construction was submitted to the City Council. The petition also included statistics from a survey of 1,102 households, showing 55–71% opposition to the project. [15] Although the City Council rejected the petition on February 21st, 2018, ENEOS ultimately announced the project's cancellation on March 27th, 2018 due to continuous public opposition and pressure from the local government. [9] [15]   Following the cancellation of the project, the citizen groups were dissolved. Regarding the subsequent land use, in 2020, Shizuoka Prefecture and ENEOS signed an agreement to explore transforming the site into a clean energy hub, including the development of a solar power plant and a hydrogen energy system. [16]   This plan has not generated any significant public opposition or reunification of the disbanded citizen groups. This case highlights not only the impact of fossil fuel power plant construction on global warming but also the unequal burden it places on local regions and residents in terms of environment, health, and social culture. Moreover, it stands as a powerful demonstration of the strength of civic action, showing how persistent resistance can mobilize authorities and ultimately force corporations to abandon even large-scale projects.

case_name: Melchorita Gas Plant in Lima and the Peru LNG Gas Pipeline in Ayacucho, Peru
headline: The Peru LNG gas pipeline, operated by Hunt Oil, EIG, and Shell, generates socio-environmental conflicts in Ayacucho due to spills, river contamination, failure to compensate communities, and greenwashing actions. Protests since 2010 demand reparations for damages, social support, and dialogue regarding impacts on health, crops, and biodiversity.
description: Introduction The Perú LNG project is an energy complex that includes a 408 km pipeline and a liquefaction plant in Pampa Melchorita, located on the coast of Lima. Operated by Hunt LNG (a subsidiary of Hunt Oil Company), it transports natural gas from the fields of the Urubamba Basin to the coast, interconnecting with the Camisea system in Ayacucho. With an initial investment of USD 3.874 billion, the project has been key for the export of LNG gas to Europe, particularly to Spain, but it has also generated recurring socio-environmental conflicts due to its impacts on local communities and ecosystems. Case History The project was designed as part of the expansion of the Camisea system , a key gas exploitation in the South American region, located in the environmentally fragile tropical Urubamba Valley of the Peruvian Amazon.  In 2010, when the project became operational , Peru LNG was owned by Hunt Oil (50%), Repsol (20%), SK Energy (20%), and Marubeni (10%) [13] . Since its launch in 2010, communities in Ayacucho denounced (in 2012) the lack of prior consultation and compensations [3] . The residents pointed out that the company Perú LNG, to date, has not fulfilled the compensations and requests of the communities affected by the passage of the Camisea gas pipeline. They specified that the company often failed to meet its promises and has not yet remedied the damages caused to their lands. In contrast to its commitments to the communities of Ayacucho, Peru LNG has carried out various actions that may align with greenwashing strategies. One example is its partnership with the NGO Prosynergy. This NGO carries out local sustainability projects funded [5] by Peru LNG and SK Energy, a shareholder of the gas company. Additionally, it has other collaborators [4] such as Pluspetrol, the International Finance Corporation of Canada, and Minsur (Breca Mineria S.A.C.), whose mining, gas, and oil businesses could create a conflict of interest with their local collaborations in favor of Peru LNG. The activity of the LNG terminal culminated in the shipment of 32 cargoes between January and June 2017, compared to 31 during the same period in 2016. Most of the shipments were destined for Spain [6] , but three also reached Mexico, two to France and Japan, while Taiwan, the United Kingdom, and South Korea received one each. Accidents and Environmental Impacts On Thursday, April 30, 2015, residents of Huayrapata, in the district of Anco (province of La Mar, Ayacucho), denounced the rupture of the Camisea gas pipeline and the consequent contamination of the river. Blandina Contreras Yance, from the Peruvian Peasant Confederation, stated that she had collected evidence showing that "at the time of the gas leak, it reached the river, where many dead fish and reptiles from the area were observed." She added: "The water is contaminated; last Tuesday we collected water from the river, and it was evident that half of what was collected was river water, and the upper part was liquid gas." Meanwhile, delegate Hugo Huamán Tovar stated that the community fears this will affect crops such as coffee, cocoa, and citrus [7] . That same day, a strong explosion surprised the residents of the district of Anco in Ayacucho. Upon leaving their homes, they observed a strange cloud in the sky. The natural gas liquids pipeline burst at kilometer 183, as confirmed by the Transportadora de Gas del Perú (TgP). After the explosion, they proceeded to close some valves to prevent the hydrocarbon from continuing to escape into the environment. According to El Comercio, nine communities were affected by the spill. These are Wayrapata, Mejorada, Pampa Aurora, Chontabamba, and San Antonio, where 1,056 residents lived. Residents of Villa Unión, Puerto Asunción, Bella Vista, and Naín were also affected. The population reported symptoms such as intense headaches, vomiting, and skin rashes [8] .  On the other hand, it is worth noting that as early as 2013, a study showed evidence of the impact of the Peru LNG pipeline on the biodiversity of the forests of Ayacucho, specifically on the rodent population [9] . Mobilization and Protests  Prior to the protests by the communities of Ayacucho, which denounced (in 2012) the lack of prior consultation and compensations by Peru LNG, in 2010 around 200 artisanal fishermen from the Association of Artisanal Fishermen and Affiliates of the Port of Tambo de Mora staged a protest against the company Perú LNG [30] . Their main demand was to be included in the company's Compensation Plan, arguing that the activity of Perú LNG had affected their daily livelihood due to the decrease in marine species in the area. After exhausting administrative channels and unsuccessfully approaching entities such as the Ministry of Production and the Ministry of Energy and Mines, the protesters temporarily blocked the Panamericana Sur highway at kilometer 115, demanding a dialogue table.  During 2020, more than 500 residents from 29 annexes of the district of Vinchos, in Huamanga, protested against Perú LNG, demanding the continuation of the social support that the company used to provide annually for community projects [10] . During the protest, they held a peaceful sit-in to demand attention to their demands, and in a second protest, an incident occurred where some community members burned company furniture a few meters from the valve. The Ombudsman's Office has urged the resumption of dialogue between the company Perú LNG and the peasant community of Vinchos, made up of more than 300 inhabitants, who are demanding social support [11] . Alfredo Canales, president of the Vinchos community, stated that there was a "verbal commitment" with Perú LNG to provide funds for projects, an agreement that was fulfilled every year but which the company now denies. “They entered the community 10 years ago and supported us every year. Now, with the pandemic, they want to cut off the support,” he denounced. Canales explained that the support consisted of delivering materials according to the community's needs. However, the company allegedly suspended this assistance, citing economic difficulties due to the pandemic. Marcelina Conga, a community member of Viscachayocc, stated that "they have always deceived us" and that they promised low-cost domestic gas, which has not been fulfilled. Canales warned that, if there is no response, the community will take action, and he will resign from his position. Meanwhile, they sent a document requesting a meeting with Perú LNG, but the company has not responded.  International Alliances between NGOs and Indigenous Organizations along with UN Pressure The lack of dialogue from the Peruvian government, the failure to consult ancestral communities, the overlapping of indigenous territories [15]  and the socio-environmental problems [16]  of the gas project led the Interethnic Association for the Development of the Peruvian Rainforest (AIDESEP) and the Native Federation of the Madre de Dios River and Affluents (FENAMAD) [17]  to lead, together with the Regional Organization Aidesep Ucayali – ORAU, and the Machiguenga Council of the Urubamba River – Comaru [18]  complaints before the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights (IACHR) in 2013 [19] , stating that the expansion of Camisea violated the rights of voluntarily isolated peoples in the Nahua-Nanti Reserve. Additionally, in 2014, Forest Peoples Programme published reports linking Camisea's operations to the reduction of ancestral territories and the threat of extinction of isolated peoples. In 2014, their investigation revealed that the expansion of the project included the construction of 18 new wells and seismic tests in critical areas for the subsistence of these communities. These organizations also presented evidence of forced contacts and historical epidemics, such as the death of more than half of the Nahua population due to respiratory diseases contracted during Shell's explorations in the 1980s [20] . Also during 2013, Survival International coordinated protests [21] at Peruvian embassies in London, Madrid, and San Francisco, delivering more than 120,000 signatures demanding the halt of the expansion of Camisea. Their technical reports exposed that 75% of Block 88 overlapped with the Nahua-Nanti Reserve, violating international standards such as ILO Convention 169. In March 2013, the UN Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination (CERD) issued a recommendation demanding that the Peruvian government "immediately suspend" the expansion plans of Camisea within the Nahua-Nanti Reserve. The committee warned that the operations, which included seismic tests and well drilling, posed a risk to the physical and cultural survival of isolated indigenous peoples [22] . This measure was a direct response to the complaints filed by Peruvian indigenous organizations, such as AIDESEP, ORAU, and COMARU, who requested the intervention of CERD under the Early Warning and Urgent Action Procedure.  This international reach led the then UN Special Rapporteur on the rights of indigenous peoples, James Anaya, to speak out about the overlapping of indigenous territories that the expansion of the Camisea gas project would entail [23] . More recently, during 2017, protests occurred in the United Kingdom over the arrival of an LNG ship from Peru, a result of the natural gas transported by the Camisea pipeline [24] .  The international alliances between NGOs, indigenous movements, and UN actors demonstrated the ability to mobilize global pressure and organizational capacity of groups in defense of human rights and the legitimate mandate of ILO Convention 169. However, although these alliances were successful, they revealed the structural limits of the Peruvian State. Despite the complaints, the Camisea consortium (Pluspetrol, Hunt Oil, Repsol) maintained operations with state backing and multilateral financing. The persistence of spills, such as the 2015 spill in Huayrapata that contaminated rivers and affected nine communities, underscores the gap between corporate commitments and local realities.  Structural Limits in the Case of Peru In this sense, the Republic of Peru and its democracy face a multidimensional crisis that, according to the Bertelsmann Transformation Index (BTI) 2024, classifies its democracy as "highly defective" [25] , highlighting the weakening of political rights, fragile institutions, and conflicts between state powers. Similarly, Freedom House, under its standards for the analysis of civil and political rights, defines Peru as a "partially free" country [26] .  Ultimately, last year in 2024, Swichinfo echoed the words of Human Rights Watch regarding the legislative reforms that the Peruvian Congress, under the protection or the sidelining of the government of Dina Boluarte (with brutal repression during her mandate, still in force in February 2025, with more than 50 deaths during the December 2022 protests), approved several laws that "undermined judicial independence and weakened democracy" [27] . Current Status of the Project and New Protests The pipeline transports 745 million cubic feet per day (MMCFD), with 83% (620 MMCFD) destined for export. Hunt Oil maintains 50%, Shell 20%, EIG Global Energy Partners 10%, Saudi Aramco 10%, and Marubeni 10% [2] [14] . Demands for damage reparations persist, while organizations such as the Peruvian Ombudsman's Office urge the resumption of dialogue with communities (2020). During 2022, restrictions on access to Russian natural gas, along with the lack of regasification infrastructure, forced European countries to resort to the spot market, driving up international prices. This increase was reflected in the company's results, which closed the year with an EBITDA of US$ 361 million, the highest since late 2018. The total volume of LNG sales reached 179 TBtus through 51 shipments to European and Asian markets, surpassing the 38 shipments made in 2021. At the end of the year, total revenues stood at US$ 3,179 million, 98% more than the US$ 1,608 million in 2021 [12] . The Camisea natural gas plant has been the target of protests in recent years, 2022 and 2023, highlighting the persistence of institutional fractures and the inability to channel citizen demands. The multidimensional crisis of Peruvian democracy led to protests across Peru. In December 2022, a group of 100 protesters from the Kepashiato Population Center (Cusco) took over the Kamani Compressor Plant of TGP, demanding the resignation of President Dina Boluarte and halting the transport of natural gas. The plant, key to generating 50% of the nation's electricity, was inoperative for 12 days, affecting exports and internal supply [28] . These protests led to the Ministry of Energy and Mines (Minem), through the General Directorate of Hydrocarbons (DGH), issuing Director's Resolution 411-2022 to suspend the export of natural gas and, with it, guarantee internal supply and national electricity production, as well as the suspension of the shipment of a vessel with nearly 3 million cubic feet of LNG to South Korea [29] .

case_name: Puerta al Sureste pipeline and LNG terminal in Coatzacoalcos, Mexico
headline: The Morena government has approved the construction of a pipeline to transport natural gas across the Gulf of Mexico from the United States to Coatzacoalcos, where Canada's TC Energy plans to build a liquefied gas terminal. Indigenous communities, environmental groups, and academics are calling for the project to be cancelled.
description: Introduction In April 2022, the then-president of Mexico, Andrés Manuel López Obrador, highlighted the importance of constructing a natural liquefied gas (LNG) liquefaction terminal at the Port of Coatzacoalcos, Veracruz. According to the former president, this project aimed to meet the growing demand for gas in Europe [1] , largely driven by the war in Ukraine, and also to strengthen Mexico's energy sovereignty. However, this initiative contrasts with the country's marked dependence on natural gas imports, 96.4% of which [2] come from the United States via pipelines that connect both countries. The future terminal is projected to be built near the mouth of the Coatzacoalcos River. A region that, according to the study by Espinosa-Reyes et al. (2013) titled "Persistent Organic Pollutants in the Lower Basin of the Coatzacoalcos River, Veracruz" [3] , the existing pollution in the area poses a serious threat to human health and the ecosystems in the region. On the other hand, in June 2024, the organizations EarthJustice and the Mexican Center for Environmental Law (CEMDA) sent a letter to the U.S. Department of Energy expressing concern about the potential export of liquefied natural gas (LNG) from Mexico. They argued that, compared to the U.S., “differences in structure, access to information, and capacity for enforcement” [4] could result in “greater contributions to climate change and an increase in air pollution” [5] . In the same year of the regasification terminal announcement, 2022, Mexico formalized its Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) under the Paris Agreement of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) for an unconditional emission reduction of 35% by 2030 [6] . In contrast, Mexico's CO2 emissions have continued to grow, increasing by 17 million tons between 2022 and 2023 [7] . Case History The liquefaction terminal project is led by CF Energía, a subsidiary of the Mexican state-owned entity Comisión Federal de Electricidad (CFE). As part of this initiative, CF Energía has begun the construction of a pipeline that will connect the future terminal. However, the execution of the project requires active participation from the private sector due to CFE's limitations in experience with large-scale developments. According to the consulting firm ICIS, CFE "lacks the necessary experience to develop such large-scale projects" [8] . Therefore, the LNG export terminal will receive financial and technical collaboration from the Canadian company TC Energy. While Mexico moved towards a “covert privatization” [9] as pointed out by CELAG (Latin American Strategic Center for Geopolitics) resulting from the energy reform of former PRI president Peña Nieto, this was a trend of Mexican governments with a turning point on January 1, 1994, with the implementation of the North American Free Trade Agreement, which led to the Zapatista uprising under the EZLN. Now, the "Sovereign Republic and Energy" project from the progressive broad front of the Morena party (initially represented by former president AMLO and now by president Claudia Sheinbaum) integrates among its objectives energy sovereignty, the reduction of pollutant emissions and greenhouse gases, as well as reducing "energy intensity," meaning increasing GDP while maintaining or reducing energy consumption. This scenario contrasts with Mexico's marked dependence on natural gas imports, 96.4% of which [10] (pp.58) comes from the United States via pipelines. This situation highlights the country's significant energy vulnerability, far from the current government's sovereign energy project, particularly in the supply of natural gas for the domestic and industrial sectors. Moreover, the noted increase of 17 million tons of CO2 between 2022 and 2023 shows that Mexico is already failing to meet its CO2 reduction commitments. Ultimately, according to the study Is Decoupling GDP Growth from Environmental Impact Possible? [11] , the relationship between GDP and energy use cannot be decoupled. Dr. Nate Hagens asserts that this relationship is 99% dependent [12] . Therefore, Mexico cannot increase its GDP without consuming more energy and consequently emitting more greenhouse gases. These contradictions of the Morena government push Mexico to fail in its emission reduction agreements, increase the risk of environmental accidents, and deepen its energy dependence. Accidents and Environmental Impacts Based on the study by Espinosa-Reyes et al., (2013) titled "Persistent Organic Pollutants in the Lower Basin of the Coatzacoalcos River, Veracruz," the analysis of persistent organic pollutants (POPs) in sediments and soils of the lower Coatzacoalcos River basin (2006-2012) revealed increasing concentrations of the isomer lindane, due to its continuous use in the control of ectoparasites in local livestock. Additionally, the industrial activity in the region, such as the continuous dredging of the river to facilitate transportation to the Lázaro Cárdenas refinery in Minatitlán, and extreme weather events, such as floods, contribute to the resuspension of contaminated sediments, increasing the availability of POPs in the environment. The report had already pointed out that the mix of industrial, urban, and agricultural activities in the area worsens the risk of pollution and its ecological impacts, while bioaccumulation and biomagnification of POPs represent a threat to human health and regional ecosystems. The industrial complex located at the Port of Coatzacoalcos, the site where the liquefied gas terminal is planned, can be considered a high-risk area due to previous fatal accidents. One of the most severe incidents occurred on April 20, 2016, when an explosion at a petrochemical complex owned by PEMEX in the area caused the deaths of 32 people, with many others injured and missing [13] . The Veracruzana University issued a statement protesting the inaction of local and national authorities. In it, they presented the results of a chemical study of the waters of the Coatzacoalcos River, as well as the dust and surface soil, revealing 59 organic chemicals, some of which are considered high-risk and carcinogenic [14] . Three years later, on October 6, 2019, another explosion occurred at the Port of Coatzacoalcos, this time in a fuel tank at the complex [15] . Given the recurrent accidents at the Coatzacoalcos Port complex, the question arises as to whether the establishment of an LNG export terminal truly addresses the needs of the Veracruz and Mexican citizens, or if it serves the interests promoted by the broad front formed by the Morena party. In any case, this is of particular relevance because it implies non-compliance with international commitments on emission reductions, the risks these facilities pose to local communities, and the environmental impact at extraction sites, where the gas is primarily obtained through fracking. International Organized Resistance The Southeast Gate Gas Pipeline, conceived as a key piece to transport natural gas from Tuxpan to Coatzacoalcos and, eventually, feed the future regasification plant of TC Energy at the Port of Coatzacoalcos, has faced a wave of opposition led by organizations such as Greenpeace Mexico and supported by academics from the Universidad Veracruzana. These actors pointed out in 2022 the ecological and social risks associated with the project, highlighting that its construction endangers critical ecosystems such as the Lobos-Tuxpan Reef System, a high-biodiversity area that sustains local fishing and livelihoods [18] . Additionally, in another occasion in May 2023, Greenpeace Mexico launched a new campaign called Mar adentro, mar afuera , in which they collaborated with academics from the Universidad Veracruzana to document and raise awareness about the risks the construction of the Southeast Gate gas pipeline poses to the reefs and coastal communities of Veracruz. They used their iconic ship, Artic Sunrise, formerly a seal-fishing vessel. According to Greenpeace, the construction of the pipeline threatens fragile marine ecosystems and the coastal communities that depend on them, while its reliance on practices like fracking exacerbates the negative environmental and human health impacts.  The organized resistance also included testimonies from local communities affected by climate change, such as El Bosque and Las Barrancas, who denounced displacement caused by coastal erosion and highlighted how the construction of this infrastructure could worsen these issues. Rubicela Mayoral Cobos, a resident of El Bosque, stated, “We are the first climate displaced people in Mexico. Today we are here to say we don’t want this to happen in more communities” [19] due to rising sea levels that have consumed their homes and streets, forcing them out of their home. The Southeast Gate pipeline project could be connected to the future LNG regasification plant planned to be built at the Port of Coatzacoalcos by TC Energy and the Mexican government. These infrastructures, primarily responsible for the Canadian company TC Energy, have been pointed out by a union of indigenous communities from Mexico and Canada, demanding an impact assessment of this company due to its failure to comply with ILO Convention 169. That is, the Southeast Gate gas pipeline, meant to transport natural gas to Coatzacoalcos, has been the subject of complaints by communities in Mexico. According to these complaints, TC Energy, the company responsible for the future regasification plant at the Port of Coatzacoalcos, has failed to comply with ILO Convention 169, which guarantees the right of indigenous communities to be consulted about projects affecting their territories. As Maribel Cervantes Cruz, a leader of these communities, said, “None of the Nahua, nuntajɨɨyi’ or other coastal indigenous communities have received adequate information either from TC Energy or the Mexican government about the pipeline they want to build in our ancestral territory” [17] . Current Status of the Project Currently, in December 2024, the project has acquired a license from the Mexican government for its construction. However, earlier in the same year, Greenpeace Mexico and environmental and social organizations, such as #EsGasFósil, Alianza Mexicana Contra el Fracking, CEDICAR (Centro de Investigación y Capacitación Rural), Conexiones Climáticas, Defensa Ambiental del Noroeste, Nuestro Futuro A.C., Padres por el Futuro Monterrey, and Planeteando, demanded that the Mexican government cancel projects [16]  they consider a threat to national sovereignty and the rights of communities in the affected territories. The groups are calling for respect for local populations and the environment, urging the reconsideration of initiatives that negatively impact these areas.

case_name: Ksi Lisims Floating LNG Terminal, British Colombia, Canada
headline: Ksi Lisims LNG project is owned by Rockies LNG, Western LNG and the Nisga's Nation, one of the indigenous groups to the area. It has been hailed the "world's first Indigenous-led, low and zero-carbon" LNG project, yet it divides opinions between various indigenous groups to the area, with many citizens voicing their concerns around the environmental and health impacts the project will have.
description: The Ksi Lisims Floating Liquid Natural Gas (FLNG) terminal, will be located at Wil Milit on the northern side of Pearse Island, close to the Nisga'a Village of Ginglox [1] . It is being pioneered as the world’s first “indigenous led”  [2]  LNG project, and is located in land financially owned by the Nisga'a Nation, who own a percentage of the project, along with two LNG companies - Western Canadian Rockies LNG and Texas-based Western LNG. The project was first presented by this consortium in July 2021 [6] , and since then other indigenous groups as well as environmental groups and concerned citizens have opposed the project, citing the environmental harms to the air, land and ocean ecosystems and how this would contribute to poor health for those living that the project would cause.  The project is set to have a capacity of 12 million tonnes of LNG per annum [2] , with an expected life span of 39 years  [7] and costing around $9 billion. Destined to transport fracked natural gas out of Canada to countries in Asia.  [12]  Shell plc has also agreed to buy 2 million metric tons of the gas annually.  [15] The area that the project is located on is contested land - both the Nisga’a and the Lax Kw’alaams nations have competing claims to it [4]   [5] , although financially the Nisga’a now have ownership. The Lax Kw’alaams have been leading the resistance against the project, filing court cases against the Nisga’a peoples proposed actions [8] - in May 2022, they were joined by another first nations group, the Metlakatla, in an attempt to halt the Nisga'a people’s purchase of 22,000-hectare parcel of land at the mouth of the Nass River. Land which they had stated in 2016 was destined to be used for the FLNG project. [9] The Lax Kw’alaams and Metlakatla succeeded, and an 18 month injunction was granted, which delayed the buyout of this plot of land.  [9]   [10] Yet, in the end the land was successfully bought by the Nisga’a and the project began.  As legal challenges represent strong disapproval of the project, public consultations also draw substantial opposition. There have been two periods for public comment on the project, as part of the environmental assessment decision. During the first which was held in September 2021, there were 67 comments made - most came from concerned citizens, listing the issues that could arise from the project and citing the lack of commitment to climate goals of reducing greenhouse gas emissions. One anonymous commenter highlighted their disdain with the decision of Nisga'a people for being involved in such a project  -  “ Shame on the Nisga'a First Nation for willingly jeopardizing the salmon run and other fisheries of the Nass River. Shame on the Nisga'a First Nation for going against the wishes of the Gitanyow and Tahltan First Nations when it comes to protecting the salmon of the Nass River. Shame on the Nisga'a First Nation for going against the will of the Luutkudziiwus House of the Gitksan First Nation, who have blocked one of the proposed pipeline routes that would supply this proposed facility. Shame on the Nisga'a First Nation for jeopardising the fishery of the Lake Babine First Nation. Shame on the Nisga'a First Nation for advocating more fracking on the traditional lands of "Treaty Eight" first nations - whose lands are already decimated by the activities of oil and gas extraction. Shame on the Nisga'a First Nation and on the BC government for even considering another mammoth FLNG facility, when the legislated GHG targets for this province will not be met with the construction of FLNG Canada and Coastal GasLink, alone .”  [14] During the second public comment period, which opened on October 31st 2023 and ran until December 1st 2023, the project received over 500 written comments, the bulk of which were negative  [6] . While many of these referred to how this project is not aligned with the provincial energy policy, and the global need to transition quickly away from fossil fuel reliance, the consortium was given the opportunity to respond to all comments. Their argument focussed around the Ksi Lisims FLNG being the “the lowest GHG-emission FLNG facility in the world and has committed to being Net-zero” [11] .  One member of the public stated that she was a doctor and a mother, before referring to the issue of FLNG being claimed as a “bridge fuel”, and voicing her concerns around the fugitive emissions of methane that occur all along the supply chain that are extremely difficult to monitor accurately, often leading to misrepresentation of methane emissions. The companies replied, absolving themselves of responsibility by stating that “activities related to upstream natural gas are outside of the scope of Ksi Lisims FLNG Project” going on to say during the operation of the FLNG…The amount [of methane] that would be released by this means is small and will be further mitigated through existing technologies such as capture and re-liquefaction.”  [11] Additionally, during the second public consultation, the Lax Kw'alaams nation representatives pointed out the Ksi Lisims FLNG relies on a pipeline that transports gas from gas fields in northeastern BC, and rather than carrying out a new environmental impact assessment, they rely on approvals given in 2014 [3] . The Lax Kw'alaams people believe that there should be a new environmental assessment seeing as it is nearly 10 years since the last, and raised this as an issue in the public consultation that took place for the project at the end of 2023.  [4] On top of this, the Lax Kw’alaams Mayor Gary Reece stated that, “neither the Lax Kw’alaams Council nor the Nine Allied Tribes of Lax Kw’alaams have approved or consented to the project, and therefore it cannot proceed on Lax Kw’alaams’ traditional territory.”  [3]  They added that if the project is approved despite their outright objection, they will be taking further legal action.  [3] Environmental groups that oppose the project include David Suzuki Foundation, Stand.earth, the Wilderness Committee, T. Buck Suzuki Environmental Foundation and Skeena Watershed Conservation Coalition. Each group raised their concerns over GHG emissions from the project, as well as the impact on marine habitats - especially for the Nass River salmon and whales - with increased ship traffic.  [7] They also raised their concerns over the project's power demand. The application omits some key information around how much energy the FLNG will require, which will be taken from the British Colombia grid. The figures that have been provided demonstrate the need for a 4,700 GWh supply of electricity, yet this would comprise almost all of the power produced at Site C dam, what is set to be a key hydroelectric facility for the region, located on the Peace River in British Columbia.  [7]  The power requirements for the project are so high due to the fact that the Ksi Lisims would use electric drive instead of natural gas powered turbines to fuel the chilling process that cools the natural gas into liquid. This is what helps them in reducing the overall GHG emission intensity of the FLNG.  [12] The David Suzuki Foundation wrote an article complaining “10 reasons to say no to LNG”. Their list highlighted LNG project’s reliance on government subsidies, police violence and colonialism surrounding pipeline construction in the country, excessive electricity consumption and the Ksi Lisims LNG becoming a stranded asset/abandoned infrastructure due to the speed of fluctuation of Asian markets.  [13] Despite the resistance to the project by different actors, on the grounds that it will threaten local ecosystems, particularly the Nass River salmon, and contradicts climate goals despite promises of low GHG emissions, the project is still underway and is expected to be in operation by 2027  [4] .

case_name: Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) Terminal in Sagunto, Spain
headline: Environmental impacts, labor issues, and opposition to the regasification plant.
description: Introduction The liquefied natural gas (LNG) regasification plant is located in the Port of Sagunto, Valencia, with a storage capacity of 600,000 m 3 . Since 2021, and especially since 2022 with the Ukraine war and sanctions on Russia, activity at the regasification plant has increased significantly due to rising imports of U.S. fracked gas. [1] This growth has led to labor conflicts, environmental risks, and protests from environmental organizations like Greenpeace and other local social movements. The plant was inaugurated in 2006 amidst real estate speculation and construction booms preceding the 2008 financial crisis, spurred by the bipartisanship of Spain’s PP and PSOE parties, despite significant local opposition [2] . Although it faced controversy from the beginning and international environmental commitments had been made (such as the 1997 Kyoto Protocol in effect since 2005), the plant was approved and inaugurated on June 26, 2006, next to a town of 44,000 people, a marshland designated as a Special Protection Area for endangered birds, and surrounded by the infrastructure of the Port of Sagunto [3] .  Case History In 2006, in Spain, during the speculative real estate and construction bubble that affected the entire country leading up to the 2008 crisis, the state, under the PSOE administration, initially financed the construction and expansion of the regasification terminal at the Port of Sagunto (Valencia) with €390 million from the European Investment Bank, eventually investing over €500 million in the project [4] . Notably, by then, the 1997 Kyoto Protocol had entered into force just a year before construction began, in 2005, alongside other conventions and agreements such as the UNFCCC, signed at the Rio Earth Summit in 1992, which paved the way for the later Paris Agreement in 2015. In this context, the construction of the Port of Sagunto regasification plant was approved on 23 hectares reclaimed from the sea. The main private investors include the operating company Saggas, whose shareholders are Enagas, Osaka Gas, and Oman Oil Company [5] holding 72.5%, 20%, and 7.5% of the shares, respectively [6] . Notably, both Enagas and Osaka Gas have major shareholders, including the U.S. fund BlackRock and Spanish billionaire Amancio Ortega [7] . However, the plant’s construction cannot be fully understood without considering the public relations strategies [8] —such as those promoted by the International Gas Union to encourage public acceptance—that Unión Fenosa (the original promoter of Saggas’ Sagunto plant) implemented. Their efforts included economic development contributions (direct and indirect), support for local industry, campaigns promoting pride and belonging in Sagunto, and essential energy infrastructure for Spain [9] . Social Mobilization and Protest The political party Esquerra Unida requested a study in the Valencian Parliament on the risks and potential accidents [10] at the regasification plant, given its proximity to Fertiberia’s fertilizer plant, which could trigger a domino effect in the event of an accident or fire. These concerns add to the allegations from the local environmental group Acció Ecologista-Agró Camp de Morvedre, who filed complaints in 2021 with the Valencian Government about Saggas' ship-to-ship LNG transfer activities at the regasification plant. The group highlighted the dangers of normalizing these operations for the environment, workers, and Sagunto’s residents.  In 2021, Greenpeace protested against fossil fuel use by blocking [11] gas unloading from a tanker at the regasification plant, leading to the arrest of the *Esperanza*’s captain by the Guardia Civil on a Sagunto judge’s order. Though released the next day, he faced charges for allegedly disobeying authorities. Police and judicial investigations were also launched against Greenpeace. The organization’s actions are part of the larger fight against climate change and the push to end fossil fuel reliance, such as LNG and fracking-derived natural gas.  Consequently, the gas terminal, along with other industrial activities at the port, has become part of a “sacrifice zone” where socio-environmental impacts are concentrated. In February 2002, Unión Fenosa’s Environmental Impact Study on the Sagunto Regasification Plant (published in the Spanish Official Gazette by the Ministry of the Environment [12] ) identified 85 negative environmental impacts versus only 28 positive ones [13] . Among them, it highlighted risks such as “Population disruption due to major accidents” and “Air quality disruption due to major accidents,” along with numerous impacts on marine vegetation and fauna, expected to last throughout the plant’s 50-year operational life. Despite these concerns, the regasification plant was installed and continues its activities as of 2024. Labor Conflict Starting in 2022 and the ramifications of the Ukraine war, there has been a surge in LNG imports derived from U.S. fracking, resulting in a substantial increase in activity at the regasification terminal. This has led the workers of Amarradores del Puerto de Sagunto CEMSA-P&REYSER to file complaints with the local council, accusing the company of violating legal working hour limits, which have increased from 1,820 to 2,500 hours annually. Additionally, they reported breaches in labor and HR standards, claiming that the company has not adequately adapted its resources to safely handle the increase in mooring and unmooring services following the rise in LNG import activities. These violations have led to work-related accidents, temporary disabilities due to stress and overwork, and have compromised worker health and safety [14] .  El Marjal del Moro A unique feature of the Saggas regasification plant’s location, as well as the Port of Sagunto, is their proximity to a marsh that provides habitat for endangered bird species: El Marjal del Moro. This ecologically valuable area was designated a Special Protection Area for Birds (SPA) in 1995 under the European Birds Directive (2009/147/EC) and is part of Spain’s Natura 2000 network. Article 8 of the directive stipulates that “the preservation, maintenance, or restoration of a diversity and sufficient area of habitats is essential for the conservation of all bird species.” [15] . According to *Métode.cat* (2013), the marsh's plight is “the result of silence from environmental organizations and the media.” [16] . The publication points out that the marsh’s proximity to chemicals, gases, noise, and truck traffic “does not seem to be a good combination of factors for its survival.” It also warns that Saggas’ massive use of seawater could impact marine currents and sedimentation and erosion areas, which over time could transform the marsh into a beach, increasing the risk of urban development speculation. EU-Funded Greenwashing In a greenwashing , twist, Saggas has committed to offsetting 20 tons of CO2 equivalent [17] , annually from its Sagunto regasification plant. For context, the average individual in Spain emits between 5 and 9 tons annually [18] . However, a 2023 report on Saggas’ emissions reveals that total emissions exceeded 170,000 tons of CO2 equivalent (direct and indirect) for that year [19] . Furthermore, a study by Robert W. Howarth (2024) [20] , found that a complete 38-day LNG shipment cycle generates 7,370 g of CO2 equivalent per kilogram of transported LNG. Given that a storage tank can hold approximately 67,500 tons of LNG, a single shipment generates an estimated 460,000 tons of CO2 equivalent during the 38-day trip.  This mitigation project estimates a reduction of “1,517.79 tons of CO2 equivalent over the project’s 10-year duration.” [21] . This is a clear example of greenwashing , supported by European institutions and public funds under the LIFE Wetlands 4 Climate project, coordinated by the Global Nature Foundation, which is part of the European Commission. Current Project Status  Since the Ukraine war began in 2022, the Sagunto regasification plant has seen a sharp increase in activity. Sanctions against Russia and the sabotage of the Nord Stream pipeline have led to a marked rise in LNG imports to Spain, primarily sourced from U.S. fracking. This practice has shown devastating effects on public health and the environment in the U.S., especially in marginalized communities. The toxins from fracking are linked to serious health issues, including leukemia, liver damage, eye and respiratory irritation, and migraines (Fractracker, 2023) [22] . Scientific studies have concluded that no fracking method is risk-free for human health or climate stability (Physicians for Social Responsibility, 2023) [23] . These activities disproportionately affect Black, Latino, and Indigenous communities, exacerbating social and health inequalities (Gonzalez et al., 2023) [23] . Furthermore, fracking threatens aquifers and has led to soil contamination in drought-affected areas like Texas (New York Times, 2023) [24] .  According to Greenpeace, these imports increased by 1422% [25] between 2017 and 2022. The increase in activity, along with that of the Port and other industrial entities in the area, has had adverse effects on El Marjal del Moro, which is not in good conservation status and has seen its ecosystem altered, as observed in the *Radiography of Spain's Wetlands* report (Global Nature Foundation, 2023) which highlights that only 13% [26] of Spanish wetlands are in good condition.

case_name: Cove Point LNG export terminal, USA
headline: Cove Point LNG export terminal, located in Lusby, Maryland, raises concerns among residents of the Calvert County. Its environmental impacts have created conflict due to its contribution to air and noise pollution, global warming, and biodiversity loss. Local environmental groups are pushing for a shift towards renewable energy to replace the LNG project.
description: The Cove Point liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminal in Calvert County, Maryland, is at the centre of a conflict between local residents, fishermen and Dominion Energy, the company that operates the facility. Originally designed to import LNG, the terminal has been converted into an export facility, in line with the growth in US gas exports to international markets [1] . J. M. Neal, along with local residents and fishermen, is leading the opposition to Dominion Energy's conversion of the Cove Point LNG terminal to an export facility, citing environmental risks such as air and water pollution, including methane emissions, that threaten the Chesapeake Bay ecosystem [2] . Dominion Energy has begun transforming the Cove Point terminal into an LNG export platform as part of a nationwide trend in the US to tap into large reserves of shale gas for sale overseas. The company has emphasized the economic benefits of the project, such as job creation, increased local revenue, and a significant contribution to US energy exports [1] . The move is designed to take advantage of growing international demand for natural gas, particularly in Europe and Asia. Stakeholders involved in this case are: Dominion Energy: the main comapny operat ing the terminal, responsible for LNG exports  [2] . Local and federal authorities: they supported the project, considering it essential for energy security and the economy [2] . Local residents and fishermen: led by Jean Marie Neal and other activists, they oppose the project because of its environmental and social impacts [2] . Environmental Justice Organizations (EJOs): groups such as the Sierra Club have joined the opposition, highlighting the risks to the Chesapeake Bay ecosystem [2] : - The Sierra Club campaigns against the project, focusing on air quality and marine life preservation [4] . - Chesapeake Climate Action Network (CCAN) opposes the project advocating for climate action and protection of the Chesapeake Bay [2] . - Earthjustice provides legal support to halt the project, filing lawsuits on behalf of community groups [5] . - Cove Point Natural Heritage Trust works to protect local biodiversity and mitigate industrial impacts [2] . - Local Homeowners' Associations (Cove of Calvert) represent residents' concerns about safety, property values, and quality of life [2] . - Calvert Citizen for a Healthy Community advocates for health and environmental protection through community outreach and awareness campaigns [2] .  - National and Local Politicians (e.g., Senator Ben Cardin, and Congressman Steny Hoyer) raised concerns and called for stricter environmental assessments and oversight [2] . Opponents of the project are expressing concerns about public health, safety, and the environment. For example, local residents fear an increase in respiratory illnesses due to high levels of nitrogen oxide and particulate emissions for the terminal's operations [2] . Methane emissions are also a major concern, as this strong greenhouse gas could increase climate change and contribute to long-term health problems, including headaches and nausea for neighbouring communities. In addition, the risk of industrial accidents, such as explosions or toxic leaks is increased by the proximity of high-pressure pipelines and storage facilities [2] . Fishermen in the Chesapeake Bay region fear that the increased maritime traffic and industrial pollution resulting from LNG exports could significantly harm fish and crab populations, which are cr itical to the local economy  [2] . Residents also fear a deterioration in the local quality of life due to the noise and visual nuisance caused by the industrial infrastructure. The expansion of Cove Point is contributing to the increasing industrialization of the region, putting biodiversity of the Chesapeake Bay at risk [3] . The Bay is home to species of fish and shelfish essential to the local economy, and pollution could affect their habitats. Environmental Justice Organizations (EJOs) like the Sierra Club have raised concerns over the project's environmental impact, particularly the risks posed to marine life and public health, arguing that the expansion of LNG infrastructure contributes to industrialization and ecological degradation [4] . Although natural gas is presented as a cleaner alternative to coal, extracting, transporting, and liquefying it requires large amounts of energy, increasing the project's carbon footprint.  The Sierra Club and other environmental groups such as the CCAN have taken legal action by filing a lawsuit against Dominion Energy, accusing the company of failing to fully assess the potential environmental and health impacts, particularly the effects on the Chesapeake Bay's biodiversity and the community's air quality [5] . However, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) in charge of taking the decision finally approved the project [6] . The EJOs are campaigning for a switch to renewable energies, believing that the expansion of fossil fuel infrastructure is a step backwards in the fight against climate change.  One of the main points of controversy is the proximity of the terminal to residential areas. The residents of Cove Point live less than two kilometers from the facility and are exposed to risks related to pollution and industrial accidents. In addition, the deterioration in air quality, the increase in maritime traffic, and the activities linked to the terminal could affect people's health, particularly by increasing the risk of respiratory illnesses [7] ,  or poisoning due to water contamination [8] . The Cove Point project illustrates the growing tension between perceived economic benefits, as defined by Dominion Energy and local authorities, and environmental protection. Dominion Energy claims that the expansion of the facility is economically beneficial because of job creation, increased local revenues and its contribution to US energy exports. However, these benefits are essentially based on short-term gains that do not take into account external costs, such as environmental degradation and public health risks. As Kapp (1950) pointed out in The Social Costs of Private Enterprise, these economic evaluations often neglect the long-term social and environmental impacts, passing on these hidden costs to local communities and ecosystems [9] .

case_name: Goldboro LNG Terminal, Nova Scotia, Canada
headline: The Goldboro LNG Terminal, a major fossil fuel infrastructure project in Nova Scotia, faced opposition from environmental and Indigenous groups over concerns about environmental degradation, land rights, and the global climate crisis, leading to its cancellation in 2023.
description: Goldboro LNG Terminal was a proposed liquefied natural gas (LNG) export terminal with a 10 mtpa capacity located in the rural community of Goldboro, Nova Scotia, Canada  [1] . The project was presented by Pieridae Energy in the early 2010s, with the intention of exporting Canadian natural gas to European markets, in particular Germany. The project attracted attention because it promised substantial economic benefits including job creation, economic growth and improved infrastructure in the region. However, the environmental, social and economic costs associated with the project were at the centre of the dispute. The project was developed within a national and historical context marked by Canada’s long-standing dependence on resource extraction and its ongoing transition toward cleaner energy sources. As a country historically reliant on oil and gas industries, particularly in the western provinces, Canada has built much of its economic development around hydrocarbon exploitation. However, since the early 2000s, the Canadian government has adopted stricter climate policies, including a carbon tax and international commitments such as the Paris Agreement, aiming to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Within this framework, the Goldboro LNG project represented both an economic opportunity and an environmental challenge. It sought to capitalize on Europe’s growing demand for natural gas, especially as Germany aimed to reduce its reliance on Russian gas. However, it quickly faced strong opposition both locally and internationally due to its ecological and social implications  [2]  . The project was to build a liquefied natural gas (LNG) export terminal on the east coast of Nova Scotia, which would make it the first in Atlantic Canada. The Goldboro LNG project planned to construct a natural gas liquefaction facility consisting of two liquefaction trains, each with a capacity of 4.8 to 5 million tonnes per annum (Mtpa), for a total estimated production of 9.6 to 10 Mtpa . The site was to include three LNG storage tanks, each with a capacity of 230,000 cubic meters, totaling 690,000 cubic meters of storage. The marine infrastructure included a 1.8 km-long jetty with two loading berths, capable of accommodating LNG carriers ranging from 125,000 to 266,000 cubic meters. To meet the facility’s energy demands, a 180 MW natural gas-fired power plant was also planned on-site [19] . The terminal was set to be connected to the Maritimes & Northeast Pipeline for its natural gas supply, primarily sourced from Western Canada for export to Europe . The aim of the project was to export natural gas by ship, mainly to Germany, which was seeking to reduce its dependence on Russian gas.  Initially, the project looked promising, with local governments expressing support because of the potential economic benefits. Nova Scotia’s Minister of Environment at the time, Randy Delorey, granted conditional environmental approval for the project in March 2014, highlighting its potential to transform Goldboro into an “energy hub” for the province. Also, according to Pieridae Energy, the project would have created approximately 3,500 jobs during construction and 280 permanent jobs once operational, thereby stimulating the local economy  [16] .  However, it soon encountered strong opposition from environmental groups, indigenous communities and some local residents. Opposition focused primarily on the environmental, social and economic impacts that the project would have on the region, which is known for its natural landscapes and ecosystems. One concrete aspect of the environmental impact that the project could have had on the region concerns the destruction of natural habitats and the risks to marine and terrestrial species. The construction of the LNG terminal would have required extensive infrastructure, which would have damaged the coastline and disrupted local biodiversity. Although Pieridae Energy obtained some initial approvals, it received a “provincial environmental assessment and approval in 2014”  [2] , the project has experienced numerous delays and financial obstacles. In 2022, Pieridae Energy scaled back its plans and the future of the Goldboro LNG project remained uncertain until it decided to cancel the project in the company's financial and operating results for the third quarter of 2023 [3] .  The company plans to sell the project's permits by June 2024, ending a 12-year saga.  The Goldboro project was cancelled after report of financial challenges surfaced and the decision of the Nova Scotia court of appeal. This decision was made after a series of court cases between Pieridae Energy and Indigenous groups and other relevant stakeholders. Pieridae Energy had requested for a loan of $4.5 billion from Germany but only received a letter of intent. The project lacked adequate funding after news of its internal financial situation became public. Evironmental activists led by Andy Gheorghiu wrote a letter to the parliament to deny Pieridae energy its request for almost $1 billion. Pieridae energy filed lawsuits began as a verdict in favor of Peridae Energy in 2022 but after a successful appeal, the Nova Scotia court of Appeal in 2023 overturned the initial verdict in favor of the Mi'kamq indigenous people represented by Ecojustice on the subject of Public Interest Standing. [4]   The cancellation of the Goldboro LNG project was the result of sustained mobilization by environmental and Indigenous groups, coupled with financial and legal setbacks [18] . Beyond legal victories, activists leveraged transnational advocacy networks to pressure potential European investors, particularly in Germany, where public opposition to LNG expansion played a role in dissuading financial backing. The Mi'kmaq Nation, supported by legal representatives from Ecojustice, secured a significant court ruling in 2023 that reinforced Indigenous rights in environmental decision-making [18] . This decision, combined with a shift in energy policies favoring renewables, rendered Goldboro LNG financially untenable, leading to Pieridae Energy’s final decision to sell its assets in 2024. The environmental concerns surrounding the Goldboro LNG Terminal project have been significant. One of the primary issues was the increase in carbon emissions due to the large-scale fossil fuel extraction, transportation, and processing involved in LNG production. The construction and operation of the terminal posed threats to local ecosystems, including potential habitat destruction and water pollution. The risk of accidents, such as gas leaks or spills, raised concerns about long-term damage to marine and terrestrial habitats. Additionally, the LNG export industry contributes to global climate change through the release of methane and other greenhouse gases.  Socially, the project faced significant opposition from local communities and Indigenous groups, particularly the Mi'kmaq people, due to concerns about environmental degradation and threats to their traditional way of life. A major point of contention was the proposed 5,000-person work camp, often referred to as a "man camp," which many feared would pose unacceptable risks to women's safety. [4]  This concern was underscored by the National Inquiry into Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls, which highlighted that such camps associated with resource extraction projects have been linked to increased violence against Indigenous women, including higher rates of sexual assault and harassment. [14]    Within the Mi'kmaq Nation, there was notable intra-community conflict regarding the project. While the 13 Mi'kmaq bands in Nova Scotia initially signed an agreement to provide catering and cleaning services for the camps, grassroots members, particularly women, felt excluded from the decision-making process and voiced strong opposition. For instance, Mi'kmaq grandmothers and their supporters held ceremonies at the proposed site to protest the project, emphasizing that community members were not consulted and expressing fears about the potential dangers posed by the influx of transient workers.  Additionally, Chief Mike Sack of the Sipekne'katik First Nation publicly withdrew support for the project, citing safety concerns for women, and criticized the Mi'kmaq Rights Initiative (KMKNO) for overruling his stance. [15]   This division highlighted the complexities within the Mi'kmaq community, as leadership and grassroots members grappled with balancing potential economic benefits against the social and cultural risks associated with the project. Beyond the Indigenous communities, residents of Goldboro and nearby areas also expressed concerns about potential displacement, noise pollution, and long-term impacts on the rural landscape. Opponents of the Goldboro LNG project employed various forms of mobilization to express their opposition and attempt to halt its development. In May 2021, eight environmental organizations, including Ecojustice, sent a letter to the federal Minister of Environment and the President of the Impact Assessment Agency of Canada, requesting a comprehensive and updated federal review of the project. They argued that previous assessments were outdated and failed to consider Canada’s current climate commitments [17] . At the same time, legal actions were initiated to challenge specific aspects of the project. In July 2021, Ecojustice, representing the Ecology Action Centre and the New Brunswick Anti-Shale Gas Alliance, filed for a judicial review regarding the realignment of Route 316 due to environmental risks, including potential contamination from historic gold mines in the area [18] .  These legal efforts aimed to highlight the shortcomings of previous environmental assessments and to demand proper consideration of the project’s environmental and social impacts. Additionally, awareness campaigns were launched to inform the public and mobilize opposition, emphasizing the risks to the environment, local communities, and Canada’s climate commitments. T he economic impacts of the project were multifaceted. It promised to bring much-needed jobs “approximately 200 once it is built to operate on site and 23 000 annually“  [5]   according to Pieridae Energy and economic investment to a rural area, which had suffered from population decline and lack of industrial development. However, there were doubts about the sustainability of these economic benefits, particularly in light of the global shift towards renewable energy sources and the eventual decline of fossil fuel markets. Additionally, some argued that the economic benefits would be unevenly distributed, with large corporations reaping most of the profits, while local communities will have to bear the environmental costs. The Goldboro LNG Terminal project involved several key actors with diverse roles and interests. Pieridae Energy, the project developer, aimed to establish the terminal as a major hub for exporting Canadian natural gas to European markets. The Mi’kmaq First Nation, whose ancestral lands were impacted by the project, opposed the terminal, citing concerns about environmental  degradation and violations of their treaty rights.“Several Mi’kmaq women have been posting critical comments on Facebook“  [6] . Environmental organizations like the Ecology Action Centre and Sierra Club Canada were also vocal critics, raising alarms over the potential harm to marine ecosystems, greenhouse gas emissions, and risks to local water resources. Local communities near Goldboro were concerned about the health and safety risks posed by the terminal, particularly regarding air quality, water contamination, and explosion risks. On the governmental side, the Nova Scotia provincial government supported the project for its potential economic benefits, though this support faced criticism for overlooking environmental and social justice concerns raised by residents and Indigenous groups. Detailed timeline of the Goldboro project :  - June 2013: Pieridae Energy entered into a 20-year agreement with E.ON Global Commodities for the annual supply of 5 million tonnes of LNG from the facility. - December 2015: The company acquired approximately 265.5 acres (107.5 hectares) of land from the Municipality of the District of Guysborough to construct the proposed facility. - June 2017: The initial agreement with E.ON was amended to supply 4.8 million tonnes per annum (Mtpa) of LNG. - July 2019: Construction of the Goldboro LNG facility was postponed until the end of September 2020. - July 2020: Kellogg Brown & Root Ltd. (KBR), initially contracted for a fixed-price engineering, procurement, construction, and commissioning (EPCC) contract, withdrew from the agreement, citing a shift away from lump-sum projects. - June 2021: Pieridae Energy missed its final investment decision (FID) deadline due to cost pressures and financing challenges, leading to the shelving of the current project proposal. - July 2021: Environmental groups, including Ecojustice, launched a judicial review challenging the rerouting of Highway 316, a development essential for the project's progression. - February 2023: The Nova Scotia Court of Appeal granted public interest standing to environmental groups, allowing them to challenge the project's environmental approval. - November 2023: Pieridae Energy announced plans to sell its Goldboro unit and associated assets, signaling a shift away from LNG projects. - July 2024: The sale of the Goldboro unit was completed for CAD 12 million, effectively concluding Pieridae's involvement in the project. [20]

case_name: Kribi Deep sea port, Cameroon
headline: The Kribi Deep-Sea Port in Cameroon promises to boost regional economic growth but instead causes significant environmental and social issues, including deforestation, coastal degradation, and displacement of local populations.
description: The Kribi Deep Sea Port, is an important infrastructural development initiated by the government of Cameroon. The project is located in the south of Cameroon and is a world-class port designed to accommodate larger vessels, which cannot dock at the Port of Douala due to its capacity and depth limitations. This port handled 95% of the country's imports and exports. The Cameroonian government first started conceptualizing the project in early 2000s, and in 2008, China Harbour Engineering Company was selected as the contractor of the first phase, valued at USD 655 million, that was initiated officially in 2012. This phase was funded by the Export-Import Bank of China (EXIM Bank) that covered 85% of the costs, while the Cameroonian government covered 15%. The first phase of the project containing a 350 meter quay and depth of 15 meters was completed in 2015 [1] [2] . The port aims to facilitate the export of raw materials, like timber, aluminum, liquified natural gas and other commodities, aligning with Cameroon’s Vision 2035 for socio-economic emergence [3] . A second phase of the project is now under construction, and there is a third phase plan to expand the capacity and infrastructure of the port. [4] One of the key infrastructure components is a Liquified Natural Gas (LNG) terminal. This project is led by the French company Perenco, in collaboration with Cameroon's National Hydrocarbons Company and the French company Engie [7] . The LNG terminal is designed to handle around 3.5 million cubic meters of the fuel annually. This facility plays a crucial role in positioning Kribi as a major player in the regional energy sector. [6] This project promises to boost Cameroon's economy [1] but its environmental and social impact have been widely diffused among the media and researchers.  The Kribi Deep Sea Port construction has raised environmental concerns, particularly regarding deforestation and marine biodiversity [2] . For the construction of the first phase, approximately 60 hectares of forest were destroyed for the construction, affecting biodiversity and risking the loss of wildlife. The development also disrupts the marine ecosystem with noise impacting fish stocks that are essential for the local communities that depend on fishing [1] . The construction also led to changes in the water quality due to pollution risks from shipping activities. Environmental NGOs have voiced concerns about the environmental impact assessment (EIA) process, denouncing that the project's rapid pace may have overlooked critical environmental aspects. Collaborative efforts with international environmental organizations aim to reduce the ecological footprint of the project [1] . One of the port activities is an LNG terminal and it can lead to increased emissions of methane known as  “methane slip” which contributes to air pollution. While spills of LNG tend to cause less environmental damage than those of heavier fuels due to its rapid vaporization, there are still risks. These include localized cooling of water surfaces and potential toxicity of methane at higher concentrations [8] , which can affect marine biodiversity. Regarding the social impacts of the development, the Kribi Deep Sea port has had mixed effects on local communities. While the project generated around 2,000 direct jobs in the community during the first phase [1] , around 60,000 people have been displaced affecting traditional communities and fishermen [5] .  Compensation programs were implemented, but they were seen as inadequate by the locals, leading to dissatisfaction and protests [1] [2] .  The principal communities that were reallocated were from the villages of Lolabé and Nlendé-Dibé. These movements disrupted their traditional lifestyles and social cohesion. Some jobs were created, but many positions were temporary and local workers competed with foreign laborers particularly from China that were brought by the construction company [3] . Communities have been affected and tensions have grown by the dissatisfaction with compensations and amenities in the relocation sites [3] . The Kribi Deep Sea port is expected to transform Cameroon’s trade industry. The aim is for the country to be able to handle large container ships and reduce the dependency on the smaller Douala port reaching an annual capacity of 1.5 million tonnes of cargo. The port's development is expected to facilitate greater foreign direct investment and improve Cameroon’s logistical infrastructure [1] . The LNG facility will support the export of natural gas resources, contributing to the industrial and economic growth of the country by increasing the country’s capacity to manage large-scale energy exports [6] . Despite this growth, the distribution of the economic benefits is concerning. The local communities fear they will not fully benefit from the economic growth as flows could go directly to multinational companies and foreign investors involved in the port’s operations [2] [3] . The potential for increased trade flow is tempered by the possibility of local communities feeling left behind as the port enhances Cameroon’s role as a logistics hub in Central Africa [3] .
