case_name: LNG terminal development at a contaminated DuPont Chemical Site, Greenwich Township, New Jersey
headline: The Repauno Chemical Company initially produced dynamite and other chemicals. The site expanded into producing various organic compounds and materials over the twentieth century. Environmental contamination from hazardous chemicals led to state-mandated cleanups and investigations starting in the 1980s. Now, the polluted site is in the process of being turned into an international shipping port.
description: The Repauno Chemical Company (Repauno) was founded in Gibbstown, New Jersey, on June 7, 1880 by Lammot du Pont, the grandson of the EI du Pont de Nemours Company (DuPont) founder. [1] Repauno produced a range of products including dynamite, acids, nitrobenzene and other organic compounds [2] . Lammot du Pont was killed in an 1884 explosion at the Repauno plant, and DuPont bought the Repauno plant and became the country's largest dynamite producer. In 1902, the Eastern Laboratory, DuPont's first research laboratory, was built at the Repauno site to conduct explosives research. [3] Prior to the onset of environmental regulations in the 1970s, companies did not keep track of and report spills. Records of spills and other releases were kept at the Repauno Site starting in 1976. Between June 4, 1976, and April 03, 2012, 506 records of incidents related to air, soil, water, and unclassified releases occurred at the Site. [3] According to the 2002 Annual Groundwater Progress report, the area previously used by DuPont as a terminal location for anhydrous ammonia is being cleaned for reuse. In addition, several different companies currently lease areas at the Repauno facility. [4]   In the 1980's, a zone on the site, referred to as the Lower Aquifer was discovered to be impacted by contamination of several organic constituents above NJ GWQC, including benzene, TCE, PCE, nitrobenzene, aniline, naphthalene, chlorobenzene, and 2,4-DNT. [4] In 1990, the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection (NJDEP) required DuPont to conduct a Remedial Investigation and Feasibility Study of 12 solid waste management units and 11 areas of concern at the site. [4] 8,500 tons of sediments were removed from the ditches in the former Nitrobenzene and Pyromellitic Dianhydride/Dimethyl Terephthalate production areas. [2] DuPont sold the remaining business operations, with Repauno Products LLC purchasing the manufacturing operation that produced sodium nitrite and nitrosylsulfuric acid in 1998. In 1999, Spring AG purchased the industrial diamond refining operation, which was closed in 2002. Despite the business sales, DuPont retained ownership of the property. [1] As of August 2003, DuPont had completed four phases of the required RI. [4] Due to the contamination, the property was labeled as a brownfield site, a "real property, the expansion, redevelopment, or reuse of which may be complicated by the presence or potential presence of a hazardous substance, pollutant, or contaminant. " [6]   Discussions began of turning the land into a port. In 2009, the Gloucester County Improvement Authority (GCIA) and the township of Greenwich entered into an agreement to be equal partners in the redevelopment of 280 acres of the 1,700-acre property, to build a port. [7] However, the recession stalled the discussions of a port. [7] [8]   In January 2012, the EPA filed a lawsuit against a company that improperly demolished and removed asbestos-tainted materials. The EPA alleged six violations of the federal Clean Air Act and the National Emission Standard for Hazardous Air Pollutants (NESHAP) regarding asbestos. “Lovett failed to take required precautions in demolishing or removing about 5,000 feet of piping and 3,000 feet of pipe insulation with amounts of asbestos that could be exposed to the air…The EPA is asking the court to assess a $32,000 penalty per violation, per day , on the company. It's also asking for the costs of the suit.” [9]   While several businesses were making bids for the land in August 2012, the mayor, George Shivery was quoted saying “I feel like we need something clean, that won't have a possible affect[sic] on the land or health” , including that Greenwich township has “first right of refusal” on any project, and would use it if the plan would negatively affect the land. [10] On February 1, 2015 DuPont's spinoff company, Chemours FC, LLC became a new site's owner. In August of 2015, State Senate President Steve Sweeney held a press conference announcing the sale of the entire property to Fortress Investment Group. The price of the sale was not disclosed. [11] The investment group “aimed to turn the dormant 1,800-acre property into a port-related industrial park for imports and exports.” [12]   On June 30, 2016, Chemours sold approximately 125 acres located along the Delaware River in the north-central portion of the property to Fortress Investment Group, who passed the property off to a subsidiary company, the Delaware River Partners LLC, who renamed the site the Repauno Port and Rail Terminal in the summer of 2016. [13] “Chemours retained all responsibility for the necessary remediation and other activities related to the contamination present on the property sold to Delaware River Partners, LLC.” [3] The plans still encompassed creating an industrial park “including a number of cold storage warehouses, underground storage tanks for butane, and an eventual port for importing and exporting goods.” Another planner stated that the plan would include “a working port for cold storage of fresh and frozen fruits and flowers. The site would also work as a new vehicle receiving depot and a location of fuel activities.” Initially, the plan had included the storage of liquid natural gas, but after the Sierra Club Chapter of New Jersey (SCCNJ) mobilized support against it, the plan was altered to store butane instead. The director of SCCNJ said in response to the proposal for the property "they must come out against this proposal because Delaware River Partners plans to transport hazardous materials through communities and ship them right on the Delaware River. This facility will have greater safety implications for people living near the River, while threatening our public health and the environment".  [14] Additional mobilization occurred with the creation of the Concerned Citizens for the Redevelopment of the Repauno Site (CCRRS), who called for the property to continue to be remediated, but not developed into a highly trafficked area. [14]   In 2017, a proposal was submitted by DRP for the state to approve a “Delaware River dredging and deep water berth construction project for the proposed DRP Gibbstown Logistics Center, a multi-use marine terminal and international logistics center. The project involves dredging 371,000 cubic yards (cy) of sediment from the Delaware River, to a depth of 40 feet below (-40) mean lower low water (MLLW) to construct the deep-water berth. The project also involves demolition of the existing wharf and bulkhead, along with the construction of a new bulkhead, a new pile-supported wharf structure, and six new storm water outfall structures.” [15]   A “duly noticed” public hearing was mentioned in the proposal. [15] On March 27th, 2019, The NJDEP Commissioner announced and filed 4 new, public lawsuits organized by the New Jersey Department Of Environmental Protection; The Commissioner Of The New Jersey Department Of Environmental Protection; And The Administrator Of The New Jersey Spill Compensation Fund against DuPont, Chemours, and 3M. Part of the lawsuit focuses on contamination of groundwater, surface water, and other natural resources caused by releases of volatile and semi-volatile organic compounds, mercury, lead and other contaminants from the DuPont Repauno site. [16] [3] [17] In April 2019, Former President Donald Trump issued an executive order expediting the approval of energy infrastructure, including but not limited to oil and gas pipelines. [18] An additional order was issued that removed much of the steps required of companies obtaining permits for infrastructure projects involving US international borders, such as bridges, tunnels, pipelines, or land transportation routes. [19]   [20] Despite immense protest from environmentalists at a public hearing, [21] the Delaware River Basin Commission unanimously approved the proposal to dredge a portion of the river and build a $96 million 1,600-foot-long pier to load tankers in June 2019. The DRP proposed to export large volumes of liquid fuels produced from fracking Pennsylvania shale gas wells, and it was approved. [22] One journalist, Meg McGuire, wrote of the hearing: “The usual routine for the DRBC is to gather (and study) between 15 and 30 "dockets' (its word for projects) and present them together at a public hearing where speakers can address the commissioners about any of the projects on the list (or submit written comments for a period of time.). Last Thursday, June 6, 2019, the DRBC called an unusual public hearing for a single project…And with a limited written public comment period that ended about 24 hours after the hearing.” [23]     Upon contacting both the DRBC, McGuire was directed to contact the NJDEP. It was then that the NJDEP disclosed in a “commitment to transparency and public engagement, including in its permit review process” that on May 20, 2019, the NJDEP had issued a Waterfront Development Individual Permit to Delaware River Partners. On June 5, 2019, the DEP had suspended the permit due to a procedural error. Corrective notice was published in the DEP Bulletin on June 5, 2019, with a 15-day public comment period from that date, at which point the DEP would reconsider the permit. [23] Activists rallied against this proposal, and formed a coalition, EMPOWER NJ. [24] In December 2019, the Trump administration approved the shipment of liquefied natural gas from fracking fields in Pennsylvania to the Repauno Site.  [25] The Trump era LNG by rail rule allows for trains with up to 100 tank cars, each with upwards of 30,000 gallons of LNG, to move through the country's cities and towns. [26] The New Jersey State, along with 14 other states, filed a challenge to the federal rule with the US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit on August, 18th, 2020. [27] Simultaneously, six environmental advocacy groups, represented by the nonprofit environmental law organization filed a separate challenge to overturn the rule. In response, the DRP filed a petition to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission  for a declaratory order, a loophole that would make LNG operations at the site not subject to the approval of the federal agency in September of 2020. [28] [29]   The Delaware Riverkeeper Network filed a challenge to the petition. [30]   In December 2020, despite the massive mobilization efforts by environmentalist groups and the community, the 2017 petition to dredge part of the Delaware River and to construct a new wharf designated specifically for LNG export was approved in a 4-0 vote. [31] [32] In November 2021, PHMSA, with the Federal Railroad Administration, proposed reversing the 2020 rule by the Trump administration that broadly allowed LNG by rail. “PHMSA said it had received 7,000 comments about reversing the Trump-era rule.” [33] In May 2022, the NJDEP proposed new rules to regulate underground storage caverns for holding “any natural or artificial gas, or any petroleum product or derivative of any petroleum product.” [34] In August 2022, an in-depth article was published regarding the May NJDEP proposal and environmental justice and overburdened communities impacted by underground storage in New Jersey [35]   In 2023, The US Department of Transportation denied the 2020 special permit request by Energy Transport Solutions (subsidiary of New Fortress Energy) which would have allowed the transportation of liquefied natural gas by rail to the Repauno port. [36] [37] [38] .

case_name: Offshore LNG Terminal, Hong Kong
headline: Hong Kong constructed an offshore Liquid Natural Gas (LNG) terminal to enhance its energy security and allegedly support its transition to cleaner energy. However, the Project has been criticized for creating environmental risk to the surrounding marine environment.
description: The LNG Terminal is located near the Soko Islands, offshore Hong Kong, in open waters approximately 4 km east of the nearest land mass, Tau Lo Chau. The location was chosen after a thorough site selection process that included engineering and marine/met-ocean studies. At least 15 meters of water are present at the site. The proposed South Lantau Marine Park (SLMP) is located northwest of the LNG Terminal Site. There is open water to the south of the site for about 500 meters , after which the South China Sea and the HKSAR waters' border are reached. The Sediment Disposal Area, which is operational and used for the disposal of uncontaminated sediment, is located east of the Site. [1] The Hong Kong offshore LNG terminal (the Project) is the world’s largest floating storage and regasification unit . It is the first LNG import terminal project to make use of a F loating S torage and R egasification U nit (FSRU) technology in Hong Kong. Construction of the terminal was completed in November 2022 , and it began commercial operations in 2023 ​ [2] ​ . The terminal is a joint venture owned by a collaboration of CLP Power and HK Energy, forming the Hong Kong LNG Terminal Ltd. (HKLTL) ​ [1] .    The terminal comprises an offshore jetty, where the Japanese owned vessel, Bauhinia Spirit is moored. The jetty and vessel feed natural gas through a 45 km long pipeline connecting the terminal to mainland Hong Kong ​ [3] . In an effort to lower emissions and enhance air quality, the HKSAR government caps the emissions of power plants. The HKSAR Government has established a n emissions policy , and to accomplish th e goal s , they created a target fuel mix of approximately 50% natural gas-fired power generation by 2020 [4] .   The terminal is owned by the Hong Kong LNG Terminal Limited (HKLTL). T he HKLTL’s ownership is divided between the CLP Power Hong Kong Limited (CLP Power) , which owns 49% of the corporation, China Southern Power Grid International (HK) Company (21%), and the Hong Kong Electric Company Limited (HK Electric), which owns 30%. ​ [5] . The purpose of the offshore terminal is to supply gas to two power plants in the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (SAR). The goal of the initiative is to alter the Black Point and Lamma power plants' current supply chains. They used to rely on gas supplies from the Chinese mainland, but now they get their natural gas from the offshore terminal, including double berth jetty, subsea gas pipelines, and gas receiving stations.   The terminal was conceptualized in response to the 201 5 Paris Agreement and its Climate Change Action Plan, pegging Natural Gas as a transition fuel on Hong Kong’s path toward carbon neutrality by 2050. Indeed, the Hong Kong government argues that the LNG terminal project is a key step towards ensuring the region’s energy security and meeting its carbon reduction commitments. It argue that LNG is a fuel needed for the transition to cleaner energy, replacing coal while closing the gap until renewable energy sources can meet energy demands [9] . Nevertheless, a study by Robert Howarth of Cornell University, showed that when LNG is taken over its entire life cycle, the greenhouse gas footprint for LNG as a fuel source is 33% higher than that of coal when analyzed using GWP20. Also, even with the 100-year post-emission time (GWP100), which seriously underestimates methane climate damage, the LNG footprint is equal to or greater than that of coal, according to this study [10] . The largest opposition to the Project is from the environmental justice organization the World Wildlife Fund (WWF), expressing concerns for the potential adverse impacts to the marine environment ​ [6] ; specifically, to the White Chinese Dolphin and Finless Porpoise. The WWF identifies that the Project is located in the Soko Waters, where a Marine Con servation Park was proposed in 2002 . It states that the Agriculture, Fisheries, and Conservation Department have not co mmented on the Project . However, the Agriculture and Fisheries are represented in the Project’s Stakeholder Liaison Group ​ [1] . The WWF also states the Project could impact the conservation of fisheries resources and fish stocks, which would affect the local fisherman ​ [6] ​ .    A petition on Change.org initiated by Kevin Laurie opposes the Project due to the Environmental Impact Assessment being “not-fit-for-purpose ”, which excludes the impacts to Green Turtles, Whale Sharks, and Birds ​ [7] ​ ​ . The petition was signed by 909 people.    Additionally, a news release from “ myNews ” expressed that the LNG terminal intends to replace coal power generation, but that environmentalists criticize the use of LNG as a hydrocarbon that still contributes to greenhouse gas emissions ​ [8] . The article includes that the Project could also impact electricity prices for 1.5 million households ​ [8] .    In response to environmental concerns, the project’s developers have promised to implement strict mitigation measures, such as restricting construction during certain times of the year to avoid disturbing marine species’ breeding seasons , as well as setting up environmental monitoring programs ​ ​ [3] . However, critics view these measures as insufficient, continuing to call for more thorough impact studies and greater public transparency in the consultation process ​ [4] ​ [2] ​ .   Furthermore, there is opposition to the project based on the merit that LNG is not renewable, and still produces greenhouse gas emissions. Critics argue that wind or other renewable power sources would make better, more long term and climate smart investments. Perhaps future government policies will become stricter to combat climate change , and the investments in LNG will not be long term ​ [4] .   Finally, part of the controversy is fueled by concerns that this project could affect electricity prices for consumers. While authorities claim that terminal will help stabilize supplies and keep prices affordable, critics warn that increased reliance on LNG, a resource still subject to volatile global markets, could lead to higher costs for households and businesses   [4] .

case_name: Toyuan Liquid Natural Gas (LNG) Terminal, Taiwan
headline: Plans to extend an LNG facility off the coast of Taiwan are met with protest from local campaigners, scientists, politicians, and doctors. The plans will devastate rare coral reefs, potentially harming thousands of species.
description: Toayuan Liquid Natural Gas (LNG) terminal will be Taiwan's 4th terminal, and is located in the Guantang Industrial Area which spans around 764.1 hectares in Taoyuan [2] . The first phase of the project was completed and operational by 2023, while the second phase is still under construction and is proposed to be complete by 2025.  [1] The project will be the third of its kind that is owned by the country's state-owned petrol and natural gas company China Petroleum Corporation (CPC Corporation).  [1]  The project will cost ¥96.562 billion (13.68 billion USD), and will have a total capacity of 3 million tonnes per annum.  [1]  Yet, scientists, local politicians from the Kuomintang (KMT) party (Chinese Nationalist Party) and environmental groups of Taiwan are campaigning to stop the planned construction , on the basis that it will cause permanent damage to the unique algal reef ecosystem , which will have reverberating impacts for wider oceanic health.  [1]  This is partly because the construction company and CPC have proposed to use land reclamation as part of the plans to build this new LNG, and partly due to the disruption to natural sand movement that the build could cause - potentially damaging the reef but exposing it to strong waves or burying it completely under displaced sand .  [6]   [1] Taiwan is still dependent on coal-fired plants - in 2020, 41.5% of its electricity came from these facilities, 40.1% came from natural gas, 14.4% from nuclear power and 5.8% from renewables.  [8] Those in favour of the new LNG facility believe it is key to helping them phase out coal by 2025.  [8] Timeline of resistance The beginning of the resistance can be traced back to 2007, when Taiwanese environmental groups such as Citizens of the Earth, Taiwan (CET), the Taiwan Environmental Information Association (TEIA) and the Society of Wildness began campaigning against construction projects in the area on the grounds of protecting Taoyuan´s slow-forming Datan Algal Reefs.  [1]  These reefs have built up for over 7500 years, through a process of calcification and accumulation of deposits of shoals of fish and spans 27 km along the northwest coast.  [3] It was on this basis that groups began campaigning, and their struggle against corporate and government interests continues 7 years on, and counting.  In October 2018, the environmental impact assessment (EIA) was passed, much to environmental groups dismay. The only amendment was that the project size was reduced from 230 to 23 hectares, and CPC had to pledge that they would build 20 metre wave breakers to 'protect' the coral reefs.  [11] Following the decision, demonstrations took place against the project in Taipei on November 3rd, 2018, during which thousands of people took to the streets to express their frustration with the government's energy plans. It was organised by Clean Air Taiwan, who is led by a doctor of Chang-Hua Christian Hospital - Dr Yen Guan-Perng. During the protest speeches, Professor Lin Hui-chen who teaches in the department of life sciences at Tughai University asked the public -”if the Formosan cypress trees over 1,000 year-old are always well protected and preserved in Taiwan high mountains, why the algal reefs grown over 7,600 years-old along the coast of Datan Borough in Guanyin District should be wiped out for LNG terminal?”.  [10] On 8th December 2021, the country held the much-anticipated referendum vote on 4 subjects that had much importance for the people of Taiwan. It was originally meant to be held on the 28th of August 2021, but was postponed due to covid-19. The first was on Algae and Energy, second was on pork imports containing ractopork from the USA, third was on nuclear energy and the fourth was about lowering the number of referendum days, as increasingly referendums are used by the KMT and the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) in political strategizing against each other, often simply making the complete opposite vote from their opponent despite this not always aligning with their “party politics”.  [4] The Algae and Energy referendum question asked “Do you agree that the Keelung City Government should reject the Hsieh-ho Power Plant and its affiliated LNG terminal to reclaim land from waters off Keelung?”  [6]  and specifically saw the DPP party in favour of the Toayuan terminal, stating that it was a necessary step in the move away from nuclear energy and strives towards improving the country's energy security in the case that China were to invade or blockade energy resources to the island. Leaving environmental groups feeling let down by the DPP, as this is the opposite of how the debate around the terminal began in the 1990s - when it was right-wing KMT who proposed the project, while the DPP party sided with environmental activists against their motion.  [4] This motion became highly politicised in the country, while traditionally the environmentalists - including politicians from the Green Party - have sided with the DPP, they are now in fear of speaking up about the issue for fears of being smeared as “pro China” in siding with the KMT  [4] . Jiang Qichen of the nationalist KMT party, in a lengthy post to his Facebook page in February 2021, conveyed his support for the campaign behind the coral coast of Taoyuan and his disdain with the DPP.  [5] The referendum was rejected. [7] With official results showing that 4,163,464 people voted against and 3,901,171 voted in favour. [9]  This included rejecting the amendment to move the project an additional 750 metres offshore (which would have made it 1200 metres from shore, rather than 450 metres).  [9]  Environmentalist Pan Chong-cheng (潘忠政) who was the individual to first initiate the referendum responded to the result, stating - “We cannot lose heart over the result, as there is still plenty of work for us to do to continue protecting the algal reefs”  [9] . He then went on to attribute the referendum's failure to the ruling DPP party, stating that there had been false information spread by officials of the government.  [9]  He stated that “We gained widespread support among young people when collecting signatures, but today the ratio of young people who voted in the referendum is much lower than expected... Why? I think some of them received false information, could not make up their mind and chose not to vote”.  [9] In March 2022 the Taiwanese Environmental Protection Agency approved the construction of the project.  [1] As of 2024, the project was halfway complete and is still expected to be operational by 2025. Protests against it, for the rights of the ocean ecosystems, continue.  [1]

case_name: Sidakarya-Bali LNG, Indonesia
headline: Construction of the Sidakarya-Bali LNG threatens cultural sites, mangrove systems and coral reefs. The project has been heavily opposed by the desa adat Intaran Sanur people, environmental groups and student groups in Bali.
description: The Sidakarya LNG in Bali was originally proposed to be located at Benoa Harbor, before being relocated to the coast of Sidakarya. The relocation troubled the people of the Intaran Sanur Traditional Village, as the chosen location was in close proximity to sacred cultural sites. Once more, it will impact delicate mangrove and coral reef ecosystems. Environmental group Wahli (friends of the earth Indonesia) together with student groups and political parties have also joined forces with the neighbours of the Desa Adat (traditional village) Intaran Sanur to try and halt the project before it is due to be built in 2023.   The project is owned by the Bali Province Regional Company PT Dewata Energi Bersih (DEB) together with PT PLN (Persero) through its subsidiary PT PLN Gas and Geothermal [9] . A memorandum of understanding was signed between the governor of Bali and the PLN on 21st of August 2019, which stipulated that if the governor provides the land, the appointed company will manage it. The LNG receives its gas from the BP Tangguh LNG project in Papua, Indonesia, which is operated by BP. [12]  The gas that Sidakarya receives will be used domestically, including power generation in Bali and some other regions of Indonesia.  [13] Timeline of project and resistance  Over 12,400 village residents in Intaran have united in opposition to the project [7] . And on 22nd of May 2022, the Socialization of the Bali Sidakarya LNG Terminal Project Plan meeting was held at Madu Sedana Meeting Hall in Intaran. It was a public consultation meeting hosted by the project owners, Dewata Clean Energy and Perusda Bali.  [1] This meeting was held only after official permits had been granted - meaning the Intaran Sanur and Walhi were only ‘involved’ in decision making subsequent to the approval of the project.  [7]   First, the companies had proposed that the LNG was to be located in the Benoa Harbor Area, yet by this meeting they had already changed the location, relocating just east of the harbour to the coast of Sidakarya. During the meeting, the director of Walhi Bali (known globally as Friends of the Earth Indonesia) [2] , Made Krisna Dinata, conveyed the organisations’ concerns around how the presence of an LNG Terminal in this coastal area would destroy sacred areas, most notably the temple in the Intaran Sanur Traditional Village which is located near to the second proposed LNG location. Additionally, he pointed out the existence of 6 more sacred temple points along this coast that would be disrupted by the LNG build and subsequent activity.  [1]  As the construction would involve dredging of 3,300,000 m3 of the sea channel, Dinata argued that “accelerate abrasion and will certainly threaten the temples on the coast”.  [1]  Others who supported Walhi Bali’s plan-rejections included Desa Adat Intaran, the NGO Kekal Bali (Environmental Advocacy Working Committee), and the student movement Frontier Bali.  [3] Another point raised was around the ecosystem impacts of the build - more specifically, the impact on the vast and treasured mangrove forest system as well as coral reefs on the coastline. Both are crucial in protecting the land and ocean ecosystems from tsunamis  [3] . The mangroves in the selected area reach 5 - 10 metres high, which demonstrates how mature this particular system is, the sheer length of time that they have had to grow and evolve.  [4] Mangrove systems help to bind loose soils, and only develop in very particular conditions depending on water acidity, tidal flows and soil type.  [5] Following the consultation, members of 7 banjars (‘neighbourhoods’) each erected billboards that conveyed their rejection of the plans to build an LNG terminal in the mangrove area.  [4]  This move was supported by Bendesa Adat Penyaringan (the head of the traditional village) together with 20 Kelihan Banjar in the Desa Adat Intaran region.  [3]  Subsequently, on the 9th of June 2022 which is also known locally as ‘Umanis Kuningan’ day (traditionally a day of cultural celebrations), a protest was carried out by the Yowana (youth groups) in the Intaran Sanur Traditional Village as well as other members of public.  [3]  During the long march through the streets, they carried banners with slogans reading “We Reject the Revision of the RTRW Which Accommodates the Development of an LNG Terminal in the Mangrove Area '', while wearing traditional balinese clothing [10] . The group walked towards the building of the Representative Council of the Province of Bali and ended the march by visiting the governor's office. Their demands included that the Governor and Representative Council of Bali must review the draft document “Regional Regulation on Spatial Plans for Residents of the Province of Bali”, as this is the document that states that the LNG can be built in the Mangrove area.  [3] Following this, on world mangrove day on 26th June 2022, protesters took to the coastline in boats to plant mangroves in Muntig Siokan, just south west of Sanur.  [3]  In conjunction with this, five Sekeha Jukung and seven Fishermen's Groups in the Intaran Traditional Village carried out a water parade in their boats to protest of the project that would impact their subsistence, slowly travelling up the coastal area.  [3]   A mass prayer was also carried out, called the Segara Kertih. Members of the Desa Adat gathered on the Sanur beach. This prayer called to God to show the project leaders the consequences of the project, if it were to go ahead.  [3] But by October 2022, Walhi were still trying to get Bali Provincial Commission for Public Information to share the documents relating to the proposed construction of an LNG Storage Terminal, and they filed a legal demand on the 6th October 2022, with the Provincial Information Commission and the Provincial Forestry and Environmental Agency with support from two representatives from the Democratic Front for the People’s Struggle – A.A. Gede Surya Sentana and I Wayan Sathya Tirtayasa. As the company plans on installing submarine piping that will transect the mangrove, the group were specifically requesting to see exactly what the environmental assessment of this plan was and if the assessment included the impacts on the Tahura Ngurah Rai Mangrove Area.  It was not until 20th of September 2022, that they received a reply - in the form of total refusal to grant them the public planning documents on the grounds that it must be the companies involved that release the documents.  [6] Yet under the Indonesian law on freedom of information and public disclosure (Pasal 17 of RUU HIP), this refusal is technically illegal, as it requires the Board of Commissioners liable in making such information available to the public, not only the companies.  [6] Once more, senior decision makers also disagreed on the project. While Bali’s Governor Wayan Koster was for the project, the Coordinating Minister for Maritime Affairs and Investment, Luhut Binsar Pandjaitan released several statements calling for the project to be halted.  [8] Latest updates  Despite this, as well as legal and civil actions from the people of Intaran SanurIn 2024, the project is going ahead. Once more, Bali is the chosen location for the 4th IndoPACIFIC LNG Summit 2024 which will take place between the 16th-17th of July 2024 [11] , during which member states learn about "LNGs role in Net Zero Emission" from fossil gas companies who have business interests in the region. The conference is led by the Indonesian Gas Society.

case_name: The Idku LNG Terminal, Egypt
headline: The Idku LNG terminal, Egypt is condemned by local fishers, farmers and members of society who make up the Idku Workers Union. Once more, it is one of the many projects that the international organisation Don't Gas Africa is campaigning against in their fight for a just transition away from fossil fuels and the dismantling of neocolonial oil relations between African nations and the global north.
location: Not specified clearly in live EJAtlas metadata.
description: The Idku LNG Terminal, also known as the Egyptian LNG Terminal or the ELNG Terminal, is located in Beheira, just 50 km east of Alexandria. It comprises two production trains originally only supplied by the Simian Sienna Gas Field and Sapphire Gas Field  [1] . Costing $2 billion, it opened in 2005 and was originally owned by Rashpetco (50% state-run Egyptian General Petroleum Corporation, 50% split between the UK’s BG Group and Malaysia’s Petronas [21] ) but is now operated by Shell Egypt, Egypt’s EGAS and EGPC, Malaysia’s Petronas, and France’s TotalEnergies.  [1]   [11]  Traditionally used for export purposes, it has fluctuated between primarily exporting or importing over the years, most notably in 2015 when it became a net-importer from Israel's Leviathan oil field, following a time of political instability and sustained power outages in Egypt  [1]   [13] . Egypt as a whole holds around 10% of Africa's total gas reserves (2020) [14] , and in 2022 the Egyptian LNG exports increased by 14% to 8 billion cubic metres - the majority of which was sent to Europe.  [35] Idku is the biggest of Egypts two LNG terminals,  [10] and is now supplied by Israeli gas to meet a portion of domestic demand, as well as being used for re-export further afield.  [5]   [32]  In 2023, Egypt’s gas production fell to its lowest level in the past 3 years, while demand for gas both domestically and within export agreements increased.  [5]  This led to an increased dependence on Israeli gas from the Tamar and Leviathan fields which, according to Rystad Energy consultant, exports around 7 billion cubic feet of natural gas per annum from these fields into Egypt.  [6]  In 2014, the undersea pipeline was built to connect Israels Leviathan gas field to Egypts Idku LNG, for transit to EU and Asian markets.  [33] Natural gas exploitation and exploration has been condemned by both local and international civil society groups, as the project has caused many issues that extend beyond simply the extraction of gas. Locally, the community has been fighting against the environmental degradation caused by the project - which has polluted the area and impacted their fishing and agricultural activities since the beginning of its operations. In 2006, the company that was employed by Rashpecto to manage waste from the build, Green Valley, was found to be illegally dumping toxic waste into the Mediterranean Sea.  [20]  Fishers and farmers in the area noticed that this not only impacted fish stocks - namely, the Om al-Kholoul fish - but also guava trees on land. In 2011, the court found Rashpecto liable in the depletion of 2428 hectares of agricultural land.  [21] In 2012, Rashpetco and Green Valley were also involved in illegal dumping of waste from the project. Activists from Idku Workers Union found that GreenValley employees were dumping industrial waste in fields, following the closure of a nearby dump site. Initially, in attempt to tackle this , March 2012 activists would capture GreenValley truck drivers and take them to the police in efforts to prove that they do not have the correct documentation provided when you dump waste legally. Along with lawyers, members of the Workers Union brought the firm to court over the polluting activities.  [21] Globally, the campaign is led by African civil society groups, who organise as Don’t Gas Africa. The group have gathered international support for their cause against the plunder of fossil fuels in African nations to, majoritively, serve the Global North.  [7]   [9] They have done so by producing reports  [14] , films [19] , organisation international street mobilisations and counter summits  [15]   [18] , hosting and participating in webinar series  [17] and circling petitions [16] , campaigning for, as Lorraine Chiponda (the Don’t Gas Africa Campaign facilitator) states, a “clear phase-out of fossil fuels, and an energy transition [without] gas as a transition fuel.”  [18]  And while plans for international gas exportation gain strong traction amongst political leaders, the people of Egypt continue to suffer blackouts and planned power cut offs. For years, Egyptian gas was sold off to Israel, Spain and Jordan for "rock bottom prices"  [37]  while officials of Egyptian-Israeli company amassied huge fortunes. Egyptians question why they are reliant on gas from Israel in the first place, while leaders and strategists know that energy dependancy is beneficial for the exporter (in this case, Israel). Israel did this first with the Palestinian Authority and Jordan, now it has the same export agreements with Lebanon and Egypt.  [31]  Such agreements have had huge impacts on Egyptian society as of late - indeed, following the beginning of the war on Gaza in October 2023, Chevron cut off Egyptian from its two Israeli gas fields (Tamar and Leviathan) as part of their move to prioritise gas supply for Israel.  [30]   Egypt - EU - Israel Natural Gas Relations In 2020, the East Mediterranean Gas Forum (EMGF) was established by representatives of 7 countries (Cyprus, Egypt, France, Greece, Israel, Italy, Jordan, and Palestine), with help from the World Bank  [3] and a collective goal of boosting gas trade between regional states, with Cyprus, Israel and Egypt being the biggest players for export.  [2]  The EU even established the "Economic and Investment Plan of Egypt" which will included mobilising 9 billion euros in food, water and energy investment in the period between 2021 - 2027. By March 2024, already over 5.8 billion euros-worth has been utilised. [29]   Following the war in Ukraine, the EU became increasingly interested in creating a partnership with these suppliers, notably following the June 2022 EMGF meet up in Cairo, the EU, Egypt and Israel signed a trilateral deal to boost gas trade from Israel to EU states, via Egypt. The gas would travel to Egypt via the EMG pipeline and then be exported out of the country to the EU via LNG terminals such as Idku LNG  [10] . Under this agreement, the EU is bound to encourage European oil companies to participate in Israeli and Egyptian exploration tenders.  [2]   Following this, just before Cop27 in 2022, a memorandum of understanding was signed between Germany and Egypt to strengthen partnership on green hydrogen and LNG, entering into an agreement to support the building of “climate friendly energy networks”.  [4] The deal stipulates the intent to expand LNG export capacity by 2050, in the view that while we wait for renewable energy provisioning to increase, we must rely on LNG as a so-called “bridge fuel”  [11]   [12] . Such is the opinion held by many of those in decision making positions as well as oil and gas firms. Yet, the viability of fossil gas as a “transitional fuel” has been widely challenged by a large and growing body of research that highlights the warming impact of methane leakage [14] . For example, back in 2022 African campaigners warned against following along with the EU’s fossil gas push, referring to the danger of locking the continent into fossil fuels for decades to come.  [8] Mohamed Adow, the Director of Power Shift Africa stated “what Africa does not need is to be shackled with expensive fossil fuel infrastructure which will be obsolete in a few years as the climate crisis worsens”  [8] . His words were supported by Lorraine Chiponda, the Africa Coal Network Coordinator, who stated that, “ The prospect that African leaders are presenting and pushing for gas developments and investment is overwhelming and reckless given the climate impacts that threaten the lives of millions of people in Africa having seen worsening droughts and hunger, recurring floods and cyclones. In addition to this as we have seen in the past, the acceleration of gas projects in Africa is another colonial and modern "Scramble and Partition of Africa" amongst energy corporations and "rich" countries. ” While Joab Okanda, Pan Africa Senior Advocacy Advisor from Christian Aid stated,  “The African Union is in danger of falling for the con of African gas at a time when other countries are investing in renewables which will be what powers development and progress in coming decades. It would be the ultimate betrayal of African people if their leaders missed the opportunity to become a renewable energy super power by locking us into a doomed experiment with fossil fuels that is hurting Africa through climate breakdown." Annexing Energy  Once more, deals such as these between the EU and Israel via Egypt are condemned by many due to their reverberated impacts on the Palestinian people.  [34]  In February 2018, the deal signed between Egypt and Israel regarding the undersea gas pipeline connecting to the Idku LNG Facility was said to have left "Palestinians out in the cold".  [36]   It was known that the subsea pipeline alone would contribute to "lethal militarey closure of Gaza's martime space enforced to secure Israel's gas platforms and pipelines". Once more, the two nations did not have explicit consent from the Palestinian Authority regarding the subseacable build, despite it crossing disputed land.  [38]  Moves such as these do not go unnoticed by the Egyptian people, who also have suffered from energy deals between the two governments of Egypt and Israel. Infact many of the Egyptian civil society stand with the Palestinians against Israel's apartheid regime. On October 20th, 2023, a huge protest broke out in Egypt against Israels treatment of Palestinian people - during which protesters called for Egypt to cut all ties with Israel, with even the riot police sent to calm the protest banging from the inside of their van in support of the people's chants.  [34] All of these voices draw attention to the danger, on a local and global scale, of the proposed scale-up of gas infrastructure and provisioning, that would be majoritively for the benefit of countries in the north. Indeed, the agreement between Germany and Egypt, as well as the trilateral agreement between EU, Egypt and Israel 2022 have sought to ensure a smooth transition for the global north while creating a carbon lock in for nations across Africa. They also help compound the genocide that is being inflicted on the Palestinian people, through adding a binding energy relation between Israel and European counties. People are increasingly understanding the attacks being carried out in Palestine as in-part related to the potential oil extraction. The Idku LNG Terminal is a key vector in fossil gas provisioning, and in order for a truly just transition to be carried out, organisations such as Don’t Gas Africa are fighting for the rights of people across the continent.

case_name: Ruwais LNG Terminal in Al Ruwais Industrial City, Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates
headline: Ruwais LNG planned Terminal will export LNG to other countries and other regions of the country. The Terminal’s construction, however, has raised concerns over potential health and safety risks faced by low-skilled migrants’ workers.
description: Liquified Natural Gas (LNG) is seeing an expansion in the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The country is currently exporting 5 mtpa (million tonnes per annum) [11] , and according to Bloomberg, it is expecting to almost double their LNG capacity by 2027, and four-fold it by the end of the decade. [1] The expansion of LNG is driven by increased global gas demand from other countries, and from Europe in particular, as Europe is attempting to find alternatives to Russian gas. [2]  According to OEC 2022 data, the top 5 destinations of LNG from UAE are India (47%), Japan (28%), South Korea (9%), Taiwan (6%), and Thailand (4%). [3]  As of 2022, exports to European countries only accounted for 2%, including France, Spain, Belgium and the UK, [3]  however, according to Climate Home News, several other European countries such as Germany or Austria are currently turning to the UAE to cover their needs. [2] The UAE currently has 3 LNG Terminals, Das Island (export), Ruwais (import) and Jebel Ali (import), which are distributed along the coast and in Das island, see Figure 1. [4]   Besides these, another LNG Export Terminal is planned in Ruwais expected to start operations in 2028. [5] The construction of LNG Terminals and distribution networks, however, has raised concerns over occupational health and safety risks faced by low-skilled migrants’ workers. Several cases have been raised by workers of the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC), [2]  who owns both Ruwais Terminals (located in Al Ruwais Industrial Park, west of Abu Dhabi) and the one at Das Island. For the purposes of this case study, Ruwais LNG export Terminals is at focus, but occupational health and safety risks could be present at any of ADNOC’s owned facilities.  Al Ruwais Industrial Park is home to many of ADNOC’s operations. Because of this, ADNOC decided to move its LNG planned export Terminal from Fujairah to Ruwais. [5]  The Terminal, with an expected  two liquefaction trains and 9.6 mtpa (million tonnes per annum) capacity , has been designed to be powered by renewable energy and nuclear power, being the first facility in the Middle East and North Africa to run on “clean” power. [5]  In 2024, BP, Mitsui & Co, Shell and TotalEnergies took 10% stake each of the Terminal, with ADNOC retaining 60% stake. [6]  Public statements from the international companies who joined Ruwais project highlight how the low-carbon aspect of the Terminal is aligned with their decarbonisation values or strategy, [6]  despite the Terminal being used to export liquified natural gas, which is not renewable. Buyers of LNG from Ruwais include China (Zhijang province), [7]  Germany, who signed a 15-year Heads of Agreement with Energie Baden-Württemberg for the delivery of 0.6 million mtpa [8] and another one with SEFE (Securing Energy for Europe), [9]  and India, with Indian Oil Corp announcing to buy one million metric tons each year from the terminal. [10] Concerns over health and safety risks of workers of ADNOC has been raised in multiple occasions and according to Climate Home News the construction of Terminals in UAE and Qatar will rely of low-skilled migrant workers. [2]  Instances of labour abuse in the UAE oil and gas sector and in ADNOC’s operations in particular have been raised by workers (anonymously) and international NGOs. [2]  Workers and industry observers state that the oil and gas sector has improved safety protocols, but there is no transparency and conflict of interests in work-related injuries, accidents or deaths. [2]  According to Fair/Square, an international NGO, not all deaths and incidents are being investigated, particularly when the accidents involve non-nationals and low-skilled jobs. [2]  An engineer of ADNOC states that accidents are rarely reported, there is no transparency or accountability. [2]  According to a low-skilled ADNOC worker, despite being aware of the dangers of his work he prefers working in the oil and gas sector as it is better paid than in other sectors. [2]  Wages, however, do not seem proportionate to the high risks low-skilled workers undertake, according to an ADNOC engineer. [2]   Moreover, ADNOC hires third party contractors for construction and engineering, who rarely hold the same standards as ADNOC. [2]

case_name: Alaska LNG Terminal, USA
headline: The state-led Alaska LNG project threatens the lives of endangered marine species, and livelihoods of the people living there - including the traditional practices of members of the native Iñupiaq, Yup’ik and Eyak Athabaskan communities.
description: The Alaska LNG Terminal is a proposed terminal located in Nikiski, Alaska, United States.  [1] Along with the Terminal on the Kenai Peninsula, the project will require the construction of a gas treatment plant and an 800 mile pipeline connecting the facility to the Prudhoe Bay and Point Thomson fields on Alaska’s North Slope.  [7]  Despite being advertised as a project that furthers Alaskan energy security, it will be an export terminal used to transport natural gas out of the country to buyers in Asia.  [11] In fact, the projects proximity to and ease in reaching Asian countries by sea is deemed as one of its strong points, compared to the US’s other LNG export terminals which must transit the Panama or Suez Canals or the Straits of Hormuz.  [12]   [13] Opponents say that the project will roughly triple the states greenhouse gas emissions for decades to come, with environmental and civil activists refuting the government's decision on the project  [7] .  Financing  With an initial estimated cost of $38.7 billion, the project had financial and operational involvement from major oil and gas companies including BP, ExxonMobil, and ConocoPhillips, as well as international engineering firm Fluor Corporation.  [4] Yet in 2016, all of these corporations pulled out of the project citing concerns with economic viability. It then became a state-led project, developed by Alaska Gasline Development Corp  [2] alongside the Alaskan Federal state. In this kind of agreement, the state's primary role is in initiating, funding (as well as finding corporate funding) and overseeing the project. The project, now projected to cost between $40 billion to $45 billion was, in 2017, seeking long-term contract buyers in Asia to invest  [6] LNG Project and resistance timeline  As much of the gas exported out of the US is for demand in countries in Asia, most notably Japan, activists in many places across the world are protesting the US's decision to continue with the LNG. In April 2023, the Japanese organisation Fossil Free Japan was condemning Japan's role as the head of he G7 summit of 2023 in promoting additional LNG facilities to be built, specifically mentioning the continuation of the Alaska LNG project [19] . On the 13th of October 2023, activists disrupted a US event with the ambassador of Japan. They shouted slogans such as "No Alaska LNG," and "No More Gas" as the Japanese ambassador made his speech about the importance of Japan as a US business ally in the Indo-Pacific area.  [17]  Additionally, on December 8th, a letter was sent to the Biden Administration from over 300 organisations based in 40 different countries calling on the president to halt all LNG projects including the Alaska LNG.  [18] On March 15th, 2024, the government made the decision to reapprove this LNG project following the Biden administration's decision to halt all new LNG projects in early 2024,  [3]   [5] despite acknowledging that the project would definitely result in a net increase of greenhouse gas emissions  [12] . The Department of Energy justified the decision, stating that the Alaska LNG was a project of public interest and that their determination predated the January 2024 decision to pause new LNG export approvals while more studies were carried out on the effects of shipping natural gas on the environment and on energy costs.  [12]  They also stated that their move was made in the interest of “energy security for US allies and trading partners”, referring to geopolitical events or natural disasters that may disrupt usual global trade.  [3] Following this, in May 2024, 8 young Alaska residents sued the state in hopes to block the project. The group were aged between 11 - 26 years old [10] , all living in native communities such as the Iñupiaq, Yup’ik and Eyak Athabaskan, or remote villages in the surrounding areas. They invoked their rights under Alaska’s constitution by making reference to two of its sections that state - 1. The right to have protected natural resources for current and future generations and 2. The right to be free from government infringement on life and property. The group received help from Our Children’s Trust, the non profit law firm that helps youth bring forward legal cases.  [7] Summer Sagoonick, one of the youth that came forward from the Iñupiat tribe, conveyed her reasons for deciding to take legal action, stating that her life is intertwined with her natural surroundings, with a “close connection” to not only other people but also to the land including knowledge of the vegetation, the mammals and weather patterns. She went on to say, “as our water warms and the land erodes, it poses a threat to our nourishment and our cultural practices,”, stating that she hopes that bringing the case to court will, “instil security and promise into our future”.  [8] This is not the first time youth activists have used legal measures to get their points heard. Both the Kanuk vs Department of Natural Resources case (2011) and the Sagoonick vs State of Alaska I (2017) are earlier examples [9]. The first was dismissed by the supreme court in 2014 which ruled that the judiciary could not mandate broad policy change on climate issues, while the second was dismissed on similar grounds in 2022. By regrouping and choosing to focus the Sagoonick vs State of Alaska II case solely on the LNG project, the group hopes to have more success.  [9] In an unrelated move, groups such as the Sierra Club, Center for Biological Diversity and Earthjustice also joined forces to file a petition  [16] against the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals on the grounds of the project doesn’t properly consider projected harms that it will have on marine animals listed on the Endangered Species Act - such as polar bears, Cook Inlet beluga whales and Eastern North Pacific right whales.  [15] This legal challenge was filed against the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service, along with the agencies’ parent departments, the Department of the Interior and Department of Commerce.  [14]   [15]  This is not the first time the groups have taken formal legal action against government departments on this project - on 11th of August 2023, the groups alleged that the federal decisions of approval overlooked both climate and non climate environmental impacts. This case (as of May 2024) is still pending, and the company released a statement of rebuttal: “These objections are misguided and do not overcome the deference due the expert agency’s scientific and technical judgments. The Natural Gas Act gives DOE broad discretion in assessing the public interest and directs DOE to deny an export application only if DOE makes an affirmative finding that proposed exports will not be consistent with the public interest. DOE properly exercised its discretion, considering all pertinent issues, and providing a reasoned explanation for its decision. The petition for review should be denied.”  [3]

case_name: Predator's 'Mag Mell'  LNG Floating Storage and Regasification Unit (FSRU), Cork, Ireland
headline: Named after the mythological Celtic Otherworld, the Mag Mell is a Floating Regasification and Storage Unit of liquid natural gas, proposed just 50km from the coast of County Cork. The facility is one of three that was proposed in the country, and met with resistance from campaigners who are fighting to keep Ireland free from fracked gas, and thus LNG-free.
description: The US company Predator Oil & Gas planned the development of ‘Mag Mell’ Floating Storage and Regasification Unit (FSRU) for Liquid Natural Gas (LNG) located in the Muir Cheilteach (Celtic Sea) 50km off the coast of County Cork. [1] Its capacity was planned to be 3.3 bcm per year, and would be composed of two floating storage units, that would use the disused Kinsale Head gas pipeline to transport gas to shore. [1] Utilising the Kinsale Pipeline was cited by the Mag Mell project organisers as a benefit of the project, allowing a “key piece of physical infrastructure” [10] to stay in use, emphasising their desire to repurpose old existing oil and gas infrastructure [11] . Following much resistance from campaigners in Ireland (with support from international anti-gas groups), the government put a ban on importing fracked gas, which led all proposed LNG projects in the country to be halted or paused. Yet, this ban was overturned by the government in 2023, who cited the necessity of “national energy security” in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the energy precarity that followed. The struggle to keep Ireland LNG free - and, thus free of fracked gas - continues.  Project and resistance timeline In 2020, Predator set up an Irish subsidiary (Predator LNG Ireland), and employed the Irish environmental consultant, SLR Environmental Consulting, as regulatory, planning and environmental advisors to help advance their project, amidst uncertainty around whether their project would be halted by the government. [2] At the same time, two other LNG facilities were further along in their planning process, with strong opposition from the public and civil society organisations such as Not Here Not Anywhere, Safety Before LNG, Love Leitrim and Friends of the Earth Ireland  [3 ]  [4] [12] , with initial support from Irish Green party politicians. These facilities were Hess Corp’s “Shannon LNG” terminal and NextDecade’s “Cork LNG” terminal. In June 2020, Eamon Ryan, the Green Party Minister for Energy in parliament tweeted Safety Before LNG stating “ be rest assured, if we can agree to the #PFG [Programme for Government] we will implement the policies which will see an end to the importation of fracked gas via any LNG terminals in Ireland”. As a result of these organisations' tireless campaigning, including several court victories [10] , in 2021, all of these LNG projects were successfully halted or paused, following the government's ban of all fracked gas imports. In the policy statement on the importation of fracked gas that was published on the 18th of May 2021, Eamon Ryan states, “Fracked gas causes environmental damage both locally where it is extracted and globally and Ireland, having banned its exploitation onshore, should not impose these environmental risks on other communities around the globe”. [5] Although the explicit statement from the government stated that they were ruling out all “commercial LNG Terminals” for the foreseeable, it was deduced that this meant all LNG terminals, seeing as LNG relies heavily on fracked gas from the US - a 2023 report from Food & Water Action Europe and Gastivists found that “fracked US gas could represent as much as one eighth of all gas the EU consumed in 2022”, adding that 87% of the gas extracted in the US is fracked [6] .  Yet, Predator’s FSRU project was only shelved, and in November 2023 when the “Energy Security in Ireland to 2030” report was released, it demonstrated the government's U-Turn on the banning of fracked gas through their support of “state-led” LNG’s to ensure energy security for the country. State led simply means commissioned by the state, and “does not preclude a public-private-partnership nor the involvement of private firms contracted to provide, build or operate the necessary infrastructure”, according to the 2023 report. [7] Following this, in March 2024, 150 groups wrote an open letter [9]   to the Green Party Minister for Energy, calling for a confirmation that he and the Green party would stand by their word, and not use the excuse of ‘national energy security’ as a reason to allow for an LNG terminal to be established in the country. Most of these groups were Irish, however there was notable international support from Concerned Health Professionals of Pennsylvania and North American fracked communities that are already negatively impacted by the fracking of gas in their regions. [8] In the lead up to local and EU elections of June 2024, Not Here Not Anywhere complied the report "Keep Ireland LNG Free" in response to the "Energy Security in Ireland to 2030" report [13] . Their report demaned that councillors must make a pledge against the Mag Mell project if they are claiming to take climate change, inlcuding the Irish Climate Action Plan of 2023 (CAP23), as well as the interests of the Irish people seriously. The report highlighted issues with this proposed FSRU, which include security concerns, pollution impacts and issues with leasing, specifically mentioning that as this units intended purpose is only "in the event of a supply shock" ,  the project is merely "an expensive insurance policy" measure [13] . On June 16th, 2024, the US-based organisation Frack Action organised an information event "Don't Blow Up Cork" about the risks of the FSRU. [15]   The event was held in Cork city, and included a panel presentation with spe akers including Julia Walsh (Director at Frack Action, Eoghan Harris (Founder at Future Generations Kerry), Amber Morningstar (Byars Choctaw activist) and moderation by Roisin Myers (Cork resident and youth climate activist).   [16] On June 19th, 2024 Not Here Not Anywhere came together with Frack Action and Friends of the Earth (FoE) to brief the politicians in Leinster House, Ireland on the dangers and risks associated with the FSRU, highlighting the work of Not Hear Not Anywhere's recent report [13] .  The event was hosted by Neasa Hourigan TD, a member of parliament for the Greens. During the briefing, Julia Walsh again discussed the 2024 Biden administration's ban on new export terminal permits. While Jerry Mac Evilly (head of policy at FoE) briefed parliament members on the importance of resisting a U-turn position on LNG by standing by the strict climate measured that the government itself have proposed. Mide Power spoke on behalf of Not Here Not Anywhere to share information from the organisations   "Keep Ireland LNG Free: Unpacking the Energy Security Review & Detailing How a Floating Storage and Regasification Unit Will Impact Ireland's Climate Goals" report.  [14]    The push by international oil and gas companies to add Ireland to their global LNG network has been tirelessly opposed by trans-atlantic activists for nearly a decade. This conflict displays an inspiring example of how civil society can hold politicians to their word, demonstrating a kind of democracy that today can seem absent in a western context.

case_name: Kochi LNG (and LPG) Terminal and pipeline across Kerala and Tamil Nadu, India
headline: Kochi LNG Terminal imports LNG and distributes it via a pipeline to other regions of the country. More recently, an LPG Terminal has also been constructed in Kochi facilities, overlapping with LNG. All these projects, however, have faced opposition from local communities who fear social and environmental impacts.
description: Liquified Natural Gas (LNG) is seeing a rapid expansion in India. According to th e Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis, the government of India has set targets to increase natural gas consumption from 51 MTPA in 2023 to 139 MTPA by 2030. [1] The expansion of LNG is mainly driven by increased demand in city gas distribution, power, fertiliser, refinery or petrochemical industry sectors, with the fertiliser sector accounting for the largest share of India’s LNG demand. [1] India currently has several existing, proposed and under-construction LNG Terminals, which are distributed mainly along the north-west coast, and multiple existing, planned and under-construction pipelines that connect Terminals with one another and with major cities and industry hubs, see Figure 1.  The construction of LNG Terminals and pipelines, however, has not always been welcomed by local communities, who have, in multiple cases, raised concerns. One of the most emblematic cases is the Kochi Terminal construction and connecting pipeline located across Kerala and Tamil Nadu (see Figure 1 circled area of focus). More concretely the Terminal is located in Puthuvype, about 12 km away from the city centre, and the pipelines in focus connects Kochi with Bangalore, Kayamkulam and Mangalore. Kochi LNG Terminal started constructions in 2007 and began operations in 2013. [2]   The Terminal is owned by Petronet LNG, a joint venture of the Oil and Natural Gas Corporation (12.5%), the Indian Oil Corporation (12.5%), Bharat Petroleum Corporation (12.5%), the Gas Authority of India Ltd (GAIL) (12.5%) and Public and Foreign Institutional Investors (50%). [2]   Kochi LNG Terminal has the capacity to receive, store and distribute 5 million tons of LNG each year, but it is currently utilised to less than 15% capacity. [3]   Currently, the Terminal imports LNG from Gorgon, Australia for a 20-year period as per a sign ed-deal from 2009. [2]  Although it could start importing LNG from Qatar as soon as that contract finishes, given that Petronet LNG (one of the owners) has signed a deal with QatarEnergy to supply 7.5 million tons of LNG each year from 2028 to 2048. [4] In January 2024   a Liquified Petroleum Gas (LPG) Terminal, owned by the Indian Oil Corporation, was inaugurated next to the LNG Terminal. Kochi LPG Terminal has a capacity to store 15,400 million tons of LPG each year, and the first LPG shipment of 5,000 tonnes came from Saudi Arabia. [6]  It is not clear, however, if all upcoming LPG shipments will be originating from the same country. The LPG Terminal is thou ght to provide energy to households and businesses in the region, [5]   whereas the LNG Terminal is thought to provide energy to businesses in other regions of the country. Both LPG and LNG Terminals, however, faced opposition from local fishermen, communities and activists who feared social and environmental impacts. [7] [9] The LNG Terminal faced opposition and protests in 2017 and 2019. In 2017, protestors allegedly disrupted the functioning of the Terminal, causing the arrest of 204 protesters who were later released on bail. [3] [8]  Despite arrests, protestors launched a satyagraha (a form of non-violent protest invented by Gandhi) and a march against the LNG Terminal at the Elamkunnappuzha panchayat village office in 2019. [3]  Despite their efforts, the LNG Terminal is still operational. With regards to LPG Terminal, protests also started in 2017 as local residents were concerned about potential leakages of the terminal and the lack of benefit received from the terminal in the form of electricity. [9]  Moreover, worries around the presence of mercaptans, a foul-smelling gas added to LPG, has also been reported in local press. [9]  Exposure to mercaptans can be irritating to the skin, eyes and respiratory tract, and cause health effects if health and safety protocols are not followed properly. [10]  Protests and worries of local communities resulted in a partial victory for communities, with Indian Oil Corporation announcing a suspension of LPG Terminal construction. [9] As a result, the initial plans to start construction in 2009 and to finalise construction by the end of 2012 were severely delayed, see Figure 2. [5] H owever, a few years later the LPG Terminal re-started construction and it was inaugurated in 2024. The Indian Oil Corporation dismissed communities’ concerns stating that international safety standards would be followed to avoid potential damages. [9]  Moreover, a statement from the company claimed that the project would generate employment for over 300 local people, and around Rs 150 crore each year of revenue for the state. Locals, however, see the statement suspicious and believe it is an attempt done by the company to silence their protests. [9] Local fishermen and communities in Puthuvype are not only concerned on safety issues, they also allegedly state that both LNG and LPG Terminals violate environmental regulations and steal their livelihoods since the terminal shrinks fishermen access to the sea. [9]  Protestors state that the construction of the Terminals has been made on marshy land, impacting the area’s environmental balance. [9]  Indian Coastal Zone Regulations only allows construction 200 meters away of the high tide line, but according to local protestors, LPG and LNG Terminals have broken those rules. [9]  Fishermen allege that the land historically belonged to the fishing community, but resulting impacts from terminals activities are forcing them to sell their land and migrate. [9]  A press release from Indian Oil Corporation stated that the Terminals offer wide access from the village to the sea, and therefore Terminals do not disturb fishermen’s activities. [8] Besides the terminals, the proposed or constructed pipelines, owned or operated by GAIL, that distribute LNG from Kochi to Kayamkulam thermal power plant , to Mangalore and to Bangalore , passing through Coimbatore, Erode, Namakkal, Salem, Dharmapuri, and Krishnagiri have received fierce oposition. [11] Fish workers’ organisations are again leading the protests against the pipeline that connects to Kayamkulam, as the project is thought to go through the coastline and fishermen fear negative impacts on their fishing activities. [12]  The Kerala Swathanthra Matsya Thozhilali Federation (a trade union of small-scale artisanal fishers of the state of Kerala) also came out against the pipeline according to local press. [12] The pipeline that connects Kochi to Mangalore also goes through the coastline crossing villages like Mukkam, whose residents headed a campaign, protest and road blockage in 2017 in an attempt to stop the construction of the pipeline through their village. [13]   Protesters voiced concerns over land acquisition of their farmland, and the demolition of houses needed to build the pipeline, claiming that the pipeline will affect 600 families in Kozhikode. [13]  The 2017 protest allegedly took a violent turn with local police forcefully removing protesters, who set tyres on fire and pelted stones at vehicles, according to local press. [13]  Police officers allegedly used lathicharge and fired tear gas to disperse the crowd and detained 32 protestors. [13]  Despite protests taking over 2018, GAIL authorities resumed gas pipeline laying. [14 ] Finally, the pipeline that connects Kochi to Bangalore is also experiencing complaints mainly in Hosur, as the pipeline is proposed to go through farmlands, while the pipelines in Kerala and other districts in Tamil Nadu are being laid following the road. [11]  The pipeline in Hosur would affect the communities of three villages (Idayanallur, Edappalli and Soothalam), who base their livelihoods on farming activities. [11]  In order to preserve their farming lands and stop the construction of the pipeline, farmers, led by the Tamil Nadu Vivasayigal Sangam (a farmers’ association) stagged multiple protests in 2024. [11]  The farmers also initiated a mass petition outside the sub-collector’s office, which resulted in several arrests. [15]  Despite protests, GAIL continues to attempt construction of the pipeline, but affected farmers are allegedly maintaining a 24h vigil to save their lands and have called the district administration to intervene and lay the pipeline along the road instead of their farmlands. [11]  However, according to the state secretary of All India Kisan Sabha it is not possible to lay the pipeline without acquiring agricultural lands, as village roads are narrower than the width needed to build the pipelines. [16]  Other protests in Tamil Nadu happened in 2022 in Palavadi village who gathered 50 farmers to protest against a land survey fearing that their lands would be acquired to build the pipeline. [16]  Fears over land acquisition led to one farmer allegedly taking his life as a result. [16] The current status of pipeline construction in farmers fields is not fully known.
