case_name: Block B Liquid Natural Gas (LNG) Project, Vietnam
headline: International financial firms and supranational organisations are influencing the government of Vietnam's 'green energy transition', pushing for increased dependancy on LNG as part of the 'solution' to climate change. Environmental justice organisations denounce the LNG project Block B threatens to contribute to already dangerous (and rising) levels of methane produced by natural gas exploration.
description: The Block B Gas Project will be located 250 kilometres from the coast of Ca Mau Province. Nationally, this project is part of the country's commitment to phase out coal by 2040 [3] , instead investing more in renewable energy and using LNG as a “bridge fuel”, as it is often misattributed by those in the natural gas market (fossil fuel corporations; energy utility companies). [1]   [4] Internationally, this project comes as part of a wider shift by governments in Asian countries, public finance institutions and private corporations that are “aggressively pursuing the expansion of Fossil Gas in the region” [5] , similar to trends occurring in other parts of the the Global South. Both nationally and internationally, climate activists have been calling for an end to investments such as these that perpetuate natural gas projects, increasing the longevity of our dependence on fossil extraction. Within Vietnam, many prominent climate activists have been arrested for voicing their opinions on LNG, often charged with crimes such as money laundering or tax evasion [6] .  Owned by a consortium of companies (including PetroVietnam), the project is a joint development which comprises three fossil extraction units, called Ac Quy Oil and Gas Field, Kim Long Oil and Gas Field and Ca Voi Oil and Gas Field [10] . Once extracted and converted to LNG, the gas will be carried onward by an interconnecting pipeline (see image 1 of this conflict case) to onshore gas-fired power plants located in Vietnam, and used for power generation. [1]   In terms of export value, Vietnam mainly exports natural gas to Cambodia. In 2022, the country exported $116M of LNG making it the 35th largest exporter of LNG globally. [13]   The project is under construction and is due to be operational by 2025. [10] Resistance  Organised to coincide with the 56th Annual Meeting of the Asian Development Bank (ADB) Board of Governors in Incheon, on May 4th, 2023 Asia-wide protests were held in 13 cities to mark the launch of a new resistance network named “Don’t Gas Asia”. The campaign seeks to end fossil extraction across Asia, pushing for a just transition away from fossil fuels towards “100% renewable energy systems that serve the people” [5] . The key city protests were in Tokyo, Incheon, Mandaluyong, Jakarta, Chiang Mai, Hanoi, Dhaka, Delhi, Kolkata, Kathmandu, Lahore, Karachi and Colombo, where there was the biggest presential turn out of protesters [5] . Creating an international network campaign such as this allows organisations in Vietnam to join, arguably creating a safer space to ‘voice’ their views - by signing petitions and showing support in this way. ActionAid Vietnam and Aid for Social Protection Program Foundation Vietnam are part of the movement. [5] Sreedhar Ramamurthi, a campaigner involved in the Don’t Gas Asia Campaign stated that, “Fossil fuel companies, for their own survival, have been pushing gas as a transition fuel. Governments are building gas infrastructure to benefit these companies which will soon get stranded. Asia needs to be saved from this catastrophe as there is a concerted effort to even call this green,”. [12] On the 15th of September 2023, Ngo Thi To Nhien, the director of the Vietnam Initiative for Energy Transition Social Enterprise was arrested for "appropriating internal documents". She had held a workshop event in June 2020 based on intergrating renewable energy sources into the country's grid, using information from the state electricity utility during the session. Her organisation of this event was used as evidence for her arrest. [6]    Her arrest was sited as particularly unusual, as she had worked previously in advisory positions for the World Bank, and was not outrightly critical of the government. Others who spoke out against the governments climate policy were arrested, often with charges such as tax evasion. [6]  Repression of such opinions can be understood to have influenced the network building and solidarity across countries in Asia.  Additionally, research from organisations such as Recourse, Friends of the Earth U.S. and Asian Peoples Movement for Debt and Development that helped to expose the depth of influence from supranational organisations and financial institutions in pushing for LNG in Vietnam. [3] .  Their 2022 joint report they uncovered the ways in which through the International Monetary Fund (IFC), the World Bank are at the forefront of pushing for an expansion to LNG infrastructure across Vietnam, by providing funding and policy advice that operates under the guise of “clean energy” [9] . This influence has contributed to the upscaling of LNG as a “bridge fuel”, through framing LNG as a less-polluting fuel that will serve as a transitional measure to support the upscaling of renewables in the coming years. [4] Overview of International influence for LNG in Vietnam The dangerous landscape for environmental campaigners in Vietnam is enforced by the government (through arrests that intend to silence contrary opinions), yet is upheld by the investment interests of other countries and international bodies. [11] Vietnam is an important player in Japan’ s strategy for energy security, and Japanese government firms have led a push for establishing LNG terminals and associated infrastructure in the country, much like they are in the Gulf Coast today (2024) [7] . The Japanese government agency for the Organisation for Metals and Energy Security has played a prominent role in the financing of Block B, providing a “loan guarantee up to 50% of the development cost” [2] that accumulate from this LNG and the associated pipeline infrastructure. Despite making a commitment to end fossil fuel development abroad, the country's energy department continues to finance the expansion of oil and gas fields. Additionally, across the whole of Asia, Japan's Bank for International Cooperation (JBIC) is the largest financier of natural gas projects in the region [7] . As mentioned previously, the IFC has played an important role in LNG projects in the Country. In the World Bank and the IFC's their 2021 report on Vietnam Country Private Sector Diagnosis, they indicated that natural gas extraction would be critical to meeting future energy demands. In the following year, they stated they will step up to help the country meet its “sustainable development targets”, in which they sighted LNG as one of the routes toward sustainable development. [3] Other projects they have invested in, such as the Chan May import terminal located on the east coast of Vietnam, have been cancelled due to immense pressure from the international sphere.  In 2022, the European Commission agreed on a political declaration with the Vietnamese government to establish a Just Energy Transition Partnership between the regions - a condition of this being that the government must consult with “the media, NGOs and other stakeholders to ensure a broad social consensus” [8] . Yet, following this, the government has been found to leave NGOs out of such discussions, and go so far as to arrest those who speak out in opposition of the governments ‘clean energy’ strategy. [6]

case_name: LNG Boom in the Verde Island Passage, The Philippines
headline: Fossil companies are on track to turn Batangas in the Philippines into a Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) import hub for Southeast Asia. Batangas is home to 5 of 6 existing gas plants in the Philippines, 8 of 35 proposed new plants and 7 of 12 planned terminals.
province: Not specified clearly in live EJAtlas metadata.
location: Not specified clearly in live EJAtlas metadata.
description: In the Philippine island region of Luzon lies the Verde Island Passage (VIP), a marine corridor housing over 300 coral species, underwater rock canyons and reef formations, and 60% of all known shore fish species in the world within a ten-kilometer area [1] . It is the most biodiverse marine habitat in the world and has been touted as the “Amazon of the oceans” [1] . In addition, the VIP holds a strategic position for the shipping industry as it connects the South China Sea with Tayabas Bay and the Sibuyan Sea, and is the main shipping route between the Port of Manila and the Visayas and Mindanao in the south [2] . Overall, the VIP provides food, livelihoods and other benefits to over 2 million people [3] . On top of several existing threats such as uncontrolled illegal fishing practices, encroachment, oil spills, declining fish catch and water quality, reclamation, pollution from shipping activities and other industries, and climate change [4] , VIP today finds itself in great peril as one of the four provinces in its vicinity, Batangas, rapidly turns into the hotspot of operation and expansion of a destructive industry: liquefied natural gas (LNG) and fossil gas [1] . In recent years, the Philippine government’s recognition of fossil gas as a supposed “transition fuel” and the vision of transforming the country into a LNG Trading and Transshipment Hub of Asia-Pacific has opened the floodgates for massive plans for fossil gas and LNG projects build-out [4] .  LNG is fossil methane gas in a liquid state. Gas producers cool methane gas down to -162°C to turn it into a more transportable liquid state. As LNG, the companies can ship the methane all over the world [5] . Currently, Batangas is home to ​5 of 6 existing gas plants in the Philippines, 8 of 35 proposed new plants (4 are active, 4 are delisted/onhold) and 7 of 12 planned LNG terminals (receiving facilities used to turn the LNG back into its gaseous state to be burned in power plants) [1] . Despite being mired in lawsuits, Atlantic Gulf & Pacific-subsidiary Linseed Field Power Corporation’s PH LNG, the first LNG terminal in the Philippines, started commissioning in April 2023 [4] . All of the projects will rely on imported LNG, representing a risk for the energy security of the country [6] . Malampaya, the largest producing gas field and the primary source of fossil gas in the country, is depleting rapidly and no new gas fields are currently in development [15] . Until recently, the Lopez Group’s First Philippine Holdings Corporation was the largest developer of gas projects in the Philippines. However, the Conglomerate made a net-zero pledge, and committed to phase-out its gas-fired power plants or consider a fuel shift to hydrogen as part of its decarbonization strategy [15] . San Miguel Corporation’s Global Power has now become the country’s leading fossil gas developer, with one gas-fired plant under construction and seven more proposed. Together with Meralco PowerGen Corporation and Aboitiz Power Corporation, they are planning a total investment of $3.3 billion in two gas-fired power plants and the LNG import and regasification terminal owned by Linseed Field Corporation [16] . In addition, I Squared Capital invested $300 million in the LNG terminal, the Japan Bank for International Cooperation and Osaka gas invested $100 million, and China Bank and Development Bank of the Philippines funded a $100 million term loan facility [15] . International financiers with net-zero pledges are fueling the country’s fossil future. The top four financiers of fossil gas expansion in the Philippines 2020-onwards contributed to almost half of the total fossil gas financing, each accounting for at least USD 1.1 billion. Financing from the United States contributed USD 1.5 billion, the largest among all countries. Japan (USD 1.2 billion), Germany (USD 1.2 billion), and the United Kingdom (USD 1.2 billion) follow behind. Local financing notably accounted for only 6.5% or USD 674 million . Among the top financiers are Deutsche Bank AG, JPMorgan Chase & Co., Standard Chartered PLC, Allianz SE, BlackRock, and GAM Holding. Notably, all of these financial institutions have made various net-zero pledges [15] . Although natural gas is regarded as a “clean” and “environmentally friendly” fuel, there are a number of harmful impacts on human health associated with the pollutants emitted from natural gas facilities, including heart disease, certain types of cancer, and damage to the reproductive system and internal organs [7] . In addition, environmental organizations and scientists warn against the negative impacts of the industrialization boom on marine ecosystems of the Verde Island Passage. Vulnerable fishing communities are already feeling these effects, catching less fish than ever before and losing access to their traditional fishing areas due to zoning restrictions from the ongoing construction projects [8] . Electricity consumer groups are also raising the implications of importing fuels to electricity rates [15] . The Philippine people, despite paying some of the highest electricity prices in Asia, would have to shoulder the costly burdens of imported LNG as power suppliers pass on risks from volatile fuel costs and foreign exchange to consumers. This would leave the electricity bills of Philippine households at the mercy of international fossil fuel markets [12] . On top of everything, residents of Santa Clara, living only a few hundred meters away from the Avion, Sta. Rita, San Lorenzo, and San Gabriel natural gas-fired power plants, are yet to be connected to power. They are among the remaining 1.58% or 210,538 unenergized households in Luzon, according to government data [9] . The coalition ProtectVIP summarizes the potential negatives impacts of the LNG boom in Batangas: toxic air and water pollution, thermal pollution from seawater intake (causing disrupted reproductive cycles of marine life and less fish catch), potential freshwater shortages (with gas terminals and plants competing with locals for supply), a massive increase in shipping activities and loss of flora and displacement of coastal communities [1] . In addition, the burning of methane will continue to contribute to global climate change. The Philippines is ranked number four on the The Long-Term Climate Risk Index (CRI) that details the 10 countries most affected from 2000 to 2019 (primarily due to tropical cyclones) [10] . According to a report from Climate Analytics on getting fossil fuels out of the Philippine power sector, the Philippines must almost entirely phase out gas-fired generation by 2040 to stay aligned to a 1.5C pathway [11] . However, a variety of different actors are coming together to take a stand against fossil gas and LNG developments in Batangas, including youth, faith-based groups, fisherfolk and other impacted sectors, civil society and people’s organizations, and academe [1] . The Protect VIP campaign network links local, national and civil society groups from across the globe to stop the expansion of LNG projects in Batangas [1] . These movements have filed complaints, organized petitions, and protested against LNG in the VIP [12] . In October of 2022, a coalition of local stakeholders and advocates filed a complaint against San Miguel Corporation subsidiary Excellent Energy Resources, Inc. (SMC-EERI) and Linseed Field Corporation with Atlantic Gulf and Pacific Company (AG&P-Linseed) before the Environmental Management Bureau of the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR-EMB) over the companies’ violation of environmental laws [13] . In November of 2022, 95 civil society, people’s organizations, and institutional representatives across the Philippines and the globe signed a call to protect the Verde Island Passage against the plan of Shell Petroleum Corporation to build the ₱3.5 billion liquefied natural gas (LNG) import terminal in Batangas [1] . In May 2023, Philippine activists traveled to Europe to meet with banks and investors and demand financial institutions to stop funding fossil fuel companies destroying the Verde Island Passage [14] . Currently, there is 29.64 GW of new fossil gas capacity in the pipeline - nearly ten times the Philippines’ existing 3.42 GW [1] . Of the 8 gas-fired power plants proposed in Batangas Province, one is under construction (expected by end of 2024), two others have been indicated for operation in 2026 and 2027, and the remaining six have been announced with the operation date to be decided [4] . Of the 7 planned gas terminals in Batangas, two have been commissioned and the remaining five only proposed.

case_name: Rio Grande LNG, Texas
headline: Construction for the Rio Grande LNG began in October 2023, despite decades of resistance from local campaigners who have fought to stop fossil fuel industry building in the area.
description: The Rio Grande Liquid Natural Gas (LNG) facility is an LNG terminal under construction on the southern Texan coast, in Cameron County. The facility is owned by Next Decade [2] , and will add to the 7 other operational LNG facilities along the Gulf Coast [1] . Despite much opposition from local Gulf Coast organisers such as the Vessel Project, Healthy Gulf, South Texas Environmental Justice Network and the Carrizo/​Comecrudo Tribe of Texas as well as national and international NGOs such as Oil Change International and Greenpeace (who together are quickly forming global networks of resistance to LNG projects) the facility build began in October 2023. This was only 3 months prior to Biden announcing a delay to all LNG facility approvals further north in the Gulf [7] , marking a pause in what climate activists are calling a “Climate Death Star” [7] .  Investment in further LNG infrastructure, such as this export terminal as well as necessary associated pipeline infrastructure, further contributes to a carbon lock in - fusing global energy commitments to fossil extraction through a set of huge financial and infrastructural investments. This makes moving towards decarbonisation, “politically, economically, and socially” increasingly difficult, as stated in a Greenpeace report. [8] Furthermore, industrial operations in the natural gas sector have been identified as causing intergenerational health effects on nearby communities. These populations are subjected to air and water pollution throughout the gas processing chain, spanning from fracking activities in Texas and other U.S. states to the liquefaction processes along the Gulf Coast. [21] Bekah Hinojosa who is an organiser in the city of Brownsville, Texas states, “We’re a Gulf Coast community, but our community doesn’t look like the rest of the Gulf Coast.” [12] This is because the Rio Grande LNG, along with the Texas LNG, are the first two big industry projects to try to move into this stretch of the Gulf Coast . The export terminal was first proposed back in 2015, and in 2016 the company committed an additional US$85 million to the project. This allowed them to advance their plans and in 2019, they applied to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) to site, construct, and operate both the LNG terminal as well as the Rio Bravo Pipeline. [2] Plans were delayed due to COVID-19, so in November 2021, the company applied to the FERC again, this time to incorporate a carbon capture and storage system into the project build, stating that it would capture “at least 90%” [9] of emissions from the terminal. The move was said to be a result of growing pressure from buyers - particularly in Europe - to curb carbon emissions of the project, ensuring that if they buy fracked gas from the terminal they would still meet their countries emissions reductions goals. [9]   However, this apprehension fails to acknowledge the intrinsically environmentally harmful consequences inherent in the process of fracking for natural gas. [10] In June 2023, TotalEnergies bought a 17.5% stake in NextDecade costing them US$219 million. [3] Following this, on October 3rd, 2023, Next Decade held a ceremony marking the beginning of construction of Phase 1 of the LNG facility. Those who spoke during the event included a representative from their building partners - Bechtel - as well as the Count Judge of Cameron County. [4] This first phase is set to be the project's biggest - costing $18.4 billion to build. [5] Upon completion, the Rio Grande LNG will span nearly 404 hectares along the Brownsville Ship Channel in Cameron. [5] In 2023, planning for the 137 mile long Rio Bravo Pipeline was underway, which is set to facilitate fuelling of the Rio Grande LNG facility with shale gas from East and West Texas . [5] The pipeline project is ultimately owned by NextDecade, through their subsidiary firm Rio Bravo Pipeline Company LLC, and will be comprised of two pipelines parallel to one another that span from the Agua Dulce Hub in the North to Port of Brownsville (look to image 4 in this conflict case to visualise) [6]   [22] . Furthermore, pipelines such as these require additional supporting infrastructure - in this case, 2 interconnect booster stations, both located in Kenedy County as well as 3 compressor stations, one in Kleberg, Kenedy, and the other in Cameron County [22] . It was noted in the Rio Bravo General Project Description, Resource Report 1, that this infrastructure will be, "likely to stimulate pipeline system enhancements (e.g., looping, additional compression, installation of larger pipelines) to further increase the throughput capacity of the relevant connecting pipelines" [22]   suggesting that building one pipeline project prompts others to be built. In the context of the Rio Bravo Pipeline, current (2024) additional proposals for pipelines include for Texas LNG, Annova LNG, and other pipelines that will cross the border to feed gas to Mexico. [22]   Resistance  Despite support from local government officials and business in favour of the project , many of the residents who live and work in the area have been campaigning against it. [5] Communities in this area of southern Texas have been learning from the resistances of other communities in the Gulf South, who have campaigned against the negative health and environmental impacts of LNG projects (such as Corpus Cristi, Sabine Pass, Cameron, Calcasieu), as well as other polluting industries for years. [17] [18] [19] [20] These networks of activists share information through talks, meetings, attending protests in support of each other's causes and, over the years, have effectively organised against industrial and fossil projects that dominate the Gulf Coast.  In efforts to disrupt the plans to construct the supporting pipeline infrastructure (Rio Bravo Pipeline), the Carrizo/​Comecrudo Tribe of Texas have bought up acres of land along the planned pipeline route. Mancias, the chair of the tribe, states that, “They're trying to justify and redefine everything as ​‘critical infrastructure,’” Mancias says of the fossil-fuel projects. ​ “But the real ​‘critical infrastructure’ is the air, the water and the land.” [5] This community does not want to shoulder the negative impacts of expansion of fossil infrastructure. What they want, instead, is “support for renewable energy that is community led”, states Bekah Hinojosa [5] .  Between the 18th-22nd of March 2024 the group, along with other campaigners such as Greenfaith US, Better Bayou, Ted Talks Dirty,  Better Brazoria, Fisherman Fight Back and 350org also protested outside the CERAWeek conference organised by S&P Global. The conference was promoting technological fixes in the energy transition, and campaigners spent 4 days outside of the conference, which was widely documented on their respective social media channels. [13] [14]   [15] Further afield, transatlantic solidarity with LNG resistance groups in Europe bolstered their fight against terminal developments. Not here not anywhere, an LNG resistance group in Ireland, managed to halt all new LNG plans by working closely with resistance groups based in the Gulf Coast, directly referencing the shale gas that would be shipped to the proposed Shannon and Cork LNG facilities through the Rio Grande Terminal. The Irish group managed to win their case, on the grounds that Ireland had banned fracking for gas, and should not offset this harm to another part of the world. [16] This move helped in the global solidarity against LNG projects, in directing potential investment away from such infrastructure.  Additionally, groups such as Food and Water Watch have facilitated transatlantic webinars , such as the one held in February 2024, to share information on individual struggles and strengthen the networks of resistance [11] . This was the first in a series of forums that will take place over the years to foster further connections. On April 1st, 2024 Earthworks and FracTracker Alliance shared their study of fracking operations in Arlington, Texas. The report included their work using specialised methane-detecting cameras, exposing 24 hour emissions of methane billowing from 24 production facilities located in the Fort Worth Basin, Arlington - the most heavily populated fracking basin in the US. [23] All of these facilities are owned by TotalEnergies, under their subsidiary of TEP Barnett USA, LLC. [23]   The cameras recorded pollution at 85 of the 305 site visits, reporting that numerous sources of these emissions were less than 100m from child care facilities, while 76% of the fracking sites were within 200 meters of homes. [23] This is allowed to happen because TotalEnergies along with all other oil and gas companies are exempt from air pollution standards intended to curb methane outputs. (Only in late 2023 did the Biden administration decided to introduce new regulations designed to significantly reduce methane emissions from both new and existing extraction sites. [24] Prior to this, oil and gas companies enjoyed lenient air pollution regulations due to their significant economic importance to the US economy). On top of this, air pollution levels are sometimes misreported by companies - in a March 2024 study published in Nature, it was found that methane emissions from oil and gas operations in the same area of Arlington, Texas in the Forth Worth Basin were 3 times higher than the companies themselves had reported. [23]   [25] Gas is fracked at these locations with the intended export out of the Rio Grande LNG.

case_name: Boca Chica SpaceX Launch Facility, TX, USA
headline: SpaceX's Boca Chica Launch Site in Texas, adjacent to a state park, jeopardizes fragile ecosystems, endangers species like the Kemp's Ridley Sea Turtle, and infringes on indigenous cultural heritage, sparking environmental and legal battles.
description: The SpaceX launch  site in Boca Chica State Park, Texas is located at the southernmost point of the state near the Mexican border. Within a sparsely populated region along the Gulf Coast, Boca Chica State Park spans 1,055 acres and encompasses a variety of diverse ecosystems such as a hypersaline bay, the Tamaulipan thorn scrub, wetlands, coastal prairies, tidal flats, and beaches. Within these diverse habitats live the critically endangered Kemp's Ridley Sea Turtle and Rice's Whale, the endangered Ocelot and Aplomado Falcon, and the threatened Piping Plover among numerous other species (mainly migratory birds)  [31] .  The Boca Chica area, considered one of North America's most biologically diverse regions, serves as a crucial wintering and stopover habitat for migratory birds traversing the central and Mississippi flyways each year, yet it's facing alarming declines in shorebird populations as noted by the American Bird Conservancy in 2023   [34 ]. The region surrounding the launch site primarily consists of undeveloped land, with Boca Chica village being the only nearby unincorporated community in Cameron County, Texas. It is situated on Texas State Highway 4 and is approximately two miles northwest of the mouth of the Rio Grande river. Adjacent to the SpaceX Tracking Station, Boca Chica Village is home to twenty-six residents; the majority of whom belong to the indigenous Carrizo community  [1] .  In 2014, the village was selected as the site for constructing a control facility for the SpaceX South Texas launch site and flight testing began in 2019  [19 ].  The primary conflicts at the site stem from two key issues: damage to the environment resulting from the SpaceX starship launch on April 20, 2023, and SpaceX's violation of the Texas Open Beaches Act by obstructing access to the beach and closing it for more than 1,000 hours. This exceeds the limit set by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) permit which allows only 300 hours of closure  [43] . The Boca Chica Launch Site, referred to as "Starbase," serves as a spaceport as well as the production and development hub for Starship rockets. Home to SpaceX's Starship spacecraft and the Super heavy rocket  (jointly termed as Starship), the "Starbase" represents a fully reusable transport system designed for missions concerning the Earth's orbit, the Moon, Mars, and beyond. Acknowledged as the most powerful launch vehicle globally, Starship can carry payloads of up to 150 metric tonnes in a fully reusable capacity and 250 metric tonnes when deployed in an expendable setup   [33] .  Starship requires over 10 million pounds of propellant, with 1/5th comprised  of methane (in the form of Liquified Natural Gas), and 4/5th comprised of liquid oxygen  [40] .  SpaceX's Boca Chica launch site employs roughly 1,600 individuals, most of whom live in Brownsville which is located twenty-three miles away from the site. According to the 2020 Census, Brownsville has a population that is 94.6% Hispanic or Latino, with a median household income of $46,735, where twenty-six percent of the population lives in poverty  [41] .  As the largest employer in Brownsville, SpaceX plays a pivotal role; estimated to contribute around $855 million in gross output for Cameron County where it's situated  [39] .   According to court filings and comments by SpaceX's CEO, SpaceX has spent over $5 billion on its Starship vehicle and launch infrastructure  [38] . The Carrizo/Comecrudo are the indigenous people who inhabit the area in the South Texas Rio Grande Delta.  The name Comecrudo comes from the Spanish explorers' observation that the food they consumed was half raw and cooked in animal paunches [3] . Carrizos,  on the other hand, is a term that was applied after the 1700's to various indigenous groups of northeastern Mexico and Texas, most likely because they lived in houses whose frames were covered by canes or reeds. As described on their website, Carrizo/Comecrudo culture is so deeply intertwined with local species that their Spanish name describes their diet as "those who eat raw" [3] . Therefore, protecting Boca Chica is not only a matter of preserving the environment but also of respecting and honoring the cultural heritage of the Carrizo Nation.  Several miles northwest of Boca Chica lies the Garcia Pasture, an ancient pre-Columbian village that existed between 1000 and 1750 CCE. This site holds significant cultural importance as a sacred burial ground for the Carrizo people. Within the Garcia Pasture there are remnants of the village and its burial grounds as well as rock art relics  [2] .  The site is not only at-risk due to SpaceX launches, but also due to the proximity of the Rio Grande Liquified Natural Gas (LNG) export terminal--slated to be constructed just 1,000 feet from the Garcia Pasture   [5] . Last year I had the privilege of speaking to the Chairman of the Carrizo Tribe, Juan Mancias and we discussed his tireless efforts in fighting for his tribe's rights. Juan expressed hesitancy toward seeking federal recognition, citing concerns about potential limitations on tribal  sovereignty. He highlighted, "I am really hesitant about federal recognition because it takes away your rights. You waive your sovereignty." According to Juan, federal recognition could subject a tribe to various regulations and oversight, potentially hindering their independence and decision-making abilities. He described recognized tribes as "wards of the state"  [29] .  However, the absence of federal recognition presents its own set of challenges for the tribe, particularly in their endeavor  to protect sacred lands. Without this recognition they face significant hurdles in accessing legal protections and resources necessary for safeguarding these culturally significant areas.   Juan Mancias descends from the sole survivor of The Devil's River Massacre. This tragic event occurred along the ninety-four mile stretch of the Devil's River which runs southwest along the Texas-Mexico border. In 1801, Spanish colonizers raided a Carrizo village along the river, which resulted in the brutal murder of over 300 individuals; homes were pillaged and bodies buried in a mass grave. Mancias' great-great-great-grandfather, Manuel Cavazos, then just eleven years old, miraculously survived by feigning death; bearing a spear wound in his back. Tragically, Mancias has not been able to visit the site as LNG companies have purchased the land and completely blocked it off from the public  [24] .  Starship's extensive use of methane, sourced in the form of LNG, may potentially be sourced from Carrizo land, thereby compounding the harm inflicted upon the tribe through its operations. In a 2022 interview Mancias expressed his concerns over the fate of Carrizo artifacts and remains at Boca Chica, "We have no idea what Musk did with the artifacts, if they just threw them over to the side, or sold them to collectors" [25] .  When I spoke to Mancias last year he mentioned that the Whitney Museum in Whitney, Texas possessed Carrizo remains, stating, "They have an infant body in the storage facility somewhere, and they say, well, we don't have it here anymore. But did they return it for us to take care of our ancestors? No, and it's ridiculous" [2 ].  In October 2021, a dispute erupted over SpaceX facilities and access to Boca Chica Beach in Texas. The conflict began when David Newstead, a local and the Director of the Bird Program at the nonprofit Coastal Bend Bays and Estuaries, frequented the beach for bird observations. However, he often found the beach closed, prompting him to meticulously track the closure times.  Speaking to a CBS reporter, Newstead shared his observations about changes in the refuge since SpaceX's operations began. As a monitor of migratory bird populations in Boca Chica State Park, he noted the beach had been closed for over 1,000 hours. Furthermore, he expressed concern about a marked decline in nesting, stating, "Where we once observed about a dozen nests, starting last year, we found only two, and this year, there is only one"  [5] .  On October 12th, 2021, the environmental NGO Save RGV [Rio Grande Valley] filed a lawsuit against Cameron County, the Texas General Land Office, and Texas Land Commissioner George P. Bush  [6] .  Newstead's findings, along with Save RGV's monitoring of beach closures prompted the lawsuit.  The suit challenged the constitutionality of a state law that allows officials to override the 1959 Texas Open Beaches Act, which made public access to Gulf Coast Beaches a constitutional right. According to the TOBA, everyone has the right to access and enjoy all Texas beaches for recreational purposes which include swimming, fishing, sunbathing, and other activities. The statute extends the public's right of access to the beach to the vegetation line, often known as the "dry beach," and it is applicable to all Texas beaches that are close to tidal water.  In a petition against Cameron County, Save RGV claimed that the 1959 Texas Open Beaches Act “is one of the nation’s strongest and most effective set of laws protecting public beach access” [7] .  Further, it states that in 2009, Texas voters adopted an amendment to the Texas constitution acknowledging that the public, “individually and collectively, has an unrestricted right to use and a right of ingress to and egress from a public beach."  This amendment was passed with a 77% majority, guaranteeing the right to access public beaches  [8] .  The lawsuit  challenges the 2013 House Bill 2623, permitting the closure of beaches for space flight  activities. This legislation allows SpaceX to conduct up to 12 rocket launches annually without additional permits or approvals   [9] .  Save RGV contends that House Bill 2623 violates the Texas Open Beaches Act, rendering it unconstitutional.  Save RGV requested a court declaration to invalidate any order by the Cameron County Commissioners Court authorizing the Cameron County Judge to close Boca Chica Beach and/or State Highway 4 to accommodate space flight activities  [10] .  In April of 2022, Juan Mancias attempted to access the beach to make offerings and say prayers but was denied access by Cameron County Policemen. This, he alleges, is a violation of the American Indian Religious Freedom Act   [26] . Juan Mancias explained  how access to Boca Chica is necessary to preserve their ancestral heritage, "We had villages here, to come together here for our life ways and to fish and to live. Our ancestors are buried in these lands. Our umbilical cords are planted in these land"  [27] .   The lawsuit was dismissed on July 7th, 2022, but Save RGV, The Sierra Club, and the Carrizo Comecrudo Tribe of South Texas jointly appealed the 445th District Court's decision on June 28th, 2022 [22] .  The General Land Office and attorney general of Cameron County argued that the groups lack standing for their suit because beach access can only be regulated by officials. On June 2nd 2023, the Save RGV’s Open Beach lawsuit appeal reached the 13th District Court, resulting in a dismissal on June 30th [23] .   On September 20th, 2023, The Sierra Club, Save RGV, and the Carrizo Tribe presented their appeals in a lawsuit, making oral arguments before the 13th Court of Appeals. If successful, the case will return to the district court in Brownsville. Otherwise, the groups might pursue an appeal to the Texas Supreme Court  [32] . On April 20th, 2023, SpaceX launched its Starship spacecraft. The spacecraft exploded in the air after being airborne for less than four minutes, at an altitude of twenty-four miles. Debris was scattered across the 385-acre land belonging to SpaceX and the Boca Chica state park, including "watermelon-sized slabs" of concrete measuring two feet in diameter. Additionally, a fire was discovered south of the launch pad within the state park, covering an area of 3.5 acres  [21] .  T he U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service reported that a debris cloud containing pulverized concrete spread as far as six and a half miles from the launch pad [30] .  On May 1st, 2023, Save RGV, the Center for Biological Diversity, Carrizo Tribe, and the American Bird Conservancy sued the FAA, releasing a complaint entitled Regulators Failed to Address Dangers of SpaceX Launches at Boca Chica. In this Complaint, they argued that mitigation by the FAA isn't enough to prevent the launch program  from causing significant environmental harm, and asked the FAA to suspend SpaceX's five year license  [42] . T he suit remains ongoing. The FAA, in collaboration with the U.S. Fish  and Wildlife Service, conducted a safety evaluation before granting a new flight license for a second launch attempt. Following the rocket launch and resulting damage to the pad infrastructure, the FWS released a report stating there were no lasting adverse impacts on the surrounding ecology. The report outlines sixty-three corrective measures that SpaceX needs to implement to prevent similar mishaps in the future. These actions involve redesigning vehicle hardware to prevent leaks and fires, fortifying the launch pad, incorporating more rigorous reviews in the design process, conducting further analysis and testing of safety-critical systems (like the Autonomous Flight Safety System), and enhancing change control practices  [35] .  On November 18th, 2023, SpaceX launched their second Starship rocket, intentionally detonating it mid-flight. The FAA will oversee a "mishap" investigation into the flight, a standard regulatory procedure, before SpaceX can launch another Starship rocket   [36] .

case_name: Sabine Pass LNG, Lousianna, USA
headline: Sabine Pass LNG Facility, located in Louisianas coastal wetlands, is threatening the health of local communities and ecosystems. Fisherfolk, civil and environmental organisations have been campaigning against the expansion of this facility, along with many other LNG facilities in the area.
description: The Sabine Pass Liquid natural gas (LNG) terminal comprises 3 phases, the first two are located in Sabine and the third - if approved- will be located in Cameron Parish, Louisiana [1] directly on the state border with Texas. Owned by Cheniere Energy, the project was approved by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission in 2012, costing $5 billion [12] . In reaction to this, the Sierra Club filed a legal protest against the proposed gas export project, urging the Department of Energy to consider the environmental and public health effects of increased gas production. [3] Since then, multiple environmental organisations have been fighting for the rights of the communities living in the area, citing the disastrous impacts that such LNG projects are having on the health of people and ecosystems in the region. The facility was originally intended for import, yet following the boom of hydraulic fracking in the US, it was converted to an export facility. [22] Overview of Sabine Pass LNG The LNG facility has been operational since 2016 [2] . As of 2024, it included 6 liquefaction units, each capable of producing ~5 mtpa of LNG [1] . In 2017, the facility was reportedly shipping gas from the Montery Shale facility, which included gas drilled from British Columbia and Alberta. And further down the distribution line, Sabine Pass LNG has supplied natural gas to Brazil's state owned company, Petrobras (in 2016) as well as Gail India Ltd. [18]   [19] . Furthermore, in June 2023, a long term agreement was signed with Equinor to supply the company (and thus Norway) with natural gas from Sabine Pass, "1.75 million tonnes per annum (MTPA)" [24] . It is owned by Cheniere Energy. [12] The Gulf Coast and LNG context Since the 1990s, coastal erosion has transformed the area, wiping away previously existing old growth forests [4] . Louisiana is especially vulnerable to storms and heavy rainfall, which are occurring at an increasing rate due to climate change [5] . And over the past years, motivated by the surge in global demand for natural gas, different locations have been cleared for the construction of new LNG terminals. [4] Only a decade ago (2014), the United States had never exported LNG. Yet by approving every single export licence that any company has requested in the Gulf of Mexico [11] , the US became the world’s top exporter of the fuel in 2023, surpassing Qatar in the ranking. [4]   The Sabine Pass is just one LNG project of the 33 (either in their planning stages or operational [1] ), that are located on the coast stretching from the southern tip of Texas to the south-east of Louisana. This stretch of coast's vulnerability to storms makes planning large energy facilities here extremely risky. In the past, export facilities have been forced to shut down all operations and evacuate all staff due to hurricanes. Indeed, this occurred at the Cheniere facility on August 25, 2020. A week later, and having found no significant storm damage, the company said it had begun the process to restore the facility's operations, though no timeline was given for how long it took to resume operation. [13] There is also a risk of chemical explosions caused by storms - expert Ivor van Heerden, a marine scientist and former Louisiana State University professor, assessed the hurricane risk coastal Louisiana could see in the coming years and how this could impact LNG facilities based here. He found that, “if a flood ever breached the plant’s levee system, there would be a high probability of chemicals being carried off the site and into homes, businesses, farmland, and fragile coastal wetlands.” [4] Local officials largely celebrate the increase in LNG terminals in the area, citing that the industry is a “ boon for economic growth and employment” [4] . Yet, the impacts of the expansion of such industry are felt by the people who live there. The Louisana coastline consists of a rich marshland ecosystem, and is home to people who have fished in the marshes and surrounding lakes for years. The fishing industry employs over 26,000 people, as Lousianna is the largest seafood producer in the lower 48 US states. Yet many people are being forced to relocate multiple times due to LNG construction and as a result of feeling the impacts of the dangerous pollution spewing from facilities located near their homes, resulting in job precarity and insecurity. [9] Furthermore, concerns around the health impacts of this industry were supported by a report commissioned by Earthworks, which sought to understand the impacts of air pollution using optical gas imaging monitoring. Sabine Pass LNG facility was found to be actively releasing excessive hydrocarbon emissions during both assessment periods, and the report found that, “emissions were significant and are likely underrepresented on permits, as pollutants were added to the airshed far beyond the company's property lines.” [6] And although the report examined multiple facilities in the area, the Sabine Pass LNG, “stood out in magnitude from the others”. [6] Pollutants from LNG facilities have been linked to adverse health outcomes, including respiratory and cardiovascular disease. [15] These findings counter how LNG is marketed by the companies who operate the facilities, touting the natural gas as “clean-burning” [7] , a “clean natural gas” [8] . Others have enlisted the gas as a vital "bridge fuel" in the climate crisis, including President Obama (who called LNG such during his 2014 State of the Union Address  [20] ) and more recently in March 2024, the president of ConocoPhillips  [21] . LNG is in fact mostly methane, one of the most potent greenhouse gases, [9]   and a 2023 study found that, “when the entire lifecycle of exported LNG is considered, it can be 24% worse than the lifecycle of coal.” [9] Project expansion The project is set to expand, with a planning application being filed by Cheniere to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission on February 29th 2024 [2] . In this, the company requested site access, a construction licence, and operational approval of the Sabine Pass Stage 5 Expansion Project, and the Sabine Crossing Pipeline -  a 48 inch diameter pipeline, stretching around 5 miles in length [2] . This project expansion, if approved, would further infringe on the Sabine National Wildlife refuge, which is a large area of marsh that stretches between the Calcasieu lake in the east, to the Sabine lake in the west.  Resistance Following campaigns and a mass outcry from national and international environmental groups against the proposed LNG Facilities along the Gulf coast (including a Washington DC protest and a petition with over 200,000 signatures) [10] [23] , on the morning of January 26, 2024 the government decided to pause pending approvals of liquefied natural gas export facilities [14] , which includes the proposed expansion of the Sabine Pass facility into its 5th phase . Environmental groups and Lousianna coastal communities celebrated this decision - Greenpeace’s USA Executive Director, Ebony Twilley-Martin, responded to the decision stating that, “Today, we celebrate an incredible win that rests squarely in the hands of people living on the frontlines, who have been fighting this nightmare tirelessly for years. With this delay, President Biden is demonstrating that the United States can and will transition away from dirty oil and gas. It’s a remarkable step that defines the stakes in the upcoming election”  [10]   .  As the government complied with their wishes, environmental organisations of Lousiana, have called off a scheduled sit-in at the Department of Energy. Roishetta Ozane stated that, “now, our focus shifts to the next steps. We're requesting a meeting with the White House and the DOE to discuss how the public interest determination should be made and how frontline communities can actively participate in the process.” [11] Others are concerned that the decision was merely an election stunt to win over voters, and call for assurance that the decision will not be overturned following the appointment of a new President. Wenonah Hauter, who is the executive director of Food & Water Watch, states, “We don’t need new criteria if they only serve to arrive at the original conclusion, and increased exports are eventually approved. President Biden should permanently halt new and existing oil and gas exports, and aggressively ramp down the fossil fuel industry once and for all.” [10] Indeed, delaying the decision does not mark a definitive end to the project.  The Louisiana Bucket Brigade is another organisation at the forefront of protecting Louisana from gas exports, working to unite local residents, fishermen and organisations to reject the dozen facilities planned for Plaquemines, Calcasieu and Cameron Parishes. They organise events and media campaigns to raise the visibility of local resistance to the expansion, and help mobilise the affected communities to get in contact with the federal government. [16] Further to this, they have created an interactive mapping tool called the iWitness Pollution Map to allow community members to document and track through crowdsourcing. [17]

case_name: Baynouna Solar Power Plant and Sun-for-Water deal with Israel, Jordan
headline: Baynouna Solar Plant is located in the Al Muwaqqar district of north west Jordan. Members of the Al-Balqa tribe have been battling against the project since its inception, because the project causes significant destruction on an environmental, societal and cultural heritage basis. Further to this, Jordan and Israel have struck a precarious water-for-energy deal, which the Jordanian people oppose.
description: The Baynouna solar photovoltaic (PV) facility is located in the Al Muwaqqar district of north west Jordan. [1] The project includes a 248-megawatt facility which was developed by Masdar, the Abu Dhabi Future Energy Company with funding from the International Finance Corporation (IFC). [3] In 2020, when construction was already underway, members of the Al-Balqa tribe lodged a formal complaint with the independent Compliance Advisory Ombudsman (CAO), the organisation that addresses the environmental and social concerns of communities affected by IFC and Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA) projects [1] [4] . This was the community's final option after years of discussions between themselves the IFC, government officials, and others since late 2018, during which members of the Al-Balqa tribe were threatened and harassed. [4] Energy context in Jordan - Jordan’s government - along with support from the IMF - began privatising its energy sector in 2007. Gradually, distribution and investment companies were introduced through new energy deals, set up to ensure that they would not experience any financial risks, only profits. Such agreements made private corporations the benefactors of energy production and distribution, while leaving the public energy sector to soak up the financial burdens. Additionally, there was no strategy to ensure energy security in its longevity. [2] Such an energy plan, bolstered by IFC funding deals that guarantee debts will fall on the public's pocket, has made Jordans energy provision increasingly unstable.  In 2011, the government decided to adopt a new plan - based on “diversification and the exploitation of local energy sources” [2] . Over the next few years, this strategy included plans to purchase Israeli gas (despite widespread public protest about this decision) [6] , building the oil shale-fuelled  Attarat  Power  Plant (funded by the international Estonian company Enefit), and finally the promotion of locally generated renewable energy. [2] By 2022, renewables made up 30% of the country's total electricity production [7] . Yet the sector is dominated by private companies and rich individuals, an arrangement that syphons profits away from the public energy sector. [2] It is important to mention the role natural gas plays in Jordan, it being the most used component in domestic power generation and the most significant contributor to energy costs. [2] Indeed, by looking at figure 5 in this conflict case you can see that in 2014, when gas supplies were cut off the country had to turn to diesel at a great expense. In 2015, the New Fortress-owned liquid natural gas (LNG) terminal in the Port of Aqaba began operation - which explains why natural gas usage in the country shot up in 2016. In 2020, only natural gas and renewable energy was being used to meet the country's consumption needs. [2] In terms of renewable energy production, the government brought in the Renewable Energy and Energy Efficiency Law 2012 which, among other things, established 2 ways of producing renewables in the country - direct bid renewable projects and self-generation renewable projects. The former promoted and encouraged direct foreign investment in public-private partnership deals, whereas the latter allowed for individuals to produce their own renewables to then sell back to the grid, benefiting from a sort of ‘free energy’ agreement in which they received monetary compensation from the government. Both ways of production left little room for the public energy sector to benefit, and therefore drove up costs for individuals who could not afford to produce their own energy. The scheme, in effect, made the most energy-vulnerable communities increasingly vulnerable with no state support. At the same time, increasing profits for the private firms and decreasing profits for the public energy sector. [2] Project and conflict timeline The Baynouna facility is part of the ‘Seven Sisters’ project - a renewable energy public-private partnership under which multiple solar PV projects are included, all financed by a single financing package [4] . This deal was struck between the IFC and the Government of Jordan in 2011, yet it wasn’t until December 2017 that the IFC arranged a sum of up to $188 million to build and operate the Baynouna solar PV facility [4] . Following this, between December 2018 and February 2020 members of the Al-Baqua tribe brought their grievances to the project planners, IFC and Government officials. Despite this, construction work began in early 2019.  Mr Farhan Al-Daboubi, who is also the chairman of the Jordanian advocacy group the East Amman Society for Environmental Protection (EASEP), was the primary member of the Al-Baqua community that then raised the issues with CAO. The official claim he lodged was supported by 66 other named members of the tribe, and brought forward issues that their tribe had with the project. In this formal complaints process, they lodged 8 official complaints which are as follows - exclusion from the stakeholder identification and pre project consultation process; land rights violations and uncompensated economic displacement of their people and livestock; exclusion from development benefits and opportunities (including lack of employment opportunities from the mega project); threats and reprisals (including intimidation, threats and harassments towards the EASEP); no compliance with environmental and social management systems; cumulative environmental degradation caused by the project; air pollution and threats to worker health and safety. [4] The IFC responded in February 2022, refuting all of the claims made by Mr Al-Daboubi, using measures drawn up by the IFC and laws of the Government to substantiate their arguments. [4] The CAO concluded that all of the Al-Baqua groups grievances were plausible, giving evidence to support their stance which included how the IFC had failed to involve them in the decision making process, how they had ignored evidence of the Al-Baqua peoples’ use of the land and further environmental issues related to the project. [4]   Sun-for-water deal with Israel  In September 2023, an agreement was made between Israel’s energy minister and the chief executive of UAE’s renewable energy firm Masdar  to trade water-for-energy with Jordan. [5] In this agreement, Jordan would supply solar energy power from a new 600 MW capacity solar plant with storage to Israel, receiving desalinated water in return. This agreement makes Jordan worryingly dependent on Israel and Jordanian people have been taking part in widespread protests against the deal since 2021, warning against making Jordan's water supply dependent on the "hostile entity" Israel [8] .

case_name: Tataouine Solar Power Plant, Tunisia
headline: The Tataouine Solar Plant in Tunisia was blocked by members of the national workers union, in protest of Tunisia's shift towards prioritising the profits of international investors over the public good through provisioning of renewable energy.
description: The Tataouine Solar power plant in the south east of Tunisia began producing energy at the end of 2022. [1] Its capacity is 10 MW, located right next to the city of Foum Tatahouine and it is owned by the Italian energy giant ENI and built by the Société Énergie Renouvelables Eni Etap (SEREE) (which is a joint venture between Eni and the Entreprise Tunisienne d'Activités Pétrolières). [1] The energy it produces is sold on to the national grid, and makes up 1% of Société Tunisienne de l'électricité et du Gaz (STEG)’s total energy production. [1] The project cost 30 million Tunisian dinar (USD 9.57m). [4] In 2020, the plant was ready for operational use, yet the connection project associated with the plant was “the victim of sabotage” [2] . According to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Energy Transition, Mongi Marzouk, who was arrested in August 2022 for charges in relation to his involvement in corruption linked to the Gafsa Phosphate Company project [2] . The sabotage involved the General Federation of Electricity and Gas, under the Tunisian General Labour Union (UGTT) refusing to connect the Tataouine solar power plant to the network. [3] Abdelkader Jelassi, secretary general of the General Federation of Electricity and Gas responded to Marzouks accusations of sabotage, stating, “we (the union) are not against renewable energy…but against people who for 60 years have continuously fed off of the state. They take without giving anything in return. If the private sector wants to use the grid, it has to pay.” [3] Events leading up to the resistance  The Tunisian governments' mission to slowly increase privatisation of the countries energy sector (heavily influenced by international law firms and the German government agency GIZ [6] ), has been met by opposition from the UGTT, the biggest Tunisian labour union who have been at the forefront of the fight. One reason for their position against privatisation is that these grand infrastructure projects do not necessarily bring tangible benefits to the Tunisian people. Indeed, i n 2020, the countries first wind turbine project was built 70km from the capital, Tunis. Yet, residents of the nearby town, Borj Salhi remained unconnected to the national grid. The example this set about international companies regard for local people and their right to electricity helped form the basis of the UGTT's understanding of how privatisation of energy could look like in Tunisia [7] . Since then, they have ran a huge public awareness campaign to disseminate information about how privatising energy can impact communities negatively, alongside holding direct negotiations with the government. This campaign used evidence from studies of the failing private power stations located south of Tunis that are run by foreign energy companies [7] . I n 2014 they spoke out in reaction to the governments amendments to a bill concerning land use for renewable energy projects (which later became the 2015-12 Law [5] , that governs Tunisia's approach to production and distribution of renewable energy) [4] . Further to this, they reacted to the decision making process behind the bill, stating that it was, “drawn up without involving the UGTT or STEG’s executives and engineers''. [3] Following from this, on 27th of March 2018, the General Federation for Oil and Gas (FGEG) formalised their demands by calling for the non-privatisation of the electricity production sector.  [3] A few months before the UGTT blocked the Tataouine power plant, the government had issued a decree that approved the rights of ‘individuals’ (read private companies) to produce their own renewable electricity and sell it back to the national grid. A move which the FGEG condemned as they believed this would disrupt the country's electricity network, and marked a definitive move towards prioritising the motives of private foreign investment, favouring investor profit over the public utility of energy. [3]   Ultimately, the UGTT believe that energy is a public good, and seek to defend the “quasi-monopoly” of STEG, which dominates the production, transport, distribution and sale of energy in Tunisia. [3] Blocking the operation of the Tataouine plant represented a subsequent step, highlighting their position against the government's swift implementation of new energy regulations aimed at market liberalisation and foreign investme nt. This action followed years of vocal opposition they had expressed prior. Latest updates  Despite the actions of the UGTT to stem operation of the Tataouine Solar plants while it is geared toward profit maximisation for private firms, it began producing power for the national grid by the end of 2022. [1]

case_name: Matabari LNG Terminal, Bangladesh
headline: Matabari LNG Terminal is one of many LNG projects destined for the south east of Bangladesh. Local communities have been displaced by the project, and their livelihoods have been disrupted with no sign of compensation. International corporations such as JERA are key funders of the project.
description: The Matabari Liquid Natural Gas (LNG) import terminal was to be located in the south east of Bangladesh, in Matabari, Cox's Bazaar, Chittagong division. The project threatened the livelihoods of the local communities who work in the area, relying largely on salt farming in the dryer months, fish and shrimp farming in the rainy season and livestock farming all year round [3] . The land acquisition process for the project forced locals from the lands that their livelihoods depended on, and people have reported no kind of compensation for their displacement. [2] [3] Committing to another LNG project serves the interests of international companies who wish to strengthen the global LNG market, and will further lock Bangladesh into years of reliance on fossil gas use as well as compounding climatic impacts felt both locally and globally. Country and Area Context Following the failure of coal mining projects, Bangladesh's economy turned to become dependent on local gas. Yet, gas exploration in the area had limited success, which is what has led them to now increasingly depend on importing liquified natural gas to meet the country's ga demands. The country first started importing LNG in 2018-19. In 2022, the country imported a substantial quantity of LNG (5.06 million metric tons) from Qatar Gas, Oman Trading, and the Spot market, costing them USD 4,555 million [16] . In 2021, Japan’s International Cooperation Agency (JICA) was given the rights to prepare Bangladesh’s national energy plan. [14] Energy experts urged JICA to design the plans “in Bangladesh’s best interests, not Japan's” [15] , suggesting a low or zero emission roadmap with no further expansion of coal and LNG should be put in place [2] . The district of Cox’s Bazaar in the south east of Bangladesh includes the town of the same name and a surrounding area of high biodiversity. Since 2017, when conflict in Rakhine State escalated, the southern tip of the region became one of the largest refugee camps in the world, called Kutupalong [10] . Around 1 million Rohingya refugees, having fled persecution in neighbouring Myanmar, live in precarious, informal settlements that are spread across the region. [8] [9]   The proposed fossil fuel projects in the area - including not only the Matabari LNG, but also coal and gas fired power plants and pipeline infrastructure - risk exacerbating issues of land use and resource scarcity further, jeopardising the livelihoods of those living in the area who rely on the natural resources. The coal and gas projects in the area have already forces hundreds of families to relocate to other areas of the country. [3] In addition to this, cyclones that hit the area typically between the months of March to July, causing floods and landslides, are increasing in frequency as an impact of climate change [9] [10] , severely impacting the lives and livelihoods of those living in the area and often forcing people to migrate north to major cities to escape these climate impacts. [3] Project Timeline The Matabari LNG is part of the larger, Matarbari Integrated Infrastructure Development Initiative (MIDI) which includes a power plant, transport infrastructure such as roads and railway, a powerplant development area and 2 ports (see image 5 in this conflict case) . In July 2018, the Bangladeshi government signed two separate agreements coming to the sum of $7.4 billion, in efforts to generate 6000 megawatts of electricity from power plants supplied with gas from LNG terminals destined to be located in the Cox’s Bazar region. [11] One of these deals was the Matabari terminal, run by the Summit Corporation Limited which is (in part owned by JERA, Japan's largest power generation company and) a subsidiary of Summit Power International Limited. [12] [13] The project also had involvement from Japan’s Mitsubishi Corporation and the US's General Electric Company. [11] The initial plan was to establish a floating LNG that was to be located in the port was later scrapped due to technical issues caused by adverse weather issues [4] . Following this, the onland Matabari LNG project was proposed in January 2019 by Rupantarita Pratkritik Gas Company, a subsidiary of Petrobangla, Bangladesh's state owned oil and gas company [1] . In 2019, a number of Japanese companies such as Japan Investment Corporation, JERA, Mitsubishi Corporation, Mitsui & Co, Marubeni, Osaka Gas, Sumitomo Corporation, Tokyo Gas showed interest in developing the project, as well as the oil and gas giants Shell and Total. [2] [5] In January 2020, the Bangladeshi Minister for Shipping Khalid Mahmud Chowdhury Chief announced that the project will be developed with financing from JICA [ 1] . The company plan on putting the Matarbari-Maheshkhali development, "at the centre of the “Bay of Bengal Industrial Growth Belt (BIG-B)” initiative.  [17] The Prime Minister of Bangladesh, Sheikh Hasina, urged JICA that they must properly compensate the local people that will be impacted by the mega project, stating, "It’s seen (at many times) that the people whose lands are acquired for development get nothing. So you’ll have to look into the matter so that they get proper compensation.” [18] Resistance to the project Fossil Free Chattogram, a campaign group set up by the Australian NGO Market Forces, is working to raise awareness of the “carbon bomb” [6] that the proposed coal and gas projects in the area would create, if approved. They draw attention to the financial risk that Bangladesh is taking by housing such projects - stating that by 2023, the annual LNG import cost will reach an estimated US$8.4 billion [3] . They created a call to action to encourage people who oppose the project to unite against it, in signing an email addressed to GE, Mitsubishi, JERA and JICA to call on them to halt the projects, on environmental and civil grounds. [7] The communities living in the surrounding area and in the city of Chattogram, just north of the project, have been speaking out about the impacts that Matabari LNG is having on their lives and the ecosystem. Market Forces reported that fisherfolk from the region count their catch regularly, each week the number of fish is getting smaller making it increasingly difficult to make a living to feed their families [3] . Additionaly, those whose work depends on the land acquirred by the project are worried that they will not be given the compensation for their losses. Pastoral cattle grazer Mohammad Redwan stated, “I graze buffaloes during monsoon and do whatever work is available to me. These lands have been acquired. What will I do to feed my family in the future? We have been told many times we will get compensation, but we have not received any.” [3] Noman, a landowner in Matabari stated that, “170 acres of land is being acquired for the LNG Terminal. We’ve been put on notice on 6 september 2002 to relocate, but no discussions [with the community] have taken place before or after” [5] .  Latest updates The project was due to be operational by 2023/2024, yet its is still under construction.

case_name: Rotterdam Industrial Port, The Netherlands
headline: The Port of Rotterdam has historically been the home to polluting industries like fossil fuels and coal transportation. Yet, with the advent of the green transition, more greenwashed industrial projects are being planned, with little regard for the health of local populations. Environmental groups are leading the campaign against the ports industrial, climatically destructive activities.
description: The Port The Port of Rotterdam is the largest in Europe, facilitating shipping logistics, import and export of manufactured goods, ferry services, chemical processing and oil and gas facilities [1] . It spans 26 miles along the mouth of the Scheur river. The two stakeholders of the port are Rotterdam municipality and the Dutch state [4] . The port is home to a Sustainable Aviation Fuel SAF projec t and will soon host a Carbon Capture and Storage (CCS) project. Neste SAF project  The SAF project in Rotterdam Port is managed by Neste Oyj. Neste’s majority shareholder is the Government of Finland, with other shareholders including The Vanguard Group, Keskinäinen Työeläkevakuutusyhtiö Varma, Norges Bank Investment Management and Capital International Ltd. [3] . The company was founded in 1948 as the state petrol company of Finland. [18] In the 1960s-70s, it became the largest company in Finland and following this is began to explore and produce oil and gas, entering into the chemical industry. [18] It was not until 2007 when the company entered into renewable fuel source research - first, looking into using algae and municipal solid waste for 'sustainable fuel', then moving toward refining "renewable diesel" at their plant in Singapore using palm oil and feed stocks to produce the fuel [19] . The company is the largest SAF producer in the world, with refineries in Singapore and now in the Netherlands [9] . In 2021, they introduced the SAF production project to their refinery in Rotterdam Port, investing an additional €190 million. Originally its capacity is to produce SAF was around 500,000 tons per year, however as their project expanded so to did the expected annual capacity - which is now at 1.2 million tons per annum. [2]   [8]   [17]  The project is expected to begin in 2026.  CCS Project The Porthos CCS project will be the first CO2 storage project in the Netherlands. It is planned to have a 2.5Mtpa storage capacity, and will be an “open access” project to capture and store carbon from many facilities in the port [5] .   Its feasibility study was completed in April 2018. Following this, it was awarded a subsidy from the Connecting Europe Facility (CEF) grant by the European Commission in July 2019. [5] It is managed by ‘Porthos joint venture’ - made up of the Port of Rotterdam Authority, Gasunie and EBN - who signed an agreement with four oil, gas and chemical companies in December 2019, these being Shell, Exxon Mobil, Air Liquide and Air Products [7] . These companies will invest in their own capture installations which will supply CO2 to Porthos. Porthos will then transport this CO2 through the port and out to sea to store in depleted gas fields in the North Sea which is located around 20 km from the coast, and at a depth of 3 - 4 km under the sea bed. The CO2 is transported by a collective pipeline that runs through the Rotterdam port area, and is 30km long - extending from the eastern end of Oude Maas, through the Botlek area then the Europoort area to the compressor station at Maasvlakte [22] .  The total investment required for the project was €1.3 billion, which it reached in October 2023. [5] In 2024 construction will begin in Rotterdam, with the Porthos system expected to be operational by 2026. [7] It has been deemed a Project of Common Interest by the EU [7] . Description of the conflict and mobilisation  At least since the 1970s, people living in the Rijnmond region have been protesting against the port's industrial activity. Back then, the steel company Koninklijke Hoogovens were the focus of the campaign as their activity produced a huge amount of air pollution. Students and residents mobilised en masse, dumping polluted dredging sludge on the city hall steps [6] demanding that the municipality take action to introduce restrictions on industrial activity in the area. 93,000 signatures were collected against large-scale steel producers. [6] The port has also historically been the target of anti-coal campaigns - it tranships the largest amounts of coal of any European port. [20]   More recently, there have been campaigns against the LNG terminal located at the port by ING Fossil Free, which is a collective ING Bank customers and other citizens that are concerned with the fact that ING Bank is the 3rd largest financier of LNG terminals in the US worldwide. [21] In 2023, although pollution remains, the cause of such has evolved along with the industrial shifts towards green energy projects at the port. Fossil fuel companies such as Shell, ExxonMobil, and BP are now the targets of the campaigns. Leading the resistance in 2023 was the Netherlands Extinction Rebellion (XR) group who state that - “Behind the symbol of a city of growth, prosperity and open gates to the world is a thick smokescreen that hides a bleak reality: the port is heavily dependent on fossil fuels, relies on polluting industries, damages our collective health & prosperity and is driven by profit over people.” [4] Their campaign seeks to "Herover de Haven" (“reclaim the port”) through four demands centred around climate futures, jobs, air pollution and recentering decision making in line with public interest - with the goal of making this key industrial hub less reliant on and focused around fossil fuels and more committed to societal well being. [4] The group has carried out a number of actions including occupying Erasmus Bridge [10] , demonstrating at the port headquarters [12] and blocking cruise liners [11] .  Throughout the years, the people campaigning against the port's activities have been highlighting the health impacts of the industrial activity on Rijnmond citizens. According to the European Environmental Agency, the 5 biggest companies in the port (Shell, Maersk, Vopak, Exxon Mobil and BP ) [13]   cause annual health damage of 2.7 billion euros for the local population, calculated in years of life lost [13] . In a study conducted on babies born in Zeeland, an area with minimal road traffic just south of the port, it was found that babies born to mothers exposed to industrial air pollution are on average 75g lighter, compared to the babies of mothers that smoked during pregnancy. [13]  In late 2023, it was also revealed that the oil companies based in the port were involved in a huge lobbying campaign against the tightening of an EU Law that would limit workers exposure to benzene, the chemical compound that raises risk of developing cancer and other deadly diseases [14] .   XR demand for the mapping of all harmful substances released from the port, to hold industries accountable. Indeed, Rotterdam airport is subject to health and pollution inspections and XR argues that the port should be subject to the same. [6] Latest developments  On the 8th of December, 2023, 130 activists from XR began occupying the access roads to Europoort. In a statement online, XR called to attention that despite promising to halve its emissions by 2025 in the “Rotterdam Climate Initiative Action Programme and Goals 2007-2010” document, almost 20 years later the emissions remain the same. With the new projects such as CCS and SAF production, the emissions are not predicted to decrease anytime soon. [16] Following this pressure the mayor of Rotterdam, Ahmed Aboutaleb, said he wishes to hold talks with the group on how to “green” the port. A spokesperson from XR stated that "These talks will focus on how the port can become more sustainable and how Rotterdam can play a leading role in the energy transition" [15] .
