case_name: Corpus Christi LNG facility, Texas, USA
headline: Cheniere's plans to expand its liquefied natural gas facility in Corpus Christi are widely disputed, both locally and internationally. The LNG industry is expanding rapidly along the Gulf Coast, particularly to fill the European supply gap created as a result of the Russian invasion of Ukraine. These heavily polluting facilities take a toll on public health and the environment
description: The erosion-prone Gulf Coast is crumbling under the vast expansion of the Unites States  liquefied natural gas (LNG)  industry [1] . In part attributable to a 2022 agreement with the EU to increase energy supply against the backdrop of the Russian invasion of Ukraine, the United States has come to be the world’s biggest LNG exporter [2] . The biggest company responsible for these exports is  Cheniere Energy , which operates two LNG facilities on the Gulf Coast: Sabine Pass LNG in Louisiana and  Corpus Christi LNG  in South Texas [3] .   Cheniere’s Corpus Christi facility is located in Gregory in San Patricio County, Texas. This county is part of the  Coastal Bend  region, which is home to a relatively large Latino population [4] . The communities living in the Coastal Bend are already at the frontline of climate change impacts, experiencing recurrent droughts, heatwaves, and hurricanes, as well as loss of land due to rising sea levels [5] . At large, the development of fossil fuel extraction infrastructure in the region has been met with fierce resistance, particularly from the indigenous Karankawa Kadla tribe  [4] .    Corpus Christi LNG consists of three liquefaction trains, vaporization facilities, LNG storage tanks, a marine terminal, a 23-mile pipeline network, compression stations, and supporting facilities [6] . In November 2023, the facility exported more than 64 billion cubic feet of LNG (1.34 million tonnes) [7] . Most of these exports are hauled to Spain, the United Kingdom, Brazil, China, Japan, and South Korea  [4] .   Soon after commissioning in 2018, the Corpus Christi facility became the second-largest emitter of nitrogen oxide in Texas  [4] . The facility is almost entirely supplied by gas from the  Permian Basin  in West Texas, which is known to be among the worst methane-emitting gas extraction sites in the country  [3] . From the start, the Corpus Christi plant has been regularly exceeding emission limits for pollutants such as carbon monoxide, soot, and volatile organic compounds (VOCs) [8] . Rather than imposing sanctions, however, the  Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ)  repeatedly increased the company’s permitted emission levels  [8] . Besides, Cheniere receives significant tax breaks facilitated by the state government (857 million USD so far)  [4] .   Naturally, these emissions negatively affect public health and the environment. Methane is a highly potent greenhouse gas, contributing significantly to global warming. Nitrogen oxide exposure can harm the respiratory system and lead to difficulty breathing, asthma, and skin irritation  [4] . Some residents report a heightened occurrence of respiratory diseases among children in the region  [1] . The facility does not only affect the environment through air pollution but also water use. Most of the water available in Corpus Christi is used by industrial facilities, and water shortages in the area motivated plans to construct several desalination plants  [4] . These plans are not well received by local communities, however. Not only would the freshwater made available simply feed further industrial development in the area, but desalination plants can also severely damage coastal ecosystems by discharging polluted brine  [4] .   Despite existing concerns over health and environmental impacts associated with Cheniere’s operations, the company plans to expand its Corpus Christi plant to increase its productive capacity by nearly twofold   [4] . This  stage III  expansion would include seven liquefaction trains and is planned to be finished in 2027 [9] . For these constructions, the company expects additional tax breaks from the local government  [4] . In 2022, Cheniere made a financing agreement with French company  Engie , who had ended its contract with the American gas company in 2020 out of concerns over methane emissions along the LNG supply chain. Engie justified the financing deal by pointing to expected emission improvements  [4] . Cheniere is planning on constructing two more trains to be operational by 2031  [4] .   In 2022, Cheniere launched a controversial certification scheme:  Cargo Emissions Tags (CETs) . The company presents the scheme as part of the solution to climate change, but a report by Greenpeace and Oil Change International found Cheniere’s analytical methods to be highly flawed, producing a severely underestimated image of the true emissions resulting from the company’s activities  [3] . Japanese  Sumitomo Mitsui Financial Group (SMBC)  and France’s  Société Générale  lead a consortium of banks financing the CETs scheme  [3] .    In June 2021, the Sierra Club, the Environmental Integrity Project, and the Portland Citizens United reached out to the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality, requesting a public case hearing to contest another air pollution permit application by Cheniere  [4] . In the following year, the Sierra Club took litigation action against the commission’s decision to grant the company an extended pollution permit for Corpus Christi Stage III [4] . According to the environmental organization, increasing LNG exports drive up domestic gas prices. Other concerns mentioned include increasing shipping traffic and the associated impacts on marine wildlife and air quality, as well as the anticipated project benefits being blown out of proportion. Not only does the Sierra Club contest the energy crisis argument Cheniere uses – pointing to the fact that it will take several years before the expansion is completed - but it also criticizes the company’s lack of consideration for the distributive dimension of the promised economic benefits. In February 2024, local opponents organized a caravan protesting Cheniere’s operations and expansion plans after the Biden administration announced a temporary halt on pending LNG export projects [10] .   Internationally, opponents have also been voicing their disapproval of Cheniere’s LNG activities in Corpus Christi. In 2021, Coastal Bend residents joined German environmental activists of Ende Gelände in demonstrations against the planned Brunsbüttel LNG terminal, which is expected to receive LNG from the Corpus Christi facility  [4] . Between May and June of 2022, an international campaign against SMBC’s investments in fossil fuel infrastructure (including Cheniere’s plants on the Gulf Coast) involved protests in Japan, Indonesia, the Philippines, Kenya, the UK, the Netherlands, and the USA [11] . Dutch multinational ING is the second biggest financer of the American LNG industry, amongst others supporting Cheniere’s operations in the Coastal Bend  [5] . In the Netherlands, ING Fossielvrij ( ING Fossil Free ), organized a protest in front of one of bank’s offices against LNG facilities in the Gulf of Mexico. International NGO Banktrack invited some residents from Corpus Christi to speak during the protest  [1] . A banner used during the protest describes the Gulf Coast as a having become a  sacrifice zone .

case_name: LNG Terminals around Calcasieu Lake, Louisiana, USA
headline: Liquified natural gas (LNG) projects in Louisiana are rapidly expanding; local populations are raising many concerns for health and environment.
description: The conflict around the Calcasieu lake LNG terminals originated in 2014, precisely when the planning stages of the Cameron/Calcasieu LNG facility project was initiated in response to the growing expansion of liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports from the United States . Since that year, a precise timeline of the conflict's evolution has emerged .  Starting in 2014, crucial environmental and societal concerns came to the forefront, encompassing the potential threat of local environmental degradation, the inherent risks associated with hydraulic fracturing, greenhouse gas emissions, and disruptions that could impact local communities.    Calcasieu Pass LNG facility is an LNG establishment put forward in Louisiana, United States. The plant would be constructed to the south of Lake Charles, Louisiana   [1] . This project engages low-income and communities of color in  Cameron  and.  Calcasieu  parishes (estimated population 210,000), close to the region often described as Louisiana's Cancer Alley.    Community complaints and regulatory scrutiny arose during the proposal and approval phases, resulting in conflicts during construction over environmental damage and interruptions. Environmental hazards and regulatory violations were the centrepieces of protests and litigation. Community groups and environmental organisations used activism to try to influence project decisions. Ongoing disagreements spilled over into operations, raising concerns about environmental damage and community well-being.   The construction of Cameron LNG and Calcasieu Pass LNG, two liquefied natural gas (LNG) export facilities in the United States, is linked with the country's transition from a natural gas importer to a strong exporter. This trend may be traced back to the United States' shale gas boom, that was triggered by hydraulic fracturing, or fracking, which liberated large supplies of natural gas trapped in shale formation  [2] . With a natural gas surplus, the emphasis moved into exporting this resource to international markets, where prices were frequently higher.   T he operation of the Cameron LNG facility has prompted major concerns, especially due to recurring equipment failures that occur at an alarming rate of roughly two breakdowns per month. These failures frequently result in the discharge of greenhouse gases and volatile organic compounds, both of which contribute to climate change and pose urgent health threats to neighbouring communities as reported by the local environmental justice organisation Louisiana Bucket Brigade [3] . These chemicals have been connected to neurological diseases and cancer. The recurrence of these equipment failures highlights the importance of advocating for stronger security standards and rigorous maintenance procedures on the premises in order to minimise the impact on the environment and safeguard the well-being of the local people   [3] .   Regulatory compliance obstacles became significant occurrences, with legal claims implying deficient adherence to environmental standards. municipal communities and environmental organisations were among those involved, as were project developers such as Venture Global LNG and regulatory agencies at the federal, state, and municipal levels. Environmental implications, community health, and economic factors were all mentioned in the claims, emphasising the difficulty of reconciling energy development with environmental and social responsibilities.     The environmental consequences of these LNG installations are significant, involving a wide range of concerns. The liquefaction process and associated activities can result in greenhouse gas and pollutant emissions, potentially harming local air quality   [4] . Furthermore, the significant water requirements for cooling and the liquefaction process place a burden on local water supplies, potentially depleting aquifers and harming aquatic habitats. Consequently, responsible use of water became vital, such facilities' construction and operation can also disrupt natural habitats, potentially impacting local species and biodiversity, forcing a delicate balance between infrastructure expansion and environmental protection  [5] .   The authorization given to the Commonwealth LNG Terminal by the US Energy Regulatory Commission one year ago has resulted in several effects. It is predicted to emit huge amounts of greenhouse gases and air pollutants, potentially endangering the well-being of surrounding populations and changing the landscape. While the development delivers economic advantages by providing jobs and raising wages in impoverished towns, concerns about the environment persist, especially in hurricane-prone areas. Local communities, environmental organisations, and legal challenges are opposing the enterprise, underscoring the difficult balance between economic progress and environmental sustainability.     In response, environmental justice organisations like the Cameron Environmental Justice Alliance, Indigenous groups such as the Atakapa-Ishak Nation, and bigger organisations such as the Sierra Club and Greenpeace have all spoken out against the LNG projects in Southwest Louisiana. Local organisations such as the Calcasieu Property Owners Association express concerns about safety and environmental damage, and social initiatives such as the Cameron Climate Action Coalition address larger climate change issues. They advocate for rights, conservation, and climate goals in the face of LNG development, addressing possible adverse effects on people, indigenous lands, and the environment.     Furthermore, Louisiana fisherman, shrimpers, and climate activists protested the expansion of LNG export terminals on the Calcasieu River. The demonstration, that occurred during a conference attended by oil and gas executives, aimed to highlight the concrete impact of such projects on the community's livelihoods and cultural practises. This collective action exemplifies the persistent conflict between energy development and the preservation of local ecosystems and traditional livelihoods [6] . The social implications of these LNG installations are numerous. These facilities are frequently located in or near small, rural areas, and while they provide economic benefits, they can also disrupt Louisiana residents' lives. It has become highly important for striking a balance between development and the preservation of local ways of life.  Proponents claim that LNG facilities generate jobs both during construction and afterward, contributing to the local economy and giving employment possibilities, particularly in economically disadvantaged areas   [1] . They often, however, have an impact on the cultural and social fabric of local communities by changing traditional practises, social dynamics, and ways of life.   Critical weather conditions are a recurring concern for LNG plants such as Cameron LNG and Calcasieu Pass LNG in Louisiana's coastal region. The Gulf Coast is subject to powerful hurricanes and winds, which can interrupt business, destroy infrastructure, and endanger worker safety  [3] . Because of these weather-related dangers, extensive disaster preparedness and mitigation techniques are required. Additionally, the violation of the Clean Air Act by miscalculating and underreporting emissions at the Cameron LNG facility raises concerns about transparency and accountability  [3] . This regulatory noncompliance not only jeopardises environmental protection efforts, but it also damages public trust. Simultaneously, communities near the Calcasieu Pass facility have expressed persistent concerns about constant flaring, which not only disrupts daily life but also causes environmental damage, as dredging activities contribute to beach erosion, harm local seafood and sea life, and disrupt local boating activities   [3] .

case_name: The Mphanda Nkuwa Hydropower Project, Mozambique
headline: The Mphanda Nkuwa Hydropower Project, fiercely opposed by local environmental and civil society organisations, on the basis that a project such as this will only benefit global corporations and governments, while leaving local lives and ecosystems to deal with the life threatening consequences. Justiça Ambiental and communities in the Tete region have been resisting the project since early 2000s.
description: The Mphanda Nkuwa Hydropower project is located on one of Africa’s most dammed rivers, the Zambezi [3] . Since its inception, local environmental and civil society organisations have opposed the project on the basis that a project such as this will only benefit global corporations and governments, while leaving local lives and ecosystems to deal with the life threatening consequences. Lack of transparency from government officials, including withholding vital project documents and lying about the existence of an updated environmental impact assessment contributed to local scepticism surrounding the project. [3] Project Timeline After years of trying to secure funding for the project, it was announced in 2010 by the government that the Export–Import Bank of China would fund the project build, investing over $2 billion. [3] It would be located only 60 km downstream from another Dam project, Cahora Bassa. This existing project already has impacts on river restoration further downstream. Yet by 2023, the dam's construction was still not underway, and in June 2023, it was announced that the European Union (EU) and the European Investment Bank (EIB) will contribute €500 million to the financing of the project. [4] The following December, shortly after COP27, it was announced that the consortium of EDF, TotalEnergies and Sumitomo Corporation had been selected by the Government of Mozambique to enter into a joint development of the controversial Mphanda Nkuwa hydropower project. [1] The total cost of the project well be $2.4bn. [11]   This partnership contract was signed before a single community consultation meeting with the people who live in the region had been carried out. [10] Energy for whom?  The dam has a projected capacity of 1,350 megawatts. [3]   Yet, excluding Mozambique's largest energy consumer (the Mozal aluminium smelter) the country's demand for electricity stands at just 350 megawatts. The government was hoping that this project would attract more energy-intensive industries to Mozambique, and that it will address rural electrification shortfalls. [5] The reality is many people living rurally do not have access due to the high cost of this electricity, as prices are driven up by extending the transmission grid. It is said that the Mphanda Nkuwa project will not contribute significantly to rural electrification. [2] Indeed, the communities surrounding the longer established Cahora Bassa Dam remain un-electrified, while the power it generates is sold well below market value to neighbouring countries. [3] In 2013, it was noted that “the majority of the electricity generated by Mphanda Nkuwa will be sold to South Africa.” [5] While the negative impacts of this dam project will be felt locally, the positive impacts - namely, huge economic gains - will be felt most by the international companies that invest in the project. These include the French energy giants EDF and TotalEnergies [1] . As has been demonstrated throughout history [7] , France's stake in water mega-projects across the continent have helped to establish long-lasting relations of neocolonial rule, entrenching a paradigm of dominance through resource control. Sara Prichard refers to this as ‘hydroimperialism’, later transforming into ‘hydrocapitalism’. [7]   The project also has clear links with TotalEnergies Mozambique Liquid Natural Gas (LNG) project , which was committed a $20 billion Final Investment Decision in 2019 [12] . In one of the companies 2023 press releases', Mike Sangster, the senior vice president of their Africa division and Vincent Stoquart, the senior vice president of the Renewables devision at TotalEnergies stated that "TotalEnergies is delighted to be able to expand its presence in Mozambique beyond the Mozambique LNG project with a large investment in renewable energy, which will benefit to the people of Mozambique. It is a new example of TotalEnergies’s ability to implement its multi-energy strategy in oil & gas countries to support them in their energy transition” [13] . Impacts on people and place The Zambezi river supports rich ecosystems and large communities of people who rely on its banks and waters for food provisioning. In 2003, its delta was declared a ‘Wetland of International Importance’, under the Ramsar convention [6] , an agreement that seeks to halt the loss of wetlands worldwide through international political cooperation.  Displacement has been a key issue caused by the heavy damming of the river. Indeed, the Cahora Bassa Dam displaced tens of thousands of people, as well as severely impacting floodplains and fishers. [6] Following this, much work was put into improving the water release patterns from the Cahora Bassa, to mimic more natural water flows. Yet, impacts of the Mphanda Nkuwa will undermine and largely reverse these changes [6] , and the dams reservoir will flood 97 squared kilometers of land. [5] In the lead up to the construction of the Mphanda project, it was projected that the project would compromise the livelihoods of the 200,000 or so subsistence farmers and fishers living downstream of the dam. [6] Climate studies have indicated the risk of longer droughts, reduced hydrological flows and increased risk of extreme flooding events in the region [5] , which suggests that increased damming of the river Zambezi is not a reliable or sustainable solution for countries experiencing a power-deficit. [5] Therefore relying on hydropower when there is such climate unpredictability will have further knock on impacts for the country, both economically and socially.  Resistance For over 2 decades, the Maputo-based grassroots organisation - Justiça Ambiental (JA!) - have been campaigning for the rights of the people impacted by the mega-dam projects. They focus on uniting different communities based along the vast river, to foster webs of solidarity. In 2006 Anabela Lemos, a member of JA!, stated that - "The Mphanda Nkuwa project may be good for the relationship between China and the Mozambique government, but it’s not good for the relationship between our government and the rural poor….If the government wants what is best for Mozambique, the dam should be stopped, and efforts to restore the Zambezi prioritised." [8] On March 14th. 2013 the organisation brought together over 50 communities that live on the river banks to drum up support and awareness of the projects impacts. [5] The group gathered in Tete, including those who would be displaced as a result of the megadam projects’ construction. They were also joined in solidarity by communities that have been affected by the mining projects of Vale, Rio Tinto and Jundal. [9] The meet up was co organised by JA!, Liga dos Direitos Humanos (Human Rights League), AAAJC (Association for Support and Legal Assistance for Communities), UNAC (National Farmers Union, Tete provincial chapter). [9] On the same day the group held an action in Maputo, against the World Bank who are another actor heavily involved in pushing the dam agenda. The group congregated outside of the World Bank Headquarters in Kenneth Kaunda Avenue, distributing flyers and spreading information. [9] Following the December 2023 announcement that the consortium of international businesses, along with support from the World Bank, EU and EIB, would finance the dams construction and operation, JA! released their new campaign. It features a video titled ‘How Many No’s Does It Take To Build A Dam?”, which shows members of the communities who are resisting the Mphanda Nkuwa project speaking about the illicit activities of the government and planning officials in regards to pushing ahead with the dam project. [10]

case_name: Göteborg LNG Terminal, Sweden
headline: In September 2019, after years of campaigning, the proposed LNG terminal project in Gothenburg was successfully brought to a close. The local environmental group Fossilgasfällan's tireless work in raising awareness of the immorality of dependence of natural gas contributed to the Swedish government's final decision.
description: In 2013, €27 millions of EU funding under the Project of Common Interest (PCI) scheme was pledged to the new Liquid Natural Gas (LNG) terminal in Göteborg . [1] The project was owned by the Dutch company Vopak and the Swedish gas infrastructure company, Swedegas. [2] Swedegas initiated the project which was due to connect with the LNG project in Rotterdam Port, together destined to comprise the EU Commission's “most prioritised Motorways of the Seas” [1] . It was due to be the largest LNG in a long list of projects proposed by the company right along the swedish coastline. [3]   Project and resistance timeline In 2017, local grassroots group Fossilgasfällan began their campaign against the LNG project in Sweden. They drummed up support against the terminal by gathering thousands of signatures for their petition against the project. Further to this, they have held talks and written articles to demystify ‘natural gas’, as well as holding many meetings with NGOs, members of government and other grassroots organisations to collectivise their ideas and build momentum. [4] In 2017, they organised an action in the Port of Göteborg , during which activists took to the sea in kayaks, holding an anti-LNG banner stating “NO 2 LNG: Not here not anywhere”. [4] It was followed by 2 more actions in 2018. They operate under the umbrella of the larger, international organisation - the Gastivists. [12] In October 2019, after years of local organising led by Fossilgasfällan, the Swedish Government refused to grant the final fossil gas permit for the project on ‘climate grounds’. This decision closely followed a mass civil disobedience resistance organised by Fossilgasfällan in September 2019, during which hundreds of protesters from the region gathered in a 12 hour blockade of the entrances and exits to block the Energy Harbour and the fossil gas terminal. [3] [4] The decision from the government prompted words of support from politicians and activists alike. The Dutch Green MEP Bas Eickhout stated that, “the decision of the Swedish Government is an important development. There is finally some waking up when it comes to the dangers of all the new gas investments that are happening around Europe.” [3] Olivia Linander from Fossilgasfällan commented on how their organisation has helped to shift the conversation around LNG terminals in Sweden entirely, stating that “ when we [Fossilgasfällan] started campaigning against the terminal in early 2017, the gas lobby’s claims that this massive piece of new fossil fuel infrastructure was a solution of sorts went unchallenged” . [3] In 2022, it was reported that Swedegas were intending to revive the project in reaction to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine [2] , an event that spurred many energy providers across Europe to justify continued fossil extraction and storage. Fossilgasfällan made a statement in response to this announcement, stating: “to Swedegas we want to say: Sweden has said no to your fossil gas terminal. You will face opposition if you submit a new formal application for a terminal. To our allies around Sweden we want to say: We have spoken to both authorities and the company ourselves, and Swedegas has not submitted a formal application to build. However, it is clear from the CEO's statement on Sweden's radio on May 9 that they are fishing for pacifiers from politicians. We invite everyone to get ready to organise and mobilise again if necessary, and to take their own initiatives.” [11] European Context  This was just one of the 112 gas projects included on the PCI (Project of Common Interest) list, which were due to receive funding from the EU. [3] Yet , the monumental decision from the Swedish government disrupted the EUs Motorways of the Sea project, which planned to create new intermodal maritime-based logistics chains in Europe [5] . The idea was first proposed in 2001 as part of the Transport White Paper- European transport policy for 2010, and the Swedish terminals were due to make up part of the Motorway of the Baltic Sea, which would link the Baltic Sea Member States with Member States in Central and Western Europe, including the route through the North Sea/Baltic Sea canal [5] . This means that the natural gas stored at the LNG transport hub was intended to be part of a larger European supply project. National Context Already by 2013, a Swedish Government commission had proposed a ‘fossil-independent transport sector’. Following this, the Swedish 2030-Secretariat was launched as a specific organisation committed to ensuring the target became a law. [6] [7] This demonstrates the country's commitment to scaling down and eliminating fossil gas from their transport sector.

case_name: Bontang / Badak LNG plant, East Kalimantan, Indonesia
headline: Badak / Bontang LNG is the largest LNG plant in Indonesia. LNG production around the city of Bontang is responsible for land conflicts, pollution, and interferences with indigenous ways of life. With exports decreasing and domestic demand increasing, the plant is undergoing some major supply shifts.
description: The Bontang LNG terminal in East Kalimantan on the island of Borneo is one of the largest liquefied natural gas (LNG) plants in the world [1] . The project is operated by PT Badak – the largest LNG company in Indonesia – and yearly produces millions of tons of LNG across its eight processing trains, only a few of which are still operational. Although the company is known for its many corporate social responsibility (CSR) programs, the alleged positive impact of gas extraction in the region is questionable.   Bontang is a city on the East coast of Borneo. The gas fields in the Bontang region were first discovered in 1972. Since 1977, the Bontang plant has been extracting LNG from four gas fields: Badak, Sambereh, Nilam, and Mutiara  [1] . PT Badak LNG, the project’s operator, is a joint venture of state-owned Pertamina , TotalEnergies ,  Pertamina Hulu Sanga Sanga (PHSS) ,   and PNA [2] . The LNG facility is supported by cooling units, storage tanks, steam power plants, and loading ports [3] . Gas extracted and processed at the Bontang facility is mostly exported to Japan , Taiwan , and South Korea   [1] . However, due to a decrease in regional gas production foreign customers are shifting their supply away from Botang towards competitors in Qatar, Malaysia and Australia, promting proposals to reconvert the facility into a regasification terminal to supply an adjacent fertiliser plant from the state-owned company  PT Pupuk Kalimantan Timur (Pupuk Kaltim) [4] .  Pupuk Kaltim facilities are responsible for large amounts of ammoniac waste in the area. The presence of these the LNG terminal and the fertiliser factory has motivated many people seeking employment to migrate to the area [5] [6] . As such, Bontang is highly ethnically diverse, with the indigenous Kutai people of East Kalimantan being native to the region  [3] [5] .   In 2004, the terminal’s processing trains were modernized. Chiyoda was in charge of the modernization effort, which was financed by a $1.1 billion loan from a group of companies led by the Bank of Taiwan, including Mitsubishi Corporation, Chase Manhattan, Bank Indonesia, and Fuji Bank  [1] . Once the plant’s modernization and expansion were concluded, the plant’s production capacity briefly peaked at approximately 24.6 million tons per annum (mtpa), only to decline shortly after due to supply issues.   Badak LNG has come to hold significant power in the Bontang region, and LNG extraction has produced serious environmental impacts. The company cut down mangrove forests that used to shield coastal villages from erosion  [5] . Villagers of Guntung have reportedly been suffering water and air pollution since industrial development took over the region. The villagers depend deeply on Badak’s presence in the region because most of the village’s young residents are employed with the company. Since LNG extraction took hold of the area, little is left of indigenous spiritual traditions, and few indigenous Kutai villages remain.   Generally, the Bontang project has been the source of land conflicts in the region. Local communities were discontent with the company claiming land for the LNG plant, leading to significant tensions and monetary compensation claims [7] . In various instances, communities held demonstrations demanding their right to land in the region. Since 1984, Badak has been responding to the unrest with efforts to support community development and reduce conflict through various CSR initiatives  [3] . In 2020, the company launched the Saung Pandu : a program aimed at establishing harmonious collaboration between local communities and the company. One of the tactics the program employs is applying processed wastewater from the company to support agriculture in the region. Like Saung Pandu, Badak has undertaken various other infrastructure assistance and community empowerment programs  [3] .   Civil society groups throughout Indonesia and in the plant’s purchasing countries have been resisting LNG extraction in the country. For instance, a petition by Friends of the Earth Indonesia (WALHI) specifically addresses the role of Japan, as a purchaser of Indonesia-sourced gas, has in prolonging LNG extraction and supporting the destruction of the environment and local livelihoods [8] . Campaigns such as Don’t Gas Asia broadly resist gas and LNG extraction in Asia. Some of the participating movements from Indonesia in this campaign are Aksi Ecologi dan Emansipasi Rakyat (AEER), KRUHA, Trend Asia, and Friends of the Earth Indonesia (WALHI) [9] .   To date, only two of the plant’s processing trains are still operational, partly due to the depletion of the gas reserves. In October 2023, Italian energy company Eni announced its plans to send newly discovered offshore gas reserves to Badak’s Bontang facility [10] .

case_name: Rügen LNG import terminal, Germany
headline: An LNG import terminal project on the East German island of Rügen has been approved by the German Ministry of Economic Affairs. The local community is strongly opposed to the project, which they consider harmful to the environment and the economy.
description: Following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, the world's economic powers are trying to find alternative sources of energy supply. This has prompted Germany to take an interest in the subject, and especially liquified natural gas (LNG). The LNG Acceleration Act of 12 July 2023 provides the basis for eleven (eight floating and three on shore) new LNG terminals in various locations such as in Mukran on the island of Rügen  [1] . The gas would arrive at Rügen by ship from all over the world and be converted and stored in a Floating Storage and Regasification Unit (FSRU). The project includes the creation of pipelines to transport the gas. The platform, located off the coast of Rügen, is connected to the gas network "with a 38-kilometre offshore pipeline through the ecologically highly sensitive Bay of Greifswald" [6] . The project was unveiled on 13 February 2023 by the Ministry of Economic Affairs [2]  and approved by the government on 7 July 2023. Deutsche ReGas began construction during the summer and the terminal is due to come on stream by the first semester of 2024 [1] . However, the project has led to a number of demonstrations and protests, as many stakeholders do not agree with it. The main criticism is that with a projected capacity of 13.5 billion cubic meters per year (bcm/y) the project regasification capacity is totally oversized for the needs of the country. The project also risks potencial damage to the environment. Rügen is a tourist island in Germany, and locals fear that tourism will decline because of the increased air pollution and the impact this will have on the island in the long term. The island will lose some of its beauty. Ecologists also fear the impact of this infrastructure on coastal and marine ecosystems. This project does not promote the use of renewable energies at all, but rather the gas industry. And it goes against existing climate legislation of the country [3] .   The main environmental impacts can be simply divided into two categories: air pollution and soil contamination. T here are methane leaks during the production, transport and processing of LNG; methane is a greenhouse gas 80 times more harmful than CO2. It leaks into the atmosphere throughout the production and supply chain and slips directly from the ship’s funnels, contributing to climate warming at a significant pace [11] [12] . As a result, producing LNG will speed up global warming and Germany will not reach its climate targets because of additional emissions of methane. As  the LNG production chain involves the use and the combustion of a huge amount of fuel which produces a lot of CO2 emissions. Indeed, air pollution is the most serious impact of LNG expansion  [4] . LNG terminals also release air pollutants that threaten the health of local residents, including tons of sulfur dioxide (which damages the lungs), nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds (both of which contribute to smog), microscopic soot or particulate matter (which can trigger asthma and heart attacks), and carbon monoxide (which can inhibit oxygen intake to the heart and brain)  [13] . LNG terminals are also reported to cause chemicals,  such as volatile organic compounds, nitrogen oxides, and benzene, seeping into the soil and groundwater. This poses social and health problems to the local population [14] . And it also presents an immediate threat to disrupt local fishing grounds [13] . There are also economic issues at stake in this project. The growing demand for gas in Europe is driving up global gas prices, with consequences in the countries of the Global South such as power shortages and power cuts [5] . In response, various protests have been taking place against the construction of the project. On 8th May 2023, Fridays for Future Germany, alongside Bürgerinitiative Lebenswertes Rügen (Rügen Worth Living citizen's initiative), Deutsche Umwelthilfe (DUH, Environmental Action Germany ), and other organisations protested in front of the Federal Chancellery while a petition to cancel the project signed by 61000 people was being discussed at the Bundestag [16] . Sascha Müller-Kraenne from DUH expressed that "The federal government is going against common sense in climate policy and against the people on the island. Rügen, like Lützerath, will thus become another symbol for the federal government's inadequate climate policy." [17] A poll confirmed that the opposition to the project is generalised, only 35.6% of Germans supports building an LNG terminal there, with 49.6% against and 14.8% undecided, a survey by Civey showed in March  [15] . On July 7th, Binz municipality announced a legal challenge against the construction of the project at the Federal Administrative Court [18] . The DUH also filed a lawsuit against the project at the Federal Administrative Court challenging the fast-tracked approval process of the project that did not meet basic environmental requirements [19] . The lawsuit specifically refers to the approval of a 38-kilometer-long connecting line from the mainland coastal town of Lubmin to Rügen, which poses a great threat to marine ecosystems.  [16] On 7 September 2023, Greenpeace activists also protested against Rügen LNG [1] . Greenpeace claims that w ith oversized LNG projects like in Rügen, Germany is cementing its dependence on fossil fuels for decades to come.  However, in order to meet the climate targets, gas consumption and thus also the volume of LNG imports must fall drastically in the coming years. This project therefore raises many questions and a great deal of discontent. The question is whether it will be completed and under what conditions and at what cost for the environment and for people. In a noteworthy demonstration opposing the use of fossil fuels, members of Greenpeace, the environmental protection organization, temporarily interrupted the construction of the pipeline conneting the future LNG terminal to the gas network in the Greifswalder Bodden, Germany. This unexpected protest featured four to five inflatable boats surrounding the pipe-laying vessel "Castoro 10." Furthermore, two individuals ascended a portion of the pipeline, unfurling a banner with the impactful statement "Gas destroys!". Ende Gelände, a civil disobedience movement occupying coal mines in Germany to raise awareness for climate justice, staged against Rügen LNG on 22-24 September in 2023. They proposed to prevent the construction of the Rügen LNG terminal before the gas infrastructure is built. The group used itscharacteristic tactics to occupy the construction site of the pipeline en masse [20] Otherwise,  ENDE GELÄNDE host two climate camps to well prepare the protest  against the expansion of fossil energies and for climate justice on 23 September  [5] . On the political front, Manuela Schwesig (SPD), Premier of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania (the state in which Rügen is located), has “publicly opposed the federal government's plans to authorize the LNG terminal on the island” [9] . In addition, Karsten Schneider and Kai Gardeja, mayor and tourism director of the seaside town of Binz on the island of Rügen, are trying to have the project cancelled so that biodiversity and tourism are not impacted by the negative effects of such a project [9] .

case_name: BP's Tangguh LNG Project, West Papua
headline: BP has been condemned for its involvement with Indonesian security forces and for failing to secure human rights in West Papua. The land acquisition process for Tangguh LNG has divided Papuan communities and although classified as a National Strategic Project, delivers little of the promised development to the local people.
location: Not specified clearly in live EJAtlas metadata.
description: In  Bintuni Bay  of West Papua, BP’s  Tangguh LNG  project has been under public scrutiny for alleged connections with excessive surveillance and violence enacted by security forces. Indigenous Papuans have been relocated, and selective compensation has led to tensions and divisions among Papuan residents, who so far have not reaped the financial benefits the project has generated.    Despite its endowment with precious natural resources, West Papua suffers poverty well above the national rate [1] . Indigenous  Melanesian  residents of coastal settlements in Bintuni Bay depend predominantly on fishing [2] . The area has a rich history of commercial resource extraction, including oil drilling, logging, fishing, and plantations [3] .   The gas fields in Bintuni Bay were first discovered by the American-owned  Atlantic Richfield Company   (ARCO)  in the 1990s [4] . Together with Indonesian state-owned oil company  Pertamina , ARCO initiated Tangguh LNG in 1997.  British Petroleum (BP)  took over the operation in 1999, and secured the 3,200 hectares of land needed for the project in the same year. After the Indonesian government approved the project’s Environmental and Social Impact Assessment in 2002, LNG production started in 2009 [4] .   The Tangguh project extracts from two super giant gas fields (Wiriagar Deep and Vorwata) and four smaller fields (Roabiva, Ofaweri, Wos, and Ubadari) through offshore production platforms that are connected to the on-land processing facility 35 kilometers away by subsea pipelines  [2] [4] . In 2020, BP finished constructing a third liquefaction plant and two additional offshore platforms  [2] . This expansion (Train 3), which cost the company 4 billion USD, generates a 50% increase in the project's production capacity to a total of 7.6 mtpa. In November 2023, Tangguh Train 3 was declared a National Strategic Project [5] .   The initial development of the processing plant necessitated the relocation of residents of Tanah Merah and Onar  [4] . All in all, BP relocated ten villages for the Tangguh operation [2]. The relocation of directly affected villages to newly built huts along the shore was not received well by other communities living in Bintuni Bay, who were left envious without access to electricity and clean water  [2] . When Indonesia gained independence from the Netherlands in 1949, West Papua continued to be held under Dutch rule until it was annexed by Indonesia in 1962  [1] . After a controversial referendum in 1969, West Papua formerly came under Indonesian control. The region, which became known as  Irian Jaya , entered an enduring period of violent conflict between Indonesian security forces and separatist groups (most prominently the  Free Papua Movement (OPM) ) who see the annexation as illegitimate and seek independence from Indonesia  [3] . The region is highly valuable to the Indonesian government for its richness in natural resources, and Indonesian efforts to secure access to natural resources have heightened militarization and securitization.   Against the backdrop of this long unfolding conflict, BP’s Tangguh LNG project was meant to break with the violent and inhumane legacy of natural resource extraction in West Papua  [3] . Central to this effort is BP’s  Integrated Community Based Security Program (ICBS)  which aims to depend predominantly on Papuan security officers  [6] .    However, it appears that indigenous Melanesians are rarely employed in highly skilled or supervisory roles, and they often face racism in the workplace  [2] . BP has been collaborating with the  Indonesian military   (TNI) , who are guilty of killing and torturing thousands of separatist activists and other civilians. Security guards working for BP are allegedly stationed at BP’s base, from where they spy on locals and betray them to the military under the guise of counterterrorism. Local islanders reported that crime has increased significantly since the arrival of BP  [2] . It may also be argued that the indigenous peoples of Papua could not exercise their right to Free, Prior, and Informed Consent (FPIC), given the precarious security conditions West Papua has been finding itself in, as well as the denial of customary land rights by the established order.   In the early days of the project development, local residents and NGOs already expressed concerns over the possible negative impacts of the LNG operation  [3] . In 2001, for instance, villagers of Weriagar reported that grasses had turned yellow and infant mortality had risen [7] . In May 2002, dozens of Papuan villagers held a peaceful sit-in at the project site. In August 2004, the Soway, Wayuri, and Simuna indigenous groups released a statement claiming that land transfers to BP had not been voluntary  [8] . According to them, the land acquisition process  “did not reflect whatsoever the value we place on land as a source of livelihoods which has been handed down to us through the generations” , making the process invalid. A collective letter from different Indonesian NGOs pointed out flaws in the project’s Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) and community discontent over the amount of compensation paid for land [9] .   In December of 2004 the Indonesia Human Rights Campaign submitted a letter to BP’s CEO on behalf of hundreds of signatories, demanding the company suspend the project as long as it has not improved transparency, continues being involved in human rights violations, and fails to address the wider political context in which its operations take place [10] . The signatories were also skeptical of the  Tangguh Independent Advisory Panel (TIAP)  BP had set up.   Although the project was expected to deliver West Papua 3.6 billion USD between 2006 and 2030, so far none of these revenues reached the region  [3] . Despite BP’s supposed commitment to community engagement and compliance with human rights, it finds itself deeply entangled with the West Papua conflict and makes itself guilty of continuing human rights violations through its support of the Indonesian military. In the Global North, BP’s involvement with human rights violations has stirred resistance as well. Fpr example, Free West Papua activists protested outside BP’s headquarters in London several times [11] [12] . In January 2019, civil society groups held a die in on Union Square in New York in solidarity with the West Papuan people mobilizing against Tangguh LNG [13] .

case_name: LNG Boom in the Verde Island Passage, Philippines
headline: The LNG boom in the Philippines adds to climate change and the destruction of the Verde Island Passage, while also stripping the livelihoods of thousands of Philippine fisherfolk.
province: The Verde Island Passage Marine Corridor is situated between Southern Luzon (Batangas) and Mindoro
description: During the spring of 2021, oil and gas companies proposed the addition of 14 new Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) power plants and shipping terminals in the Batangas region of the Philippines [2] . These facilities are proposed by several assertive energy corporations that believe LNG facilities will produce cleaner fossil fuel and become a reliable energy source for the country [1] . The Department of Energy (DOE) is backing these proposals, viewing LNG as a commodity that will generate economic growth [3] . By 2023, there were two LNG terminals receiving international shipments in Batangas Bay: FGEN Batangas FSRU operated by First Gen, and the Linseed Field terminal (PHLNG) operated by AG&P . The Batangas region is an extension of t he Verde Island Passage (VIP), a marine corridor housing over 300 coral species, underwater rock canyons and reef formations, and 60% of all known shore fish species in the world within a ten-kilometer area [8] . It is the most biodiverse marine habitat in the world and has been touted as the “Amazon of the oceans” [9] [10] . In addition, the VIP holds a strategic position for the shipping industry as it connects the South China Sea with Tayabas Bay and the Sibuyan Sea, and is the main shipping route between the Port of Manila and the Visayas and Mindanao in the south . Overall, the VIP provides food, livelihoods and other benefits to over 2 million people [11] . p { line-height: 115%; margin-bottom: 0.1in; background: transparent }a:visited { color: #800000; text-decoration: underline }a:link { color: #000080; text-decoration: underline } p { line-height: 115%; margin-bottom: 0.1in; background: transparent }a:visited { color: #800000; text-decoration: underline }a:link { color: #000080; text-decoration: underline } p { line-height: 115%; margin-bottom: 0.1in; background: transparent }a:visited { color: #800000; text-decoration: underline }a:link { color: #000080; text-decoration: underline } p { line-height: 115%; margin-bottom: 0.1in; background: transparent }a:visited { color: #800000; text-decoration: underline }a:link { color: #000080; text-decoration: underline } Background In 2021, fossil gas had a 4-6% share in the country’s total energy supply, forecast to increase to 11% of the total share by 2040 [12] and 18% by 2050 [13] . Domestic supply of gas from Malampaya field is delivered to Batangas City via pipeline , supplying several power plants there, including Santa Rita Power Station (1000 MW), San Lorenzo Power Station (500 MW); Ilijan (1200 MW); and San Gabriel (450 MW). Sixteen Special Economic Zones in Batangas also host a variety of active or prospective industrial LNG customers [13] . Gas resources in Malampaya are dwindling, and several plant s w ere taken offline or forced to switch to more expensive fuels, beginning in 2021. These shortages prompted the development of LNG import terminals in the region. The VIP has already been impacted by fossil fuel shipping. In February of 2023, the oil tanker MT Princess Empress carrying industrial fuel oil sank in the neighboring Tablas Strait, spilling over 800,000 L of industrial oil. A month later, the oil reached the Verde Island Passage [14] [15] . Residents of surrounding coastal towns were unable to fish, which they rely on for a living [2] p { line-height: 115%; margin-bottom: 0.1in; background: transparent }a:visited { color: #800000; text-decoration: underline }a:link { color: #000080; text-decoration: underline } LNG Projects Until recently, the Lopez Group’s First Philippine Holdings Corporation was the largest developer of gas projects in the Philippines. However, the Conglomerate made a net-zero pledge, and committed to phase-out its gas-fired power plants or consider a fuel shift to hydrogen as part of its decarbonization strategy [17] . San Miguel Corporation’s Global Power has now become the country’s leading fossil gas developer, with one gas-fired plant under construction and seven more proposed. Together with Meralco PowerGen Corporation and Aboitiz Power Corporation, they are planning a total investment of $3.3 billion in two gas-fired power plants and the LNG import and regasification terminal owned by Linseed Field Corporation [18] In addition, I Squared Capital invested $300 million in the LNG terminal, the Japan Bank for International Cooperation and Osaka gas invested $100 million, and China Bank and Development Bank of the Philippines funded a $100 million term loan facility [17] . p { line-height: 115%; margin-bottom: 0.1in; background: transparent }a:visited { color: #800000; text-decoration: underline }a:link { color: #000080; text-decoration: underline } p { line-height: 115%; margin-bottom: 0.1in; background: transparent }a:visited { color: #800000; text-decoration: underline }a:link { color: #000080; text-decoration: underline } p { line-height: 115%; margin-bottom: 0.1in; background: transparent }a:visited { color: #800000; text-decoration: underline }a:link { color: #000080; text-decoration: underline } International financiers with net-zero pledges are fueling the country’s fossil future. The top four financiers of fossil gas expansion in the Philippines 2020-onwards contributed to almost half of the total fossil gas financing, each accounting for at least USD 1.1 billion. Financing from the United States contributed USD 1.5 billion, the largest among all countries. Japan (USD 1.2 billion), Germany (USD 1.2 billion), and the United Kingdom (USD 1.2 billion) follow behind. Local financing notably accounted for only 6.5% or USD 674 million. Among the top financiers are Deutsche Bank AG, JPMorgan Chase & Co., Standard Chartered PLC, Allianz SE, BlackRock, and GAM Holding. Notably, all of these financial institutions have made various net-zero pledges [17] . p { line-height: 115%; margin-bottom: 0.1in; background: transparent }a:visited { color: #800000; text-decoration: underline }a:link { color: #000080; text-decoration: underline } Impacts Although natural gas is regarded as a “clean” and “environmentally friendly” fuel, there are a number of harmful impacts on human health associated with the pollutants emitted from natural gas facilities, including heart disease, certain types of cancer, and damage to the reproductive system and internal organs [19 ] . In addition, environmental organizations and scientists warn against the negative impacts of the industrialization boom on marine ecosystems of the Verde Island Passage. Vulnerable fishing communities are already feeling these effects, catching less fish than ever before and losing access to their traditional fishing areas due to zoning restrictions from the ongoing construction projects [20] . T he fisherfolk of Batangas have been blocked off from entering their fishing grounds, as the area near the bay has become an exclusive zone for the fossil fuel industry [2] . I t is estimated that over 26,000 people can no longer earn a living [2] . In addition to local fisherfolk, the Bajau—a nomadic sea people that may be the “world’s only community of self-sufficient sea nomads” [5] — a lso rely on the vast marine life that spans from the Philippines to Malaysia, including the VIP [6] . Electricity consumer groups are also concerned that importing fuel may increase electricity rates [17]. The Philippine people, despite paying some of the highest electricity prices in Asia, would have to shoulder the costly burdens of imported LNG as power suppliers pass on risks from volatile fuel costs and foreign exchange to consumers. This would leave the electricity bills of Philippine households at the mercy of international fossil fuel markets [2]. On top of everything, residents of Santa Clara, living only a few hundred meters away from the Avion, Sta. Rita, San Lorenzo, and San Gabriel natural gas-fired power plants, are yet to be connected to power. They are among the remaining 1.58% or 210,538 unenergized households in Luzon, according to government data [21] . The coalition ProtectVIP summarizes the potential negatives impacts of the LNG boom in Batangas: toxic air and water pollution, thermal pollution from seawater intake (causing disrupted reproductive cycles of marine life and less fish catch), potential freshwater shortages (with gas terminals and plants competing with locals for supply), a massive increase in shipping activities and loss of flora and displacement of coastal communities [8]. In addition, the burning of methane will continue to contribute to global climate change. The Philippines is ranked number four on the The Long-Term Climate Risk Index (CRI) that details the 10 countries most affected from 2000 to 2019 (primarily due to tropical cyclones) [22] . According to a report from Climate Analytics on getting fossil fuels out of the Philippine power sector, the Philippines must almost entirely phase out gas-fired generation by 2040 to stay aligned to a 1.5C pathway [23] p { line-height: 115%; margin-bottom: 0.1in; background: transparent }a:visited { color: #800000; text-decoration: underline }a:link { color: #000080; text-decoration: underline } Opposition A variety of different actors are coming together to take a stand against fossil gas and LNG developments in Batangas, including youth, faith-based groups, fisherfolk and other impacted sectors, civil society and people’s organizations, and academe . The Protect VIP campaign network links local, national and civil society groups from across the globe to stop the expansion of LNG projects in Batangas [8] . These movements have filed complaints, organized petitions, and protested against LNG in the VIP [2] . In October of 2022, a coalition of local stakeholders and advocates filed a complaint against San Miguel Corporation subsidiary Excellent Energy Resources, Inc. (SMC-EERI) and Linseed Field Corporation with Atlantic Gulf and Pacific Company (AG&P-Linseed) before the Environmental Management Bureau of the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR-EMB) over the companies’ violation of environmental laws [24] . p { line-height: 115%; margin-bottom: 0.1in; background: transparent }a:visited { color: #800000; text-decoration: underline }a:link { color: #000080; text-decoration: underline There are “95+ civil society organizations and representatives from around the world demanding gas companies to cancel their LNG terminals in Batangas” [2] . In addition, Philippine activists have traveled all around the world, demanding financial institutions take back the investments that support the companies destroying the Verde Island Passage [2] [25] .  In the past, Philippine communities, activists, and organizations have successfully convinced the Philippine government to drop plans for coal energy expansion, so they are confident in their ability to create the same fate for LNG expansion [2] . Moreover, strong advocacy for the Verde Island Passage has begun in the US as well. At the beginning of November, the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History launched an exhibit that showcased the Verde Island Passage. The exhibit displayed a multitude of photographs of marine life, along with infographics explaining how the passage is in danger due to climate change and the expansion of gas facilities. The exhibit had a section with a petition that viewers of the exhibit could sign with a QR code. This petition was for the “Philippine government to make the Verde Island Passage a protected area under the Expanded National Integrated Protected Areas System Act (ENIPAS)” [7] .  The organizers of this exhibit plan to showcase it in several places around the world, to build advocacy for the Philippines [7] . 2025 update Health and Environmental Impact In early 2024, the Philippine Movement for Climate Justice along with other groups petitioned the Department of Health (DOH) to declare a public health emergency in Batangas, reporting thousands of people suffering respiratory or cardiovascular disease resulting from air pollution from the LNG plants. Water testing in Batangas Bay indicated that the environment was not conducive to marine life, fishing, or recreational activities. [33] Following residents’ protests to financers of the SMC–Meralco–Aboitiz consortium that took over AG&P’s Linseed Field, the Japan Bank for International Cooperation issued a report denying environmental degradation in the VIP, although locals continue to report coral bleaching, reduced catch, and also fish that taste like gasoline. [34] p { line-height: 115%; margin-bottom: 0.1in; background: transparent }a:visited { color: #800000; text-decoration: underline }a:link { color: #000080; text-decoration: underline } Regulatory On 8 January 2025, the Philippine Natural Gas Industry Development Act, was signed into law, requiring development of natural gas as a fuel source in the country and conversion of existing fossil fuel infrastructure to use natural gas wherever feasible. [13] p { line-height: 115%; margin-bottom: 0.1in; background: transparent }a:visited { color: #800000; text-decoration: underline }a:link { color: #000080; text-decoration: underline } Ongoing projects In October 2025, the Economic Research Insititute for ASEAN and East Asia reported three infrastructure projects under construction in Batangas, (in addition to the Linseed and FGEN terminals) expected to be operational between 2025 and 2028. [13] Tabangao In 2021, Shell converted its Tabangao oil refinery in Batangas into an import terminal for diesel, gasoline and other fuels. [26]   This is the company’s largest import terminal. In 2022, the company announced plans to invest P3.5 billion (US$ 59 million) for a LNG import terminal at Tabangao, [27] and in May 2025, the company announced an additional P2-3 billion in development of the terminal [28] . Linseed Gas to the SMC-Meralco-Aboitiz owned Linseed Field is supplied by Abu Dhabi National Oil Co. through its FSU Ish under a 15-year contract signed in 2022 [29] . Gas is also supplied by Vitol Asia Pte. Ltd., a supply and trading unit of Vitol Group. By April 2025, the new power station was partially completed, with SMC subsidiary Excellent Energy Resources, Inc (EERI) announcing that units 1 and 2 of the LNG plant were producing a combined 850 MW [30] . p { line-height: 115%; margin-bottom: 0.1in; background: transparent }a:visited { color: #800000; text-decoration: underline }a:link { color: #000080; text-decoration: underline } p { line-height: 115%; margin-bottom: 0.1in; background: transparent }a:visited { color: #800000; text-decoration: underline }a:link { color: #000080; text-decoration: underline } p { line-height: 115%; margin-bottom: 0.1in; background: transparent }strong { font-weight: bold }a:visited { color: #800000; text-decoration: underline }a:link { color: #000080; text-decoration: underline } FGEN In January 2025, the FGEN Batangas terminal was expanded with additional on-shore infrastructure . case_name: Woodfibre LNG, Squamish, Canada
headline: Woodfibre LNG in Squamish, BC, Canada claims it will be the world's first net zero emission LNG facility. Their words are comforting upon initial glance, but a closer inspection reveals the potential harm for to the Squamish community and environment.
description: Woodfibre LNG is a proposed liquid natural gas export site located at the southern end of Squamish, Howe Sound, BC, Canada. The site consists of 212 acres of land situated on the industrial waterfront with an additional 202 acres of floating storage space which would sit in the water directly next to the facility [1] . Nine kilometers of tunnels for gas lines w o uld also be drilled beneath the soil and rivers to connect the site to a railway in the town of Squamish [6] . The body of surrounding water is an inlet off of the north pacific, which then leads into the Squamish river and Estuary channel. The site where Woodfibre LNG is located was originally a pulp/paper mill built in 1912. The small town built around the mill for the workers was in turn named Woodfibre in dedication towards the pulp facility. However, in 1973, as business slowed, the surrounding town closed, forcing many of the workers to find residence and jobs elsewhere [2] . While the mills technically remained open following the town closure, it was not until 33 years later, in 2006, all mill operations were seized and the site was officially put up for sale. Not long after, this site was sold to Pacific Energy Corporation Limited which immediately set its sights on building a liquid natural gas manufacturing and exportation site [3] .  Although natural gas extraction does not occur at this coastal site it’s still important to know the process of where natural gas comes from. Some natural gas extraction is conducted via hydraulic fracturing (fracking), and includes a process of collecting natural gas that is usually found inside shale rock within the Earth [4] . This process includes drilling down somewhere between 5,000 and 20,000 feet to allow the natural gas to come to the surface where it can be collected. For more extraction, pressurized water is sent into the drilled holes which cause horizontal and diagonal fractures in the shale which allow more release of natural gas. Nowadays, fracking has become a controversial means of energy production due to its high rate of greenhouse gas emissions and adverse health effects from toxins used in the fracking process, sometimes affecting the surrounding communities. What will be done at the coastal site is the process of liquifying and shipping of the gas. To liquify this gas, it is cooled to about -260 degrees Fahrenheit [5] . This allows a much more efficient way of storing and transporting long distances as the liquid only takes up 1/600th of the volume, compared to if it was in gas form. However, the process of cooling a gas to such temperatures is extremely energy intensive. In standard LNG manufacturers, roughly 8% of the total natural gas going into the facility will be used solely as power to condense it into a liquid state for transport [8] . This in turn contributes several greenhouse gasses to the environment such as carbon dioxide and methane. However, when it's time to use the liquified natural gas, the process to get it back into a gaseous state also takes a considerable amount of energy [9] . Of course, transportation also needs to be considered as only specially equipped boats can store and haul liquified natural gas. While the liquid natural gas warms up during transport, some of it will begin to evaporate. The ships are specially designed to use this natural gas as power. The main problem with this is that it then exhausts greenhouse gasses into the environment wherever they travel. When all parts are considered, LNG contributes about twice as much greenhouse gas emissions compared to natural gas in its regular gaseous state. Water pollution is also frequent near these facilities [11] . As many types of machinery are necessary for the process, lots of oils and fuels will be located in the area. It is common for these oils to end up in groundwater or nearby bodies of water especially during the construction phase. When pipes break or require maintenance, natural gas and other chemicals will be released into the environment. This is especially of concern for the Woodfibre facility as not only is it situated right on the water, but they are also drilling a new tunnel to house a gas line which travels beneath two rivers in order to get material to the rail site [6] .  Once pollutants find their way into the water they will harm all local species including sea lions and the endangered glass sponge reefs. These reefs are primarily found in BC Canada, in close proximity to Woodfibre’s shipping route. Sea lions are also especially at risk, as the underwater noise produced by this facility is enough to cause them permanent hearing loss. This will of course be detrimental to their wellbeing. Other species will also face increased threats, including humpback whales. As large ships will be the main mode of export for this site, the frequency of ship strikes are projected to increase six fold.  The negative impacts don’t just stop at the environment and wildlife. Emissions from burning natural gas include compounds like methane, nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, volatile organic compounds, and particulate matter [12] . Short term exposure to these compounds includes symptoms of irritated skin and eyes, headaches, and respiratory illnesses [10] . It is also known that long term exposures could lead to consequences of damaged reproductive organs, cancer, and heart disease. Considering the constant emissions from the LNG boats coming to the facility combined with the high potential for leakages, residents living in the surrounding area will absolutely notice a difference in their health. This is also not to mention the increased car and train traffic in the area which will also contribute to worsening air quality.   Woodfibre LNG is being marketed as an environmentally friendlier and safer source of energy production compared to coal [3] . Its main goal is to ship natural gas to developing Asian nations (many of which currently rely on coal) in order to ‘help the environment.’ While it is true that natural gas is 50% cleaner than burning coal, the world cannot rely on natural gas or fossil fuels to avoid the most catastrophic effects of global climate change, and must soon transition to a renewable and carbon free emissions future. Especially in 2023 when there are numerous cleaner energy alternatives, Canada and industry should avoid investments into fossil fuel infrastructure - this is an unsustainable direction for the world in terms of energy production and usage. It is no secret that the history of fracking and LNG sites have been built in predominantly poor or minority areas. Woodfibre LNG is no different. Looking at the numbers for the 2020 Squamish, Canada census the median after tax income for the area was $45,600 [7] . Compared to the rest of Canada, in 2020, the median after-tax income was $66,800. While the majority of the Squamish population is not technically considered to be in poverty, it is still interesting to note how the median income is more than $20,000 dollars lower than that compared to the rest of Canada. It is also important to note how 27.9% of the current Squamish population has recently (within the past 5 years) moved into the area from other parts of Canada, and 5.3% of the population have migrated from another country. Combining these two factors of lower income, and about one third of the citizens being new to the area shows, whether intentional or not, this is an environmental justice issue.  In September of 2021, the region of Howe Sounds was designated a United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) biosphere region [14] . Something being declared a UNESCO biosphere region means that the specific area was recognized for its distinct beauty and incentivizes conservation projects and sustainable development within the area. While this doesn’t impose any new laws regarding sustainability efforts, it does promote sustainable edvelopment for any company operating within the region. Considering Howe Sound’s past as a fairly industrial area, this declaration was a huge win for the area, especially as it is a very diverse landscape home to many different species - including some of which that are designated as endangered. The reason it has only recently been declared is because the recent efforts for sustainable living in the area combined with the acknowledgment of increased ecotourism.  The problem here is that Woodfibre LNG will be placed within Howe Sound on a former industrial location. For an area that is looking to move on from its own industrialized past, this is not the place where residents in the region want a fossil fuel operation. However, Woodfibre LNG did respond to the biosphere declaration by congratulating the region [3] . They also go on to state its efforts in cleaning up the former industrial site, and how it's committed to protecting and supporting all preservation efforts within Howe Sound. Their words are comforting upon initial glance, but when looking into every other LNG exporter in the world, their environmental effect many times a net negative. Developmental stages of Woodfibre LNG have not gone the smoothly. While this can be attributed to several factors including environmental assessments and protests of the facility, one of the main road blocks for them was the concern for adhering to wildlife safety guidelines. One of the restrictions set a maximum noise level of 160 decibels during construction in order to protect the hearing of all aquatic life [15] . While this may slow construction, it wouldn't halt it as much as the policy stating they have to stop construction if sea mammals are spotted within 4.4 miles of the construction. As this location in Howe Sound is a popular spot for seals and sea lions, a very curious group of mammals, construction would be very time consuming and could often be called off for long periods at a time. This is considered a success for locals/protestors, but a burdensome task for Woodfibre LNG. However in August of 2023, the BC Environmental Assessment Office changed the guidelines in favor of Woodfibre. Underwater noise levels can now no longer exceed 190 decibels, a 30 decibel increase, and sea mammals can get as close as 1,500 feet before construction is halted. Considering that seal's hearing has often been compared to that of a humans, sounds of that magnitude would absolutely cause problems for the curious mammals. While it is unclear what led to the recent change in guidelines, it may be due to a governmental push to help support this lucrative exporter. Several protesting environmental organizations have been formed in order to stop the construction of Woodfibre LNG from occurring. A notable one includes My Sea to Sky [6] . Beginning the fight from before 2014, they have had some success in slowing the approval and construction. This fight includes changing the design of Woodfibre from using sea water cooling to a more environmentally friendly air cooling. They’ve drawn attention to and stopped illegal donations occurring from Woodfibre to the government in order to bribe approval.  They’ve also successfully delayed the construction by more than six years, as it was originally supposed to be operational by 2017. Despite constant work by multiple NGOs, Woodfibre LNG has officially received approval and began sight preparation as of November 3, 2023 [3] . This includes mobilization of heavy machinery, sweeping for invasive species, and relocating equipment to prepare for the beginning of construction. With no policies in their way, and a government supporting the lucrative LNG market, Woodfibre LNG is set to be fully operational by the year 2027.
