case_name: Le Havre LNG Floating Storage and Regasification Unit, France
headline: Le Havre LNG Floating Storage and Regasification Unit aims at breaking away from Russian gas imports and obtain other sources of gas supply for France. Several environmentalists are opposed to this project as they believe it undermines the local environment and that it is not useful.
location: Bougainville Sud dock - In the port of the city Le Havre
description: Le Havre Liquefied natural gas (LNG) Floating Storage and Regasification Unit (FRSU) is located in the Bougainville Sud Dock in the port of the city Le Havre in Normandy. It was prompted by the war between Ukraine and Russia. The EU, including France, had been importing gas from Russia in large quantities before the war. The main purpose of this project is to break away from Russian gas imports and obtain other sources of gas supply for France [1] [2] [3] .   The FRSU vessel is named Cape Ann and is managed by TotalEnergies through its subsidiary TotalEnergies LNG Services France (TELSF). GRTgaz (a subsidiary of Engie) is in charge of the 3.5 km pipeline running under the city canal that links the FRSU to the French gas network. Haropa Port, manages the port of Le Havre and is in charge of the reception of the FRSU. The FRSU arrived in the port of Le Havre on September 18, 2023, but was not yet in use at the beginning of October 2023. As for now, the plan is to use it for 5 years at a capacity of 5 bcm /y [1] [2] [4] [5] [6] .     The project was actually adopted by the public authorities on Friday, July 29, 2022   [7] . From the decision to conduct no environmental assessment for the construction of the pipeline, several administrative authorizations were granted for onshore installations as well as derogations  [8] . Le Havre FRSU is a controversial project as many environmentalists are opposed to it due to its environmental impacts  [4] .  It contributes to greenhouse gas emissions and therefore to global warming, as it requires the use of fossil fuels, notably shale gas for LNG [9] . The carbon footprint of this project is significant, as it requires considerable energy to cool it at the start and to heat it on arrival. This leads to air pollution [10] . Le Havre FRSU may also lead to a loss of biodiversity, particularly in marine spaces [11] . The four land-based LNG terminals located in France (Loon-Plage, Montoir-de-Bretagne, and two in Fos-sur-Mer) are subject to the Seveso-III Directive on the control of major-accident hazards involving dangerous substances. Because the Le Havre gas terminal is a floating installation, it escapes the Seveso directive. However it is at the heart of an area comprising 21 Seveso factories and t he proximity to these sites multiplies the dangers to the environment  [9] [12] . Proponents of Le Havre FRSU have claimed that the project has potential economic impacts benefits such as job creation. However, it can also affect energy prices on a local level as LNG is known to be expensive  [13] .   Le Havre FRSU has potential social impacts particularly related to health and safety of local populations. The project is located less than 2 km from the "Les Neiges" housing quarter in the city of Le Havre, which due to its proximity, may be exposed to various safety issues such as accidents involving leaks or explosions, or noise pollution  [11] [14] . In addition, the proximity of this project to Seveso sites (containing materials that are hazardous to humans) multiplies the risks that could affect the health and safety of local populations  [9] [12] [15] . There may be a lack of safety in the workplace, with negative consequences coming from industrial activity on workers’ health [16] .     The firms TELSF, GRTgaz and Haropa were chosen to deal with one aspect of the project and they are driven by economic interests since by exploiting le Havre FRSU, they are making money. Haropa port which manages the port of the city Le Havre is in charge of the reception of the FRSU and by charging its own fees for the use of its infrastructures, it makes money [17] . GRTgaz is in charge of the pipeline that connects the FRSU to the French gas network and by exploiting it, it generates revenues [18] . TELFSF, the subsidiary of TotalEnergies is the main company in this project as it is responsible for the management of the FRSU and therefore by exploiting it, it can generate revenues. With this project, TotalEnergies can increase its LNG gas production capacity and resell it to other European countries while making profits in the process due to the strong demand for LNG in Europe  [18] [19] . The involved French public environmental authorities  (Ministry of Ecological Transition, the Seine Maritime préfecture, the Regional Directorate for Environment, Planning and Housing, and the intercommunal body Le Havre Seine)  [2] [18]   claim that this project is needed to meet energy needs and energy independence as well as to avoid the risk of a energy shortage  [17] [20] [21] .   The groups opposing to the project are mostly environmentalists, who are concerned about the damage to the environment associated with Le Havre FRSU. It includes the NGO Greenpeace, members of the group Scientifiques en Rebellion, representatives of the French environmentalist political party "Europe Ecologie-Les Verts" now called "Les Ecologistes", the Normandy branch of this same party, environmental assocations such as the association "Ecologie pour le Havre", Collectif Climat Le Havre, the French federation of nature and environmental protection associations called "France Nature Environnement" and the "Extinction Rebellion" movement. To better understand their role and position of each of these environmentalists, a chronology of different events is provided. Following a meeting on October 14, 2022 by the Normandy prefecture which aimed at presenting Le Havre FRSU to the public, Le Havre climate collective created a petition to obtain 1,000 signatures in order to create a public debate  [9] [15] .  On November 30, 2022, Julien Bayou, a deputy from the political party "les Ecologistes" of Paris announced his decision to file an appeal with the Council of State, aiming to stop the decree allowing this project. He has his own position regarding Le Havre FRSU: he said that no real danger weighs on the gas supply with the high level of gas stocks in Europe and that this should not validate its creation. He also added this project has negative impacts on the environment. He was supported by the Normandy branch of the political party and local environmental associations during that day  [20] . The “Ecologistes” party filed two other appeals aimed at stopping two building permits linked to the FRSU in Le Havre which were rejected on January 19, 2023  [21] . On Wednesday April 19, 2023, the France Nature Environnement federation said that it filed an appeal with the administrative court of Rouen (Seine-Maritime) against the FRSU project in Le Havre. It shares its position by saying that this project goes against the recommendations of the scientific community as well as French environmental objectives. Furthermore, the federation does not share the government's vision saying that a danger weighs on the gas supply and that there is no proof while France is doing well in terms of its gas stocks  [22] . In a press release on Wednesday, June 28, 2023 coupled with an investigation in partnership with Disclose (an NGO of investigative journalism), Greenpeace shares its position regarding the usefulness of the FRSU project in Le Havre. The investigation carried out by Disclose focuses more on the usefulness of the project and assumes that the creation of this FRSU is not necessary due to the fact that France already has enough stocks to meet its gas needs. The press release from Greenpeace contains two major points. LNG represents a fossil energy and contributes to GHG emissions even than more conventional gas. The NGO wants to move away from gas and fossil fuels and shifts towards renewable energies    [18] [19] [23] . On August 22, 2023, a fourth appeal was filed by Julien Bayou, the Normandy branch of Les Écologistes party as well as by the association Ecologie pour le Havre against an order taken by the prefect which authorized GHG emissions. Julien Bayou once again shared his opinion on the negative impact of this project on the environment as well as its uselessness  [24] . On September 16, 2023, members of the Extinction Rebellion movement and the association Ecologie pour le Havre joined in protest against the arrival of the FRSU in Le Havre. They carried out different actions such as giving leaflets  [10] . On September 18, 2023, members of Greenpeace blocked the route of the FRSU Cap Anne in the port of Le Havre with kayaks. They painted “gas kills” on the FRSU. Members of the group Scientifiques en Rebellion attended this event too claiming that the project is “an ecological, social and economic aberration”     [1] [10] . The last event dates from September 22, 2023 when members of Collectif Climat Le Havre demonstrated in front of the University of Le Havre at the time when a scientific festival conference was taking place. They intervened to point out the presence of TotalEnergies at this conference. They distributed leaflets to students and showed a banner revealing the FRSU threats  [25] .

case_name: NextDecade Liquid Natural Gas (LNG) Terminal, Cork, Ireland
headline: Plans for a LNG terminal to be built in the Port of Cork City by US Firm NextDecade have been shelved following much resistance from local, national and international civil society organisations.
description: NextDecade Cork FSRU is a Liquid Natural Gas (LNG) terminal proposed to be built in Ringaskiddy located in the western side of Cork’s industrial port. The project is owned by the US company NextDecade, and is designed to be an import terminal receiving gas from the USA. The project costs €125 million (151 million USD) in total, and would have the capacity of 4.0 billion cubic metres per year, that is 2.9 million metric tonnes of natural gas being transported through and stored annually. [1] It was in 2017 when the Port of Cork signed a memorandum of understanding with NextDecade and Flex LNG to install a Floating Storage Regasification Unit (FSRU) and associated LNG import terminal infrastructure in the port [1] , which marked the beginning of the consultation process [2] . The port is an ‘Irish semi-state’ [3] , meaning it is owned by the government, and is already a hub of industry and a major port for the country and, more widely, Europe. The terminal would be located right next to a Bord Gáis plant which is the state-owned gas company in Ireland, therefore it is in the Bord Gáis’ interest that the project goes ahead. Although it was never explicitly stated by the company that the purpose would be to import fracked gas, NextDecade already uses fracked gas in some of its explorations [2] and from the outset it was decided that gas from the Rio Grande LNG export terminal in South Texas was destined for the proposed LNG terminal in Cork. The gas would then be turned into fossil gas and pumped onto the main gas line from the Kinsale gas fields which run onshore in the Whitegate area [3] .  Resisting the project from its beginnings was the grassroots Irish environmental network Not Here Not Anywhere that is campaigning to end fossil fuel exploration and the development of new fossil fuel projects. It is a volunteer-run organisation at the forefront of campaigning for introducing an amendment to the Planning and Development Act to stop all LNG applications being granted in the country. [4] Other than their legislative campaigns, they also organised demonstrations, created a petition against the Cork LNG terminal [6] and communicated educational content on their social media platforms around the drawbacks and dangers of LNG [3]   that are often glossed over by fossil gas companies.  In 2018, they wrote an open letter to the Port of Cork signed by over 50 civil society organisations, including local organisations (Cork Climate Action, UCC Environmental Society, Cork Environmental Forum), national organisations (An Taisce Climate Committee, Irish Doctors for the Environment, Frack Free Clare), international organisation (350.org, Oil Change International, Friends of the Earth) and allied environmental organisation from around the world ( New Brunswick Anti-Shale Gas Alliance - resisting export terminals in eastern Canada, Citizens Movement Climate and health - a German group fighting the LNG terminal in Brunsbuettel, Save Rio Grande Valley and the Carrizo/Comecrudo Tribe - fighting NextDecade's Rio Grande LNG in Texas, US). The letter decried the hypocrisy of the Irish government if it were to accept the project: "In 2017 the Republic of Ireland banned fracking on health and environmental grounds. It would be morally corrupt to allow this project to proceed as it would facilitate the importation of fracked gas from the United States which has devastating impacts on communities, local environments and the climate." [5] .  Following this letter, in 2019, the Green party in Ireland brought forward the motion that encouraged councillors in the area to write to the Port of Cork and the Minister for Communications, Climate Change and the Environment (Richard Bruton) to immediately halt any plans that could involve the “the importation of Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) extracted using hydraulic fracturing” [7] . All but one councillor voted in favour of the motion. The Green councillor for north central Cork, Oliver Moran, stated that “locating a storage terminal in Cork would be a test of the government’s credibility in meeting the challenges of the global climate and biodiversity crisis”. [7] Also in 2019, fellow activists from the southern Texas community group Save Rio Grande Valley joined local groups to hand in a petition against the project to the port authority. Rebekah Hinojosa from Save Rio Grande Valley said they “don’t want their communities to be sacrificed” so that “dirty fracked gas” can be exported to Ireland. Local activist believed that forging alliances with groups directly affected by the production of fracked gas would be could be an important way to stop the project [10] . For NextDecade’s LNG to progress to the next stages of development, it was dependent on a few things - European markets demand for shale gas being one of them. In November 2020, Engie, the French energy company, halted talks over a long-term supply agreement with NextDecade. This was due to pressures not to import shale gas [8] .  In January 2021, the Environment Minister Eamon Ryan announced it would not renew the licence to develop the project acknowledging the incompatibility of the project with the climate commitments of the country [9] . The project has therefore been shelved. This decision came following the resistance of the local environmental groups, supported by local communities and the work of the Green party politicians in parliament. This case marks the rise in popular sovereignty against fossil gas in Ireland and, more widely, Europe.

case_name: LNG Shannon terminal, Ireland
headline: The Shannon LNG terminal aims to facilitate the import of gas to Ireland, the UK and the rest of Europe. Opponents argue that building new fossil fuel infrastructure is not in line with COP21 commitments and directly pushes Europe into a carbon lock-in.
location: South West Ireland – near Ballylongford and Tarbert
description: Shannon Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) terminal would be the first of its kind to be built in Ireland. It would be  located in the rural area of Kilcolgan, which lies between the two north Kerry villages of Tarbert and Ballylong ford on the southern shores of the Shannon [1] . The purpose of building this terminal is to facilitate gas imports from non-EU countries (such as the US) to Ireland, the UK and the rest of Europe. The terminal’s proposed capacity is said to offer up to 180,000 m3 of LNG storage capacity and regasification capacity of up to 22.6 million m3/d [16] . In 2003, the terminal was first proposed by Paddy Power, an Irish oil executive [2] . The company Shannon LNG was then established in 2006 - as a subsidiary of “Hess LNG”, a 50/50 joint venture between Hess Corporation and Poten & Partners [2] which are US multinational corporations.  Traditionally, the importation of gas has been bound physically by the location of pipelines - often coming from places such as Russia, Central Asia or North Africa. LNGs have opened up possibilities for gas transportation, making it easier than ever to store and transport fuel with less reliance on pipelines, diversifying supplier opportunities to places such as the US, Western Africa and the Middle East. Patrick Bresnihan, a geography lecturer at Maynooth University, refers to the way in which LNG developments such as Shannon LNG illustrate how “energy provision is always embedded in wider networks, which connect geographies, finance, state and private interests” [3] . This project was never solely about national or regional development - from its beginnings it was embedded in wider networks. Seeking to develop European energy supply and security.  In 2008, the An Bord Pleanala (Ireland’s national planning board) granted the company planning permission for a new interconnector pipeline [2] to be built between Ireland and the UK. This was an essential part of the project - the current interconnector pipeline is owned by Ervia (formerly Bord Gais), a state-owned utility, meaning that the costs of maintaining it would continue to be borne by Irish customers [3] . Both Ervia and the Commission for Energy Regulation of Ireland (CER) celebrated this decision, stating it was a victory for the Irish people, as it meant that the cost of pipe  maintenance would now fall onto Shannon LNG. The Shannon LNG Terminal would result in the old  interconnector gas pipeline with the UK becoming redundant. As a result, CER ruled that Shannon LNG would have to contribute to the costs of the two new necessary interconnecting pipes which transport gas between Ireland and the UK. Shannon LNG claimed the tariffs would cost them tens of millions and serve to subsidise their competition in the UK. Shannon LNG failed in a High Court action against the CER tariff scheme in December 2013 [4] .  Legal disputes such as these resulted in huge financial difficulties for Hess, and eventually led them to sell Shannon LNG in 2016 [5] . They had spent more than €67m trying to progress the project [5] . It is now under management by the US multinational New Fortress. The sale includes the rights to develop land owned by the Shannon Group (formerly Shannon Development) and planning permission for the terminal [6] .  Despite being financed by US multinationals, the project is also eligible for political and financial support (CEF-Energy funding) from the EU through its inclusion on the 2015 PCI (Projects of Common Interest) list [8] . The decision to include this project on the PCI list was contested by Friends of the Irish Environment [15] . The project was also cited by the European Commission as a future strategic hub for Europe's gas supply, which means it is eligible for low cost financing from the European Investment Bank (EIB) and accelerated planning and permit granting [8] .  Action from Environmental Groups: In 2008, Friends of the Irish Environment Ltd (FIE) and Raymond O’Mahony (a welder and representative from the Kilcolgan Residents Association) brought forward legal proceedings challenging the proposed development [9] . Kilcolgan Residents Association first formed in 2006, in efforts to mobilise community members against the project. It brings together people campaigning for environmental reasons, economic reasons (such as farming) and those concerned with the health safety of the local population - creating alliances within the community. With traction building, the association expanded into “Safety Before LNG”, a national campaign group [1] . FIE was first established in 1997 to create and maintain a network of conservationists and  environmentalists in Ireland. It works with these networks, often assisting them with legal cases for the environment in Ireland [10] . In the 2008 legal case both parties submitted their concerns in the court, arguing that the Health and Safety Association (HSA) had applied major accident regulations to the project, yet subsequently the technical advice on the development was inadequate [10] . These shortcomings were the foundation for their legal battle and successfully brought proceedings to a halt. Since then, Safety Before LNG has sought to bring a wide scope of issues concerning usage of the Shannon estuary to the public's attention. They set out arguments for why Shannon LNG should not go ahead. The first poses the option of “Farming or Fracking” [10] - stating that Shannon LNG emissions would equate to the methane emissions from 1 million cattle and would severely impact Ireland’s strict carbon budget, meaning that cattle farming practices will have to be altered. As many people living in rural Ireland’s work in agriculture and animal husbandry, this draws alliances between the environmentalists and the farmers of the area. The group is opposed to fracking due to the various associated environmental and societal impacts. These feelings are echoed by other environmental activist groups across Ireland, such as Love Leitrim - an anti fracking group based in the north of the country [14] . The second argument focuses on how the proposed LNG is not necessarily for the Irish people. They pose that the real issue of resource use in Ireland is because the country has become home to many international data centres - it is said that data centres in Ireland are now consuming more metered electricity than all of our rural homes put together [11] . Indeed, certain political decisions made by the government encourage international companies to establish headquarters in the country, as it remains strategically based within the European Union and in close proximity to the UK. Famously, part of the Irish government's enterprise policy includes large tax breaks for these companies and their employees [13] . Safety Before LNG argues that the government should really re-centre the debate around energy usage inequality before signing deals that put people and the environment at further risk. Addressing the needs of the Irish people instead of using their lands to house international companies.  The third points to controversial payments made from Shannon LNG to Kerry Council, that raises ethical questions. It is reported that a total of €4.1 million has been paid from Shannon LNG to the council in relation to the project [11] . Councillor Finucane of Kerry stated that these payments were simply “good faith contributions” [11] made by a company that was committed to the area. Safety Before LNG state that these payouts are a potential sign that agreements are being made on the basis of financial gain, with no regard for environmental or social impacts.  By June 2023, planning permission for the LNG Terminal had expired, meaning US firm New Fortress Energy is still seeking planning permission and the project remains in its assessment stage [7] almost 20 years following its conception. This case highlights the intricate web of connections that financial institutions, investors and global corporations have with national and European governments surrounding global energy provisioning [3] . It raises concerns about EU and investor commitment to a just transition, especially as there has been much local  concern surrounding this development. In September 2023, An Board Pleanàla finally rejected New Fortress' request, stating that "the development would be inappropriate pending review of Ireland’s  energy supply" [17] . The decision was based mainly on the governments stance on importation of fracked gas.

case_name: The Kariba REDD+ Project, Zimbabwe
headline: A flagship REDD+ project for carbon credit brokers is riddled with allegations of financial corruption and selling worthless offsets to fossil fuel companies claiming to sell "carbon-neutral gas."
province: Matabeleland North, Midlands, Mashonaland West, and Mashonaland Central
description: The Kariba REDD+ Project (KCRP), covering approximately 785,000 hectares in northern Zimbabwe near lake Kariba, was started in 2011 by a private investor who founded Carbon Green Investments (CGI) and its subsidiary Carbon Green Africa (CGA) to manage the project with the four local Rural District Councils (RDC) and communities [1] . While there are conflicting claims about the amount, one source states that the 30-year project will generate 52 million carbon credits, certified by the carbon non-profit Verra, through reductions in deforestation [1] . Carbon offsets from the project have led companies like Total Energies to claim they “have completed [their] first shipment of carbon neutral LNG” [2] . Even South Pole, a project partner selling carbon offsets, said “ it’s such  obvious nonsense” [3] .  Green Choice, another energy company purchasing carbon credits from the project, claims to sell "100% green electricity" and "forest-compensated gas." [18] The project claims to offer a variety of benefits to the local communities and strategies to reduce deforestation: promoting conservation farming to strengthen food security and reduce slash and burn practices by locals, creating nutritional community gardens, repairing and digging new boreholes in order to access clean drinking water and prevent burning trees to boil water, apiculture training to prevent cutting trees for collecting honey, reducing overgrazing by livestock, hiring anti-poaching units helping to prevent veldt fires caused by poachers, promoting more efficient use of fuelwood for domestic purposes and alternatives for curing tobacco, and investing in environmental education for the communities and local schools. [4] [5] [6] [7] From the beginning, the four RDCs from Hurungwe, Mbire, Nyaminyami and Binga had little say in the decision making as partners in the project with CGA, leading to disenfranchisement of the local councils as the only formal representation of community members [5] [7] According to researchers from the University of Zimbabwe: " The local authority is more like a sleeping  partner, with very little knowledge of what the project is all about and with  no voice on its direction. As one of the officers at the local authority  remarked: ‘These guys have the money, and what do we have? Nothing [ …] and these guys have the lawyers. They even have experts who know what  carbon credit is. Some of us do not know what it is, nor do we know the  details.’” [5] Another council member said:  “I am telling you we are in the dark about what these  guys are doing. These people are not straightforward at all.” [5] In 2014, a councilor from Binga complained about unmet promises and the lack of transparency around the funds owed to the district: “We have not seen anything really tangible, financially  or otherwise (from CGA). [...] We do not understand what REDD+ is all about. These g uys are not clear on the amount that is due to Binga as a district. We do not  know how many credits they have sold. Those issues need to be made clear to the  rural council and to the community” [8] . Nevertheless, there are some benefits for the communities and not all districts have complained about the aid from the project. A Zimbabwean newspaper reported in 2017 that “Since the inception of Kariba REDD+ in 2011, up to 1,200 Farmers have been trained per year by Carbon Green Africa on conservation farming and where necessary, material inputs have been provided. [By 2017] more than 6,000 farmers have benefited from the training programme” [9] . At the same time, the RDC members complained when the resources offered to the community were not always available, which CGA claimed was due to budget shortfalls [9] . On top of the RDCs' claims of malpractice by CGA, Transparency International Zimbabwe (TIZ) alleged in 2015 that “rural district councils were taking the lion’s share of the benefits from REDD+ projects through corrupt practices by benefiting from carbon credits while local communities benefit nothing” [10] . From the beginning, many community groups did not favor the project. According to local researchers “In practice, the project undermines livelihoods,  forbidding access to foraging, agriculture and hunting across large areas that  were traditionally used. All this makes the KCRP strongly opposed by migrants -  mainly Karanga – who need land for petty commodity production, and women and  hunters who forage and hunt in the forests for household food security. The KCRP i s also opposed by squatters wanting land and who wish to avoid intervention  that would entangle them with the state and the private sector” [5] . The only supporters from the community were the Korekore, who mostly thought that the strict rules set up around land use could help stem the tide of immigration of outsiders onto their ancestral territory [5] .  Furthermore, the project narrative around the reasons for deforestation did not always seem to coincide with the views of locals. Slash and burn practices had not been prevalent for decades and were not observed by the local NGO, Environment Africa, who was tasked with socio-economic studies as a partner in the project [5] . The project documents also claimed that overgrazing by local farmers was a cause of deforestation, but the livestock was very limited due to high mortality rates from the tsetse fly [5] . Nevertheless, increasing mechanization and expansion of tobacco fields is evident in the area, and many migrants rely on this cash crop, burning wood from the forests for curing the tobacco leaves and consequently denying this to be a factor of deforestation in the area [5] . Investigations revealed that the amount of carbon offsets generated by the project are much higher than they should be, bringing CGI and their partner, South Pole (responsible for selling carbon credits to international clients), under increasing scrutiny. In 2022, a remote sensing scientist from a ratings agency “argued that the Kariba REDD+ project could be generating 30 times as many offsets as it should. [He] wrote that the project uses ‘ridiculous  baseline math’ ” [11] .  Other ratings firms say that the project has generated excess credits by a factor of 5 to 8 [12] . The rate of deforestation without the  intervention by the REDD project is alleged to be overestimated by a factor of 14 [13] . This lead to one rating agency to announce that the project has been put on a “watch list” with the risk of fraudulent sales of carbon credits [14] . Both Verra and South Pole have conflicts of interest that provide a financial incentive to overestimate the amount of carbon offsets created by REDD projects, and leaked internal documents from South Pole estimate 2/3 of the credits sold from Kariba are basically worthless [15] . Only recently, after initially denying any problems, has South Pole admitted that offsets were “overestimated by 50 percent” [11] [12] .  South Pole also has multiple employees that sit on Verra's advisory committees [19] . The motives of many of the actors involved in the Kariba REDD+ project seem to be more tied to financial gain rather than environmental protection.  The CGI founder, Steve Wentzel, admitted that he “didn’t care about trees and the people [in the project area]” until he realized there was a great business opportunity in the REDD project [15] . In fact, both CGI and impactChoice, a partnering company that founded a cryptocurrency to sell carbon credits from the project, are registered in tax havens [1] [15] .  In addition, South Pole has taken a 43% commission from the sales of credits generated by the Kariba REDD+ project, much higher rate than the agreed 25% [15] . South Pole also admits that it cannot confirm the amount of money that has reached the RDCs and local communities, relying on promises from CGI [15] . Wentzel, failed to respond to inquires about funding discrepancies for local communities, showing a complete lack of transparency about where millions of dollars have ended up [15] . Among increasing scrutiny, South Pole promised to “publish the funds distributed to the project beneficiaries on [their] webpage” [3] . As of May of 2023, the national government of Zimbabwe has made new laws on carbon credits generated within the country and has declared all previous carbon contracts with international companies and institutions “null and void” [16] . The continuing viability of the REDD+ project in the country seems doubtful with South Pole saying that it is “assessing the implications that this new potential regulation might have on [it]” [13] .

case_name: Liquefied Natural Gas Project, Papua New Guinea
headline: Landowners decry ExxonMobil's PNG LNG botched promises to share benefits leading to violent protests. In 2022, TotalEnergies' Papua LNG is set to repeat the mantra: benefits for multinationals and national elites, and impacts for local communities.
location: Not specified clearly in live EJAtlas metadata.
description: In 2010, Exxon-Mobils subsidiary Esso Highlands started the construction of the PNG LNG (Papua New Guinea Liquefied Natural Gas), a US $19 billion project aiming to produce and export 6.9 million tons of natural gas per year over a period of 30 years. The project integrates gas production and processing in the Southern Highlands and Western Provinces, mainly in Kutubu and Tari districts, and the subsequent liquefaction and storage at Port Moresby on the Gulf of Papua to be sent to foreign hungry Asian markets mainly in China, Taiwan and Japan. The project is currently at the preparatory stages with the company currently developing the infrastructure to extract and transport the gas. The construction of the pipeline will stretch around 700 kilometers (248 km onshore and 407 km offshore), connecting the provinces to the port. The project is estimated to obtain $ 20 billion in revenues during the first year of extraction in 2014, coming from 200 million barrels of liquefied gas. Yet one year in the PNG LNG project has already been linked with a number of worrying incidents, including tribal conflict, local landowner unrest, alleged abuses by the companies involved, and concerns over the transparency of government decisions. In Feb. 2011 the project reached a boiling point when landowners closed down gas plants and mobilised on project sites following increased discontent over their benefits payments. Land-related violence between 2 communities as a result of the project caused four deaths in January 2010. Another work stoppage in January 2011 was led by an angry group of landowners who mobilised when a local boy lost his life after consuming a toxic substance obtained from one of the project sites. Locals have also reported feeling the effects of inflation on PNG’s economy, with prices for basic staples being distorted by extreme inflation. The Ex-Im Bank estimates that PNG LNG will emit 3, 100, 000 tons of CO2 every year in direct emissions, yet even this figure omits the much greater indirect (lifecycle) emissions associated with LNG schemes. Finally, activists claim that the projects Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) and Social Impact Assessment (SIA) are grossly inadequate and fail to address the environmental and social impacts and provide appropriate mitigation measures. The most affected population will be the Huli people. UPDATE 2022 - Papua LNG (TotalEnergies) In 2019 Total SA, now TotalEnergies, and the PNG government inked an agreement to develop a new project called Papua LNG to exploit the Elk and Antelope gas fields in Baimuru, Gulf Province, the traditional lands of Pawaian people. The extracted gas is to be transported via a pipeline to the existing PNG LNG terminal near Port Moresby, where a third liquefaction train would be added to accommodate the increased capacity. The operator of the project is TotalEnergies through its Total E&P PNG subsidiary (31.1%), other partners are ExxonMobil (28.7%), Papua New Guinea government (22.5%) and Santos Limited (17.7%) [1] . Like the PNG LNG project this new extractivist development is ridden with promises of local economic development, which are welcomed by some in the community but resisted by other landowners demanding to receive a fair part of the benefits of the project. These landowners have threatened to block the wellheads and shut-down operations. Additionally, the landowners accuse the french company of adopting "divide and rule tactics" [2] . The government is totally on the side of the multinational and it has urged claimants not to protest. "As leaders of that community, they needed to be wary of the words they use and the actions they take, because the project is going to be there for the long term..." said the Minister for Petroleum, Krenenga Kua [2] . Local villagers accuse the national political leaders to rip the benefits of the country's resources and denounce they have not been informed of the project planned in their lands. There is also a confusing process to vet which clans are the rightful owners of the land, as traditional ownership regimes clash with a western-imposed conception of property [3] . The haphazard process of stablishing who and by how much benefits from the new wave of gas extractivism has caused political turmoil at the highest spheres of government, leading to the resignation of the finance minister two days after the signing of the deal, who ultimately forged an aliance with the opposition to force a change of government and become the new prime minister two months later [2] [3] . Citing concerns of the failed benefit sharing scheme conflict with PNG LNG project in Southern Highlands, Chief Solomon Lae from Kapai Aikavalavi village said " Our people in this country, they never learn from the previous experiences. Southern Highlanders are waiting ten years and are yet to receive royalties. The leaders of this country, they're elected to represent our people. But that is never the case. They're milking us. Daylight robbery. " [3] At the moment of publishing this update TotalEnergies was pushing forward with the project with the first phase of front-end engineering and design (FEED) [4] .

case_name: Planta de licuefacción de gas de Sempra Energy en Ensenada, Baja California, México
headline: En Ensenada la población local se opone al proyecto de la empresa Sempra Energy de ampliación de su planta regasificadora para añadir la capacidad de licuefacción con el objetivo de exportar gas proveniente de Estados-Unidos hacia Asia.
description: A inicios de los años 2000, después de ser rechazada para operar en Estados Unidos por ser considerada actividad de riesgo, los principales impulsores del Consorcio Costa Azul, filial de la empresa mexicana IEnova, a su vez filial de la empresa estadounidense Sempra Energy, empezaron la construcción de una planta regasificadora en Ensenada, Baja California, que inició operaciones en el 2008 [1] . Esta planta tiene por función recibir buques de gas natural licuado (GNL) desde Asia y transformarlo de estado líquido a gaseoso, para luego ser exportado hacia Estados-Unidos por medio de una red de gasoductos propiedad también de Sempra Energy. Esta multinational fue una de las primeras empresas extranjeras en distribuir gas natural en territorio mexicano, con la red EcoGas de Mexicali, y tiene también varios proyectos de generación eléctrica en Baja California: una planta termoeléctrica de ciclo combinado en Mexicali y un parque eólico en La Rumorosa (Energía Sierra Juárez), ambos para exportar electricidad hacia Estados Unidos, y un parque fotovoltaico (Rumorosa Solar) para abastecer el mercado local [2] . La empresa tiene actualmente un nuevo proyecto que consiste en la ampliación de su planta regasificadora para añadir la capacidad de licuefacción, es decir, en lugar de importar buques de GNL y transformarlos a estado gaseoso, ahora podrá recibir gas natural proveniente de Estados Unidos (incluyendo las cuencas de fracking ubicadas en Texas), convertirlo a estado líquido (enfriándolo a -162°C) y exportarlo en buques a los países del Pacífico. De concretarse este proyecto, Sempra convertirá a Baja California en una plataforma de exportación e importación de gas natural entre Estados Unidos y el Pacífico, o dicho de otra forma, como una “servidumbre de paso” de gas entre ambos espacios. Mediante estos proyectos, la transnacional podrá cambiar a conveniencia el sentido de los flujos de sus gasoductos: cuando le sea más barato comprar el energético en Texas podrá transportarlo hasta Ensenada y utilizar su planta de licuefacción para exportarlo al Pacífico; cuando le sea más rentable adquirirlo en un país de la Cuenca del Pacífico como Indonesia, Rusia u otros, podrá recibirlo en su planta de regasificación y después transportarlo por territorio bajacaliforniano y exportarlo a Estados Unidos. También planea construir una terminal de almacenamiento de productos refinados del petróleo (gasolina, diesel, turbosina y etanol) llamada Baja Refinados [2] [3] . Sempra Energy, por medio de su filial IEnova, ha firmado acuerdos preliminares con empresas afiliadas de Total, Mitsui y Tokyo Gas para la compraventa a 20 años del conjunto del gas natural licuado (GNL) que pretende transformar en la planta durante la fase 1 [4] . La multinacional petrolera de capital francés Total adquirió además una participación del 16.6% en el proyecto de planta, de la misma manera que lo tiene con el otro proyecto de planta de licuefacción Cameron LNG de Sempra Energy en Luisiana [5] [6] . Sempra tiene también un contrato con Chevron para que su filial Chevron Combustibles de México pueda utilizar aproximadamente el 50% de la capacidad de almacenamiento de una nueva terminal marina de recibo, almacenamiento y entrega de hidrocarburos que Sempra proyecta construir al lado de la su planta de gas [14] .  Estos proyectos representan potenciales afectaciones ambientales, por las emisiones de metano y otros gases tóxicos (benceno), además de afectaciones a los ecosistemas marinos por verter al mar aguas residuales a muy bajas temperaturas. Eso podría tener afectaciones en las actividades pesqueras, turísticas y recreativas así como el proceso reproductivo de las ballenas grises, debido a la circulación cotidiana de buques [2] . También conlleva grandes peligros, al ser consideradas industrias de alto riesgo, los cuales se potencian por la cercanía de los proyectos entre sí, en una área geológica inestable, con presencia de fallas y fracturas, en la que se encuentra una planta de recepción y almacenamiento de grandes cantidades de gas LP [1] [2] . Desde 2003 se despertó una oposición local contra la planta regasificadora por parte de los habitantes del complejo habitacional Bajamar situado a menos de 4km de la planta. Interpusieron varios recursos legales y obtuvieron un juicio de amparo que otorga la suspensión definitiva de la planta [7] . Existe además un litigio agrario por el hecho que esta planta se construyó sobre varios lotes, entre ellos el número 2, que corresponden a la colonia Agrícola Costa Azul, razón por la cual empresarios de esta colonia interpusieron una demanda ante el Tribunal Agrario denunciando anómala situación jurídica de los títulos de propiedad y la errónea localización física [8] . Con el anuncio del proyecto de ampliación de la planta empezó una movilización más amplia por parte de la población de Ensenada por medio del movimiento social Ensenada Resiste. Personal académicos del Centro de Investigación Científica y de Educación Superior de Ensenada (CICESE) y de la Universidad del Sur de California (USC) han pronunciado también su rechazo a la la expansión de la planta de gas natural, denunciando las afectaciones ambientales que provocaría y el hecho que el proyecto no forma parte de ningún plan energético nacional y que es contradictorio con un proceso de transición energética [9] . La población ha denunciado y se ha manifestado contra el proceso de consulta ciudadana realizado de manera fraudulenta e ilegal en octubre del 2020. Existieron varias irregularidades y faltas de transparencia en el proceso de votación (las boletas no tenían folio, se utilizaron tinta que se borra y casillas que no estaban plenamente identificadas en la folletería). Además denunciaron que la consulta había sido manipulada por el hecho que la empresa Sempra condicionó el voto, con coacción del alcalde de Ensenada Armando Ayala, ofreciendo destinar 430 millones de pesos para la construcción de 24 obras públicas si la población aceptaba el proyecto durante la consulta [7] [10] .

case_name: Militarisation of LNG Gas Liquefaction plant, Yemen
headline: Yemen LNG gas liquefaction plant in Balhalf, Yemen, has been militarized by the Saudi Arabian government and used as a secret military base and prison during the Yemeni conflict. Foreign shareholders deny responsibility.
description: Before the start of the civil war in 2015, Yemen, a resource-rich nation in proximity to the Arabian Sea, depended on oil and gas exports for economic growth despite never being a significant producer of the two [6] . Yemen’s liquefied natural gas (LNG) project was one of the largest investments the country had made and had many foreign shareholders such as French company Total, as well as other American and Korean companies [1] . The plant in Balhalf opened in 2005 on the Gulf of Aden, which allowed transportation to any port neighboring the Arabian sea [1] [6] . The purpose of the plant served as a method to stimulate the nation’s economy while protecting and establishing Yemen’s coral biodiversity in the process, implemented with guidelines set by the World Bank and IFC standards [7] . A civil war started in 2015 in Yemen and Saudi Arabian military intervention stopped the exports at the Balhalf plant to target Houthi rebels [2] . Due to the ongoing war, Yemen’s oil and gas resources are continuously used as a weapon [6] . Oil pipelines are regularly destroyed, along with attacks on the electricity grid, causing nationwide blackouts. The nation’s economic dependence on oil and gas has caused horrible consequences for the people and the institutional development and capacity of the country [6] . The Balhalf plant was shut off after about 4 years of operating due to being taken over by UAE forces [7] and was forced to shut down due to militant occupation of the plant [3] .  L'Observatoire des armaments and SumOfUs, global consumer groups that challenge corporate power, began investigating the facilities considering many foreign shareholders finance the LNG plant [5] . They revealed that the Yemen LNG plant in Balhaf has been set up as a military base since 2009 and a secret prison from 2017 to 2018 [5] . Open sources reveal that French company Total has partaken in militarization activities in Yemen since the 1980s, and questions are being raised as to the company’s involvement in the militarization of the plant, as well as the climate financing and impacts of the plant by social and environmental justice organizations [5] . The reports show that Saudi Arabians were likely to be torturing Yemenis in the plant, as well as inhumane and degrading treatment and denying medical care, all while the French government must have had awareness of the matter [5] . In 2014, the Yemeni youth embarked on demonstrations and protests that demanded their government to cut the LNG gas deals [11] .  The protests were led by Yemeni politician, journalist, and Nobel Peace Prize winner Tawakkol Karman who draws major concern about bribery as the gas is being sold for 10% of its market price [11] . She additionally urged the South Korean prime minister to reconsider their partner agreement with Yemen LNG, mentioning that the people of Yemen are disappointed in the agreement and believe it is unjust [12] .  Organizations outside of Yemen such as EKO, an organization holding corporations accountable to protect the environment, treat workers well, and respect democracy, as well as other organizations such as the Business & Human Rights Resource Center, have been demanding the French company Total to speak on the matter [4] [5] . They more specifically demand: why this plant has not been included in Total’s 2019 Vigilance Plan despite the control it has over the plant, to clarify the presence of UAE troops on their plant, and demand withdrawal from the Yemen LNG project in light of the human right violations [4]. Eko asks the French parliament to end public guarantees in the gas and oil industries in response to the violations [5] . TotalEnergies, formally known as Total, responded to the Business & Human Rights Resource Center’s list of demands stating that the plant also has American, Yemeni, and South Korean shareholders and therefore is not solely responsible for the presence of UAE’s troops and therefore has no information on how the Saudi coalition has been able to access their restricted area [1] [4]. There has been no other comment from any stakeholders or governments about the conflict at this time [1] [2] [3] [4].

outcome_text: Notes from the author: "Despite that corporations and governments are at the very least knowledgeable about the human rights violations occurring in their plants, the issue becomes an environmental dilemma as well. It becomes clear that when the resources of the environment are commodified, nature and people suffer as well. Corporations that take part in environmental destruction are also taking part in destroying the lives of humans as well. Although this is a very obvious and extreme example, it goes to show how corporations who have as much if not more power than governments are able to do as they please, genocide of people and the environment comes next. It should be the first priority of governments to protect the people and environment rather than prioritizing the economy and exploitation of resources. Governments and corporations should be held responsible for their wrongdoings."

case_name: Afungi LNG airport and construction camps, Mozambique
headline: Afungi Airstrip and workers' camps, constructed to serve Mozambique LNG project, became the epicentre of the worst COVID-19 outbreak in the country. Gas development proceeds in the midst of violent insurgency and a worker building the airstrip was killed.
description: Farming and fishing communities are being displaced for offshore gas development in Cabo Delgado, the northernmost province of Mozambique. The situation is complicated by Islamist insurgency; villages have been raided and people killed. The root motivations of these attacks are complex. Sudden arrival of gas companies, in a region that has endured decades of poverty, led to young men suffering high levels of unemployment and lack of livelihoods becoming targets for enrolment by Islamist armed rebels. [1] The  first flight to land at Afungi Airstrip, built to serve the Mozambique LNG  project in Cabo Delgado, was reported on 20th February 2020. [2] In a  24th February 2020 Al Jazeera article Ilham Rawoot of environmental  non-governmental organization Justica Ambiental reported from discussions with  villagers from communities being forcibly displaced for gas development in Cabo  Delgado. Their concerns and objections to the resettlement process had ‘fallen  on deaf ears’. Farming and fishing livelihoods were being lost. Many affected people  said compensation was inadequate and in some cases allocation of new plots of  arable land triggered conflict because the land encroached on other  communities’ farmland. Gas industry jobs they had been promised had not  materialized. [3]   Mozambique LNG project acquired 6,625 hectares of land on the Afungi Peninsula, in the form of a DUAT (Direito de Uso e Aproveitamento da Terra) - a right to use and benefit from the land. The project includes an airstrip and adjoining project camps. Mozambique LNG: Resettlement Action Plan (RAP) Summary, published in April 2019, includes a graphic indicating the locations of 556 households (2,446 people) who will be displaced by the project. Many of these people will lose access to agricultural land, fishing grounds and intertidal gathering areas. Women are anticipated to be more severely affected due to patriarchal social structures affording them lower status regarding property ownership, land rights and participation in fishing. A small number of the households to be displaced are shown to be located within the site of Afungi airstrip and project camps on the southwest border of the site. The resettlement village site, in the area of the Quitunda settlement, is on the outside of the DUAT boundary, just 300 kilometres from the northern portion of the Afungi airstrip runway. [4] A map in the DUAT Encroachment Management Plan shows sites allocated for the airstrip, camps adjoining the runway and other project camps. [5] Mozambican state oil and gas company Empresa Nacional deHidrocarbonetos (ENH) acquired the DUAT from the Ministry of Agriculture in 2012. Subsequently the DUAT was transferred to Rovuma Basin LNG Land, LDA (RBLL), a joint venture between AMA1, Eni and ENH. Project components specified in Mozambique LNG: Environmental and Social Impact Assessment (ESIA) Summary include airstrips and worker housing. Impacts on community health anticipated in the ESIA from Project workforce and in-migration include communicable diseases, increased demand on health infrastructure, food and nutrition-related issues, community accidents and sexually transmitted diseases. Environmental impacts of the projected influx of people to the project area detailed in the ESIA include reduction of bird habitat quality and indirect impacts on mammals. [6] Afungi Airstrip conflict On 21st February 2019 an employee of Gabriel Couto, a company contracted to build the airport in the LNG project site, was murdered in a fatal attack on a convoy of sub-contractors working for Anadarko, operator of the Cabo Delgado LNG project. The worker was be headed, and the attack left another six people injured. Sources in Mozambique’s security and logistics sectors told Petroleum Economist that the convoy had been transporting Anadarko contractors to the project site when it came upon a village in flames, under attack by insurgents. The convoy turned around but was shot at by another group of insurgents in a village through which it had passed earlier. The man who was murdered was travelling in a separate car and appeared to have been killed when he got out of the car upon encountering the attack. The Afungi airport project is designed to help LNG projects avoid road travel as much as possible. At this juncture the airport facility was at least two years away from completion. It was the first incidence of international oil companies being directly caught up in the armed insurgency in the Cabo Delgado province. Whether the attack specifically targeted Mozambique’s emerging gas industry was unknown, but it highlighted future security problems for the region. The attack led to talk of a shift in insurgents’ strategy towards targeting gas projects. In response the government promised to step up security in the province. Interior minister Basilio Monteiro promised to send various units of Mozambique’s defence and security forces to bolster security around the gas projects. Anadarko, whilst stating that the evidence indicated that their contract personnel, LNG project and airstrip were not targeted in the attack, expressed gratitude for the government action to increase security. The company stated that thanks to the government response it was expected that the project would continue according to its current schedule. But authorities’ response to the attack stoked resentment among the local population who were already concerned that their safety was a lower priority for the government than the gas projects. Hundreds of villagers had been killed since the insurgency in the Cabo Delgado province began. [7] Afungi COVID-19 outbreak On 30th September 2019 French oil and gas  company Total became the main operator of Mozambique LNG upon acquiring  Anadarko’s 26.5% stake. [8] On 2nd April 2020 Total confirmed a COVID-19 case at Afungi, the tenth case to be confirmed in Mozambique. An employee working at the LNG project site at Afungi had tested positive for Covid-19, having worked on the site since 9th March and beginning to feel unwell on 27th March. The individual was reported to be in self- isolation since 29th March after being tested in a facility in Maputo. [9] On 9th April it was reported that five cases of COVID-19 had been confirmed among 35 Total workers who had been in contact with the first worker at the site to test positive. Total announced a decision to place ‘the entire project in quarantine’, reducing site operations to a minimum with only ‘critical activities, such as aerodrome safety operations’ continuing. Total stated that all of the almost 500 workers, of various nationalities, at the Afungi site would be required to stay in their rooms and be tested for COVID-19 and that, in collaboration with the Ministry of Health all local contacts of the confirmed cases outside the project site would be traced. [10] On 14th April it was reported that Total’s Afungi project was Mozambique’s COVID-19 epicentre, with 17 of Mozambique’s 28 confirmed cases linked to the site. The first worker at the site to test positive had transmitted the disease to at least 10 other people and seven new cases, all connected to the LNG project, had been confirmed. Total said in a statement that “business continuity plans in place to ensure the impact to the project of an event like this is mitigated as much as possible…We are focused on critical activity including security, logistics and forward planning.” [11] In a Foreign Policy News article Kate DeAngelis, international policy analyst at Friends of the Earth, raised concerns over the measures being taken by Total to contain the virus. Reportedly, Total had ‘at first refused to halt or even slow its work in northern Mozambique’, a failure to take early action that would have stemmed an increase in COVID cases. The virus would spread easily in camps housing thousands of fossil fuel workers in cramped quarters. Having placed the site ‘under lockdown’, it was unclear which activities had been halted on the Total site and what safety measures the firm had put in place to protect workers and nearby communities. De Angelis writes ‘Total’s delay in stopping activities and unclear plans for controlling the virus’s spread puts not only its workers, but also surrounding villages at unnecessary risk’.  She points out that the host community has only scarce resources to manage COVID-19 and local health systems would likely be ‘strained beyond the breaking point’ if the virus spreads more widely in the area, arguing that fossil fuel companies should halt all work while the region works to contain coronavirus. [12] On 26th April 2020 National Director of Public Health, Dr. Rosa Marlene, stated that contact tracing had discovered five more COVID-19 cases in Mozambique, all workers at Total’s Afungi camp, taking the country’s total number of cases to 70. [13] The following day five more COVID-19 cases among Total workers at Afungi were reported, with this being the only detected active transmission chain in the country. A further COVID-19 case, Mozambique’s 76th, was a child, the daughter of a resident of Pemba who contracted the virus from professional contact with a patient in Afungi. Director general of INS (National Institute of Health), Dr. Ilesh Vinodrai Jani, announced that almost 1,000 workers and subcontractors on the Afungi Peninsula would be tested, informing a press conference: “There is active transmission in the Afungi camps, and we need a process of mass testing, isolation and decontamination. It is a process that will take at least two or three weeks… and we will definitely see an increase in the number of positive cases.” Testing all Afungi workers for Covid-19 would not be possible as more than 2,000 people had left the Total camp since identification of the ‘index case’. This movement of workers meant that attempts to contain the outbreak within Cabo Delgado province would not be unfeasible. [14]   Concerns over continuing Afungi flights   On 8th May A Verdade reported concerns over possible risk of spreading infection from continuing flights, by Mozambican flag carrier LAM, between the Afungi LNG facility, epicentre of Mozambique COVID-19 outbreak, and Pemba, the capital city of Cabo Delgado province. Air passengers were Total workers leaving the Afungi site and health workers conducting tests at the camps. A Verdade reported that air crew operating these flights, five people including two pilots, were not subject to the screening tests and quarantine that applied to all citizens and that after each flight these crew stayed at a hotel in Pemba where they interacted freely with other people. National Director of Public Health, Dr. Rosa Marlene, stated that LAM crew “observe quarantine, depending on the time they have on land. We can guarantee that they are isolated and not in contact with other people, so as not to transmit the infection, but we will see what is happening and reinforce the measures if we are relaxing”. She informed a press conference “We will see what happened with the non-testing of the crews of Airlines of Mozambique, but testing is planned to ensure crew is not a source of infection”.  A Verdade raised concerns that COVID-19 measures pertaining to aviation might be insufficiently stringent to contain the Afungi outbreak. A circular prepared by the Ministry of Transport and Communications made recommendations related to air transport including disinfection of shoes and hands, and temperature measurement, when boarding aircraft. In accordance with recommendations of health authorities cabin crew must wear masks during flights. But the circular did not specify procedures for transport of passengers considered to be at risk of COVID-19 infection, which was the case regarding Total workers at Afungi camps. [15]   Continued  increase in Afungi COVD-19 cases The number of COVID-19 cases at Total’s Afungi oil facilities climbed to 59 by 11th May 2020. Samples had been collected from all of the 886 Total workers at three operational camps. Dr. Ilesh Vinodrai Jani explained that positive and negative cases would be identified and non-essential workers relocated to different areas according to risk. 415 workers would remain on site to ensure continuation of minimum services and be tested for COVID-19 every 10 days. Dr. Jani announced that transmission chains had been interrupted so, as the camp was closed, there was no reason for testing in the wider Afungi Peninsula.[16] On 15th May it was reported that the 75th worker at Total’s construction camps on the Afungi Peninsula had tested positive for COVID-19. The patient was a 30-year-old woman and health officials said her low viral load indicated her infection had occurred several weeks previously and was in its final phase. The cumulative total of known COVID-19 cases in the country had reached 115 and a new outbreak of four cases had emerged in the District of Palma. Dr Sergio Chicumbe, National Director for the Health Survey and Monitoring Area, said it was “not possible to establish a direct relationship with the Afungi camp” but admitted that the transmission mechanism was not known. [17] Three new cases in the Afungi Peninsula were reported on 17th May, all Total employees diagnosed in re-testing of the 415 individuals remaining at the camps maintaining minimum services in the Mozambique LNG project. The new cases brought the number of COVID-19 positive Total workers to 78. [18]

case_name: Liquefied natural gas project -LNG 2,  Gydan peninsula, Arctic Russia
headline: Across the Yamal penninsula where already a mega Arctic LNG1 is in operation, a new LNG 2 project is under construction. Total (France) is very much involved.
description: Just across the Yamal peninsula, in the autonomous administrative region of Yamal-Nenets, where already a mega Arctic LNG1 is in operation [2] ; a new  LNG 2 project has been under construction [1] [2] . Namely, on the opposite side in the western part of the Gydan Peninsula [1] [3] .  Companies involved in this project are Novatek (Russia) (60%)- out of which Total (France) (10%), y Ekropromstroy (China) (40%) with an estimated investment of $25.5bn [1] . In 2018 it was announced in Paris on 24 May  in the presence of the President of the Russian Federation, Vladimir Putin, and the President of the French Republic, Emmanuel Macron, that Total signed an agreement with Novatek outlining the terms upon which Total shall acquire a direct working interest of 10% in Arctic LNG 2, a giant liquefied natural gas project lead by Novatek on the Gydan Peninsula in thevnorth of Siberia. Taking account of Total’s approximate 19% stake in Novatek and Novatek’s intention to retain 60% of the project, the Total Group's overall economic interest in this new LNG project will be approximately 21.5%. Should Novatek decide to reduce its participation below 60%, Total will have the possibility to increase its direct share up to 15%.  Novatek and Total have also agreed that Total will have the opportunity to acquire a 10 to 15% direct interest in Novatek'sfuture LNG projects in Yamal and Gydan.(13).  “Total is delighted to be part of this new world class LNG project alongside its partner Novatek, leveraging the positive experience acquired in the successful Yamal LNG project. This project fits into our strategic partnership with Novatek and also with our sustained commitment to contribute to developing the vast gas resources in Russia’s far north which will primarily be destined for the strongly growing Asian market." said Patrick Pouyanné, Chairman and CEO of Total. “Arctic LNG 2 will contribute to our strategy of growth in LNG by developing competitive projects based on giant low cost resources.”(13).  With a production capacity of approximately 19.8 million tons per year (Mt/year), or 535,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day (boe/d), Arctic LNG 2 will unlock more than 7 billion boe of hydrocarbons’ resources in the onshore Utrenneye gas and condensate field. The project will involve the installation of three gravity-based structures in the Gulf of Ob on which will be installed the three liquefaction trains of 6.6 Mt/year capacity each. In the same way as for Yamal LNG, Arctic LNG 2 production will be delivered to international markets by a fleet of ice-class LNG carriers that will be able to use the Northern Sea Route for cargoes destined for Asia. (13). However, Gydan peninsula is home to Indigenous Nenets communities [2] [4] . They are already strongly affected by climate change. In winter 2020/2021 temperature variations connected to global warming led to the death of about 80,000 thousand reindeer in the Yamal Region [6] . Nenets are highly dependent on reindeer herding as a traditional way of life and feels increasingly powerless in the face of this "land grab". But this also leads to resistance, f.i. in the activities of an open group on social media [7] . The Arctic LNG 2 Project was also opposed by representatives of the reindeer herders themselves in an official complaint letters  to local municipality (early January 2021)  [2] . Further, the complain was also officially stated by community leaders in a newspaper [see 11]. Nenets strongly believe that a recent starvation of about 80,000 reindeers is directly related to gas projects and climate change of the whole peninsula [11] .  The degree of environmental protection of the area is decreasing: the federal Gydan reserve has lost its status and was converted into a national park in December 2019, which was interpreted by experts as making way for the development of the northernmost license area to secure long-term LNG production on the Gydan peninsula [10] .

case_name: Sabetta port, Arctic Russia
headline: The Sabetta port is related to the Yamal gas mega project. Scientists and environmentalist warn about consequences of the accelerated Russian Arctic development.
description: Sabetta is one of the largest Russian Arctic ports situated on the Yamal peninsula, on the bank of the Ob River [2]. The port project was iniciated by the Russian Government as a project of strategic importance for the development of gas-rich Yamal Peninsula. The port is directely related to the Yamal Gas Mega Project. The extensive construction of transportation infrastructure is still ongoing in the scope of the Yamal project, including the Sabetta sea port [7] . Key companies of the port development include Novatek, the Federal Agency of Sea and River Transport, and the state enterprise Rosmorport [1] [4] .  The port covers an area of 60 ha. The project involves the construction of a 50km sea channel, a 6 kilometre long and 420m wide approach channel, and berths for construction materials cargo as well as gas tankers. The port also has a 4km  long canal for storage of ships, and a control station [1] . The port’s construction is being carried out in two phases. The piers for handling liquified natural gas plant modules and construction materials are being constructed in the phase one. Phase two includes the construction of berths for handling liquified natural gas and gas condensate [1] .  The dredging works performed at the port amounted to 1.5 million m³ of earthworks. A total of 25 million cubic meters of permafrost was excavated from the dredging of sea area and approach channel [1] . A cargo-vessel named "Yuri Arshenevsky", brought construction loads to the port with the help of nuclear powered ice-breaker called Taimyr [1] [6] . Activists from the Norwegian environmental group Bellona think that "Running a ship on LNG doesn't help the climate at all". Scientist working on the Arctic similarly stated "We are not sure how long the project will go on because of climate change"... "They build and sell  cheap gas and oil, but in the meantime, the Arctic continues to warm at twice the rate of the rest of the world." [2].  Also, the alternative environmental  media the Barents Observer and Eye on the Arctic -- web journalists from circumpolar countries-- constantly report on the project and rise concerns related to climate change, especially if the Arctic region will proceed with developments at the current speed or even more if it accelerates [4] [5] : "The whole route is now free of ice. "That is upsetting"... "This includes the East Siberian Sea, a region that normally has the longest-lasting ice cover" . ... "Air temperatures along the Siberian coast are generally 2 to 7 degrees Celsius above the 1981-2010 average" [8] ...Total of 94 vessels were sailing in the waters, many of them are transporting liquefied natural gas from the Yamal plant" ..."The ice had almost vanished in July 2019"  [8] . Navigation is helped by climate change that melts the ice, while the burning of fossil fuels increases climate change worldwide, and in particular in the Arctic. While activists, journalists, and scientist rise their concerns about the climate change, the government has a different perspective on the Arctic: the goal of the Sabetta port is an annual shipment of 80 million tons by 2024" [8] .  Scientist furthermore warn how developments on the Northern Sea Route are closely connected with current "dramatic" climate changes in the area: "2019 become the warmest year on record and ice melting is reaching unprecedented levels" [8] .

case_name: Novatek's two gas fields in Yamalsky nature reserve, Yamal, Russia
headline: Novatek obtained Arkticheskoye and Neytinskoye field for exploration which are a protected Arctic tundra and Indigenous lands. Chemical processing is part of the bigger project on the peninsula, including the Ob river case.
description: Novatek company from Russian Federation is operating the Yamal LNG and the company ambition is flourishing. These include the development of the Arctic LNG 2 and adjacent Gydan peninsula, and more recently, the Ob project based on the resources of the Verkhnetiuteyskoye and Zapadno-Seyakhinskoye fields [1] (see conflicts already documented in EJAtlas). However, a new natural gas project is underway [1,2]. Namely Arkticheskoye and Neytinskoye fields [1] . These newly obtained licence for exploitation are situated in  Yamalsky natural reserve, fragile Arctic tundra  [1] . Tundra refers to slow growing Arctic forest or no forest area of high biological and cultural values for Nenets Indigenous people, who use these lands for their livelihoods and local economise, such as reindeer herding [2] .  The Yamalsky reserve covers a 4,1 million hectare area, out of which  3,7 million are located in the central and southern part of the peninsula (see photos). According to Russian law, industrial activities are prohibited in nature reserves [1] . In fact, the Yamal-Nenets Autonomous Area is home to 13 specially protected areas of different categories [5] . Yet, this has not stop the company from exploiting the reserve and profit seeking. On the contrary, the borders of the Yamalsky reserve has  been adjusted following pressure from oil and gas companies, according to Barents Observer [1] .  For instance,  the first adjustment of the reserve was in 2013, at the same time as Gazprom moved ahead with the development of the Bovanenkovo project (see conflictive event in EJAtlas too). The latest border adjustment of the Yamalsky reserve was formalised in May 2021, only few weeks before Novatek had secured control over the licenses.  According to Interfax [3] , the field auction included special conditions that favoured Novatek and apparently no other company submitted interest in the fields. Moreover, this new conflict directly relates to the Ob LNG project. At present, Obsky LNG has been renamed into Obsky Mining and Chemical Combine - NOVATEK decided to produce ammonia and, possibly, methanol on its resource base. In addition to filling the resource base of Ob LNG, these fields "will make it possible to ensure the volume of production at Yamal LNG" ( it has already been built and is operating ), as well as to direct part of the LNG produced to the gasification of the Kamchatka Territory, "the head of NOVATEK noted [3] . This is why  the government of the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug to recommend changing the boundaries of the reserve [2,3].

case_name: Yamal Mega natural gas project, Arctic Russia
headline: Russia’s biggest gas field covers two-thirds of the peninsula which the Nenets people need for nomadic reindeer-herding. For protesting, Nenets activists are accused of preventing economic development.
description: Nenets are an indigenous group that inhabits Yama peninsula, known as the Yamal-Nenets autonomous region in Russian Siberia [1] [4]. Being a nomad group, the Nenets migrate between forests or taiga to their grazing lands way up to Russia's northern fringe [6] . In the 1990s, however, as  90% of Russian gas can be found on the Yamal peninsula, Gazprom company under the Yamal LNG (Liquefied natural gas)   initiated preparations for one of its biggest gas projects, the Yamal Megaproject gas exploitation project promoted as renewable source of energy  [1] [6] .   Due to this mega project, Nentes' traditional lands have been transformed and environmental degradation started to take place [1].  “For them it is fortune, for us terror,” said 20-year-old herder. “The fact they’ve found deposits here is catastrophic”, another member of Nenets community stated [2] . Due to this project, some Nentes members left their traditional lands on the peninsula, as they refused a life in permanent settlements [1].  For those who stayed, the main problems are biophysical land degradation and the disappearance of cultural tradition. Their nomadic lifestyle and migration routes have been disrupted by gas infrastructure, pollution, and the effects of climate change [1].  But Nenets depend on reindeer-herding for their cultures and livelihoods. For example, warmer climate in the Arctic lead to a denser shrub growth across the tundra, making it more difficult for Nenets to gather and move reindeer herds. Extreme temperatures can cause freezing rain and ice that the reindeer herds can not graze or pass across easily [1]. In addition, the new pipelines and other industrial infrastructure are creating further obstacles to traditional migration routes [1]. Many activists from the Nenets community, especially the Forest Nenets, involved in Indigenous rights group alliances of Siberia, have publicly raised their concerns about the environmental challenges facing their community in order to raise awareness about the environmental and cultural issues of gas and oil industries on their traditional territories [1]. The activists have been holding seminars and training sessions, including legal issues, economic development, pollution and climate change [5]. In 2019, a Moscow court ordered the closing down of the Indigenous rights group, saying that the organization has not provided the correct documentation which is needed to be recognized by the Russian law [5]. But the group argued how the Russian Government accuses the community of trying to thwart Russian economic development [5].   The group’s allies say "this is a nonsense" and continue: "the alleged sentence is nothing but a pretext to silence the organization" [5]. “It’s not a legal issue. It’s a political one,”  Indigenous People of the North/Russian said. “There’s a big conflict of interest between corporations and indigenous people” [5]. The aim is “to frighten the society” [5].  "The organization also argued how the government built the gas plant ignoring climate change and crisis issues. The organization also argues how the development of such huge gas fields has other issues with permafrost holes, that can explode very easily, bringing a danger of large scale accidents to the community as well [5].  Gazprom, on the other hand, argues how they provide the Yamal province with $665 million a year, but did not comment on how exactly the money is distributed and to whom [2] . Herders and administration officials argue that compensations for pasture degradation and land are meant for local government but they do not reach Nenets people [2] . The community still argues how they do not want their cultural landscapes change: “I want my grandchildren to see our land as it is: beautiful, fresh, full of berries and deer” [2]
